arXiv:1212.5341v1 [cond-mat.quant-gas] 21 Dec 2012

Mathematical theory and numerical methods for Bose-Einstein condensation

Abstract.

In this paper, we mainly review recent results on mathematical theory and numerical methods for Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC), based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE). Starting from the simplest case with one-component BEC of the weakly interacting bosons, we study the reduction of GPE to lower dimensions, the ground states of BEC including the existence and uniqueness as well as nonexistence results, and the dynamics of GPE including dynamical laws, well-posedness of the Cauchy problem as well as the finite time blow-up. To compute the ground state, the gradient flow with discrete normalization (or imaginary time) method is reviewed and various full discretization methods are presented and compared. To simulate the dynamics, both finite difference methods and time splitting spectral methods are reviewed, and their error estimates are briefly outlined. When the GPE has symmetric properties, we show how to simplify the numerical methods. Then we compare two widely used scalings, i.e. physical scaling (commonly used) and semiclassical scaling, for BEC in strong repulsive interaction regime ( Thomas-Fermi regime), and discuss semiclassical limits of the GPE. Extensions of these results for one-component BEC are then carried out for rotating BEC by GPE with an angular momentum rotation, dipolar BEC by GPE with long range dipole-dipole interaction, and two-component BEC by coupled GPEs. Finally, as a perspective, we show briefly the mathematical models for spin-1 BEC, Bogoliubov excitation and BEC at finite temperature.

Key words and phrases: 
Bose-Einstein condensation, Gross-Pitaevskii equation, numerical method, ground state, quantized vortex, dynamics, error estimate.

1. Introduction

Quantum theory is one of the most important science discoveries in the last century. It asserts that all objects behave like waves in the micro length scale. However, quantum world remains a mystery as it is hard to observe quantum phenomena due to the extremely small wavelength. Now, it is possible to explore quantum world in experiments due to the remarkable discovery of a new state of matter, Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). In the state of BEC, the temperature is very cold (near absolute zero). In such case, the wavelength of an object increases extremely, which leads to the incredible and observable BEC.

1.1. Background

The idea of BEC originated in 1924-1925, when A. Einstein generalized a work of S. N. Bose on the quantum statistics for photons [58] to a gas of non-interacting bosons [94, 95]. Based on the quantum statistics, Einstein predicted that, below a critical temperature, part of the bosons would occupy the same quantum state to form a condensate. Although Einstein’s work was carried out for non-interacting bosons, the idea can be applied to interacting system of bosons. When temperature TT is decreased, the de-Broglie wavelength λd​B\lambda_{dB} of the particle increases, where λd​B=2​π​ℏ2/m​kB​T\lambda_{dB}=\sqrt{2\pi\hbar^{2}/mk_{B}T}, mm is the mass of the particle, ℏ\hbar is the Planck constant and kBk_{B} is the Boltzmann constant. At a critical temperature TcT_{c}, the wavelength λd​B\lambda_{dB} becomes comparable to the inter-particle average spacing, and the de-Broglie waves overlap. In this situation, the particles behave coherently as a giant atom and a BEC is formed.

Einstein’s prediction did not receive much attention until F. London suggested the superfluid 4He as an evidence of BEC in 1938 [137]. London’s idea had inspired extensive studies on the superfluid and interacting boson system. In 1947, by developing the idea of London, Bogliubov established the first microscopic theory of superfluid in a system consisting of interacting bosons [57]. Later, it was found in experiment that less then 10%10\% of the superfluid 4He is in the condensation due to the strong interaction between helium atoms. This fact motivated physicists to search for weakly interacting system of Bose gases with higher occupancy of BEC. The difficulty is that almost all substances become solid or liquid at temperature which the BEC phase transition occurs. In 1959, Hecht [116] pointed out that spin-polarized hydrogen atoms would remain gaseous even at 0K. Hence, H atoms become an attractive candidate for BEC. In 1980, spin-polarized hydrogen gases were realized by Silvera and Walraven [167]. In the following decade, extensive efforts had been devoted to the experimental realization of hydrogen BEC, resulting in the developments of magnetically trapping and evaporative cooling techniques. However, those attempts to observe BEC failed.

In 1980s, due to the developments of laser trapping and cooling, alkali atoms became suitable candidates for BEC experiments as they are well-suited to laser cooling and trapping. By combining the advanced laser cooling and the evaporative cooling techniques together, the first BEC of dilute 87Rb gases was achieved in 1995, by E. Cornell and C. Wieman’s group in JILA [12]. In the same year, two successful experimental observations of BEC, with 23Na by Ketterle’s group [86] and 7Li by Hulet’s group [59], were announced. The experimental realization of BEC for alkali vapors has two stages: the laser pre-cooling and evaporative cooling. The alkali gas can be cooled down to several μ\muK by laser cooling, and then be further cooled down to 50nK–100nK by evaporative cooling. As laser cooling can not be applied to hydrogen, it took atomic physicists much more time to achieve hydrogen BEC. In 1998, atomic condensate of hydrogen was finally realized [99]. For better understanding of the long history towards the Bose-Einstein condensation, we refer to the Nobel lectures [80, 126].

The experimental advances [12, 86, 59] have spurred great excitement in the atomic physics community and condensate physics community. Since 1995, numerous efforts have been devoted to the studies of ultracold atomic gases and various kinds of condensates of dilute gases have been produced for both bosonic particles and fermionic particles [11, 84, 97, 129, 144, 146, 151]. In this rapidly growing research area, numerical simulation has been playing an important role in understanding the theories and the experiments. Our aim is to review the numerical methods and mathematical theories for BEC that have been developed over these years.

1.2. Many body system and mean field approximation

We are interested in the ultracold dilute bosonic gases confined in an external trap, which is the case for most of the BEC experiments. In these cold dilute gases, only binary interaction is important. Hence, the many body Hamiltonian for NN identical bosons held in a trap can be written as [132, 129]

HN=∑j=1N(−ℏ22​m​Δj+V⁡(𝐱j))+∑1≤j<k≤NVint​(𝐱j−𝐱k),H_{N}=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{N}\left(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\Delta_{j}+V(\mathbf{x}_{j})\right)+\sum\limits_{1\leq j<k\leq N}V_{\rm int}(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{k}), (1.1)

where 𝐱j∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} (j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N) denote the positions of the particles, mm is the mass of a boson, Δj\Delta_{j} is the Laplace operator with respect to 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}, V⁡(𝐱j)V(\mathbf{x}_{j}) is the external trapping potential, and Vint​(𝐱j−𝐱k)V_{\rm int}(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{k}) denotes the inter-atomic two body interactions. The wave function ΨN:=ΨN​(𝐱1,…,𝐱N,t)∈L2​(ℝ3​N×ℝ)\Psi_{N}:=\Psi_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{N},t)\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3N}\times\mathbb{R}) is symmetric, with respect to any permutation of the positions 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j}. The evolution of the system is then described by the time-dependent Schrödinger equation

i​ℏ​∂tΨN​(𝐱1,…,𝐱N,t)=HN​ΨN​(𝐱1,…,𝐱N,t).i\hbar\partial_{t}\Psi_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{N},t)=H_{N}\Psi_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{N},t). (1.2)

Here ii denotes the imaginary unit. In the sequel, we may omit time tt when we write the NN body wave function ΨN\Psi_{N}.

In principle, the above many body system can be solved, but the cost increases quadratically as NN goes large, due to the binary interaction term. To simplify the interaction, mean-field potential is introduced to approximate the two-body interactions. In the ultracold dilute regime, the binary interaction VintV_{\rm int} is well approximated by the effective interacting potential:

Vint​(𝐱j−𝐱k)=g​δ​(𝐱j−𝐱k),V_{\rm int}(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{k})=g\,\delta(\mathbf{x}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{k}), (1.3)

where δ⁡(⋅)\delta(\cdot) is the Dirac distribution and the constant g=4​π​ℏ2​asmg=\frac{4\pi\hbar^{2}a_{s}}{m}. Here asa_{s} is the ss-wave scattering length of the bosons (positive for repulsive interaction and negative for attractive interaction), and it is related to the potential VintV_{\rm int} [132]. The above approximation (1.3) is valid for the dilute regime case, where the scattering length asa_{s} is much smaller than the average distance between the particles.

For a BEC, all particles are in the same quantum state and we can formally take the Hartree ansatz for the many body wave function as

ΨN​(𝐱1,…,𝐱N,t)=∏j=1NψH​(𝐱j,t),\Psi_{N}(\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{N},t)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x}_{j},t), (1.4)

with the normalization condition for the single-particle wave function ψH\psi_{H} as

∫ℝ3|ψH​(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=1.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}=1. (1.5)

Then the energy of the state (1.4) can be written as

E=N​∫ℝ3[ℏ22​m​|∇ψH​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψH​(𝐱,t)|2+N−12​g​|ψH​(𝐱,t)|4]​𝑑𝐱.E=N\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left[\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}|\nabla\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+\frac{N-1}{2}g|\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{4}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}. (1.6)

Let us introduce the wave function for the whole condensate

ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=N​ψH​(𝐱,t).\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\sqrt{N}\psi_{H}(\mathbf{x},t). (1.7)

Neglecting terms of order 1/N1/N, we obtain the energy of the NN body system as

E⁡(ψ)=∫ℝ3[ℏ22​m​|∇ψ​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2+12​g​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|4]​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle E(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left[\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}|\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}g|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{4}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}, (1.8)

where the wave function is normalized according to the total number of the particles,

∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=N.\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}=N. (1.9)

Eq. (1.8) is the well-known Gross-Pitaevskii energy functional. The equation governing the motion of the condensate can be derived by [150]

i​ℏ​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=δ​E​(ψ)δ​ψ¯=[−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+g​|ψ|2]​ψ,\displaystyle i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{\delta E(\psi)}{\delta\overline{\psi}}=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+g|\psi|^{2}\right]\psi, (1.10)

where ψ¯\overline{\psi} denotes the complex conjugate of ψ:=ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi:=\psi(\mathbf{x},t). Eq. (1.10) is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) with cubic nonlinearity, known as the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE).

In the derivation, we have used both the dilute property of the gases and the Hartree ansatz (1.4). Eq. (1.4) requires that the BEC system is at extremely low temperature such that almost all particles are in the same states. Thus, mean field approximation (1.8) and (1.10) are only valid for dilute boson gases (or usually called weakly interacting boson gases) at temperature TT much smaller than the critical temperature TcT_{c}.

The Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) theory (1.10) was developed by Pitaevskii [149] and Gross [109] independently in 1960s. For a long time, the validity of this mean field approximation lacks of rigorous mathematical justification. Since the first experimental observation of BEC in 1995, much attention has been paid to the GP theory. In 2000, Lieb et al. proved that the energy (1.8) describes the ground state energy of the many body system correctly in the mean field regime [132, 133]. Later H. T. Yau and his collaborators studied the validity of GPE (1.10) as an approximation for (1.2) to describe the dynamics of BEC [96], without the trapping potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}).

GP theory, or mean field theory, has been proven to predict many properties of BEC quite well. It has become the fundamental mathematical model to understand BEC. In this review article, we will concentrate on the GP theory.

1.3. The Gross-Pitaevskii equation

As shown in section 1.2, at temperature T≪TcT\ll T_{c}, the dynamics of a BEC is well described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE) in three dimensions (3D)

i​ℏ​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+N​g​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2]​ψ​(𝐱,t),𝐱∈ℝ3,t>0,\displaystyle i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+Ng|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\right]\psi(\mathbf{x},t),\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3},\,t>0, (1.11)

where 𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is the Cartesian coordinates, ∇\nabla is the gradient operator and ∇2:=∇⋅∇=Δ\nabla^{2}:=\nabla\cdot\nabla=\Delta is the Laplace operator. In fact, the above GPE (1.11) is obtained from the GPE (1.10) by a rescaling ψ→N​ψ\psi\to\sqrt{N}\psi, noticing (1.9), the wave function ψ\psi in (1.11) is normalized by

‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖22=∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑x=1.\displaystyle\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,dx=1. (1.12)

1.3.1. Different external trapping potentials

In the early BEC experiments, a single harmonic oscillator well was used to trap the atoms in the condensate [84, 60]. Recently more advanced and complicated traps are applied in studying BEC in laboratory [150, 143, 61, 72]. Here we present several typical trapping potentials which are widely used in current experiments.

I. Three-dimensional (3D) harmonic oscillator potential [150]:

Vho(𝐱)=Vho(x)+Vho(y)+Vho(z),Vho(α)=m2ωα2α2,α=x,y,z,\displaystyle V_{\rm ho}({\mathbf{x}})=V_{\rm ho}(x)+V_{\rm ho}(y)+V_{\rm ho}(z),\quad V_{\rm ho}(\alpha)=\frac{m}{2}\omega_{\alpha}^{2}\alpha^{2},\ \alpha=x,y,z, (1.13)

where ωx\omega_{x}, ωy\omega_{y} and ωz\omega_{z} are the trap frequencies in xx-, yy- and zz-direction, respectively. Without loss of generality, we assume that ωx≤ωy≤ωz\omega_{x}\leq\omega_{y}\leq\omega_{z} throughout the paper.

II. 2D harmonic oscillator + 1D double-well potential (Type I) [143]:

Vdw(1)​(𝐱)=Vdw(1)​(x)+Vho​(y)+Vho​(z),Vdw(1)​(x)=m2​νx4​(x2−a^2)2,\displaystyle V_{\rm dw}^{(1)}({\mathbf{x}})=V_{\rm dw}^{(1)}(x)+V_{\rm ho}(y)+V_{\rm ho}(z),\quad V_{\rm dw}^{(1)}(x)=\frac{m}{2}\nu_{x}^{4}\left(x^{2}-\hat{a}^{2}\right)^{2}, (1.14)

where ±a^\pm\hat{a} are the double-well centers in xx-axis, νx\nu_{x} is a given constant with physical dimension 1/[s m]1/2.

III. 2D harmonic oscillator + 1D double-well potential (Type II) [118, 67]:

Vdw(2)​(𝐱)=Vdw(2)​(x)+Vho​(y)+Vho​(z),Vdw(2)​(x)=m2​ωx2​(|x|−a^)2.\displaystyle V_{\rm dw}^{(2)}({\mathbf{x}})=V_{\rm dw}^{(2)}(x)+V_{\rm ho}(y)+V_{\rm ho}(z),\quad V_{\rm dw}^{(2)}(x)=\frac{m}{2}\omega_{x}^{2}\left(|x|-\hat{a}\right)^{2}. (1.15)

IV. 3D harmonic oscillator + optical lattice potential [79, 150, 3]:

Vhop​(𝐱)=Vho​(𝐱)+Vopt​(x)+Vopt​(y)+Vopt​(z),Vopt​(α)=Iα​Eα​sin2⁡(q^α​α),\displaystyle V_{\rm hop}({\mathbf{x}})=V_{\rm ho}(\mathbf{x})+V_{\rm opt}(x)+V_{\rm opt}(y)+V_{\rm opt}(z),\quad V_{\rm opt}(\alpha)=I_{\alpha}\;E_{\alpha}\sin^{2}(\hat{q}_{\alpha}\alpha), (1.16)

where q^α=2​π/λα\hat{q}_{\alpha}=2\pi/\lambda_{\alpha} is fixed by the wavelength λα\lambda_{\alpha} of the laser light creating the stationary 1D lattice wave, Eα=ℏ2​q^α2/2​mE_{\alpha}=\hbar^{2}\hat{q}_{\alpha}^{2}/2m is the so-called recoil energy, and IαI_{\alpha} is a dimensionless parameter providing the intensity of the laser beam. The optical lattice potential has periodicity Tα=π/q^α=λα/2T_{\alpha}=\pi/\hat{q}_{\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha}/2 along α\alpha-axis (α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z).

V. 3D box potential [150]:

Vbox​(𝐱)={0,0<x,y,z<L,∞,otherwise.\displaystyle V_{\rm box}({\mathbf{x}})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0,&\quad 0<x,y,z<L,\\ \infty,&\quad\hbox{otherwise}.\end{array}\right. (1.17)

where LL is the length of the box in the xx-, yy-, zz-direction.

For more types of external trapping potential, we refer to [150, 148]. When a harmonic potential is considered, a typical set of parameters used in experiments with 87Rb is given by

m=1.44×10−25​[k​g],ωx=ωy=ωz=20​π​[r​a​d/s],a=5.1×10−9​[m],N: 102∼107m=1.44\times 10^{-25}[kg],\ \omega_{x}=\omega_{y}=\omega_{z}=20\pi[rad/s],\ a=5.1\times 10^{-9}[m],\ N:\ 10^{2}\sim 10^{7}

and the Planck constant has the value

ℏ=1.05×10−34​[J​s].\hbar=1.05\times 10^{-34}\ [Js].

1.3.2. Nondimensionlization

In order to nondimensionalize Eq. (1.11) under the normalization (1.12), we introduce

t~=tts,𝐱~=𝐱xs,ψ~​(𝐱~,t~)=xs3/2​ψ​(𝐱,t),E~​(ψ~)=E⁡(ψ)Es,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=\frac{t}{t_{s}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{\mathbf{x}}{x_{s}},\quad\tilde{\psi}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{x}},\tilde{t}\right)=x_{s}^{3/2}\psi\left({\mathbf{x}},t\right),\quad\tilde{E}(\tilde{\psi})=\frac{E(\psi)}{E_{s}}, (1.18)

where tst_{s}, xsx_{s} and EsE_{s} are the scaling parameters of dimensionless time, length and energy units, respectively. Plugging (1.18) into (1.11), multiplying by ts2/m​xs1/2t_{s}^{2}/mx_{s}^{1/2}, and then removing all ~\tilde{}, we obtain the following dimensionless GPE under the normalization (1.12) in 3D:

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi({\mathbf{x}},t) =\displaystyle= −12​∇2ψ​(𝐱,t)+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ​(𝐱,t)+κ​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​ψ​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)+V({\mathbf{x}})\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)+\kappa|\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{2}\psi({\mathbf{x}},t), (1.19)

where the dimensionless energy functional E⁡(ψ)E(\psi) is defined as

E⁡(ψ)=∫ℝ3[12​|∇ψ|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ|2+κ2​|ψ|4]​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle E(\psi)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi|^{2}+\frac{\kappa}{2}|\psi|^{4}\right]\;d\mathbf{x}, (1.20)

and the choices for the scaling parameters tst_{s} and xsx_{s}, the dimensionless potential V⁡(𝐱)V({\mathbf{x}}) with γy=ts​ωy\gamma_{y}=t_{s}\omega_{y} and γz=ts​ωz\gamma_{z}=t_{s}\omega_{z}, the energy unit Es=ℏ/ts=ℏ2/m​xs2E_{s}=\hbar/t_{s}=\hbar^{2}/mx_{s}^{2}, and the interaction parameter κ=4​π​as​N/xs\kappa=4\pi a_{s}N/x_{s} for different external trapping potentials are given below [135]:

I. 3D harmonic oscillator potential:

ts=1ωx,xs=ℏm​ωx,V⁡(𝐱)=12​(x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2).t_{s}=\frac{1}{\omega_{x}},\quad x_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega_{x}}},\quad V({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\left(x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right).

II. 2D harmonic oscillator + 1D double-well potential (type I):

ts=(mℏ​νx4)1/3,xs=(ℏm​νx2)1/3,a=a^xs,V⁡(𝐱)=12​[(x2−a2)2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2].t_{s}=\left(\frac{m}{\hbar\nu_{x}^{4}}\right)^{1/3},\ x_{s}=\left(\frac{\hbar}{m\nu_{x}^{2}}\right)^{1/3},\ a=\frac{\hat{a}}{x_{s}},\ V({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(x^{2}-a^{2}\right)^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right].

III. 2D harmonic oscillator + 1D double-well potential (type II):

ts=1ωx,xs=ℏm​ωx,a=a^xs,V⁡(𝐱)=12​[(|x|−a)2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2].t_{s}=\frac{1}{\omega_{x}},\quad x_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega_{x}}},\quad a=\frac{\hat{a}}{x_{s}},\quad V({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{2}\left[(|x|-a)^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right].

IV. 3D harmonic oscillator + optical lattice potentials:

ts=1ωx,xs=ℏm​ωx,kτ=2​π2​xs2​Iτλτ2,qτ=2​π​xsλτ,τ=x,y,z,\displaystyle t_{s}=\frac{1}{\omega_{x}},\quad x_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega_{x}}},\quad k_{\tau}=\frac{2\pi^{2}x_{s}^{2}I_{\tau}}{\lambda_{\tau}^{2}},\quad q_{\tau}=\frac{2\pi x_{s}}{\lambda_{\tau}},\quad\tau=x,y,z,
V⁡(𝐱)=12​(x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2)+kx​sin2⁡(qx​x)+ky​sin2⁡(qy​y)+kz​sin2⁡(qz​z).\displaystyle V({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{2}(x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2})+k_{x}\sin^{2}(q_{x}x)+k_{y}\sin^{2}(q_{y}y)+k_{z}\sin^{2}(q_{z}z).

V. 3D Box potential:

ts=m​L2ℏ,xs=L,V⁡(𝐱)={0,0<x,y,z<1,∞,otherwise.t_{s}=\frac{mL^{2}}{\hbar},\quad x_{s}=L,\quad V({\mathbf{x}})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0,&0<x,y,z<1,\\ \infty,&\textrm{otherwise}.\end{array}\right.

1.3.3. Dimension reduction

Under the external potentials I–IV, when ωy≈1/ts=ωx\omega_{y}\approx 1/t_{s}=\omega_{x} and ωz≫1/ts=ωx\omega_{z}\gg 1/t_{s}=\omega_{x} (⇔\Leftrightarrow γy≈1\gamma_{y}\approx 1 and γz≫1\gamma_{z}\gg 1), i.e. a disk-shape condensate, the 3D GPE can be reduced to a two dimensional (2D) GPE. In the following discussion, we take potential I, i.e. the harmonic potential as an example.

For a disk-shaped condensate with small height in zz-direction, i.e.

ωx≈ωy,ωz≫ωx,⟺γy≈1,γz≫1,\displaystyle\omega_{x}\approx\omega_{y},\quad\omega_{z}\gg\omega_{x},\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\gamma_{y}\approx 1,\quad\gamma_{z}\gg 1, (1.21)

the 3D GPE (1.19) can be reduced to a 2D GPE by assuming that the time evolution does not cause excitations along the zz-axis since these excitations have larger energies at the order of ℏ​ωz\hbar\omega_{z} compared to excitations along the xx and yy-axis with energies at the order of ℏ​ωx\hbar\omega_{x}.

To understand this [31], consider the total condensate energy E⁡(ψ⁡(t))E\left(\psi(t)\right) with ψ⁡(t):=ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(t):=\psi(\mathbf{x},t):

E⁡(ψ⁡(t))\displaystyle E\left(\psi(t)\right) =\displaystyle= 12​∫ℝ3|∇ψ​(t)|2​𝑑𝐱+12​∫ℝ3(x2+γy2​y2)​|ψ⁡(t)|2​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\nabla\psi(t)|^{2}d\mathbf{x}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left(x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}\right)|\psi(t)|^{2}d\mathbf{x} (1.22)
+γz22∫ℝ3z2|ψ(t)|2d𝐱+κ2∫ℝ3|ψ(t)|4d𝐱.\displaystyle+\frac{\gamma_{z}^{2}}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}z^{2}|\psi(t)|^{2}d\mathbf{x}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi(t)|^{4}d\mathbf{x}.

Multiplying (1.19) by ψt¯\overline{\psi_{t}} and integrating by parts show the energy conservation

E⁡(ψ⁡(t))=E⁡(ψI),t≥0,\displaystyle E\left(\psi(t)\right)=E\left(\psi_{I}\right),\qquad t\geq 0, (1.23)

where ψI=ψ⁡(t=0)\psi_{I}=\psi(t=0) is the initial function which may depend on all parameters γy\gamma_{y}, γz\gamma_{z} and κ\kappa. Now assume that ψI\psi_{I} satisfies

E⁡(ψI)γz2→0,asγz→∞.\displaystyle\frac{E(\psi_{I})}{\gamma_{z}^{2}}\to 0,\qquad\hbox{as}\quad\gamma_{z}\to\infty. (1.24)

Take a sequence γz→∞\gamma_{z}\to\infty (and keep all other parameters fixed). Since ∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(t)|2​𝑑𝐱=1\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi(t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=1, we conclude from weak compactness that there is a positive measure n0​(t)n^{0}(t) such that

|ψ⁡(t)|2⇀n0​(t)weakly asγz→∞.|\psi(t)|^{2}\rightharpoonup n^{0}(t)\quad\hbox{weakly as}\quad\gamma_{z}\to\infty.

Energy conservation implies

∫ℝ3z2​|ψ⁡(t)|2​𝑑𝐱→0,asγz→∞,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\;z^{2}|\psi(t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}\to 0,\quad\hbox{as}\quad\gamma_{z}\to\infty,

and thus we conclude concentration of the condensate in the plane z=0z=0:

n0​(x,y,z,t)=n20​(x,y,t)​δ​(z),n^{0}(x,y,z,t)=n_{2}^{0}(x,y,t)\delta(z),

where n20​(t):=n20​(x,y,t)n_{2}^{0}(t):=n_{2}^{0}(x,y,t) is a positive measure on ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2}.

Now let ψ3=ψ3​(z)\psi_{3}=\psi_{3}(z) be a wave function with

∫ℝ|ψ3​(z)|2​𝑑z=1,\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\;|\psi_{3}(z)|^{2}\;dz=1,

depending on γz\gamma_{z} such that

|ψ3​(z)|2⇀δ⁡(z),asγz→∞.\displaystyle|\psi_{3}(z)|^{2}\rightharpoonup\delta(z),\qquad\hbox{as}\quad\gamma_{z}\to\infty. (1.25)

Denote by SfacS_{\rm fac} the subspace

Sfac={ψ=ψ2​(x,y)​ψ3​(z)|ψ2∈L2​(ℝ2)}\displaystyle S_{\rm fac}=\{\psi=\psi_{2}(x,y)\psi_{3}(z)\;|\;\psi_{2}\in L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{2})\} (1.26)

and let

Π:L2​(ℝ3)→Sfac⊆L2​(ℝ3)\displaystyle\Pi:\;L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{3})\to S_{\rm fac}\subseteq L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}^{3}) (1.27)

be the projection on SfacS_{\rm fac}:

(Π​ψ)​(x,y,z)=ψ3​(z)​∫ℝψ3¯​(z′)​ψ​(x,y,z′)​d​z′.\displaystyle(\Pi\psi)(x,y,z)=\psi_{3}(z)\int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\;\overline{\psi_{3}}(z^{\prime})\;\psi(x,y,z^{\prime})\;dz^{\prime}. (1.28)

Now write the equation (1.19) in the form

i​∂tψ=𝒜​ψ+ℱ⁡(ψ),\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi={\mathcal{A}}\psi+{\mathcal{F}}(\psi), (1.29)

where 𝒜​ψ{\mathcal{A}}\psi stands for the linear part and ℱ⁡(ψ){\mathcal{F}}(\psi) for the nonlinearity. Applying Π\Pi to the GPE gives

i​∂t(Π​ψ)=\displaystyle i\partial_{t}(\Pi\psi)= Π​𝒜​ψ+Π​ℱ​(ψ)\displaystyle\,\Pi{\mathcal{A}}\psi+\Pi{\mathcal{F}}(\psi)
=\displaystyle= Π​𝒜​(Π​ψ)+Π​ℱ​(Π​ψ)+Π⁡((Π​𝒜−𝒜​Π)​ψ+(Π​ℱ​(ψ)−ℱ⁡(Π​ψ))).\displaystyle\,\Pi{\mathcal{A}}(\Pi\psi)+\Pi{\mathcal{F}}(\Pi\psi)+\Pi\left((\Pi{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{A}}\Pi)\psi+(\Pi{\mathcal{F}}(\psi)-{\mathcal{F}}(\Pi\psi))\right). (1.30)

The projection approximation of (1.19) is now obtained by dropping the commutator terms and it reads

i​∂t(Π​σ)=Π​𝒜​(Π​σ)+Π​ℱ​(Π​σ),\displaystyle i\partial_{t}(\Pi\sigma)=\Pi{\mathcal{A}}(\Pi\sigma)+\Pi{\mathcal{F}}(\Pi\sigma), (1.31)
(Π​σ)​(t=0)=Π​ψI,\displaystyle(\Pi\sigma)(t=0)=\Pi\psi_{I}, (1.32)

or explicitly, with

(Π​σ)​(x,y,z,t)=:ψ2​(x,y,t)​ψ3​(z),\displaystyle(\Pi\sigma)(x,y,z,t)=:\psi_{2}(x,y,t)\psi_{3}(z), (1.33)

we find

i​∂tψ2=−12​∇2ψ2+12​(x2+γy2​y2+C)​ψ2+(κ​∫−∞∞ψ34​(z)​𝑑z)​|ψ2|2​ψ2,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}{\psi_{2}}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi_{2}+\frac{1}{2}\left(x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+C\right)\psi_{2}+\left(\kappa\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi_{3}^{4}(z)\,dz\right)|\psi_{2}|^{2}\psi_{2}, (1.34)

where

C=γz2​∫−∞∞z2​|ψ3​(z)|2​𝑑z+∫−∞∞|d​ψ3d​z|2​𝑑z.C=\gamma_{z}^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\;z^{2}|\psi_{3}(z)|^{2}\;dz+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\;\left|\frac{d\psi_{3}}{dz}\right|^{2}\;dz.

Since this GPE is time-transverse invariant, we can replace ψ2→ψe−iC/2\psi_{2}\to\psi\;e^{-iC/2} and drop the constant CC in the trap potential. The observables are not affected by this. For the same reason, we will always assume that V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 in (1.11).

The ‘effective’ GPE (1.34) is well known in the physical literature, where the projection method is often referred to as ‘integrating out the zz-coordinate’. However, an analysis of the limit process γz→∞\gamma_{z}\to\infty has to be based on the derivation as presented above, in particular on studying the commutators Π​𝒜−𝒜​Π\Pi{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{A}}\Pi, Π​ℱ−ℱ​Π\Pi{\mathcal{F}}-{\mathcal{F}}\Pi . In the case of small interaction β=o⁡(1)\beta=o(1) [53], a good choice for ψ3​(z)\psi_{3}(z) is the ground state of the harmonic oscillator in zz-dimension:

ψ3(z)=(γzπ)1/4e−γzz2/2.\displaystyle\psi_{3}(z)=\left(\frac{\gamma_{z}}{\pi}\right)^{1/4}\;e^{-\gamma_{z}z^{2}/2}. (1.35)

For condensates with interaction other than small interaction the choice of ψ3\psi_{3} is much less obvious. Often one assumes that the condensate density along the zz-axis is well described by the (x,y)(x,y)-trace of the ground state position density |ϕg|2|\phi_{g}|^{2}

|ψ⁡(x,y,z,t)|2≈|ψ2​(x,y,t)|∫ℝ22⁡|ϕg​(x1,y1,z)|2​d​x1​d​y1\displaystyle|\psi(x,y,z,t)|^{2}\approx|\psi_{2}(x,y,t)|^{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\;|\phi_{g}(x_{1},y_{1},z)|^{2}\;dx_{1}dy_{1} (1.36)

and (taking a pure-state-approximation)

ψ3​(z)=(∫ℝ2|ϕg​(x,y,z)|2​𝑑x​𝑑y)1/2.\displaystyle\psi_{3}(z)=\left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\;|\phi_{g}(x,y,z)|^{2}\;dxdy\right)^{1/2}. (1.37)

Similarly, when ωy≫1/ts=ωx\omega_{y}\gg 1/t_{s}=\omega_{x} and ωz≫1/ts=ωx\omega_{z}\gg 1/t_{s}=\omega_{x} (⇔\Leftrightarrow γy≫1\gamma_{y}\gg 1 and γz≫1\gamma_{z}\gg 1), i.e. a cigar-shaped condensate, the 3D GPE can be reduced to a 1D GPE. For a cigar-shaped condensate [31, 148, 150]

ωy≫ωx,ωz≫ωx,⟺γy≫1,γz≫1,\displaystyle\omega_{y}\gg\omega_{x},\quad\omega_{z}\gg\omega_{x},\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\gamma_{y}\gg 1,\quad\gamma_{z}\gg 1, (1.38)

the 3D GPE (1.11) can be reduced to a 1D GPE by proceeding analogously.

Then the 3D GPE (1.11), 2D and 1D GPEs can be written in a unified way

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=−12​∇2ψ​(𝐱,t)+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ​(𝐱,t)+β​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​ψ​(𝐱,t),𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}{\psi(\mathbf{x},t)}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)+V(\mathbf{x})\psi(\mathbf{x},t)+\beta\;|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\psi(\mathbf{x},t),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, (1.39)

where

β=κ​{∫ℝ2ψ234​(y,z)​dy​dz,∫ℝψ34​(z)​dz,1,​V​(𝐱)={12​γx2​x2,d=1,12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2),d=2,12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2),d=3;\displaystyle\beta=\kappa\;\begin{cases}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}\psi_{23}^{4}(y,z)\;dydz,\\ \int_{{\mathbb{R}}}\psi_{3}^{4}(z)\;dz,\\ 1,\end{cases}\,V(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2},&d=1,\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}\right),&d=2,\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right),&d=3;\end{cases} (1.40)

where γx≥1\gamma_{x}\geq 1 is a constant and ψ23​(y,z)∈L2​(ℝ2)\psi_{23}(y,z)\in L^{2}({\mathbb{R}^{2}}) is often chosen to be the xx-trace of the ground state ϕg​(x,y,z)\phi_{g}(x,y,z) in 3D as ψ23​(y,z)=(∫ℝ|ϕg​(x,y,z)|2​𝑑x)1/2\psi_{23}(y,z)=\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\phi_{g}(x,y,z)|^{2}\,dx\right)^{1/2} which is usually approximated by the ground state of the corresponding 2D harmonic oscillator [31, 148, 150]. The normalization condition for (1.39) is

∫ℝd|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=1,\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=1, (1.41)

and the energy of (1.39) is given by

E⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t)):=∫ℝd[12​|∇ψ​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2+β2​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|4]​𝑑𝐱.\displaystyle E(\psi(\cdot,t)):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\;\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{4}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}. (1.42)

For a weakly interacting condensate, choosing ψ23\psi_{23} and ψ3\psi_{3} as the ground states of the corresponding 2D and 1D harmonic oscillator [31, 148, 150], respectively, we derive,

β:=κ​{(γy​γz)1/22​π,d=1,γz2​π,d=2,1,d=3.\displaystyle\beta:=\kappa\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{(\gamma_{y}\gamma_{z})^{1/2}}{2\pi},&\qquad d=1,\\ \sqrt{\frac{\gamma_{z}}{2\pi}},&\qquad d=2,\\ 1,&\qquad d=3.\\ \end{array}\right. (1.43)

1.3.4. BEC on a ring

BEC on a ring has been realized by choosing Toroidal potential (3D harmonic oscillator +2D Gaussian potential) [158]:

Vtor​(𝐱)=Vho​(𝐱)+Vgau​(x,y),Vgau​(x,y)=V0​e−2​x2+y2w02,\displaystyle V_{\rm tor}(\mathbf{x})=V_{\rm ho}(\mathbf{x})+V_{\rm gau}(x,y),\quad V_{\rm gau}(x,y)=V_{0}e^{-2\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{w_{0}^{2}}}, (1.44)

where VgauV_{\rm gau} is produced by a laser beam, w0w_{0} is the beam waist, and V0V_{0} is related to the power of the plug-beam.

In the quasi-1D regime [158], ωx=ωy=ωr\omega_{x}=\omega_{y}=\omega_{r}, the toroidal potential can be written in cylindrical coordinate (r,θ,z)(r,\theta,z) as

Vtor​(r,θ,z)=m2​ωr2​r2+m2​ωz2​z2+V0​e−2​r2w02.\displaystyle V_{\rm tor}(r,\theta,z)=\frac{m}{2}\omega_{r}^{2}r^{2}+\frac{m}{2}\omega_{z}^{2}z^{2}+V_{0}e^{-2\frac{r^{2}}{w_{0}^{2}}}. (1.45)

When ωr,ωz≫1\omega_{r},\omega_{z}\gg 1, the dynamics of BEC in the ring trap (1.44) would be confined in r=Rr=R and z=0z=0, where m2​ωr2​r2+V0​e−2​r2w02\frac{m}{2}\omega_{r}^{2}r^{2}+V_{0}e^{-2\frac{r^{2}}{w_{0}^{2}}} attains the minimum at RR. Then similar to the above dimension reduction process and nondimensionlization, we can obtain the dimensionless 1D GPE for BEC on a ring as [110]:

i∂tψ(θ,t)=−12∂θ​θψ(θ,t)+β|ψ|2ψ(θ,t),θ∈[0,2π],t>0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\theta,t)=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\theta\theta}\psi(\theta,t)+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi(\theta,t),\quad\theta\in[0,2\pi],\quad t>0, (1.46)

with periodic boundary condition, where ψ:=ψ⁡(θ,t)\psi:=\psi(\theta,t) is the wave function and β\beta is a dimensionless parameter.

1.4. Outline of the review

Concerning the GPE (1.39), there are two basic issues, the ground state and the dynamics. Mathematically speaking, the dynamics include the time dependent behavior of GPE, such as the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem, finite time blow-up, stability of traveling waves, etc. The ground state is usually defined as the minimizer of the energy functional (1.42) under the normalization constraint (1.41). In the remaining part of the paper, we will review the mathematical theories and numerical methods for ground states and dynamics of BECs.

In section 2, we review the theories of GPE for single-component BEC. Existence and uniqueness, as well as other properties for the ground states are presented. Well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for GPE is also reviewed. The rigorous analysis on the convergence rates for the dimension reduction is introduced in section 2.3. After an overview on the mathematical results for GPE, we list the numerical methods to find the ground states and compute the dynamics for GPE in sections 3 and 4, respectively. The most popular way for computing the ground states of BEC is the gradient flow with discrete normalization (or imaginary time) method. Section 3 provides a solid mathematical background on the method and details on the full discretizations. For computing the dynamics of GPE, the traditional finite difference methods and the popular time splitting methods are taken into consideration in section 4, with rigorous error analysis.

In section 5, we investigate the rotating BEC with quantized vortices. There exist critical rotating speeds for the vortex configuration. In order to compute the ground states and dynamics of rotating BEC in the presence of the multi-scale vortex structure, we report the efficient and accurate numerical methods in section 6. For fast rotating BEC, the semiclassical scaling is usually adopted other than the physical scaling used in the introduction. We demonstrate these two different scalings in section 7, for the whole space case (harmonic trap) and the bounded domain case (box potential). In fact, the semiclassical scaling is very useful in the case of Thomas-Fermi regime.

Section 8 is devoted to the mathematical theory and numerical methods for dipolar BEC. There are both isotropic contact interactions (short range) and anisotropic dipole-dipole interactions (long range) in a dipolar BEC, and the dipolar GPE involves a highly singular kernel representing the dipole-dipole interaction. We overcome the difficulty caused by the singular kernel via a reformulation of the dipolar GPE, and carry out accurate and efficient numerical methods for dipolar BECs. In section 9, we consider a two component BEC, which is the simplest multi component BEC system. Ground state properties as well as dynamical properties are described. Efficient numerical methods are proposed by generalizing the existing methods for single component BEC. Finally, we briefly introduce some other important topics that are not covered in the current review in section 10, such as spinor BEC, Bogoliubov excitations and BEC at finite temperatu re.

Throughout the paper, we adopt the standard Sobolev spaces and write the ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} for standard Lp​(ℝd)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) norm when there is no confusion on the spatial variables. The notations are consistent in each section, and the meaning of notation remains the same if not specified.

2. Mathematical theory for the Gross-Pitaevskii equation

In this section, we consider the dimensionless GPE in dd (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) dimensions (1.39),

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=−12​∇2ψ​(𝐱,t)+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ​(𝐱,t)+β​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​ψ​(𝐱,t),𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)+V(\mathbf{x})\psi(\mathbf{x},t)+\beta\;|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\psi(\mathbf{x},t),\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (2.1)

where V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 is a real-valued potential and β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} is treated as an arbitrary dimensionless parameter. The GPE (2.1) can be generalized to any dimensions and many results presented here are valid in higher dimensions, but we focus on the most relevant cases d=1,2,3d=1,2,3 for BEC.

There are two important invariants, i.e., the normalization (mass),

N⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t))=∫ℝd|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱≡N⁡(ψ0)=∫ℝd|ψ⁡(𝐱,0)|2​𝑑𝐱=1,t≥0,\displaystyle N(\psi(\cdot,t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{2}\;d{\mathbf{x}}\equiv N(\psi_{0})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\psi({\mathbf{x}},0)|^{2}\;d{\mathbf{x}}=1,\quad t\geq 0, (2.2)

and the energy per particle

E⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t))=∫ℝd[12​|∇ψ|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ|2+β2​|ψ|4]​𝑑𝐱≡E⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,0)),t≥0.\displaystyle E(\psi(\cdot,t))=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+V({\mathbf{x}})|\psi|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi|^{4}\right]d{\mathbf{x}}\equiv E(\psi(\cdot,0)),\quad t\geq 0. (2.3)

In fact, the energy functional E⁡(ψ)E(\psi) can be split into three parts, i.e. kinetic energy Ekin​(ψ)E_{\rm kin}(\psi), potential energy Epot​(ψ)E_{\rm pot}(\psi) and interaction energy Eint​(ψ)E_{\rm int}(\psi), which are defined as

Eint​(ψ)=∫ℝdβ2​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|4​𝑑𝐱,Epot​(ψ)=∫ℝdV⁡(𝐱)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle E_{\rm int}(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{4}d{\mathbf{x}},\qquad E_{\rm pot}(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V({\mathbf{x}})|\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{2}d{\mathbf{x}}, (2.4)
Ekin​(ψ)=∫ℝd12​|∇ψ​(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱,E⁡(ψ)=Ekin​(ψ)+Epot​(ψ)+Eint​(ψ).\displaystyle E_{\rm kin}(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{2}\;d{\mathbf{x}},\quad E(\psi)=E_{\rm kin}(\psi)+E_{\rm pot}(\psi)+E_{\rm int}(\psi).\qquad (2.5)

For convenience, we introduce the following function spaces:

LV​(ℝd)={ϕ|∫ℝdV⁡(𝐱)​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱<∞},X:=X⁡(ℝd)=H1​(ℝd)∩LV​(ℝd).\displaystyle L_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d})=\left\{\phi|\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}d\mathbf{x}<\infty\right\},\quad X:=X(\mathbb{R}^{d})=H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L_{V}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). (2.6)

2.1. Ground states

To find the stationary solution of (2.1), we write

ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=ϕ⁡(𝐱)​e−i​μ​t,\displaystyle\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)=\phi({\mathbf{x}})\;e^{-i\mu t}, (2.7)

where μ\mu is the chemical potential of the condensate and ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi({\mathbf{x}}) is a function independent of time. Substituting (2.7) into (2.1) gives the following equation for (μ,ϕ⁡(𝐱))(\mu,\phi({\mathbf{x}})):

μ​ϕ​(𝐱)=−12​Δ​ϕ​(𝐱)+V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ​(𝐱)+β​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​ϕ​(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle\mu\;\phi({\mathbf{x}})=-\frac{1}{2}\Delta\phi({\mathbf{x}})+V({\mathbf{x}})\phi({\mathbf{x}})+\beta|\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{2}\phi({\mathbf{x}}),\qquad{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (2.8)

under the normalization condition

‖ϕ‖22:=∫ℝd|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=1.\displaystyle\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{2}d{\mathbf{x}}=1. (2.9)

This is a nonlinear eigenvalue problem with a constraint and any eigenvalue μ\mu can be computed from its corresponding eigenfunction ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi({\mathbf{x}}) by

μ\displaystyle\mu =\displaystyle= μ⁡(ϕ)=∫ℝd[12​|∇ϕ​(𝐱)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2+β​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4]​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle\mu(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{2}+V({\mathbf{x}})|\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{2}+\beta|\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{4}\right]d{\mathbf{x}} (2.10)
=\displaystyle= E⁡(ϕ)+∫ℝdβ2​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4​𝑑𝐱=E⁡(ϕ)+Eint​(ϕ).\displaystyle E(\phi)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{\beta}{2}|\phi({\mathbf{x}})|^{4}d{\mathbf{x}}=E(\phi)+E_{\rm int}(\phi).

The ground state of a BEC is usually defined as the minimizer of the following minimization problem:

Find ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S such that

Eg:=E⁡(ϕg)=minϕ∈S⁡E⁡(ϕ),\displaystyle E_{g}:=E(\phi_{g})=\min_{\phi\in S}E(\phi), (2.11)

where S={ϕ|∥ϕ∥2=1,E(ϕ)<∞}S=\{\phi\ |\ \|\phi\|_{2}=1,\ E(\phi)<\infty\} is the unit sphere.

It is easy to show that the ground state ϕg\phi_{g} is an eigenfunction of the nonlinear eigenvalue problem. Any eigenfunction of (2.8) whose energy is larger than that of the ground state is usually called as excited states in the physics literatures.

2.1.1. Existence

In this section, we discuss the existence and uniqueness of the ground state (2.11). Denote the best Sobolev constant CbC_{b} in 2D as

Cb=inf0≠f∈H1​(ℝ2)‖∇f‖L2​(ℝ2)2​‖f‖L2​(ℝ2)2‖f‖L4​(ℝ2)4.\displaystyle C_{b}=\inf_{0\neq f\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\frac{\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}\,\|f\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{2}}{\|f\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}^{4}}. (2.12)

The best constant CbC_{b} can be attained at some H1H^{1} function [184] and it is crucial in considering the existence of ground states in 2D.

For existence and uniqueness of the ground state, we have the following results.

Theorem 2.1.

(Existence and uniqueness) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies the confining condition

lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞,\displaystyle\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty, (2.13)

there exists a ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S for (2.11) if one of the following holds

(i) d=3d=3, β≥0\beta\geq 0;

(ii) d=2d=2, β>−Cb\beta>-C_{b};

(iii) d=1d=1, for all β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}.

Moreover, the ground state can be chosen as nonnegative |ϕg||\phi_{g}| , and ϕg=ei​θ​|ϕg|\phi_{g}=e^{i\theta}|\phi_{g}| for some constant θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}. For β≥0\beta\geq 0, the nonnegative ground state |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is unique. If potential V⁡(𝐱)∈Lloc2V(\mathbf{x})\in L_{\rm loc}^{2}, the nonnegative ground state is strictly positive.

In contrast, there exists no ground state, if one of the following holds:

(i′) d=3d=3, β<0\beta<0;

(ii′) d=2d=2, β≤−Cb\beta\leq-C_{b}.

To prove the theorem, we present the following lemmas.

Lemma 2.1.

Suppose that V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty, the embedding X↪Lp​(ℝd)X\hookrightarrow L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is compact, where p∈[2,∞]p\in[2,\infty] for d=1d=1, p∈[2,∞)p\in[2,\infty) for d=2d=2, and p∈[2,6)p\in[2,6) for d=3d=3.

Proof.

It suffices to prove the case for p=2p=2 and the other cases can be obtained by interpolation in view of the Sobolev inequalities. Since XX is a Hilbert space, we need show that any weakly convergent sequence in XX has a strong convergent subsequence in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Taking a bounded sequence {ϕn}n=1∞⊂X\{\phi^{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\subset X such that

ϕn⇀ϕ​ in ​X,\displaystyle\phi^{n}\rightharpoonup\phi\text{ in }X, (2.14)

in order to prove the strong L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) convergence of the sequence, we need only prove that

‖ϕn‖L2​(ℝd)→‖ϕ‖L2​(ℝd).\displaystyle\|\phi^{n}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\to\|\phi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}. (2.15)

Using the weak convergence, there exists C>0C>0 such that ∫ℝdV⁡(𝐱)​|ϕn|2​𝑑𝐱≤C\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V(\mathbf{x})|\phi^{n}|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}\leq C. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, from lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty, there exists R>0R>0 such that V⁡(𝐱)≥CεV(\mathbf{x})\geq\frac{C}{\varepsilon} for |𝐱|≥R|\mathbf{x}|\geq R, which implies that

∫|𝐱|≥R|ϕn|2≤ε.\displaystyle\int_{|\mathbf{x}|\geq R}|\phi^{n}|^{2}\leq\varepsilon. (2.16)

For |𝐱|≥R|\mathbf{x}|\geq R, applying Sobolev embedding theorem, we obtain

∫|𝐱|≤R|ϕ|2​𝑑𝐱=limn→∞∫|𝐱|≤R|ϕn|2​𝑑𝐱.\displaystyle\int_{|\mathbf{x}|\leq R}|\phi|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}=\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\int_{|\mathbf{x}|\leq R}|\phi^{n}|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}. (2.17)

Combining (2.16) and (2.17) together as well as the lower semi-continuity of the L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) norm, we have

lim supn→∞‖ϕn‖L2​(ℝd)2−ε≤‖ϕ‖L2​(ℝd)2≤lim infn→∞‖ϕn‖L2​(ℝd)2.\displaystyle\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty}\|\phi^{n}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}-\varepsilon\leq\|\phi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}\leq\liminf\limits_{n\to\infty}\|\phi^{n}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}. (2.18)

Hence we get ‖ϕn‖L2​(ℝd)→‖ϕ‖L2​(ℝd)\|\phi^{n}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\to\|\phi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})} and the strong convergence in L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) holds true. The conclusion then follows.

The following lemma ensures that the ground state must be nonnegative.

Lemma 2.2.

For any ϕ∈X⁡(ℝd)\phi\in X(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and energy E⁡(⋅)E(\cdot) (2.3), we have

E⁡(ϕ)≥E⁡(|ϕ|),\displaystyle E(\phi)\geq E(|\phi|), (2.19)

and the equality holds iff ϕ=ei​θ​|ϕ|\phi=e^{i\theta}|\phi| for some constant θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}.

Proof.

Noticing the inequality for ϕ∈H1​(ℝd)\phi\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N})[130],

‖∇|ϕ|‖L2​(ℝd)≤‖∇ϕ‖L2​(ℝd),\displaystyle\|\nabla|\phi|\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq\|\nabla\phi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}, (2.20)

where the equality holds iff ϕ=ei​θ​|ϕ|\phi=e^{i\theta}|\phi| for some constant θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}, a direct application implies the conclusion.

The minimization problem (2.11) is nonconvex, but it can be transformed to a convex minimization problem through the following lemma when β≥0\beta\geq 0.

Lemma 2.3.

([133]) Considering the density ρ⁡(𝐱)=|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2≥0\rho(\mathbf{x})=|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\geq 0, for ρ∈S\sqrt{\rho}\in S, the energy E⁡(ρ)E(\sqrt{\rho}) (2.3) is strictly convex in ρ\rho if β≥0\beta\geq 0.

Proof.

The potential energy (2.4) is linear in ρ\rho and the interaction energy (2.4) is quadratic in ρ\rho. Hence, Epot+EintE_{\rm pot}+E_{\rm int} is convex in ρ\rho. For ϕ1​(𝐱)=ρ1​(𝐱),ϕ2​(𝐱)=ρ2​(𝐱)∈S\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\sqrt{\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})},\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})=\sqrt{\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})}\in S (ρ1,ρ2≥0\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\geq 0), we have ϕθ​(𝐱)=θ​ρ1​(𝐱)+(1−θ)​ρ2​(𝐱)∈S\phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\sqrt{\theta\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\theta)\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})}\in S for any θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1). Using Cauchy inequality, we get

|∇ϕθ​(𝐱)|2=\displaystyle\left|\nabla\phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}= |θ​ρ1​(𝐱)θ∇ϕ1(𝐱)+(1−θ)​ρ2​(𝐱)1−θ∇ϕ2(𝐱)|2θ​ρ1​(𝐱)+(1−θ)​ρ2​(𝐱)\displaystyle\frac{\left|\sqrt{\theta\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})}\sqrt{\theta}\nabla\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})+\sqrt{(1-\theta)\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})}\sqrt{1-\theta}\nabla\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}}{\theta\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\theta)\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})}
≤\displaystyle\leq (θ​ρ1​(𝐱)+(1−θ)​ρ2​(𝐱))​(θ​|∇ϕ1​(𝐱)|2+(1−θ)​|∇ϕ2​(𝐱)|2)θ​ρ1​(𝐱)+(1−θ)​ρ2​(𝐱)\displaystyle\frac{\left(\theta\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\theta)\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})\right)\left(\theta|\nabla\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}+(1-\theta)|\nabla\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\right)}{\theta\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})+(1-\theta)\rho_{2}(\mathbf{x})}
=\displaystyle= θ​|∇ϕ1​(𝐱)|2+(1−θ)​|∇ϕ2​(𝐱)|2,\displaystyle\theta|\nabla\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}+(1-\theta)|\nabla\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2},

which implies the convexity of the kinetic energy EkinE_{\rm kin} (2.5) (with possible approximation procedure). The conclusion then follows.

Proof of Theorem 2.1: We separate the proof into the existence and nonexistence parts.

(1) Existence. First, we claim that the energy EE (2.3) is bounded below under the assumptions. Case (i) is clear. For case (ii), using the constraint ‖ϕ‖22=1\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}=1 and Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality, we have

β∥ϕ∥44≥−∥ϕ∥22⋅∥∇ϕ∥22=−∥∇ϕ∥22.\beta\|\phi\|_{4}^{4}\geq-\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\|\nabla\phi\|_{2}^{2}=-\|\nabla\phi\|_{2}^{2}.

For case (iii), using Cauchy inequality and Sobolev inequality, for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists Cε>0C_{\varepsilon}>0 such that

‖ϕ‖44≤‖ϕ‖∞2​‖ϕ‖22≤‖ϕ‖∞2≤‖∇ϕ‖2​‖ϕ‖2≤ε​‖∇ϕ‖22+Cε,\|\phi\|_{4}^{4}\leq\|\phi\|_{\infty}^{2}\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|\phi\|_{\infty}^{2}\leq\|\nabla\phi\|_{2}\|\phi\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon\|\nabla\phi\|_{2}^{2}+C_{\varepsilon},

which yields the claim. Hence, in all cases, we can take a sequence {ϕn}n=1∞\{\phi^{n}\}_{n=1}^{\infty} minimizing the energy EE in SS, and the sequence is uniformly bounded in XX. Taking a weakly convergent subsequence (denoted as the original sequence for simplicity) in XX, we have

ϕn⇀ϕ∞,weakly in ​X.\displaystyle\phi^{n}\rightharpoonup\phi^{\infty},\quad\text{weakly in }X. (2.21)

Lemma 2.1 ensures that {ϕn}n=1∞\left\{\phi^{n}\right\}_{n=1}^{\infty} converges to ϕ∞\phi^{\infty} in LpL^{p} where pp is given in Lemma 2.1. Combining the lower-semi-continuity of the H1H^{1} and LVL_{V} norms, we conclude that ϕ∞∈S\phi^{\infty}\in S is a ground state [133]. Lemma 2.2 ensures that the ground state can be chosen as the nonnegative one. Actually, the nonnegative ground state is strictly positive [133]. The uniqueness comes from the strict convexity of the energy in Lemma 2.3.

(2) Nonexistence. Firstly, we consider the case d=3d=3, i.e. case (i′). If β<0\beta<0, let ϕ(𝐱)=π−34e−|𝐱|2/2∈S\phi(\mathbf{x})=\pi^{-\frac{3}{4}}e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^{2}/2}\in S and denote

ϕε(𝐱)=ε−3/2ϕ(𝐱/ε)∈S,ε>0,\displaystyle\phi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})=\varepsilon^{-3/2}\phi(\mathbf{x}/\varepsilon)\in S,\quad\varepsilon>0, (2.22)

we find

E⁡(ϕε)=C1ε2+β​C2ε3+C3+O⁡(1),C1,C2>0.\displaystyle E(\phi^{\varepsilon})=\frac{C_{1}}{\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{\beta C_{2}}{\varepsilon^{3}}+C_{3}+O(1),\quad C_{1},C_{2}>0. (2.23)

Hence E⁡(ϕε)→−∞E(\phi^{\varepsilon})\to-\infty as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+} which shows that there exists no ground state.

Secondly, we consider the case d=2d=2. Let ϕb​(𝐱)\phi_{b}(\mathbf{x}) (𝐱∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}) be the smooth, radial symmetric (decreasing) function such that the best constant CbC_{b} is attained in (2.12). If β<−Cb\beta<-C_{b}, let ϕbε​(𝐱)=ε−1​ϕb​(𝐱/ε)\phi_{b}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})=\varepsilon^{-1}\phi_{b}(\mathbf{x}/\varepsilon) (ε>0\varepsilon>0), and we have

E⁡(ϕbε)=β+Cb2​ε2+C4+O⁡(1)​ as ​ε→0+.\displaystyle E(\phi_{b}^{\varepsilon})=\frac{\beta+C_{b}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}+C_{4}+O(1)\text{ as }\varepsilon\to 0^{+}. (2.24)

As ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}, E⁡(ϕbε)→−∞E(\phi_{b}^{\varepsilon})\to-\infty, which shows that there exists no ground state. For β=−Cb\beta=-C_{b}, as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}, ϕbε\phi_{b}^{\varepsilon} will converge to the Dirac distribution and the infimum of the energy EE will be the minimal of V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) (suppose V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) take minimal at origin), given by the sequence ϕbε\phi_{b}^{\varepsilon}. Thus, there exists no ground state for β=−Cb\beta=-C_{b}. The proof is complete. □\Box

Remark 2.1.

The conclusions in Theorem 2.1 hold for potentials satisfying the confining condition, including the box potential as in (1.17). Since box potentials are not in Lloc2L^{2}_{\rm loc}, there exists zeros in the ground state at the points where V⁡(𝐱)=+∞V(\mathbf{x})=+\infty. Results for the 3D case were first obtained by Lieb et al. [133].

2.1.2. Properties of ground states

In this section, when we refer to the ground state, the conditions guaranteeing the existence in Theorem 2.1 are always assumed and potentials are locally bounded.

For the ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S, we have the following Virial theorem when V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is homogenous.

Theorem 2.2.

(Virial identity) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) is homogenous of order s>0s>0, i.e. V⁡(λ​𝐱)=λs​V​(𝐱)V(\lambda\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{s}V(\mathbf{x}) for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, then the ground state solution ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S for (2.11) satisfies

2​Ekin​(ϕg)−s​Epot​(ϕg)+d​Eint​(ϕg)=0.\displaystyle 2E_{\rm kin}(\phi_{g})-s\;E_{\rm pot}(\phi_{g})+d\;E_{\rm int}(\phi_{g})=0. (2.25)
Proof.

Consider ϕε(𝐱)=ε−d/2ϕg(𝐱/ε)∈S\phi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})=\varepsilon^{-d/2}\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}/\varepsilon)\in S (ε>0\varepsilon>0), and use the stationary condition of the energy E⁡(ϕε)E(\phi^{\varepsilon}) at ε=1\varepsilon=1, then we get d​E​(ϕε)d​ε|ε=1=0\frac{d{E(\phi^{\varepsilon})}}{d\varepsilon}\big|_{\varepsilon=1}=0, which yields the Virial identity (2.25).

Many properties of the ground state are determined by the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}).

Theorem 2.3.

[133](Symmetry) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is spherically symmetry and monotone increasing, then the positive ground state solution ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S for (2.11) must be spherically symmetric and monotonically decreasing.

Proof.

This fact comes from the symmetric rearrangements.

To learn more on the ground state, we study the Euler-Lagrange equation (2.8).

Theorem 2.4.

The ground state of (2.11) satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation (2.8). Suppose V⁡(𝐱)∈Lloc∞V(\mathbf{x})\in L_{\rm loc}^{\infty}, the ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of (2.11) is Hloc2H^{2}_{\rm loc}. In addition, if V∈C∞V\in C^{\infty}, the ground state is also C∞C^{\infty}.

Proof.

It is easy to show the ground state satisfies the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (2.8). The regularity follows from the elliptic theory.

For confining potentials, we can show that ground states decay exponentially fast when |𝐱|→∞|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty.

Theorem 2.5.

Suppose that 0≤V⁡(𝐱)∈Lloc20\leq V(\mathbf{x})\in L_{\rm loc}^{2} satisfies (2.13) and ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S is a ground state of (2.11). When β≥0\beta\geq 0, for any ν>0\nu>0, there exists a constant Cν>0C_{\nu}>0 such that

|ϕg(𝐱)|≤Cνe−ν​|𝐱|,𝐱∈ℝd,d=1,2,3.\displaystyle|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})|\leq C_{\nu}e^{-\nu|\mathbf{x}|},\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,\,d=1,2,3. (2.26)
Proof.

The proof for d=3d=3 is given in [133] and the cases for d=1,2d=1,2 are the same. For any ν>0\nu>0, rewrite the Euler-Lagrange equation (2.8) for ϕg\phi_{g} as

(−12​∇2+ν22)​ϕg=(μ+ν22−V−β​|ϕg|2)​ϕg.\displaystyle\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}\right)\phi_{g}=\left(\mu+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}-V-\beta|\phi_{g}|^{2}\right)\phi_{g}. (2.27)

Making use of the dd-dimensional Yukawa potential Ydν​(𝐱)Y_{d}^{\nu}(\mathbf{x}) (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) [130] associated with −12​∇2+ν22-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}, ϕg\phi_{g} can be expressed as

ϕg​(𝐱)=∫ℝdYdν​(𝐱−𝐲)​[μ+ν22−V⁡(𝐲)−β​|ϕg​(𝐲)|2]​𝑑𝐲.\displaystyle\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}Y_{d}^{\nu}(\mathbf{x}-{\bf y})\left[\mu+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}-V(\mathbf{y})-\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{y})|^{2}\right]\,d\,\mathbf{y}. (2.28)

Noticing that ϕg\phi_{g} and the Yukawa potential are positive and VV is confining potential, we see that for sufficiently large R>0R>0, μ+ν22−V⁡(𝐱)−β​|ϕg​(𝐱)|2≤0\mu+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\leq 0 for |𝐱|≥R|\mathbf{x}|\geq R. Thus, we get

ϕg​(𝐱)≤∫|𝐲|<RYdν​(𝐱−𝐲)​[μ+ν22−V⁡(𝐲)−β​|ϕg​(𝐲)|2]​𝑑𝐲.\displaystyle\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\leq\int_{|\mathbf{y}|<R}Y_{d}^{\nu}(\mathbf{x}-{\bf y})\left[\mu+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}-V(\mathbf{y})-\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{y})|^{2}\right]\,d\,{\mathbf{y}}. (2.29)

Noticing that Ydν∈Lloc2Y_{d}^{\nu}\in L_{\rm loc}^{2} (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) and |Ydν​(𝐱)|≤C​e−ν​|𝐱||Y_{d}^{\nu}(\mathbf{x})|\leq Ce^{-\nu|\mathbf{x}|} for sufficiently large |𝐱||\mathbf{x}|, we find

Cν=sup𝐱∫|𝐲|<Reν​|𝐱|​Ydν​(𝐱−𝐲)​[μ+ν22−V⁡(𝐲)−β​|ϕg​(𝐲)|2]​𝑑𝐲<∞,\displaystyle C_{\nu}=\sup_{\mathbf{x}}\int_{|\mathbf{y}|<R}e^{\nu|\mathbf{x}|}Y_{d}^{\nu}(\mathbf{x}-{\bf y})\left[\mu+\frac{\nu^{2}}{2}-V(\mathbf{y})-\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{y})|^{2}\right]\,d\,\mathbf{y}<\infty, (2.30)

and the conclusion (2.26) holds.

Remark 2.2.

Results (2.26) can be generalized to 1D case for arbitrary β\beta, where ‖ϕg‖∞\|\phi_{g}\|_{\infty} is bounded by Sobolev inequality. The proof is the same.

For convex potentials, the ground states are shown to be log concave.

Theorem 2.6.

Suppose V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) is convex, then the positive ground state ϕg\phi_{g} of (2.11) is log concave, i.e. ln⁡(ϕg​(𝐱))\ln(\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})) is concave,

ln⁡(ϕg​(λ​𝐱+(1−λ)​𝐲))≥λ​ln⁡(ϕg​(𝐱))+(1−λ)​ln⁡(ϕg​(𝐲)),𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd,λ∈[0,1].\ln(\phi_{g}(\lambda\mathbf{x}+(1-\lambda)\mathbf{y}))\geq\lambda\ln(\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}))+(1-\lambda)\ln(\phi_{g}(\mathbf{y})),\quad\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,\,\lambda\in[0,1].
Proof.

See [133].

When β>0\beta>0, we can actually estimate the L∞L^{\infty} bound for the ground state.

Theorem 2.7.

Suppose that 0≤V⁡(𝐱)∈Clocα0\leq V(\mathbf{x})\in C^{\alpha}_{\rm loc} (α>0\alpha>0) satisfies (2.13) and β>0\beta>0. Let ϕg\phi_{g} be the unique positive ground state of (2.11), we have

‖ϕg‖∞≤μgβ,μg=E⁡(ϕg)+β2​‖ϕg‖44.\displaystyle\|\phi_{g}\|_{\infty}\leq\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{g}}{\beta}},\quad\mu_{g}=E(\phi_{g})+\frac{\beta}{2}\|\phi_{g}\|_{4}^{4}. (2.31)

The chemical potential μg≤2​E​(ϕg)\mu_{g}\leq 2E(\phi_{g}) and hence can be bounded by choosing arbitrary testing function.

Proof.

Applying elliptic theory to the Euler-Lagrange equation,

μg​ϕg=(−12​∇2+V+β​|ϕg|2)​ϕg,\displaystyle\mu_{g}\phi_{g}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V+\beta|\phi_{g}|^{2}\right)\phi_{g}, (2.32)

we get ϕg∈Cloc2,α\phi_{g}\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\rm loc}. From Theorem 2.5, ϕg\phi_{g} is bounded in L∞L^{\infty}. Consider the point 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} where ϕg\phi_{g} takes its maximal, we can obtain

μg​ϕg​(𝐱0)\displaystyle\mu_{g}\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0}) =(−12​∇2ϕg+V+β​|ϕg|2)|𝐱0​ϕg​(𝐱0)\displaystyle=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi_{g}+V+\beta|\phi_{g}|^{2}\right)\bigg|_{\mathbf{x}_{0}}\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0})
≥[V⁡(𝐱0)+β​|ϕg​(𝐱0)|2]​ϕg​(𝐱0)≥β​|ϕg​(𝐱0)|2​ϕg​(𝐱0),\displaystyle\geq\left[V(\mathbf{x}_{0})+\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0})|^{2}\right]\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0})\geq\beta|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0})|^{2}\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0}),

and so

‖ϕg‖∞2=|ϕg​(𝐱0)|2≤μgβ.\displaystyle\|\phi_{g}\|_{\infty}^{2}=|\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}_{0})|^{2}\leq\frac{\mu_{g}}{\beta}. (2.33)


Remark 2.3.

In 2D and 3D, for small β>0\beta>0 or β<0\beta<0, the L∞L^{\infty} estimate above can be improved by employing the W2,pW^{2,p} estimates for (2.32) and the embedding H2​(ℝd)↪L∞​(ℝd)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d=2,3d=2,3). In 1D, L∞L^{\infty} bound can be simply obtained by H1​(ℝ)↪L∞​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R})\hookrightarrow L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), while the H1H^{1} norm can be estimated by the energy.

2.1.3. Approximations of ground states

For a few external potentials, we can find approximations of ground states in the weakly interaction regime, i.e. |β|=o⁡(1)|\beta|=o(1), and strongly repulsive interaction regime, i.e. β≫1\beta\gg 1 [33, 37]. These approximations show the leading order behavior of the ground states and they can be used as initial data for computing ground states numerically.

Under a box potential, i.e. we take

V⁡(𝐱)={0,𝐱=(x1,…,xd)T∈U=(0,1)d,+∞,otherwise,\displaystyle V(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}0,&\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})^{T}\in U=(0,1)^{d},\\ +\infty,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (2.34)

in (2.8). When β=0\beta=0, i.e. linear case, (2.8) collapses to

μ​ϕ=−12​∇2ϕ,ϕ|∂U=0,‖ϕ‖22=∫U|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=1.\displaystyle\mu\phi=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi,\quad\phi|_{\partial U}=0,\quad\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{U}|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}d\mathbf{x}=1. (2.35)

For this linear eigenvalue problem, it is easy to find an orthonormal set of eigenfunctions as [31, 148, 150]

ϕ𝐉​(𝐱)=∏m=1dϕjm​(xm),ϕl​(x)=2​sin⁡(l​π​x),l∈ℕ,𝐉=(j1,⋯,jd)∈ℕd,\displaystyle\phi_{\bf J}({\mathbf{x}})=\prod_{m=1}^{d}\phi_{j_{m}}(x_{m}),\ \phi_{l}(x)=\sqrt{2}\sin(l\pi x),\ l\in{\mathbb{N}},\ {\bf J}=(j_{1},\cdots,j_{d})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{d}, (2.36)

with the corresponding eigenvalues as

μ𝐉=∑m=1dμjm,μl=12​l2​π2,l∈ℕ.\displaystyle\mu_{\bf J}=\sum_{m=1}^{d}\mu_{j_{m}},\qquad\mu_{l}=\frac{1}{2}l^{2}\pi^{2},\qquad l\in{\mathbb{N}}. (2.37)

Thus, for linear case, we can find the exact ground state as ϕg​(𝐱)=ϕ(1,⋯,1)​(𝐱)\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})=\phi_{(1,\cdots,1)}(\mathbf{x}). In addition, when |β|=o⁡(1)|\beta|=o(1), we can approximate the ground state as ϕg​(𝐱)≈ϕ(1,⋯,1)​(𝐱)\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\approx\phi_{(1,\cdots,1)}(\mathbf{x}). The corresponding energy and chemical potential can be found as

Eg=E⁡(ϕg)≈E⁡(ϕ(1,⋯,1)​(𝐱))=d​π2/2+O⁡(β),\displaystyle E_{g}=E(\phi_{g})\approx E(\phi_{(1,\cdots,1)}(\mathbf{x}))=d\pi^{2}/2+O(\beta),
μg=μ⁡(ϕg)≈μ⁡(ϕ(1,⋯,1)​(𝐱))=d​π2/2+O⁡(β).\displaystyle\mu_{g}=\mu(\phi_{g})\approx\mu(\phi_{(1,\cdots,1)}(\mathbf{x}))=d\pi^{2}/2+O(\beta).

On the other hand, when β≫1\beta\gg 1, by dropping the diffusion term (i.e. the first term on the right hand side of (2.8)) – Thomas-Fermi (TF) approximation – [130, 11], we obtain

μgTF​ϕgTF​(𝐱)=β​|ϕgTF​(𝐱)|2​ϕgTF​(𝐱),𝐱∈U.\displaystyle\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})=\beta|\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U. (2.38)

From (2.38), we obtain

ϕgTF​(𝐱)=μgTFβ,𝐱∈U.\displaystyle\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}({\mathbf{x}})=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}}{\beta}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U. (2.39)

Plugging (2.39) into the normalization condition, we obtain

1=∫U|ϕgTF​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=∫UμgTFβ​𝑑𝐱=μgTFβ⇒μgTF=β.\displaystyle 1=\int_{U}|\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}({\mathbf{x}})|^{2}\;d{\mathbf{x}}=\int_{U}\frac{\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}}{\beta}\;d{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}}{\beta}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}=\beta. (2.40)

The TF energy EgTFE_{g}^{\rm TF} is obtained via (2.10),

EgTF=μgTF−β2​∫U|ϕgTF|4​𝑑𝐱=μgTF2=β2.\displaystyle E_{g}^{\rm TF}=\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}-\frac{\beta}{2}\int_{U}|\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}|^{4}\;d{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}}{2}=\frac{\beta}{2}. (2.41)

Therefore, we get the TF approximation for the ground state, the energy and the chemical potential when β≫1\beta\gg 1:

ϕg​(𝐱)≈ϕgTF​(𝐱)=1,𝐱∈U,\displaystyle\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\approx\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})=1,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U, (2.42)
Eg≈EgTF=β2,μg≈μgTF=β.\displaystyle E_{g}\approx E_{g}^{\rm TF}=\frac{\beta}{2},\qquad\mu_{g}\approx\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}=\beta. (2.43)

It is easy to see that the TF approximation for the ground state does not satisfy the boundary condition ϕ|∂U=0\phi|_{\partial U}=0. This is due to removing the diffusion term in (2.8) and it suggests that a boundary layer will appear in the ground state when β≫1\beta\gg 1. Due to the existence of the boundary layer, the kinetic energy does not go to zero when β→∞\beta\to\infty and thus it cannot be neglected. Better approximation with matched asymptotic expansion can be found in [37].

Under a harmonic potential, i.e. we take V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) as (1.40). When β=0\beta=0, the exact ground state can be found as [31, 148, 150]

μg0={γx2,γx+γy2,γx+γy+γz2,ϕg0​(𝐱)={(γx)1/4(π)1/4e−(γxx2)/2,d=1,(γx​γy)1/4(π)1/2e−(γxx2+γyy2)/2,d=2,(γx​γy​γz)1/4(π)3/4e−(γxx2+γyy2+γzz2)/2,d=3.\mu_{g}^{0}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{\gamma_{x}}{2},\\ \frac{\gamma_{x}+\gamma_{y}}{2},\\ \frac{\gamma_{x}+\gamma_{y}+\gamma_{z}}{2},\\ \end{array}\right.\quad\phi_{g}^{0}(\mathbf{x})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{(\gamma_{x})^{1/4}}{(\pi)^{1/4}}\;e^{-(\gamma_{x}x^{2})/2},&d=1,\\ \frac{(\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y})^{1/4}}{(\pi)^{1/2}}\;e^{-(\gamma_{x}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}y^{2})/2},&d=2,\\ \frac{(\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y}\gamma_{z})^{1/4}}{(\pi)^{3/4}}\;e^{-(\gamma_{x}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}z^{2})/2},&d=3.\\ \end{array}\right.

Thus when |β|=o⁡(1)|\beta|=o(1), the ground state ϕg\phi_{g} can be approximated by ϕg0\phi_{g}^{0}, i.e.

ϕg​(𝐱)≈ϕg0​(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd.\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\approx\phi_{g}^{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}.

Again, when β≫1\beta\gg 1, by dropping the diffusion term (i.e. the first term on the right hand side of (2.8)) – Thomas-Fermi (TF) approximation – [130, 11], we obtain

μgTF​ϕgTF​(𝐱)=V⁡(𝐱)​ϕgTF​(𝐱)+β​|ϕgTF​(𝐱)|2​ϕgTF​(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd.\displaystyle\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})=V(\mathbf{x})\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})+\beta|\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. (2.44)

Solving the above equation, we get

ϕg​(𝐱)≈ϕgTF​(𝐱)={(μgTF−V⁡(𝐱))/β,V⁡(𝐱)<μgTF,0,otherwise,\displaystyle\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\approx\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}(\mathbf{x})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\sqrt{\left(\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}-V(\mathbf{x})\right)/\beta},&\ V(\mathbf{x})<\mu_{g}^{\rm TF},\\ 0,&\hbox{otherwise},\end{array}\right. (2.45)

where μgTF\mu_{g}^{\rm TF} is chosen to satisfy the normalization ‖ϕgTF‖2=1\|\phi_{g}^{\rm TF}\|_{2}=1. After some tedious computations [33, 37], we get

μgTF={12​(3​β​γx2)2/3,(β​γx​γyπ)1/2,12​(15​β​γx​γy​γz4​π)2/5,EgTF={310​(3​β​γx2)2/3,d=1,23​(β​γx​γyπ)1/2,d=2,514​(15​β​γx​γy​γz4​π)2/5,d=3.\displaystyle\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{3\beta\gamma_{x}}{2}\right)^{2/3},\\ \left(\frac{\beta\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y}}{\pi}\right)^{1/2},\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{15\beta\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y}\gamma_{z}}{4\pi}\right)^{2/5},\\ \end{array}\right.\qquad E_{g}^{\rm TF}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\frac{3}{10}\left(\frac{3\beta\gamma_{x}}{2}\right)^{2/3},&d=1,\\ \frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{\beta\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y}}{\pi}\right)^{1/2},&d=2,\\ \frac{5}{14}\left(\frac{15\beta\gamma_{x}\gamma_{y}\gamma_{z}}{4\pi}\right)^{2/5},&d=3.\\ \end{array}\right.

It is easy to verify that the Thomas-Fermi approximation (2.45) does not have limit as β→∞\beta\to\infty.

Remark 2.4.

For the harmonic potential (1.40), the energy of the Thomas-Fermi approximation is unbounded, i.e.

E⁡(ϕgTF)=+∞.E(\phi_{g}^{\rm TF})=+\infty. (2.47)

This is due to the low regularity of ϕgTF\phi_{g}^{\rm TF} at the free boundary V⁡(𝐱)=μgTFV(\mathbf{x})=\mu_{g}^{\rm TF}. More precisely, ϕgTF\phi_{g}^{\rm TF} is locally C1/2C^{1/2} at the interface. This is a typical behavior for solutions of free boundary value problems, which indicates that an interface layer correction has to be constructed in order to improve the approximation quality.

2.2. Dynamics

Many properties of dynamics for BEC can be reported by solving GPE (2.1). In this section, we will consider the well-posedness for Cauchy problem of GPE (2.1). For BEC, energy (2.3) is an important physical quantity and thus it is natural to study the well-posedness in the energy space X⁡(ℝd)X(\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) (2.6).

2.2.1. Well-posedness

To investigate the Cauchy problem of (2.3), dispersive estimates (Strichartz estimates) have played very important roles. For smooth potentials V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) with at most quadratic growth in far field, i.e.,

V(𝐱)∈C∞(ℝd) and D𝐤V(𝐱)∈L∞(ℝd),for all 𝐤∈ℕ0dwith|𝐤|≥2,\displaystyle V(\mathbf{x})\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\hbox{ and }D^{{\bf k}}V(\mathbf{x})\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\quad\hbox{for all }{\bf k}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{d}\ \hbox{with}\ |{\bf k}|\geq 2, (2.48)

where ℕ0={0}∪ℕ\mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0\}\cup{\mathbb{N}}, Strichartz estimates are well established [73, 172].

Definition 2.1.

In dd dimensions (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3), let q′q^{\prime} and r′r^{\prime} be the conjugate index of qq and rr (1≤q,r≤∞1\leq q,r\leq\infty), respectively, i.e. 1=1/q′+1/q=1/r′+1/r1=1/q^{\prime}+1/q=1/r^{\prime}+1/r, we call the pair (q,r)(q,r) admissible and (q′,r′)(q^{\prime},r^{\prime}) conjugate admissible if

2q=d⁡(12−1r),\displaystyle\frac{2}{q}=d\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{r}\right), (2.49)

and

2≤r<2​dd−2,(2≤r≤∞ifd=1; 2≤r<∞ifd=2).\displaystyle 2\leq r<\frac{2d}{d-2},\quad(2\leq r\leq\infty\quad\text{if}\quad d=1;\;2\leq r<\infty\quad\text{if}\quad d=2). (2.50)

Consider the unitary group ei​t​𝐇𝐱Ve^{it{\bf H}_{\mathbf{x}}^{V}} generated by 𝐇𝐱V=−12​∇2+V⁡(𝐱){\bf H}_{\mathbf{x}}^{V}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x}), for V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) satisfying (2.48), then the following estimates are available.

Lemma 2.4.

(Strichartz’s estimates) Let (q,r)(q,r) be an admissible pair and (γ,ϱ)(\gamma,\varrho) be a conjugate admissible pair, I⊂ℝI\subset{\mathbb{R}} be a bounded interval satisfying 0∈I0\in I, then we have

(i) There exists a constant CC depending on II and qq such that

‖e−i​t​𝐇𝐱V​φ‖Lq​(I,Lr​(ℝd))≤C⁡(I,q)​‖φ‖L2​(ℝd).\displaystyle\left\|e^{-it{\bf H}_{\mathbf{x}}^{V}}\varphi\right\|_{L^{q}(I,L^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))}\leq C(I,q)\|\varphi\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}. (2.51)

(ii) If f∈Lγ​(I,Lϱ​(ℝd))f\in L^{\gamma}(I,L^{\varrho}(\mathbb{R}^{d})), there exists a constant CC depending on II, qq and ϱ\varrho, such that

‖∫I​⋂s≤te−i⁡(t−s)​𝐇𝐱V​f​(s)​𝑑s‖Lq​(I,Lr​(ℝd))≤C⁡(I,q,ϱ)​‖f‖Lγ​(I,Lϱ​(ℝd)).\displaystyle\left\|\int_{I\bigcap s\leq t}e^{-i(t-s){\bf H}_{\mathbf{x}}^{V}}f(s)\,ds\right\|_{L^{q}(I,L^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))}\leq C(I,q,\varrho)\|f\|_{L^{\gamma}(I,L^{\varrho}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))}. (2.52)

Using the above lemma, we can get the following results [73, 173].

Theorem 2.8.

(Well-posedness of Cauchy problem) Suppose the real-valued trap potential satisfies V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) and the condition (2.48), then we have

(i) For any initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱)∈X⁡(ℝd)\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\in X(\mathbb{R}^{d}), there exists a Tmax∈(0,+∞]T_{{\rm max}}\in(0,+\infty] such that the Cauchy problem of (2.1) has a unique maximal solution ψ∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X)\psi\in C\left([0,T_{{\rm max}}),X\right). It is maximal in the sense that if Tmax<∞T_{{\rm max}}<\infty, then ‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖X→∞\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{X}\to\infty when t→Tmax−t\to T^{-}_{{\rm max}}.

(ii) As long as the solution ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(\mathbf{x},t) remains in the energy space XX, the L2L^{2}-norm ‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖2\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{2} and energy E⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t))E(\psi(\cdot,t)) in (2.3) are conserved for t∈[0,Tmax)t\in[0,T_{\rm max}).

(iii) The solution of the Cauchy problem for (2.1) is global in time, i.e., Tmax=∞T_{\rm max}=\infty, if d=1d=1 or d=2d=2 with β>Cb/‖ψ0‖22\beta>C_{b}/\|\psi_{0}\|_{2}^{2} or d=3d=3 with β≥0\beta\geq 0.

2.2.2. Dynamical properties

From Theorem 2.8, the GPE (2.1) conserves the energy (2.3) and the mass (L2L^{2}-norm) (2.2). There are other important quantities that measure the dynamical properties of BEC. Consider the momentum defined as

𝐏(t)=∫ℝdIm(ψ¯(𝐱,t)∇ψ(𝐱,t))d𝐱,t≥0,\displaystyle{\bf P}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\rm Im}({\overline{\psi}}(\mathbf{x},t)\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x},t))\,d\mathbf{x},\quad t\geq 0, (2.53)

where Im⁡(c){\rm Im}(c) denotes the imaginary part of cc. Then we can get the following result.

Lemma 2.5.

Suppose ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi({\mathbf{x}},t) is the solution of the problem (2.1) and |∇V​(𝐱)|≤C⁡(V⁡(𝐱)+1)|\nabla V(\mathbf{x})|\leq C(V(\mathbf{x})+1) (V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0) for some constant CC, then we have

𝐏˙(t)=−∫ℝd|ψ(𝐱,t)|2∇V(𝐱)d𝐱.\displaystyle\qquad\dot{{\bf P}}(t)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\nabla V(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}. (2.54)

In particular, for V⁡(𝐱)≡0V(\mathbf{x})\equiv 0, the momentum is conserved.

Proof.

Differentiating (2.53) with respect to tt, noticing (2.1), integrating by parts and taking into account that ψ\psi decreases to 0 exponentially when |𝐱|→∞|{\mathbf{x}}|\to\infty (see also [73]), we have

𝐏˙​(t)=\displaystyle\dot{{\bf P}}(t)= −i∫ℝd[ψ¯t∇ψ−∇ψ¯ψt]d𝐱=∫ℝd[(−iψ¯t)∇ψ+iψt∇ψ¯]d𝐱\displaystyle-i\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[\;{\overline{\psi}}_{t}\nabla\psi-\nabla{\overline{\psi}}\psi_{t}\right]d{\mathbf{x}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[\left(-i{\overline{\psi}}_{t}\right)\nabla\psi+i\psi_{t}\nabla{\overline{\psi}}\;\right]d{\mathbf{x}}

The proof is complete.

σα​(t)=δα​(t),where​δα​(t)=∫ℝdα2​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle\sigma_{\alpha}(t)=\sqrt{\delta_{\alpha}(t)},\quad\mbox{where}\;\;\delta_{\alpha}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\alpha^{2}|\psi({\mathbf{x}},t)|^{2}d{\mathbf{x}}, (2.55)

Suppose ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi({\mathbf{x}},t) is the solution of (2.1) in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) with initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,0)=ψ0​(𝐱)\psi(\mathbf{x},0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}), then we have

Remark 2.5.

When V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is the harmonic potential (1.40), Eq. (2.66) can be rewritten as

where AA is a d×dd\times d diagonal matrix as A=(γx2)A=(\gamma_{x}^{2}) when d=1d=1, A=diag⁡(γx2,γy2)A={\rm diag}(\gamma_{x}^{2},\gamma_{y}^{2}) when d=2d=2 and A=diag⁡(γx2,γy2,γz2)A={\rm diag}(\gamma_{x}^{2},\gamma_{y}^{2},\gamma_{z}^{2}) when d=3d=3. For the harmonic potential (1.40), Remark 2.5 provides a way to construct the exact solution of the GPE (2.1) with a stationary state as initial data. Let ϕe​(𝐱)\phi_{e}(\mathbf{x}) be a stationary state of the GPE (2.1) with a chemical potential μe\mu_{e} [43, 46], i.e. (μe,ϕe)(\mu_{e},\phi_{e}) satisfying
