2.2.3. Finite time blow-up and damping

According to Theorem 2.8, there is a maximal time TmaxT_{\rm max} for the existence of the solution in energy space. If Tmax<∞T_{\rm max}<\infty, there exists finite time blow up.

Theorem 2.9.

(Finite time blow-up) In 2D and 3D, assume V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) satisfies (2.48) and d​V​(𝐱)+𝐱⋅∇V​(𝐱)≥0d\,V(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (d=2,3d=2,3). When β<0\beta<0, for any initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱)∈X\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\in X with finite variance ∫ℝd|𝐱|2​|ψ0|2​𝑑𝐱<∞\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\mathbf{x}|^{2}|\psi_{0}|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}<\infty to the Cauchy problem of (2.1), there exists finite time blow-up, i.e., Tmax<∞T_{\rm max}<\infty, if one of the following holds:

(i) E⁡(ψ0)<0E(\psi_{0})<0;

(ii) E⁡(ψ0)=0E(\psi_{0})=0 and Im⁡(∫ℝdψ¯0​(𝐱)​(𝐱⋅∇ψ0​(𝐱))​𝑑𝐱)<0{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\overline{\psi}}_{0}(\mathbf{x})\ (\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}))\,d\mathbf{x}\right)<0;

(iii) E⁡(ψ0)>0E(\psi_{0})>0 and Im⁡(∫ℝdψ¯0​(𝐱)​(𝐱⋅∇ψ0​(𝐱))​𝑑𝐱)<−d​E​(ψ0)​‖𝐱​ψ0‖L2{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\overline{\psi}}_{0}(\mathbf{x})\ (\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}))\,d\mathbf{x}\right)<-\sqrt{d\;E(\psi_{0})}\|\mathbf{x}\psi_{0}\|_{L^{2}}.

Proof.

Define the variance

δV(t)=∫ℝd|𝐱|2|ψ(𝐱,t)|2d𝐱.\displaystyle\delta_{{}_{V}}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\mathbf{x}|^{2}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}. (2.76)

Lemma 2.6 indicates that δV′(t)=2Im(∫ℝdψ¯(𝐱,t)(𝐱⋅∇ψ(𝐱,t))d𝐱)\delta^{\prime}_{{}_{V}}(t)=2\,{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}{\overline{\psi}}(\mathbf{x},t)(\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x},t))\,d\mathbf{x}\right) and

δ¨V(t)=\displaystyle\ddot{\delta}_{{}_{V}}(t)= 2​d​∫ℝd(1d​|∇ψ|2+β2​|ψ|4−1d​|ψ|2​𝐱⋅∇V​(𝐱))​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle 2d\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\frac{1}{d}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi|^{4}-\frac{1}{d}|\psi|^{2}\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla V(\mathbf{x})\right)\,d\mathbf{x}
=\displaystyle= 2​𝑑E​(ψ)−(d−2)​∫ℝd|∇ψ|2​𝑑𝐱−2​∫ℝd|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​(d​V​(𝐱)+𝐱⋅V⁡(𝐱))​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle 2d\,E(\psi)-(d-2)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\nabla\psi|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}-2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}(d\,V(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{x}\cdot V(\mathbf{x}))\,d\mathbf{x}
≤\displaystyle\leq 2dE(ψ)=2dE(ψ0),d=2,3.\displaystyle 2d\,E(\psi)=2d\,E(\psi_{0}),\qquad d=2,3.

Thus,

δV(t)≤dE(ψ0)t2+δV′(0)t+δV(0).\displaystyle\delta_{{}_{V}}(t)\leq d\,E(\psi_{0})t^{2}+\delta^{\prime}_{{}_{V}}(0)t+\delta_{{}_{V}}(0). (2.77)

When one of the conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) holds, there exists a finite time t∗>0t^{*}>0 such that δV(t∗)≤0\delta_{{}_{V}}(t^{*})\leq 0, which means that there is a singularity at or before t=t∗t=t^{*}.

Theorem 2.9 shows that the solution of the GPE (2.1) may blow up for negative β\beta (attractive interaction) in 2D and 3D. However, the physical quantities modeled by ψ\psi do not become infinite which implies that the validity of (2.1) breaks down near the singularity. Additional physical mechanisms, which were initially small, become important near the singular point and prevent the formation of the singularity. In BEC, the particle density |ψ|2|\psi|^{2} becomes large close to the critical point and inelastic collisions between particles which are negligible for small densities become important. Therefore a small damping (absorption) term is introduced into the NLSE (2.1) which describes inelastic processes. We are interested in the cases where these damping mechanisms are important and, therefore, restrict ourselves to the case of focusing nonlinearity, i.e. β<0\beta<0, where β\beta may also be time dependent. We consider the following damped nonlinear Schrödinger equation:

i​∂tψ=−12​∇2ψ+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​σ​ψ−i​f​(|ψ|2)​ψ,t>0,𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle i\;\partial_{t}\psi=-\frac{1}{2}\;\nabla^{2}\psi+V(\mathbf{x})\;\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2\sigma}\psi-i\;f(|\psi|^{2})\psi,\quad t>0,\;\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\qquad (2.78)
ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, (2.79)

where f⁡(ρ)≥0f(\rho)\geq 0 for ρ=|ψ|2≥0\rho=|\psi|^{2}\geq 0 is a real-valued monotonically increasing function.

The general form of (2.78) covers many damped NLSE arising in various different applications. In BEC, for example, when f⁡(ρ)≡0f(\rho)\equiv 0, (2.78) reduces to the usual GPE (2.1); a linear damping term f⁡(ρ)≡δf(\rho)\equiv\delta with δ>0\delta>0 describes inelastic collisions with the background gas; cubic damping f⁡(ρ)=δ1​|β|​ρf(\rho)=\delta_{1}|\beta|\rho with δ1>0\delta_{1}>0 corresponds to two-body loss [159, 152]; and a quintic damping term of the form f⁡(ρ)=δ2​β2​ρ2f(\rho)=\delta_{2}\beta^{2}\rho^{2} with δ2>0\delta_{2}>0 adds three-body loss to the GPE (2.1) [159, 152]. It is easy to see that the decay of the normalization according to (2.78) due to damping is given by

N˙(t)=dd​t∫ℝd|ψ(𝐱,t)|2d𝐱=−2∫ℝdf(|ψ(𝐱,t)|2)|ψ(𝐱,t)|2d𝐱≤0,t>0.\displaystyle\dot{N}(t)=\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;|\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2}\;d{\bf x}=-2\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;f(|\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2})|\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2}\;d{\bf x}\leq 0,\quad t>0. (2.80)

Particularly, if f⁡(ρ)≡δf(\rho)\equiv\delta with δ>0\delta>0, the normalization is given by

N⁡(t)=∫ℝd|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=e−2​δ​t​N​(0)=e−2​δ​t​∫ℝd|ψ0​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱,t≥0.\displaystyle N(t)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;|\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2}\;d{\bf x}=e^{-2\delta\;t}N(0)=e^{-2\delta\;t}\;\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;|\psi_{0}({\bf x})|^{2}\;d{\bf x},\quad t\geq 0. (2.81)

For more discussions, we refer to [30].

2.3. Convergence of dimension reduction

In an experimental setup with harmonic potential (1.40), the trapping frequencies in different directions can be very different. Especially, disk-shaped and cigar-shaped condensate were observed in experiments. In section 1.3.3, the 3D GPE is formally reduced to 2D GPE in disk-shaped condensate and to 1D GPE in cigar-shaped condensate. Mathematical and numerical justification for the dimension reduction of 3D GPE is only available in the weakly interaction regime, i.e. β=o⁡(1)\beta=o(1) [38, 53, 52]. Unfortunately, in the intermediate (β=O⁡(1)\beta=O(1)) or strong repulsive interaction regime (β≫1\beta\gg 1), no mathematical results are available and numerical studies can be found in [29].

For weak interaction regime, the dimension reduction is verified by energy type method with projection discussed in section 1.3.3 [38, 53]. Later, Ben Abdallah et al. developed an averaging technique and proved the more general forms of the lower dimensional GPE [52] without using the projection method. A more refined model in lower dimensions is developed in [51]. Here, we introduce this general approach. We refer to [52] and references therein for more discussions.

Consider the 3D GPE for (𝐱,𝐳)∈ℝd×ℝn(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} with d+n=3d+n=3 (d=1d=1 or d=2d=2)

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,𝐳,t)=[−12​(Δ𝐱+Δ𝐳)+Vε​(𝐱,𝐳)+β​|ψ|2]​ψ​(𝐱,𝐳,t),ψ(𝐱,𝐳,0)=Ψinit(𝐱,𝐳),Vε(𝐱,𝐳)=|𝐱|22+|𝐳|22​ε2,𝐱∈ℝd,𝐳∈ℝn,\begin{split}&i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\Delta_{\mathbf{z}}\right)+V^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})+\beta|\psi|^{2}\right]\psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t),\\ &\psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},0)=\Psi^{\rm init}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}),\quad V^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})=\frac{|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}{2}+\frac{|\mathbf{z}|^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}},\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\ \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\end{split} (2.82)

where Δ𝐱\Delta_{\mathbf{x}} and Δ𝐳\Delta_{\mathbf{z}} are the Laplace operators in 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and 𝐳∈ℝn\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, respectively. The wave function is normalized as ‖Ψinit‖L2​(ℝ3)2=1\|\Psi^{\rm init}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}^{2}=1. Compared with the situation in section 1.3.3 (1.39), we have 0<ε=1/γz≪10<\varepsilon=1/\gamma_{z}\ll 1 (d=2d=2) with γy=1\gamma_{y}=1 in disk-shaped BEC (2D) and 0<ε=1/γ≪10<\varepsilon=1/\gamma\ll 1 (d=1d=1) with γy=γz=γ\gamma_{y}=\gamma_{z}=\gamma in cigar-shaped BEC (1D). Our purpose is to describe the limiting dynamics of (2.82) for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1.

First, we introduce the rescaling 𝐳→ε1/2​𝐳\mathbf{z}\to\varepsilon^{1/2}\mathbf{z} and rescale ψ→e−itn/2εε−n/4ψε(𝐱,𝐳,t)\psi\to e^{-itn/2\varepsilon}\varepsilon^{-n/4}\psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t) to keep the normalization. Then Eq. (2.82) becomes

i​∂tψε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)=𝐇𝐱​ψε+1ε​𝐇𝐳​ψε+βεn/2​|ψε|2​ψε,(𝐱,𝐳)∈ℝd×ℝn,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\psi^{\varepsilon}+{1\over\varepsilon}\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}\psi^{\varepsilon}+\frac{\beta}{\varepsilon^{n/2}}|\psi^{\varepsilon}|^{2}\psi^{\varepsilon},\quad(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}, (2.83)

with initial data

ψε​(t=0)=Ψinit∈L2​(ℝd×ℝn),\displaystyle\psi^{\varepsilon}(t=0)=\Psi^{\rm init}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}), (2.84)

where

𝐇𝐱=12​(−Δ𝐱+|𝐱|2),𝐇𝐳=12​(−Δ𝐳+|𝐳|2−n),βεn/2:=δ∈ℝ.\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(-\Delta_{\mathbf{x}}+|\mathbf{x}|^{2}\right),\quad\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(-\Delta_{\mathbf{z}}+|\mathbf{z}|^{2}-n\right),\quad\frac{\beta}{\varepsilon^{n/2}}:=\delta\in\mathbb{R}. (2.85)

Here β=δ​εn/2\beta=\delta\varepsilon^{n/2} with a constant δ∈ℝ\delta\in\mathbb{R} means that we are working in the weak interaction regime, i.e., β=O⁡(ε1/2)\beta=O(\varepsilon^{1/2}) in 2D disk-shaped BEC and β=O⁡(ε)\beta=O(\varepsilon) in 1D cigar-shaped BEC. Notice that the singularly perturbed Hamiltonian 𝐇𝐳\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}} is a harmonic oscillator (conveniently shifted here such that it admits integer eigenvalues).

By introducing the filtered unknown

Ψε=ei​t​𝐇𝐳/ε​ψε,\displaystyle\Psi^{\varepsilon}=e^{it\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}/\varepsilon}\,\psi^{\varepsilon}, (2.86)

we get the equation

i​∂tΨε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)=𝐇𝐱​Ψε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)+F⁡(tε,Ψε),Ψε​(t=0)=Ψinit,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\Psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\Psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)+F\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon},\Psi^{\varepsilon}\right),\qquad\Psi^{\varepsilon}(t=0)=\Psi^{\rm init}, (2.87)

where FF is equal to

F⁡(s,Ψ)=δ​ei​s​𝐇𝐳​(|e−i​s​𝐇𝐳​Ψ|2​e−i​s​𝐇𝐳​Ψ).\displaystyle F(s,\Psi)=\delta\,e^{is\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}}\left(\left|e^{-is\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}}\Psi\right|^{2}e^{-is\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}}\,\Psi\right). (2.88)

When ε\varepsilon is small, (2.83) (or, equivalently, (2.87)) couples the high oscillations in time generated by the strong confinement operator with a nonlinear dynamics in the 𝐱\mathbf{x} plane, which is the only phenomenon that we want to describe.

In [52], Ben Abdallah et al. have developed an averaging technique and proved that, for general confining potentials in the zz direction, the limiting model as ε\varepsilon goes to zero is

i​∂tΨ=𝐇𝐱​Ψ+Fav​(Ψ),Ψ⁡(t=0)=Ψinit,i\partial_{t}\Psi=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\Psi+F_{\rm av}\left(\Psi\right),\qquad\Psi(t=0)=\Psi^{\rm init}, (2.89)

where the long time average of FF is defined by

Fav​(Ψ)=limT→+∞1T​∫0TF⁡(s,Ψ)​𝑑s.\displaystyle F_{\rm av}(\Psi)=\lim_{T\to+\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}F(s,\Psi)\,ds. (2.90)

For general confining operator 𝐇𝐳\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}, the convergence is proved using the fact that F⁡(s,Ψ)F(s,\Psi) is almost periodic [52], but the convergence rates are generally unclear. In the specific case of a harmonic confinement operator, like here, this convergence result can be quantified. The important point is that 𝐇𝐳\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}} admits only integer eigenvalues and the function FF is 2​π2\pi-periodic with respect to the ss variable. Therefore, the expression of Fa​vF_{av} is not a limit but a simple integral, and we have in fact

Fav​(Ψ)=12​π​∫02​πF⁡(s,Ψ)​𝑑s.\displaystyle F_{\rm av}(\Psi)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}F(s,\Psi)\,ds. (2.91)

On top of that, one can characterize the rate of convergence and prove that Ψ\Psi is a first order approximation of Ψε\Psi^{\varepsilon} in ε\varepsilon.

Rigourously, in order to state the convergence, we introduce the convenient scale of functional spaces. For all ℓ∈ℝ+\ell\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, we set

ℬℓ:={ψ∈Hℓ​(ℝ3)|(|𝐱|2+|𝐳|2)ℓ/2​ψ∈L2​(ℝ3)}{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}:=\left\{\psi\in H^{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\bigg|(|\mathbf{x}|^{2}+|\mathbf{z}|^{2})^{\ell/2}\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\right\}

endowed with one of the two following equivalent norms:

‖u‖ℬℓ2:=‖u‖L2​(ℝ3)2+‖𝐇𝐱ℓ/2​u‖L2​(ℝ3)2+‖𝐇𝐳ℓ/2​u‖L2​(ℝ3)2\displaystyle\|u\|_{{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}}^{2}:=\|u\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}^{2}+\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}^{\ell/2}u\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}+\|\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}^{\ell/2}u\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})} (2.92)

or

‖u‖ℬℓ2:=‖u‖Hℓ​(ℝ3)2+‖(|𝐱|2+|𝐳|2)ℓ/2​u‖L2​(ℝ3)2.\displaystyle\|u\|_{{\mathcal{B}}_{\ell}}^{2}:=\|u\|_{H^{\ell}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}^{2}+\|(|\mathbf{x}|^{2}+|\mathbf{z}|^{2})^{\ell/2}u\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}. (2.93)

For the equivalence, see e.g. Theorem 2.1 in [52].

We have the convergence as the following.

Theorem 2.10.

For some real number m>3/2m>3/2, assume that the initial datum Ψinit\Psi^{\rm init} belongs to ℬm+4{\mathcal{B}}_{m+4}. Let Ψε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)=ei​t​𝐇𝐳/ε​ψε\Psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=e^{it\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}/\varepsilon}\psi^{\varepsilon} be the solution of the filtered equation

i​∂tΨε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)=𝐇𝐱​Ψε​(t,x,z)+F⁡(tε,Ψε),Ψε​(t=0)=Ψinit,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\Psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\Psi^{\varepsilon}(t,x,z)+F\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon},\Psi^{\varepsilon}\right),\quad\Psi^{\varepsilon}(t=0)=\Psi^{\rm init}, (2.94)

where

F⁡(s,Ψ)=δ​ei​s​𝐇𝐳​|e−i​s​𝐇z​Ψ|2​e−i​s​𝐇𝐳​Ψ.\displaystyle F(s,\Psi)=\delta\,e^{is\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}}\,\left|e^{-is\mathbf{H}_{z}}\Psi\right|^{2}e^{-is\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}}\,\Psi\,. (2.95)

Define also Ψ~\widetilde{\Psi} as the solution of the averaged problem

i​∂tΨ~=𝐇𝐱​Ψ~+Fa​v​(Ψ~),Ψ~​(t=0)=Ψinit,i\partial_{t}\widetilde{\Psi}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}\widetilde{\Psi}+F_{av}\left(\widetilde{\Psi}\right),\qquad\widetilde{\Psi}(t=0)=\Psi^{\rm init}, (2.96)

where Fa​vF_{av} is defined by (2.91). Then, we have the following conclusions.

  1. (i)

    There exists T0>0T_{0}>0, depending only on ‖Ψinit‖ℬm+4\|\Psi^{\rm init}\|_{{\mathcal{B}}_{m+4}}, such that Ψε\Psi^{\varepsilon} and Ψ~\widetilde{\Psi} are uniquely defined and are uniformly bounded in the space C⁡([0,T0],ℬm+4)C([0,T_{0}];{\mathcal{B}}_{m+4}), independently of ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1].

  2. (ii)

    The function Ψ~\widetilde{\Psi} is a first order approximation of the solution Ψε\Psi^{\varepsilon} in C⁡([0,T0],ℬm)C([0,T_{0}];{\mathcal{B}}_{m}), i.e., for some C>0C>0, we have

    ‖Ψε​(t)−Ψ~​(t)‖ℬm≤C​ε,∀t∈[0,T0].\displaystyle\|\Psi^{\varepsilon}(t)-\widetilde{\Psi}(t)\|_{{\mathcal{B}}_{m}}\leq C\varepsilon,\quad\,\forall t\in[0,T_{0}]. (2.97)

The readers are referred to [52, 51] for a detailed proof of Theorem 2.10.

Remark 2.6.

The key property here is the periodicity of F⁡(s,Ψ)F(s,\Psi), and the result can be generalized to other dimensions ℝp=ℝd×ℝp−d\mathbb{R}^{p}=\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{p-d}, more general nonlinearities f⁡(|ψ|2)​ψf(|\psi|^{2})\psi in (2.83) and other operators 𝐇𝐳\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}} such that F⁡(s,Ψ)F(s,\Psi) defined by (2.88) is periodic.

Theorem 2.10 implies results of lower dimensional GPE (1.39). Let us take disk-shaped BEC as an example, i.e., n=1n=1 and d=2d=2. Thus, the eigenvalues of 𝐇𝐳\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}} are the nonnegative integers. Let χp​(𝐳)\chi_{p}(\mathbf{z}) be the normalized eigenfunction associated to the eigenvalue p∈ℕ0p\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:

𝐇𝐳​χp=p​χp,∫χp2​𝑑𝐳=1.\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{z}}\chi_{p}=p\chi_{p}\,,\qquad\int\chi_{p}^{2}\,d\mathbf{z}=1. (2.98)

In particular,

χ0(𝐳)=e−𝐳2/2/π1/4,𝐳∈ℝ.\displaystyle\chi_{0}(\mathbf{z})=e^{-\mathbf{z}^{2}/2}/\pi^{1/4},\quad\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}. (2.99)

Consider a function Ψ∈ℬm\Psi\in{\mathcal{B}}_{m} expanded on this basis as

Ψ⁡(𝐱,z)=∑p=0+∞φp​(𝐱)​χp​(𝐳).\displaystyle\Psi(\mathbf{x},z)=\sum_{p=0}^{+\infty}{\varphi}_{p}(\mathbf{x})\chi_{p}(\mathbf{z})\,. (2.100)

Then we have

F⁡(s,Ψ)=δ​∑p1,p2,p3,p4ap1​p2​p3​p4​ei​s​Ωp1​p2​p3​p4​φp2​(𝐱)​φp3​(𝐱)​φp4¯​(𝐱)​χp1​(𝐳),\displaystyle F(s,\Psi)=\delta\sum_{p_{1},p_{2},p_{3},p_{4}}a_{\mbox{\tiny$p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}$}}\,e^{is\Omega_{\mbox{\tiny$p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}$}}}\,{\varphi}_{p_{2}}(\mathbf{x}){\varphi}_{p_{3}}(\mathbf{x})\overline{{\varphi}_{p_{4}}}(\mathbf{x})\,\chi_{p_{1}}(\mathbf{z}), (2.101)

where we define the coefficients

Ωp​q​r​s=p+s−q−r,ap​q​r​s=⟨χp​χq​χr​χs⟩.\Omega_{pqrs}=p+s-q-r,\,\quad a_{pqrs}=\langle\chi_{p}\chi_{q}\chi_{r}\chi_{s}\rangle.

Here and in the sequel, ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle denotes the integration over the 𝐳\mathbf{z} variable. We write the expansion (2.101) shortly as

F⁡(s,Ψ)=δ​∑p1,p2,p3,p4a1234​ei​s​Ω1234​φp2​φp3​φp4¯⊗χp1.\displaystyle F(s,\Psi)=\delta\sum_{p_{1},p_{2},p_{3},p_{4}}a_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}\,e^{is\Omega_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}}\,{\varphi}_{p_{2}}{\varphi}_{p_{3}}\overline{{\varphi}_{p_{4}}}\otimes\chi_{p_{1}}\,. (2.102)

In the above sums, and in the sequel, a1234a_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}} and Ω1234\Omega_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}} stand for ap1​p2​p3​p4a_{p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}} and Ωp1​p2​p3​p4\Omega_{p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}}, respectively.

The expansion of FavF_{\rm av} (2.91) is obtained by averaging F⁡(s,Ψ)F(s,\Psi) over time ss. Noticing that the average of ei​s​Ω1234e^{is\Omega_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}} vanishes if Ω1234≠0\Omega_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}\neq 0, let us define the following index set, whose information is preserved after averaging F⁡(s,Ψ)F(s,\Psi) given by (2.102), for any p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N},

Λ(p)={(q,r,s),suchthatp+s=q+r}.\displaystyle\Lambda(p)=\{(q,r,s),\,\,\mathrm{such\,\,that}\,\,p+s=q+r\}. (2.103)

Then we have

Fav​(Φ)=δ​∑p1=0∞∑(p2,p3,p4)∈Λ⁡(p1)a1234​φp2​φp3​φp4¯⊗χp1.F_{\rm av}(\Phi)=\delta\sum_{p_{1}=0}^{\infty}\,\,\sum_{\scriptsize(p_{2},p_{3},p_{4})\in\Lambda(p_{1})}a_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}\,{\varphi}_{p_{2}}{\varphi}_{p_{3}}\overline{{\varphi}_{p_{4}}}\otimes\chi_{p_{1}}. (2.104)

The solution of (2.94) is written as Ψε​(𝐱,𝐳,t)=∑p=0∞φpε​(𝐱,t)​χp​(𝐳)\Psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\sum\limits_{p=0}^{\infty}{\varphi}^{\varepsilon}_{p}(\mathbf{x},t)\chi_{p}(\mathbf{z}) and the solution of (2.96) is written as Ψ⁡(𝐱,𝐳,t)=∑p=0∞φp​(𝐱,t)​χp​(𝐳)\Psi(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z},t)=\sum\limits_{p=0}^{\infty}{\varphi}_{p}(\mathbf{x},t)\chi_{p}(\mathbf{z}). If the initial data is polarized on the ground mode of the confinement Hamiltonian, i.e., we have

∀p∈ℕ∖{0},φpε(t=0)=0andφ0ε(t=0)=φinit.\forall p\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\},\qquad{\varphi}^{\varepsilon}_{p}(t=0)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad{\varphi}^{\varepsilon}_{0}(t=0)={\varphi}^{\rm init}.

In this case, the averaged system (2.96) reads

i​∂tφp1=𝐇𝐱​φp1+δ​∑(p2,p3,p4)∈Λ⁡(p1)a1234​φp2​φp3​φp4¯,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}{\varphi}_{p_{1}}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}{\varphi}_{p_{1}}+\delta\sum_{\scriptsize(p_{2},p_{3},p_{4})\in\Lambda(p_{1})}a_{\mbox{\tiny 1234}}\,{\varphi}_{p_{2}}{\varphi}_{p_{3}}\overline{{\varphi}_{p_{4}}},
φp1​(t=0)=δ0​p1​φinit,\displaystyle{\varphi}_{p_{1}}(t=0)=\delta_{0p_{1}}\,{\varphi}^{\rm init},

where δ0​p1\delta_{0p_{1}} is the Kronecker delta. It is readily seen from this expression that φp​(t)=0{\varphi}_{p}(t)=0 for all tt as soon as p≠0p\neq 0. Hence the averaged system (2.96) reduces to the single equation for φ0{\varphi}_{0} as

i​∂tφ0=𝐇𝐱​φ0+δ​a0000​|φ0|2​φ0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}{\varphi}_{0}=\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}}{\varphi}_{0}+\delta a_{0000}|{\varphi}_{0}|^{2}{\varphi}_{0}, (2.105)

where a0000=12​πa_{0000}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. This is exactly the 2D GPE (1.39) with the choice (1.43) (notice that we adopt a rescaling here).

Similarly, for a cigar-shaped BEC, i.e. n=2n=2, when initial data is polarized on the ground mode of the confinement Hamiltonian, we recover the 1D GPE (1.39).

This averaging technique has solved the dimension reduction of 3D GPE in the weak interaction regime β=o⁡(1)\beta=o(1) (2.82). However, there seems no progress for the intermediate interaction regime β=O⁡(1)\beta=O(1) (2.82) yet.

3. Numerical methods for computing ground states

In this section, we review different numerical methods for computing the ground states of BEC (2.11). Due to the presence of the confining potential, the ground state decays exponentially fast when |𝐱|→∞|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty and thus it is natural to truncate the whole space problem (2.1) to a bounded domain U⊂ℝdU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Thus, we consider the GPE (2.1) in UU as

i​ψt=−12​∇2ψ+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​ψ,t>0,𝐱∈U⊂ℝd,\displaystyle i\;\psi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\;\nabla^{2}\psi+V(\mathbf{x})\;\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi,\qquad t>0,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, (3.1)
ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=0,𝐱∈Γ=∂U,t≥0.\displaystyle\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=0,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma=\partial U,\quad t\geq 0. (3.2)

The normalization (2.2) and energy (2.3) then become

N⁡(ψ)=‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖22:=∫U|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=1,t≥0,N(\psi)=\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{U}\;|\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2}\;d{\bf x}=1,\qquad t\geq 0, (3.3)

and

E⁡(ψ)=∫U[12​|∇ψ​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2+β2​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|4]​𝑑𝐱,t≥0.E(\psi)=\int_{U}\;\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi({\bf x},t)|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{4}\right]\;d\mathbf{x},\quad t\geq 0. (3.4)

Replacing ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with UU, many results presented in section 2 can be directly generalized to bounded domain case. Similarly, finding the ground state ϕg\phi_{g} of (3.1), i.e. minimizing energy E⁡(ϕ)E(\phi) (3.4) under normalization constraint N⁡(ϕ)=1N(\phi)=1 (3.3), is equivalent to solving the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (2.8) with boundary condition (3.2). According to Theorem 2.1, ground state ϕg\phi_{g} can be chosen as nonnegative, and we will restrict ourselves in real-valued wave function ϕ\phi throughout this section.

3.1. Gradient flow with discrete normalization

One of the most popular techniques for dealing with the normalization constraint (3.3) is through the following construction: choose a time sequence 0=t0<t1<t2<⋯<tn<⋯0=t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{n}<\cdots with τn:=Δ​tn=tn+1−tn>0\tau_{n}:=\Delta t_{n}=t_{n+1}-t_{n}>0 and τ=maxn≥0⁡τn\tau=\max_{n\geq 0}\;\tau_{n}. To adapt an algorithm for the solution of the usual gradient flow to the minimization problem under a constraint, it is natural to consider the following gradient flow with discrete normalization (GFDN) which is widely used in physical literatures for computing the ground state solution of BEC [15, 27]:

ϕt=−12​δ​E​(ϕ)δ​ϕ=12​∇2ϕ−V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ−β​|ϕ|2​ϕ,𝐱∈U,tn<t<tn+1,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\delta E(\phi)}{\delta\phi}=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi-V(\mathbf{x})\phi-\beta\;|\phi|^{2}\phi,\ \mathbf{x}\in U,\ t_{n}<t<t_{n+1},\ n\geq 0,\quad (3.5)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1)=△ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1+)=ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1−)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖2,𝐱∈U,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\triangle}}{{=}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{+})=\frac{\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{-})}{\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad n\geq 0, (3.6)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)=0,𝐱∈Γ,ϕ⁡(𝐱,0)=ϕ0​(𝐱),𝐱∈U,\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t)=0,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma,\qquad\quad\phi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U, (3.7)

where ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn±)=limt→tn±ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n}^{\pm})=\lim_{t\to t_{n}^{\pm}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t) and ‖ϕ0‖2=1\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}=1. In fact, the gradient flow (3.5) can be viewed as applying the steepest decent method to the energy functional E⁡(ϕ)E(\phi) without constraint and (3.6) then projecting the solution back to the unit sphere in order to satisfy the constraint (3.3). From the numerical point of view, the gradient flow (3.5) can be solved via traditional techniques and the normalization of the gradient flow is simply achieved by a projection at the end of each time step. In fact, Eq. (3.5) can be obtained from the GPE (3.1) by t→i​tt\to it. Thus GFDN is also known as the imaginary time method in physics literatures.

The GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) possesses the following properties [27].

Lemma 3.1.

Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for all 𝐱∈U\mathbf{x}\in U, β≥0\beta\geq 0 and ‖ϕ0‖2=1\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}=1, then

(i) ‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖2≤‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn)‖2=1\|\phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}\leq\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{2}=1 for tn≤t≤tn+1t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}, n≥0n\geq 0.

(ii) For any β≥0\beta\geq 0,

E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,t))≤E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,t′)),tn≤t′<t≤tn+1,n≥0.\displaystyle E(\phi(\cdot,t))\leq E(\phi(\cdot,t^{\prime})),\qquad t_{n}\leq t^{\prime}<t\leq t_{n+1},\qquad n\geq 0. (3.8)

(iii) For β=0\beta=0,

E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖2)≤E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,tn)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn)‖2),tn≤t≤tn+1,n≥0.\displaystyle E\left(\frac{\phi(\cdot,t)}{\|\phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}}\right)\leq E\left(\frac{\phi(\cdot,t_{n})}{\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n})\|_{2}}\right),\quad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1},\quad n\geq 0. (3.9)

The property (3.8) is often referred as the energy diminishing property of the gradient flow. It is interesting to note that (3.9) implies that the energy diminishing property is preserved even with the normalization of the solution of the gradient flow for β=0\beta=0, that is, for linear evolutionary equations.

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for all 𝐱∈U\mathbf{x}\in U and ‖ϕ0‖2=1\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}=1. For β=0\beta=0, the GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) is energy diminishing for any time step τ\tau and initial data ϕ0\phi_{0}, i.e.

E(ϕ(⋅,tn+1))≤E(ϕ(⋅,tn))≤⋯≤E(ϕ(⋅,0))=E(ϕ0),n=0,1,2,⋯.\displaystyle E(\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}))\leq E(\phi(\cdot,t_{n}))\leq\cdots\leq E(\phi(\cdot,0))=E(\phi_{0}),\;\;n=0,1,2,\cdots. (3.10)

For β>0\beta>0, the GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) does not preserve the diminishing property for the normalization of the solution (3.9) in general.

In fact, the normalized step (3.6) is equivalent to solving the following ODE exactly

ϕt​(𝐱,t)=μϕ​(t,τ)​ϕ​(𝐱,t),𝐱∈U,tn<t<tn+1,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi_{t}(\mathbf{x},t)=\mu_{\phi}(t,\tau)\phi(\mathbf{x},t),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad t_{n}<t<t_{n+1},\quad n\geq 0, (3.11)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+)=ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1−),𝐱∈U;\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n}^{+})=\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{-}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U; (3.12)

where

μϕ​(t,τ)≡μϕ​(tn+1,τn)=−12​τn​ln⁡‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖22,tn≤t≤tn+1.\displaystyle\mu_{\phi}(t,\tau)\equiv\mu_{\phi}(t_{n+1},\tau_{n})=-\frac{1}{2\;\tau_{n}}\ln\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}^{2},\qquad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}. (3.13)

Thus the GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) can be viewed as a first-order splitting method for the gradient flow with discontinuous coefficients [27]:

ϕt=12​∇2ϕ−V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ−β​|ϕ|2​ϕ+μϕ​(t,τ)​ϕ,𝐱∈U,t>0,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi-V(\mathbf{x})\phi-\beta\;|\phi|^{2}\phi+\mu_{\phi}(t,\tau)\phi,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad t>0, (3.14)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)=0,𝐱∈Γ,ϕ⁡(𝐱,0)=ϕ0​(𝐱),𝐱∈U.\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t)=0,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma,\qquad\quad\phi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U. (3.15)

Let τ→0\tau\to 0, we see that

limτ→0+μϕ​(t,τ)=μϕ​(t)=1‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖22​∫U[12​|∇ϕ​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ2​(𝐱,t)+β​ϕ4​(𝐱,t)]​𝑑𝐱.\lim_{\tau\to 0^{+}}\mu_{\phi}(t,\tau)=\mu_{\phi}(t)=\frac{1}{\|\phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}}\int_{U}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})\phi^{2}(\mathbf{x},t)+\beta\phi^{4}(\mathbf{x},t)\right]d\mathbf{x}.

This suggests us to consider the following continuous normalized gradient flow (CNGF) [27]:

ϕt=12​∇2ϕ−V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ−β​|ϕ|2​ϕ+μϕ​(t)​ϕ,𝐱∈U,t≥0,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi-V(\mathbf{x})\phi-\beta\;|\phi|^{2}\phi+\mu_{\phi}(t)\phi,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad t\geq 0, (3.16)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)=0,𝐱∈Γ,ϕ⁡(𝐱,0)=ϕ0​(𝐱),𝐱∈U.\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t)=0,\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\Gamma,\qquad\quad\phi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U. (3.17)

In fact, the right hand side of (3.16) is the same as (2.10) if we view μϕ​(t)\mu_{\phi}(t) as a Lagrange multiplier for the constraint (3.3).

Furthermore, for the above CNGF, as observed in [5, 27, 91], the solution of (3.16) also satisfies the following theorem:

Theorem 3.2.

Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for all 𝐱∈U\mathbf{x}\in U, β≥0\beta\geq 0 and ‖ϕ0‖2=1\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}=1. Then the CNGF (3.16)-(3.17) is normalization conservative and energy diminishing, i.e.

‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖22=∫Uϕ2​(𝐱,t)​𝑑𝐱=‖ϕ0‖22=1,t≥0,\displaystyle\|\phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{U}\phi^{2}(\mathbf{x},t)\;d\mathbf{x}=\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}^{2}=1,\qquad t\geq 0, (3.18)
dd​t​E​(ϕ)=−2​‖ϕt​(⋅,t)‖22≤0,t≥0,\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}E(\phi)=-2\left\|\phi_{t}(\cdot,t)\right\|_{2}^{2}\leq 0\;,\qquad t\geq 0, (3.19)

which in turn implies

E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,t1))≥E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,t2)),0≤t1≤t2<∞.E(\phi(\cdot,t_{1}))\geq E(\phi(\cdot,t_{2})),\qquad 0\leq t_{1}\leq t_{2}<\infty.

3.2. Backward Euler finite difference discretization

In this section, we will present a backward Euler finite difference method to discretize the GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) (or a full discretization of the CNGF (3.16)-(3.17)). For simplicity of notation, we introduce the method for the case of one spatial dimension d=1d=1 with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Generalizations to higher dimension with a rectangle U=[a,b]×[c,d]⊂ℝ2U=[a,b]\times[c,d]\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and a box U=[a,b]×[c,d]×[e,f]⊂ℝ3U=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f]\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} are straightforward for tensor product grids and the results remain valid without modifications. For d=1d=1, we have [27]

ϕt=12​ϕx​x−V⁡(x)​ϕ−β​|ϕ|2​ϕ,x∈U=(a,b),tn<t<tn+1,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\phi_{xx}-V(x)\phi-\beta\;|\phi|^{2}\phi,\quad x\in U=(a,b),\ t_{n}<t<t_{n+1},\ n\geq 0,\qquad (3.20)
ϕ⁡(x,tn+1)=△ϕ⁡(x,tn+1+)=ϕ⁡(x,tn+1−)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖2,a≤x≤b,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi(x,t_{n+1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\triangle}}{{=}}\phi(x,t_{n+1}^{+})=\frac{\phi(x,t_{n+1}^{-})}{\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}},\qquad a\leq x\leq b,\quad n\geq 0, (3.21)
ϕ⁡(x,0)=ϕ0​(x),a≤x≤b,ϕ⁡(a,t)=ϕ⁡(b,t)=0,t≥0;\displaystyle\phi(x,0)=\phi_{0}(x),\quad a\leq x\leq b,\qquad\phi(a,t)=\phi(b,t)=0,\qquad t\geq 0; (3.22)

with ‖ϕ0‖22=∫abϕ02​(x)​𝑑x=1\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{a}^{b}\phi_{0}^{2}(x)\;dx=1.

We choose the spatial mesh size h=Δ​x>0h=\Delta x>0 with Δ​x=(b−a)/M\Delta x=(b-a)/M, choose the time step τ=Δ​t>0\tau=\Delta t>0 and define the index sets

𝒯M={j|j=1,2,…,M−1},𝒯M0={j|j=0,1,2,…,M}.{\mathcal{T}}_{M}=\{j\ |\ j=1,2,\ldots,M-1\},\qquad{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}=\{j\ |\ j=0,1,2,\ldots,M\}. (3.23)

We denote grid points and time steps by

xj:=a+jh,j∈𝒯M0;tn:=nτ,n=0,1,2,⋯.\displaystyle x_{j}:=a+j\;h,\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0};\qquad t_{n}:=n\;\tau,\qquad n=0,1,2,\cdots. (3.24)

Let ϕjn\phi^{n}_{j} be the numerical approximation of ϕ⁡(xj,tn)\phi(x_{j},t_{n}) and ϕn\phi^{n} the solution vector at time t=tn=n​τt=t_{n}=n\tau with components ϕjn\phi_{j}^{n}. Introduce the following finite difference operators:

δx+ϕnj=1h(ϕj+1n−ϕjn),δx−ϕjn=1h(ϕjn−ϕj−1n),δxϕjn=ϕj+1n−ϕj−1n2​h,δt+ϕjn=1τ(ϕjn+1−ϕjn),δt−ϕjn=1τ(ϕjn−ϕjn−1),δtϕjn=ϕjn+1−ϕjn−12​τ,δx2ϕjn=ϕj+1n−2​ϕjn+ϕj−1nh2,δt2ϕjn=ϕjn+1−2​ϕjn+ϕjn−1τ2.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\delta_{x}^{+}\phi^{n}_{j}=\frac{1}{h}(\phi_{j+1}^{n}-\phi_{j}^{n}),\quad\delta_{x}^{-}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{1}{h}(\phi_{j}^{n}-\phi_{j-1}^{n}),\quad\delta_{x}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{\phi_{j+1}^{n}-\phi_{j-1}^{n}}{2\,h},\\ &\delta_{t}^{+}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{1}{\tau}(\phi_{j}^{n+1}-\phi_{j}^{n}),\quad\delta_{t}^{-}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{1}{\tau}(\phi_{j}^{n}-\phi_{j}^{n-1}),\quad\delta_{t}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{\phi_{j}^{n+1}-\phi_{j}^{n-1}}{2\tau},\\ &\delta_{x}^{2}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{\phi_{j+1}^{n}-2\phi_{j}^{n}+\phi_{j-1}^{n}}{h^{2}},\quad\delta_{t}^{2}\phi_{j}^{n}=\frac{\phi_{j}^{n+1}-2\phi_{j}^{n}+\phi_{j}^{n-1}}{\tau^{2}}.\end{split} (3.25)

We denote

XM={v=(vj)j∈𝒯M0|v0=vM=0}⊂ℂM+1,\displaystyle X_{M}=\left\{v=\left(v_{j}\right)_{j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}}\ |\ v_{0}=v_{M}=0\right\}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{M+1}, (3.26)

and define the discrete lpl^{p}, semi-H1H^{1} and l∞l^{\infty} norms over XMX_{M} as

∥v∥pp=h∑j=0M−1|vj|p,∥δx+v∥22=h∑j=0M−1|δx+vj|2,∥v∥∞=supj∈𝒯M0|vj|,(u,v)=∑j=0M−1ujv¯j,⟨u,v⟩=∑j=1M−1ujv¯j,∀u,v∈XM.\begin{split}&\|v\|_{p}^{p}=h\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}|v_{j}|^{p},\qquad\|\delta_{x}^{+}v\|_{2}^{2}=h\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}\left|\delta_{x}^{+}v_{j}\right|^{2},\qquad\|v\|_{\infty}=\sup\limits_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{M}^{0}}|v_{j}|,\\ &\left(u,v\right)=\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}u_{j}{\overline{v}}_{j},\qquad\langle u,v\rangle=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M-1}u_{j}{\overline{v}}_{j},\quad\forall u,v\in X_{M}.\end{split} (3.27)

The Backward Euler finite difference (BEFD) method is to use backward Euler for time discretization and second-order centered finite difference for spatial derivatives. The detailed scheme is [27]:

ϕj(1)−ϕjnτ=12​δx2​ϕj(1)−V⁡(xj)​ϕj(1)−β​(ϕjn)2​ϕj(1),j∈𝒯M,\displaystyle\frac{\phi_{j}^{(1)}-\phi_{j}^{n}}{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}\phi^{(1)}_{j}-V(x_{j})\phi_{j}^{(1)}-\beta\left(\phi_{j}^{n}\right)^{2}\phi_{j}^{(1)},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}, (3.28)
ϕ0(1)=ϕM(1)=0,ϕj0=ϕ0(xj),ϕjn+1=ϕj(1)‖ϕ(1)‖2,j∈𝒯M0,n=0,1,⋯.\displaystyle\phi_{0}^{(1)}=\phi_{M}^{(1)}=0,\quad\phi_{j}^{0}=\phi_{0}(x_{j}),\quad\phi_{j}^{n+1}=\frac{\phi_{j}^{(1)}}{\|\phi^{(1)}\|_{2}},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\quad n=0,1,\cdots.

The above BEFD method is implicit and unconditionally stable. The discretized system can be solved by Thomas’ algorithm. The memory cost is O⁡(M)O(M) and computational cost per time step is O⁡(M)O(M). In higher dimensions (such as 2D or 3D), the associated discretized system can be solved by iterative methods, for example the Gauss-Seidel or conjugate gradient (CG) or multigrid (MG) iterative method [15, 27, 45]. With the approximation ϕn\phi^{n} of ϕ\phi by BEFD, the energy and chemical potential can be computed as

E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,tn))≈En=h​∑j=0M−1[12​|δx+​ϕjn|2+V⁡(xj)​|ϕjn|2+β2​|ϕjn|4],\displaystyle E(\phi(\cdot,t_{n}))\approx E^{n}=h\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left|\delta_{x}^{+}\phi_{j}^{n}\right|^{2}+V(x_{j})|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{4}\right],
μ⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,tn))≈μn=En+h​∑j=0M−1β2​|ϕjn|4,n≥0.\displaystyle\mu(\phi(\cdot,t_{n}))\approx\mu^{n}=E^{n}+h\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\frac{\beta}{2}|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{4},\qquad n\geq 0.

For β=0\beta=0, i.e., linear case, the BEFD discretization (3.28) is energy diminishing and monotone for any τ>0\tau>0 (see [27]).

3.3. Backward Euler pseudospectral method

Spectral method enjoys high accuracy for smooth problems such as the ground state problems in BEC. Thus, it is favorable to use spectral method in numerical computation of ground states. For simplicity, we shall introduce the method in 1D (3.20)-(3.22), i.e. d=1d=1. Generalization to d>1d>1 is straightforward for tensor product grids and the results remain valid without modifications. We adopt the same mesh strategy and notations as those in section 3.2.

For any function ψ​(x)∈L2​(U)\psi(x)\in L^{2}(U) (U=(a,b)U=(a,b)), ϕ​(x)∈C0​(U¯)\phi(x)\in C_{0}({\overline{U}}), and vector ϕ=(ϕ0,ϕ1,…,ϕM)T∈XM\phi=(\phi_{0},\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{M})^{T}\in X_{M} with MM an even positive integer, denote finite dimensional spaces

YM=span{Φl(x)=sin(μl(x−a)),μl=π​lb−a,x∈U,l∈𝒯M}.\displaystyle Y_{M}={\rm span}\left\{\Phi_{l}(x)=\sin\left(\mu_{l}(x-a)\right),\quad\mu_{l}=\frac{\pi l}{b-a},\quad x\in U,\,l\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}\right\}. (3.29)

Let PM:L2​(U)→YMP_{M}:L^{2}\left(U\right)\to Y_{M} be the standard L2L^{2} projection onto YMY_{M} and IM:C0​(U¯)→YMI_{M}:C_{0}(\overline{U})\to Y_{M} and IM:XM→YMI_{M}:X_{M}\to Y_{M} be the standard sine interpolation operator as

(PM​ψ)​(x)=∑l=1M−1ψ^l​sin⁡(μl​(x−a)),(IM​ϕ)​(x)=∑l=1M−1ϕ~l​sin⁡(μl​(x−a)),\displaystyle\left(P_{M}\psi\right)(x)=\sum\limits_{l=1}^{M-1}\hat{\psi}_{l}\sin\left(\mu_{l}(x-a)\right),\quad\left(I_{M}\phi\right)(x)=\sum\limits_{l=1}^{M-1}\tilde{\phi}_{l}\sin\left(\mu_{l}(x-a)\right), (3.30)

and the coefficients are given by

ψ^l=2b−a​∫abψ⁡(x)​sin⁡(μl​(x−a))​𝑑x,ϕ~l=2M​∑j=1M−1ϕj​sin⁡(j​l​πM),l∈𝒯M,\displaystyle\hat{\psi}_{l}=\frac{2}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b}\psi(x)\sin\left(\mu_{l}(x-a)\right)\,dx,\;\tilde{\phi}_{l}=\frac{2}{M}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{M-1}\phi_{j}\sin\left(\frac{jl\pi}{M}\right),\;l\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}, (3.31)

where ϕj=ϕ⁡(xj)\phi_{j}=\phi(x_{j}) when ϕ\phi is a function instead of a vector.

The backward Euler sine spectral discretization for (3.5)-(3.7) reads [25]:
Find ϕn+1​(x)∈YM\phi^{n+1}(x)\in Y_{M} (i.e. ϕ+​(x)∈YM\phi^{+}(x)\in Y_{M}) such that

ϕ+​(x)−ϕn​(x)τ=12​∇2ϕ+​(x)−PM​[(V⁡(x)+β​|ϕn​(x)|2)​ϕ+​(x)],x∈U,\displaystyle\frac{\phi^{+}(x)-\phi^{n}(x)}{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi^{+}(x)-P_{M}\left[\left(V(x)+\beta|\phi^{n}(x)|^{2}\right)\phi^{+}(x)\right],\quad x\in U, (3.32)
ϕn+1(x)=ϕ+​(x)‖ϕ+​(x)‖2,x∈U,n=0,1,⋯;ϕ0(x)=PM(ϕ0(x)).\displaystyle\phi^{n+1}(x)=\frac{\phi^{+}(x)}{\|\phi^{+}(x)\|_{2}},\quad x\in U,\quad n=0,1,\cdots;\quad\phi^{0}(x)=P_{M}\left(\phi_{0}(x)\right). (3.33)

The above discretization can be solved in phase space and it is not suitable in practice due to the difficulty of computing the integrals in (3.31). We now present an efficient implementation by choosing ϕ0​(x)\phi^{0}(x) as the interpolation of ϕ0​(x)\phi_{0}(x) on the grid points {xj,j∈𝒯M0}\{x_{j},\ j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}^{0}\}, i.e ϕ0​(xj)=ϕ0​(xj)\phi^{0}(x_{j})=\phi_{0}(x_{j}) for j∈𝒯M0j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}^{0}, and approximating the integrals in (3.31) by a quadrature rule on the grid points. Let ϕjn\phi_{j}^{n} be the approximations of ϕ⁡(xj,tn)\phi(x_{j},t_{n}), which is the solution of (3.5)-(3.7). Backward Euler sine pseudospectral (BESP) method for discretizing (3.5)-(3.7) reads [25]:

ϕj(1)−ϕjnτ=12​Dx​xs​ϕ(1)|x=xj−V⁡(xj)​ϕj(1)−β​|ϕjn|2​ϕj(1),j∈𝒯M,\displaystyle\frac{\phi_{j}^{(1)}-\phi_{j}^{n}}{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\left.D_{xx}^{s}\phi^{(1)}\right|_{x=x_{j}}-V(x_{j})\phi_{j}^{(1)}-\beta|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\phi_{j}^{(1)},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}, (3.34)
ϕ0(1)=ϕM(1)=0,ϕj0=ϕ0(xj),ϕjn+1=ϕj(1)‖ϕ(1)‖2,j∈𝒯M0,n=0,1,⋯.\displaystyle\phi_{0}^{(1)}=\phi_{M}^{(1)}=0,\;\phi_{j}^{0}=\phi_{0}(x_{j}),\;\phi_{j}^{n+1}=\frac{\phi_{j}^{(1)}}{\|\phi^{(1)}\|_{2}},\;j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\;n=0,1,\cdots. (3.35)

Here Dx​xsD_{xx}^{s}, a pseudospectral differential operator approximation of ∂x​x\partial_{xx}, is defined as

Dx​xsu|x=xj=−∑l=1M−1μl2u~lsin(μl(xj−a)).j∈𝒯M.\displaystyle\left.D_{xx}^{s}u\right|_{x=x_{j}}=-\sum_{l=1}^{M-1}\;\mu_{l}^{2}\tilde{u}_{l}\;\sin(\mu_{l}(x_{j}-a)).\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}. (3.36)

In the discretization (3.34), at every time step, a nonlinear system has to be solved. Here we present an efficient way to solve it iteratively by introducing a stabilization term with constant coefficient and using discrete sine transform (DST):

ϕj(1),m+1−ϕjnτ=12​Dx​xs​ϕ(1),m+1|x=xj−α​ϕj(1),m+1+(α−V⁡(xj)−β​|ϕjn|2)​ϕj(1),m,\frac{\phi_{j}^{(1),m+1}-\phi_{j}^{n}}{\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\left.D_{xx}^{s}\phi^{(1),m+1}\right|_{x=x_{j}}-\alpha\phi_{j}^{(1),m+1}+\left(\alpha-V(x_{j})-\beta|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\right)\phi_{j}^{(1),m}, (3.37)

where m≥0m\geq 0, ϕj(1),0=ϕjn\phi_{j}^{(1),0}=\phi_{j}^{n} and j∈𝒯M0j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}. Here α≥0\alpha\geq 0 is called as a stabilization parameter to be determined. Taking discrete sine transform at both sides of (3.37), we obtain

(ϕ(1),m+1~)l−(ϕn~)lτ=−(α+12​μl2)​(ϕ(1),m+1~)l+(Gm~)l,l∈𝒯M,\frac{(\widetilde{\phi^{(1),m+1}})_{l}-(\widetilde{\phi^{n}})_{l}}{\tau}=-\left(\alpha+\frac{1}{2}\mu_{l}^{2}\right)(\widetilde{\phi^{(1),m+1}})_{l}+(\widetilde{G^{m}})_{l},\qquad l\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}, (3.38)

where (Gm~)l(\widetilde{G^{m}})_{l} are the sine transform coefficients of the vector Gm=(G0m,⋯,GMm)TG^{m}=(G_{0}^{m},\cdots,G_{M}^{m})^{T} defined as

Gjm=(α−V⁡(xj)−β​|ϕjn|2)​ϕj(1),m,j∈𝒯M0.\displaystyle G_{j}^{m}=\left(\alpha-V(x_{j})-\beta|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\right)\phi_{j}^{(1),m},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}. (3.39)

Solving (3.38), we get

(ϕ(1),m+1~)l=22+τ⁡(2​α+μl2)​[(ϕn~)l+τ​(Gm~)l],l∈𝒯M.(\widetilde{\phi^{(1),m+1}})_{l}=\frac{2}{2+\tau(2\alpha+\mu_{l}^{2})}\left[(\widetilde{\phi^{n}})_{l}+\tau\;(\widetilde{G^{m}})_{l}\right],\qquad l\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}. (3.40)

Taking inverse discrete sine transform for (3.40), we get the solution for (3.37) immediately.

In order to make the iterative method (3.37) for solving (3.34) converges as fast as possible, the ‘optimal’ stabilization parameter α\alpha in (3.37) is suggested as [36]:

αopt=12​(bmax+bmin),\alpha_{\rm opt}=\frac{1}{2}\left(b_{\rm max}+b_{\rm min}\right), (3.41)

where

bmax=max1≤j≤M−1⁡(V⁡(xj)+β​|ϕjn|2),bmin=min1≤j≤M−1⁡(V⁡(xj)+β​|ϕjn|2).\displaystyle b_{\rm max}=\max_{1\leq j\leq M-1}\left(V(x_{j})+\beta|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\right),\qquad b_{\rm min}=\min_{1\leq j\leq M-1}\left(V(x_{j})+\beta|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\right). (3.42)

Similarly, with the approximation ϕn\phi^{n} of ϕ\phi by BESP, the energy and chemical potential can be computed as

E⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,tn))≈En=b−a4​∑l=1M−1μl2​|(ϕn)~l|2+h​∑j=0M−1[V⁡(xj)​|ϕjn|2+β2​|ϕjn|4],\displaystyle E(\phi(\cdot,t_{n}))\approx E^{n}=\frac{b-a}{4}\sum_{l=1}^{M-1}\mu_{l}^{2}|\widetilde{(\phi^{n})}_{l}|^{2}+h\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\left[V(x_{j})|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{4}\right],
μ⁡(ϕ⁡(⋅,tn))≈μn=En+h​∑j=0M−1β2​|ϕjn|4,n≥0.\displaystyle\mu(\phi(\cdot,t_{n}))\approx\mu^{n}=E^{n}+h\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\frac{\beta}{2}|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{4},\qquad n\geq 0.
Remark 3.1.

In practice, Fourier pseudospectral method or cosine pseudospectral method can also be applied to spatial discretization for discretizing (3.20)-(3.22) when the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition in (3.22) is replaced by periodic boundary condition or homogeneous Neumann boundary condition, respectively.

3.4. Simplified methods under symmetric potentials

The ground state ϕg\phi_{g} of (2.11) shares the same symmetric properties with V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3). In such cases, simplified numerical methods, especially with less memory requirement, for computing the ground states are available.

Radial symmetry in 1D, 2D and 3D. When the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is radially symmetric in d=1,2d=1,2 and spherically symmetric in d=3d=3, the problem is reduced to 1D. Due to the symmetry, the GPE (2.1) essentially collapses to a 1D problem with r=|𝐱|∈[0,+∞)r=|\mathbf{x}|\in[0,+\infty) for ψ:=ψ⁡(r,t)\psi:=\psi(r,t) (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3):

i​∂tψ⁡(r,t)=−12​rd−1​∂∂r​(rd−1​∂∂r​ψ)+(V⁡(r)+β​|ψ|2)​ψ,r∈(0,+∞),\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(r,t)=\frac{-1}{2r^{d-1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{d-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\psi\right)+\left(V(r)+\beta|\psi|^{2}\right)\psi,\;r\in(0,+\infty), (3.43)
∂ψ⁡(0,t)∂r=0,ψ(r,t)→0,asr→∞.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\psi(0,t)}{\partial r}=0,\qquad\qquad\psi(r,t)\to 0,\quad{\rm as}\quad r\to\infty. (3.44)

The normalization condition (2.2) becomes

Nr​(ψ)=ω⁡(d)​∫0∞|ψ⁡(r,t)|2​rd−1​𝑑r=1.\displaystyle N_{r}(\psi)=\omega(d)\int_{0}^{\infty}|\psi(r,t)|^{2}r^{d-1}\,dr=1. (3.45)

Here ω⁡(d)\omega(d) is the area of unit sphere in dd dimensions, where ω⁡(1)=2\omega(1)=2, ω⁡(2)=2​π\omega(2)=2\pi and ω⁡(3)=4​π\omega(3)=4\pi. The energy (2.3) can be rewritten for radial wave function as

Er​(ψ)=ω⁡(d)​∫0∞(12​|∂rψ⁡(r,t)|2+V⁡(r)​|ψ⁡(r,t)|2+β2​|ψ⁡(r,t)|4)​rd−1​𝑑r.\displaystyle E_{r}(\psi)=\omega(d)\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{2}|\partial_{r}\psi(r,t)|^{2}+V(r)|\psi(r,t)|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}|\psi(r,t)|^{4}\right)r^{d-1}\,dr. (3.46)

Then, the minimization problem (2.11) collapses to :

Find φg∈Sr{\varphi}_{g}\in S_{r} such that

Eg:=Er​(φg)=minφ∈Sr⁡Er​(φ),\displaystyle E_{g}:=E_{r}({\varphi}_{g})=\min_{{\varphi}\in S_{r}}E_{r}({\varphi}), (3.47)

where Sr={φ|ω(d)∫0∞|φ(r)|2rd−1dr=1,Er(φ)<∞}S_{r}=\{{\varphi}\ |\omega(d)\int_{0}^{\infty}|\varphi(r)|^{2}r^{d-1}\,dr=1,\ E_{r}({\varphi})<\infty\}.

The nonlinear eigenvalue problem (2.8) collapses to

μ​φ​(r)=−12​rd−1​dd​r​(rd−1​dd​r​φ​(r))+V⁡(r)​φ​(r)+β​|φ⁡(r)|2​φ​(r),r∈(0,+∞),\displaystyle\mu{\varphi}(r)=-\frac{1}{2r^{d-1}}\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}r}\left(r^{d-1}\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}r}{\varphi}(r)\right)+V(r){\varphi}(r)+\beta|{\varphi}(r)|^{2}{\varphi}(r),\;r\in(0,+\infty), (3.48)

with boundary conditions

φ′(0)=0,φ(r)→0,whenr→∞,\displaystyle\varphi^{\prime}(0)=0,\qquad{\varphi}(r)\to 0,\quad{\rm when}\quad r\to\infty, (3.49)

under the normalization constraint (3.45) with ψ=φ\psi=\varphi.

The eigenvalue problem (3.48)-(3.49) is defined in a semi-infinite interval (0,+∞)(0,+\infty). In practical computation, this is approximated by a problem defined on a finite interval. Since the full wave function vanishes exponentially fast as r→∞r\to\infty, choosing R>0R>0 sufficiently large, then the eigenvalue problem (3.48)-(3.49) can be approximated by

μ​φ​(r)=−12​rd−1​dd​r​(rd−1​dd​r​φ​(r))+[V⁡(r)+β​|φ|2]​φ​(r),0<r<R,\displaystyle\mu\;{\varphi}(r)=-\frac{1}{2r^{d-1}}\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}r}\left(r^{d-1}\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}r}{\varphi}(r)\right)+[V(r)+\beta|{\varphi}|^{2}]{\varphi}(r),\quad 0<r<R, (3.50)

with boundary conditions

φ′​(0)=0,φ⁡(R)=0,\displaystyle\varphi^{\prime}(0)=0,\qquad{\varphi}(R)=0, (3.51)

under the normalization

ω⁡(d)​∫0R|φ⁡(r)|2​rd−1​𝑑r=1.\displaystyle\omega(d)\int_{0}^{R}|\varphi(r)|^{2}r^{d-1}\,dr=1. (3.52)

To compute the ground state φg\varphi_{g}, a method based on GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) can be simplified. Here, we only present full discretization using a simplified BEFD method.

Choose time steps as (3.24), mesh size Δ​r=2​R/(2​M+1)\Delta r=2R/(2M+1) with positive integer MM and grid points as

rj=j​Δ​r,rj+12=(j+12)​Δ​r,j∈𝒯M0.\displaystyle r_{j}=j\Delta r,\quad r_{j+\frac{1}{2}}=\left(j+\frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta r,\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}. (3.53)

We adopt the same notation for finite difference operator as (3.25). Let φj+12n{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n} be the numerical approximation of φ⁡(rj+12,tn)\varphi(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}},t_{n}) and φn{\varphi}^{n} be the solution vector at time t=tnt=t_{n} with components φj+12n{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n}. Then a simplified BEFD method for computing the ground state of (3.47) by GFDN with an initial guess φ0​(r){\varphi}_{0}(r) is given as [27]

φj+12(1)−φj+12nτ=[12​δr,d2−V⁡(rj+12)−β​(φj+12n)2]​φj+12(1),j∈𝒯M∪{0},\displaystyle\frac{{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)}-{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n}}{\tau}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\delta_{r,d}^{2}-V(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}})-\beta\left({\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n}\right)^{2}\right]{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}\cup\{0\}, (3.54)
φ−12(1)=φ12(1),φM+12(1)=0,φj+120=φ0​(rj+12),j∈𝒯M0,\displaystyle{\varphi}_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)}={\varphi}_{\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)},\qquad{\varphi}_{M+\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)}=0,\quad{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{0}={\varphi}_{0}(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}}),\quad\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},
φj+12n+1=φj+12(1)‖φ(1)‖r,j∈𝒯M0,n=0,1,⋯,\displaystyle\quad{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n+1}=\frac{{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)}}{\|{\varphi}^{(1)}\|_{r}},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\quad n=0,1,\cdots, (3.55)

where

δr,d2​φj+12(1)=1(Δ​r)2​rj+12d−1​[rj+1d−1​φj+32(1)−(rj+1d−1+rjd−1)​φj+12(1)+rjd−1​φj−12(1)],\delta_{r,d}^{2}\;{\varphi}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(1)}=\frac{1}{(\Delta r)^{2}r_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{d-1}}\left[r_{j+1}^{d-1}{\varphi}^{(1)}_{j+\frac{3}{2}}-(r_{j+1}^{d-1}+r_{j}^{d-1}){\varphi}^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}+r_{j}^{d-1}{\varphi}^{(1)}_{j-\frac{1}{2}}\right],

and the norm is defined as

‖φ(1)‖r2=ω⁡(d)​Δ​r​∑j=0M−1|φj+12(1)|2​(rj+12)d−1.\displaystyle\|{\varphi}^{(1)}\|_{r}^{2}=\omega(d)\Delta r\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}|{\varphi}^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}|^{2}(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}})^{d-1}. (3.56)

Here, we have introduced a ghost point r−12r_{-\frac{1}{2}} so that the Neumann boundary condition φ′​(0)=0{\varphi}^{\prime}(0)=0 is approximated with second order accuracy. The linear system (3.54) can be solved very efficiently by the Thomas’ algorithm, where the computational cost is O⁡(M)O(M) per time step, for all dimensions d=1,2,3d=1,2,3. The memory cost is O⁡(M)O(M). This tremendously reduces memory and computation complexity in higher dimensions (d=2,3d=2,3) from O⁡(Md)O(M^{d}) to O⁡(M)O(M) compared with the proposed BEFD (3.28) with Cartesian coordinates.

Cylindrical symmetry in 3D. For 𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, when VV is cylindrically symmetric, i.e., VV is of the form V⁡(r,z)V(r,z) (r=x2+y2r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}), the problem is reduced to 2D. Due to the symmetry, the GPE (2.1) essentially collapses to a 2D problem with r∈(0,+∞)r\in(0,+\infty) and z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R} for ψ:=ψ⁡(r,z,t)\psi:=\psi(r,z,t) :

where

and Sc={φ|2π∫ℝ+∫ℝ|φ(r,z)|2rdzdr=1,Ec(φ)<∞}S_{c}=\{{\varphi}\ |2\pi\int_{\mathbb{R}^{+}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\varphi(r,z)|^{2}r\,dzdr=1,\ E_{c}({\varphi})<\infty\}.

μ​φ​(r,z)=−12​[1r​∂∂r​(r​∂φ∂r)+∂2φ∂z2]+(V⁡(r,z)+β​|φ|2)​φ,r>0,z∈ℝ,\displaystyle\mu{\varphi}(r,z)=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial{\varphi}}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{\partial^{2}{\varphi}}{\partial z^{2}}\right]+\left(V(r,z)+\beta|{\varphi}|^{2}\right){\varphi},\ \ r>0,\ {z\in\mathbb{R}}, (3.62)

under the normalization constraint (3.59) with ψ=φ\psi=\varphi.

μ​φ​(r,z)=−12​[1r​∂∂r​(r​∂φ∂r)+∂2φ∂z2]+(V⁡(r,z)+β​|φ|2)​φ,\displaystyle\mu\;{\varphi}(r,z)=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial{\varphi}}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{\partial^{2}{\varphi}}{\partial z^{2}}\right]+\left(V(r,z)+\beta|{\varphi}|^{2}\right){\varphi}, (3.64)

Remark 3.2.

When the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is an even function, BEFD (3.28) and BESP (3.34)-(3.35) can be used to compute the first excited states by choosing proper initial guess (see [27, 36]).

3.5. Numerical results

In this section, we report numerical results on the ground state by the proposed BEFD and BESP methods.

Example 3.1.

Ground and first excited states (Remark 3.2) in 1D, i.e., we take d=1d=1 in (2.1) and study two kinds of trapping potentials

Case I. A harmonic oscillator potential V⁡(x)=x22V(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{2} and β=400\beta=400;

Case II. An optical lattice potential V⁡(x)=x22+25​sin2⁡(π​x4)V(x)=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+25\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi x}{4}\right) and β=250\beta=250.

The initial data (3.7) is chosen as ϕ0(x)=e−x2/2/π1/4\phi_{0}(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}/\pi^{1/4} for computing the ground state, and resp., ϕ0(x)=2​xπ1/4e−x2/2\phi_{0}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{2}x}{\pi^{1/4}}e^{-x^{2}/2} for computing the first excited state. We solve the problem with BESP (3.34)-(3.35) on [−16,16][-16,16], i.e. a=−16a=-16 and b=16b=16, and take time step τ=0.05\tau=0.05 for computing the ground state, and resp., τ=0.001\tau=0.001 for computing the first excited state. The steady state solution in our computation is reached when max1≤j≤M−1⁡|ϕjn+1−ϕjn|<10−12\max_{1\leq j\leq M-1}\;|\phi_{j}^{n+1}-\phi_{j}^{n}|<10^{-12}. Let ϕg\phi_{g} and ϕ1\phi_{1} be the ‘exact’ ground state and first excited state, respectively, which are obtained numerically by using BESP with a very fine mesh h=132h=\frac{1}{32} and h=1128h=\frac{1}{128}, respectively. We denote their energy and chemical potential as Eg:=E⁡(ϕg)E_{g}:=E(\phi_{g}), E1:=E⁡(ϕ1)E_{1}:=E(\phi_{1}), and μg:=μ⁡(ϕg)\mu_{g}:=\mu(\phi_{g}), μ1:=μ⁡(ϕ1)\mu_{1}:=\mu(\phi_{1}). Let ϕg,hSP\phi_{g,h}^{\rm SP} and ϕ1,hSP\phi_{1,h}^{\rm SP} be the numerical ground state and first excited state obtained by using BESP with mesh size hh, respectively. Similarly, ϕg,hFD\phi_{g,h}^{\rm FD} and ϕ1,hFD\phi_{1,h}^{\rm FD} are obtained by using BEFD in a similar way. Tabs. 3.1 and 3.2 list the errors for Case I, and Tabs. 3.3 and 3.4 show the errors for Case II. Furthermore, we compute the energy and chemical potential for the ground state and first excited state based on our ‘exact’ solution ϕg\phi_{g} and ϕ1\phi_{1}. For Case I, we have Eg:=E⁡(ϕg)=21.3601E_{g}:=E(\phi_{g})=21.3601 and μg:=μ⁡(ϕg)=35.5775\mu_{g}:=\mu(\phi_{g})=35.5775 for ground state, and E1:=E⁡(ϕ1)=22.0777E_{1}:=E(\phi_{1})=22.0777 and μ1:=μ⁡(ϕ1)=36.2881\mu_{1}:=\mu(\phi_{1})=36.2881 for the first excited state. Similarly, for Case II, we have Eg=26.0838E_{g}=26.0838, μg=38.0692\mu_{g}=38.0692, E1=27.3408E_{1}=27.3408 and μ1=38.9195\mu_{1}=38.9195. Fig. 3.1 plots ϕg\phi_{g} and ϕ1\phi_{1} as well as their corresponding trapping potentials for Cases I&II. Fig. 3.2a shows the excited states ϕ1\phi_{1} for potential in Case I with different β\beta.

From Tabs. 3.1-3.4, Figs. 3.1 and 3.2a, we can draw the following conclusions. For BESP, it is spectrally accurate in spatial discretization; where for BEFD, it is only second-order accurate. The error in the ground and first excited states is only due to the spatial discretization. Thus when high accuracy is required or the solution has multiscale structure [37], BESP is much better than BEFD in terms that it needs much less grid points. Therefore BESP can save a lot of memory and computational time, especially in 2D & 3D.

Example 3.2.

Ground states in 2D with radial symmetric trap, i.e. we take d=2d=2 in (2.1) and

V⁡(x,y)=V⁡(r)=12​r2,(x,y)∈ℝ2,r=x2+y2≥0.\displaystyle V(x,y)=V(r)=\frac{1}{2}r^{2},\qquad(x,y)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2},\qquad r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\geq 0. (3.69)

The GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) is solved in polar coordinate with R=8+1/128R=8+1/128 under mesh size Δ​r=164\Delta r=\frac{1}{64} and time step τ=0.1\tau=0.1 by using the simplified BEFD (3.54)-(3.55) with initial data ϕ0(x,y)=ϕ0(r)=1πe−r2/2\phi_{0}(x,y)=\phi_{0}(r)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}}\,e^{-r^{2}/2}. Fig. 3.2b shows the ground state solution ϕg​(r)\phi_{g}(r) with different β\beta. Tab. 3.5 displays the values of ϕg​(0)\phi_{g}(0), radius mean square rrms=2​π​∫0∞r2​|ϕg​(r)|2​r​𝑑rr_{\rm rms}=\sqrt{2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}r^{2}|\phi_{g}(r)|^{2}rdr}, energy E⁡(ϕg)E(\phi_{g}) and chemical potential μg\mu_{g} for different β\beta.

3.6. Comments of different methods

In literatures, different numerical methods have been introduced to compute ground states of BEC. In [157], Ruprecht et al. used Crank-Nicolson finite difference method to compute the ground states of BEC based on the Euler-Lagrange equation (2.8). Later, Edwards et al. proposed a Runge-Kutta method to find the ground states in 1D and 3D with spherical symmetry. Dodd [90] gave an analytical expansion of the energy E⁡(ϕ)E(\phi) using the Hermite polynomials when the trap VV is harmonic. By minimizing the energy in terms of the expansion, approximated ground state results were reported in [90]. In [78], Succi et al. used an imaginary time method (equivalent to GFDN) to compute the ground states with centered finite-difference discretization in space and explicit forward discretization in time. Lin et al. designed an iterative method in [77]. After discretization in space, they transformed the problem to a minimization problem in finite dimensional vector space. Gauss-Seidel iteration methods were proposed to solve the corresponding problem. Bao and Tang proposed a finite element method to find the ground state by directly minimizing the energy functional in [43]. In [27, 36], Bao et al. developed the GFDN method to calculate the ground state, which contains a gradient flow and a projection at each step. Different discretizations have been discussed, including the finite difference discretization or spectral discretization in space, explicit (forward Euler) discretization or implicit (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson) discretization in time.

In the current studies of BEC, the most popular method for computing the ground state is the GFDN method. In fact, imaginary time method [78] is the same as the GFDN method, while imaginary time is preferred in the physics community. There are many different discretizations for GFDN (3.5)-(3.7) [27, 36], including backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson, forward Euler, backward Euler for linear part and forward Euler for nonlinear part, time-splitting for the time discretization and centered finite difference or spectral method for spatial discretization. From our experience, among these discretizations, BEFD and BESP are very easy to use, robust, very efficient and accurate in practical computation. Furthermore, energy diminishing is observed in linear case under any time step τ>0\tau>0 and nonlinear case when time step τ\tau is not too big [27]. If high accuracy is crucial in computing ground states in BEC, e.g. under an optical lattice potential or in a rotational frame, BESP is recommended.

4. Numerical methods for computing dynamics of GPE

In this section, we review different numerical methods to discretize the Cauchy problem of the GPE (2.1) for computing the dynamics of BEC. In fact, many efficient and accurate numerical methods have been proposed for discretizing the above GPE, or the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) in general, such as time-splitting sine pseudospectral method [31, 33, 34, 47], time-splitting finite difference method [180, 42], time-splitting Laguerre-Hermite pseudospectral method [40], conservative Crank-Nicolson finite difference method [76, 21, 20], semi-implicit finite difference method [21, 20], etc. Each method has its own advantages and disadvantages. Here we present the detailed algorithms for some of these methods.

In practice, we truncate the problem on a bounded domain U⊂ℝdU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) as Eq. (3.1), with either homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions (3.2) or periodic boundary conditions when UU is an interval (1D), a rectangle (2D) or a box (3D). For simplicity of notation, we shall introduce the method in one space dimension (d=1d=1). Generalizations to d>1d>1 are straightforward for tensor product grids and the results remain valid without modifications. In 1D, the equation (3.1) becomes

i​∂ψ⁡(x,t)∂t=−12​ψx​x​(x,t)+V⁡(x)​ψ​(x,t)+β​|ψ|2​ψ​(x,t),a<x⁡<b,t>​0,\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi(x,t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{xx}(x,t)+V(x)\psi(x,t)+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi(x,t),\ a<x<b,\;t>0,\qquad (4.1)
ψ⁡(x,t=0)=ψ0​(x),a≤x≤b,\displaystyle\psi(x,t=0)=\psi_{0}(x),\qquad a\leq x\leq b, (4.2)

with the homogenous Dirichlet boundary condition

ψ⁡(a,t)=ψ⁡(b,t)=0,t>0.\displaystyle\psi(a,t)=\psi(b,t)=0,\qquad t>0. (4.3)

The following periodic boundary condition

ψ⁡(a,t)=ψ⁡(b,t),∂xψ⁡(a,t)=∂xψ⁡(b,t),t>0,\displaystyle\psi(a,t)=\psi(b,t),\quad\partial_{x}\psi(a,t)=\partial_{x}\psi(b,t),\qquad t>0, (4.4)

or homogeneous Neumann boundary condition

∂xψ⁡(a,t)=∂xψ⁡(b,t)=0,t>0,\displaystyle\partial_{x}\psi(a,t)=\partial_{x}\psi(b,t)=0,\qquad t>0, (4.5)

is also widely used in the literature.

To discretize Eq. (4.1), we use uniform grid points. Choose the spatial mesh size h=Δ​x>0h=\Delta x>0 with Δ​x=(b−a)/M\Delta x=(b-a)/M (MM an even positive integer), the time step τ\tau, the grid points and the time step as in (3.24). Let ψjn\psi^{n}_{j} be the approximation of ψ⁡(xj,tn)\psi(x_{j},t_{n}) and ψn\psi^{n} be the solution vector with components ψjn\psi_{j}^{n}.

In the following, we will introduce two widely used schemes: the time-splitting methods and the finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods.

4.1. Time splitting pseudospectral/finite difference method

The time splitting procedure was presented for differential equations in [171] and applied to Schrödinger equations in [114, 175]. For the simplest two-step case, consider an abstract initial value problem for u:[0,T]→ℬu:[0,T]\to{\mathcal{B}} (ℬ{\mathcal{B}} Banach space),

dd​t​u​(t)=(A+B)​u​(t),u⁡(0)∈ℬ,\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}u(t)=(A+B)u(t),\quad u(0)\in{\mathcal{B}}, (4.6)

where AA and BB are two operators, the solution can be written in the abstract form as u⁡(t)=et⁡(A+B)​u​(0)u(t)=e^{t(A+B)}u(0). For a given time step τ>0\tau>0, let tn=n​τt_{n}=n\tau, n=0,1,…n=0,1,\ldots, and unu^{n} be the approximation of u⁡(tn)u(t_{n}). The time-splitting approximation, or operator splitting (split-step) is usually given as [171, 189]

un+1=eτ​A​eτ​B​un,Lie-Trotter splitting,\displaystyle u^{n+1}=e^{\tau A}e^{\tau B}u^{n},\qquad\text{Lie-Trotter splitting}, (4.7)

or

un+1≈eτ​A/2​eτ​B​eτ​A/2​un,Strang splitting.\displaystyle u^{n+1}\approx e^{\tau A/2}e^{\tau B}e^{\tau A/2}u^{n},\qquad\text{Strang splitting}. (4.8)

Formally, from Taylor expansion, it is easy to see that the approximation error of Lie-Trotter splitting is of first order O⁡(τ)O(\tau), and the error of Strang splitting is of second order O⁡(τ2)O(\tau^{2}). In principle, splitting approximations of higher order accuracy can be constructed as [189]

un+1≈ea1​τ​Aeb1​τ​Bea2​τ​Aeb2​τ​B⋯eam​τ​Aebm​τ​Bun,m≥1,\displaystyle u^{n+1}\approx e^{a_{1}\tau A}e^{b_{1}\tau B}e^{a_{2}\tau A}e^{b_{2}\tau B}\cdots e^{a_{m}\tau A}e^{b_{m}\tau B}u^{n},\quad m\geq 1, (4.9)

where coefficients aja_{j} and bjb_{j} (j=1,⋯,mj=1,\cdots,m) are chosen properly. One of the most frequently used higher order splitting scheme is the fourth-order symplectic time integrator (cf. [189, 40]) for (4.6) as:

u(1)=eθ​τ​Aun,u(2)=e2​θ​τ​Bu(1),u(3)=e(0.5−θ)​τ​Au(2),u(4)=e(1−4​θ)​τ​Bu(3),u(5)=e(0.5−θ)​τ​Au(4),u(6)=e2​θ​τ​Bu(5),un+1=eθ​τ​A​u(6),\displaystyle\begin{split}&u^{(1)}=e^{\theta\tau A}\;u^{n},\quad u^{(2)}=e^{2\theta\tau B}\;u^{(1)},\quad u^{(3)}=e^{(0.5-\theta)\tau A}\;u^{(2)},\\ &u^{(4)}=e^{(1-4\theta)\tau B}\;u^{(3)},\quad u^{(5)}=e^{(0.5-\theta)\tau A}\;u^{(4)},\quad u^{(6)}=e^{2\theta\tau B}\;u^{(5)},\\ &u^{n+1}=e^{\theta\tau A}\;u^{(6)},\end{split} (4.10)

where the coefficient θ\theta can be calculated as

θ=16(2+21/3+2−1/3)≈0.67560359597982881702.\displaystyle\theta=\frac{1}{6}\left(2+2^{1/3}+2^{-1/3}\right)\approx 0.67560359597982881702. (4.11)

4.1.1. Time splitting sine pseudospectral method

In this section we present a time-splitting sine pseudospectral method, to numerically solve the GPE (4.1) with homogenous Dirichlet boundary condition (4.3). The merit of this method is that it is unconditionally stable, time reversible, time-transverse invariant, and that it conserves the total particle number.

Time-splitting sine pseudospectral (TSSP) method. From time t=tnt=t_{n} to t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, the GPE (4.1) is solved in two splitting steps. One solves first

i​ψt=−12​ψx​x,\displaystyle i\psi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{xx}, (4.12)

for the time step of length τ\tau, followed by solving

i​∂ψ⁡(x,t)∂t=V⁡(x)​ψ​(x,t)+β​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2​ψ​(x,t),\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi(x,t)}{\partial t}=V(x)\psi(x,t)+\beta|\psi(x,t)|^{2}\psi(x,t), (4.13)

for the same time step. Eq. (4.12) will be discretized in space by the sine spectral method and integrated in time exactly. For t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}], the ODE (4.13) leaves |ψ||\psi| invariant in tt [31, 33] and therefore becomes

i​∂ψ⁡(x,t)∂t=V⁡(x)​ψ​(x,t)+β​|ψ⁡(x,tn)|2​ψ​(x,t)\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi(x,t)}{\partial t}=V(x)\psi(x,t)+\beta|\psi(x,t_{n})|^{2}\psi(x,t) (4.14)

and thus can be integrated exactly. This is equivalent to choosing operators AA, BB in (4.6) as

A​ψ=i2​∂x​xψ,B​ψ=−i⁡(V⁡(x)+β​|ψ|2)​ψ.\displaystyle A\psi=\frac{i}{2}\partial_{xx}\psi,\qquad B\psi=-i(V(x)+\beta|\psi|^{2})\psi. (4.15)

From time t=tnt=t_{n} to t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, we combine the splitting steps via the standard Strang splitting [31, 33, 47]:

ψj(1)=2M∑l=1M−1e−iτμl2/4(ψn)~lsin(μl(xj−a)),ψ(2)j=e−i⁡(V⁡(xj)+β​|ψj(1)|2)​τψj(1),j∈𝒯M,ψn+1j=2M∑l=1M−1e−iτμl2/4(ψ(2))~lsin(μl(xj−a)),ψ0n+1=ψMn+1=0,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\psi_{j}^{(1)}=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{l=1}^{M-1}e^{-i\tau\mu_{l}^{2}/4}\;\widetilde{(\psi^{n})}_{l}\;\sin(\mu_{l}(x_{j}-a)),\\ &\psi^{(2)}_{j}=e^{-i(V(x_{j})+\beta|\psi_{j}^{(1)}|^{2})\tau}\;\psi_{j}^{(1)},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\\ &\psi^{n+1}_{j}=\frac{2}{M}\sum_{l=1}^{M-1}e^{-i\tau\mu_{l}^{2}/4}\;\widetilde{(\psi^{(2)})}_{l}\;\sin(\mu_{l}(x_{j}-a)),\qquad\psi_{0}^{n+1}=\psi_{M}^{n+1}=0,\end{split} (4.16)

where μl=l​π/(b−a)\mu_{l}=l\pi/(b-a) for l∈𝒯Ml\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M} and (ψn)~l\widetilde{(\psi^{n})}_{l} and (ψ(2))~l\widetilde{(\psi^{(2)})}_{l} are the discrete sine transform coefficients of ψn\psi^{n} and ψ(2)\psi^{(2)}, respectively, which are defined in (3.31). One can also exchange the order of the steps (4.13) and (4.14) in TSSP (4.16), and the numerical results are almost the same.

Remark 4.1.

For the GPE (4.1) truncated in a bounded domain with periodic boundary condition (4.4) or homogenous Neumann boundary condition (4.5), a time splitting Fourier or cosine pseudospectral method similar to TSSP (4.16) is straightforward [44, 31, 33], i.e., solve the linear part (4.12) by Fourier or cosine spectral discretization instead of sine spectral discretization.

4.1.2. Time splitting finite difference method

In section 4.1.1, a sine pseudospectral method (or a Fourier pseudospectral method) is used to solve Eq. (4.12). Spectral method is favorable in view of its high accuracy if the solution of continuous problem (2.1) is smooth. For non-smooth potentials V⁡(x)V(x) (random potential), the regularity of the solution of the GPE (2.1) would be low. In such case, finite difference method is suggested instead of spectral method.

Time-splitting finite difference (TSFD) method From time t=tnt=t_{n} to t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, the GPE (4.1) with homogenous Dirichlet boundary condition (4.3) is solved in two splitting steps, (4.12) and (4.14). As indicated in section 4.1.1, Eq. (4.14) can be integrated exactly. For the linear part (4.12), we use Crank-Nicolson finite difference method. From time t=tnt=t_{n} to t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, we combine the splitting steps via the standard Strang splitting [42]:

ψ(1)j=e−iτ(V(xj)+β|ψjn|2)/2ψjn,j∈𝒯M0,iψj(2)−ψj(1)τ=−14(δx2ψj(2)+δx2ψj(1)),j∈𝒯M,ψ0(2)=ψM(2)=0,ψn+1j=e−iτ(V(xj)+β|ψj(2)|2)/2ψj(2),j∈𝒯M0.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\psi^{(1)}_{j}=e^{-i\tau(V(x_{j})+\beta|\psi_{j}^{n}|^{2})/2}\;\psi_{j}^{n},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\\ &i\frac{\psi_{j}^{(2)}-\psi^{(1)}_{j}}{\tau}=-\frac{1}{4}(\delta_{x}^{2}\psi_{j}^{(2)}+\delta_{x}^{2}\psi_{j}^{(1)}),\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\qquad\psi_{0}^{(2)}=\psi_{M}^{(2)}=0,\\ &\psi^{n+1}_{j}=e^{-i\tau(V(x_{j})+\beta|\psi_{j}^{(2)}|^{2})/2}\;\psi_{j}^{(2)},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}.\end{split} (4.17)

This method is also unconditionally stable, time reversible, time-transverse invariant, and it conserves the total particle number. The linear part of TSFD (4.17) can be solved by the Thomas’ algorithm in 1D and discrete sine transform (DST) in 2D and 3D. Thus, the computational costs of TSFD and TSSP are the same in 2D and 3D, while the cost of TSFD is cheaper in 1D due to the Thomas’ algorithm.

4.2. Finite difference time domain method

Finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods for NLSE have been extensively studied in the literature [9, 76] and are widely used. In this section, we present the most popular finite difference discretizations for the GPE (4.1) with homogenous Dirichlet boundary condition (4.3).

4.2.1. Crank-Nicolson finite difference method

The conservative Crank-Nicolson finite difference (CNFD) discretization of GPE (4.1) reads [76, 106, 34, 21, 20]

i​δt+​ψjn=[−12​δx2+Vj+β2​(|ψjn+1|2+|ψjn|2)]​ψjn+1/2,j∈𝒯M,n≥0,i\delta^{+}_{t}\psi_{j}^{n}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}+\frac{\beta}{2}(|\psi_{j}^{n+1}|^{2}+|\psi_{j}^{n}|^{2})\right]\psi_{j}^{n+1/2},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\ n\geq 0, (4.18)

where

Vj=V(xj),ψjn+1/2=12(ψjn+1+ψjn),j∈𝒯M0,n=0,1,2,….V_{j}=V(x_{j}),\qquad\psi_{j}^{n+1/2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\psi_{j}^{n+1}+\psi_{j}^{n}\right),\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\quad n=0,1,2,\ldots.

The boundary condition (4.3) is discretized as

ψn+10=ψn+1M=0,n=0,1,…,\displaystyle\psi^{n+1}_{0}=\psi^{n+1}_{M}=0,\qquad n=0,1,\ldots\;, (4.19)

and the initial condition (4.2) is discretized as

ψj0=ψ0​(xj),j∈𝒯M0.\displaystyle\psi^{0}_{j}=\psi_{0}(x_{j}),\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}. (4.20)

The above CNFD method conserves the mass and energy in the discretized level. However, it is a fully implicit method, i.e., at each time step, a fully nonlinear system must be solved, which may be very expensive, especially in 2D and 3D. In fact, if the fully nonlinear system is not solved numerically to extremely high accuracy, e.g., at machine accuracy, then the mass and energy of the numerical solution obtained in practical computation are no longer conserved [21]. This motivates us also consider the following semi-implicit discretization for the GPE.

4.2.2. Semi-implicit finite difference method

The semi-implicit finite difference (SIFD) discretization of the GPE (4.1), is to use Crank-Nicolson/leap-frog schemes for discretizing linear/nonlinear terms, respectively, as [21, 20]

i​δt​ψjn=[−12​δx2+Vj]​ψjn+1+ψjn−12+β​|ψjn|2​ψjn,j∈𝒯M,n≥1.i\delta_{t}\psi_{j}^{n}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right]\frac{\psi_{j}^{n+1}+\psi_{j}^{n-1}}{2}+\beta|\psi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\psi_{j}^{n},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\quad n\geq 1. (4.21)

Again, the boundary condition (4.3) and initial condition (4.2) are discretized in (4.19) and (4.20), respectively. In addition, the first step can be computed by any explicit second or higher order time integrator, e.g., the second-order modified Euler method, as

ψj1=ψj0−i​τ​[(−12​δx2+Vj)​ψj(1)+β​|ψj(1)|2​ψj(1)],j∈𝒯M,\displaystyle\psi_{j}^{1}=\psi_{j}^{0}-i\tau\left[\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right)\psi_{j}^{(1)}+\beta|\psi_{j}^{(1)}|^{2}\psi_{j}^{(1)}\right],\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\qquad (4.22)
ψj(1)=ψj0−i​τ2​[(−12​δx2+Vj)​ψj0+β​|ψj0|2​ψj0].\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\psi_{j}^{(1)}=\psi_{j}^{0}-i\frac{\tau}{2}\left[\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right)\psi_{j}^{0}+\beta|\psi_{j}^{0}|^{2}\psi_{j}^{0}\right].

For this SIFD method, at each time step, only a linear system is to be solved, which is much more cheaper than that of the CNFD method in practical computation.

4.3. Simplified methods for symmetric potential and initial data

Similar to section 3.4, when the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) (𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) and the initial data ψ0\psi_{0} are symmetric, then the solution of the GPE (2.1) is symmetric. In such cases, simplified numerical methods, especially with less memory requirement, are available for computing the dynamics of GPE.

4.3.1. Radial symmetry in 1D, 2D and 3D

When potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) and initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,0)=ψ0​(𝐱)\psi(\mathbf{x},0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}) are radially symmetric for d=1,2d=1,2 and spherically symmetric for d=3d=3, the problem is reduced to 1D. In such case, the GPE (2.1) collapse to the 1D equation (3.43) for ψ:=ψ⁡(r,t)\psi:=\psi(r,t) with r=|𝐱|≥0r=|\mathbf{x}|\geq 0.

In practical computation, the equation (3.43) is approximated on a finite interval. Since the wave function vanishes as r→∞r\to\infty, choosing R>0R>0 sufficiently large, equation (3.43) can be approximated by

i​∂tψ⁡(r,t)=−12​rd−1​∂∂r​(rd−1​∂∂r​ψ)+V⁡(r)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​ψ,0<r<R,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(r,t)=-\frac{1}{2r^{d-1}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{d-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\psi\right)+V(r)\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi,\quad 0<r<R, (4.23)

with boundary conditions

∂rψ⁡(0,t)=0,ψ⁡(R,t)=0,t≥0,\displaystyle\partial_{r}\psi(0,t)=0,\qquad\psi(R,t)=0,\qquad t\geq 0, (4.24)

and initial condition

ψ⁡(r,0)=ψ0​(r),0≤r≤R.\displaystyle\psi(r,0)=\psi_{0}(r),\qquad 0\leq r\leq R. (4.25)

For this 1D problem, an efficient and accurate method is the time-splitting finite difference (TSFD) method. Choose time steps as (3.24) and mesh size Δ​r=2​R/(2​M+1)\Delta r=2R/(2M+1) for some integer M>0M>0. We use the same notations for the grid points as (3.53), and let ψj+12n\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n} be the numerical approximation of ψ⁡(rj+12,tn)\psi(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}},t_{n}) and ψn\psi^{n} be the solution vector at time t=tnt=t_{n} with components ψj+12n\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n}. The time-splitting finite difference (TSFD) discretization for (4.23) reads

ψ(1)j+12=e−iτβ|ψj+12n|2/2ψj+12n,j∈𝒯M0,\displaystyle\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}=e^{-i\tau\beta|\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n}|^{2}/2}\;\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{n},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},
i​ψj+12(2)−ψj+12(1)τ=[−12​δr,d2+V⁡(rj+12)]​ψj+12(2)+ψj+12(1)2,0≤j≤M−1,\displaystyle i\frac{\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)}-\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}}{\tau}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{r,d}^{2}+V(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}})\right]\frac{\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)}+\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}}{2},\quad 0\leq j\leq M-1,
ψ−12(2)=ψ12(2),ψM+12(2)=0,ψj+120=ψ0​(rj+12),j∈𝒯M0,\displaystyle\psi_{-\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)}=\psi_{\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)},\qquad\psi_{M+\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)}=0,\qquad\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{0}=\psi_{0}(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}}),\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},
ψn+1j+12=e−iτβ|ψj+12(2)|2/2ψj+12(2),j∈𝒯M0,n≥0.\displaystyle\psi^{n+1}_{j+\frac{1}{2}}=e^{-i\tau\beta|\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)}|^{2}/2}\;\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}}^{(2)},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\quad n\geq 0. (4.26)

This method is second-order accurate in space and time, unconditionally stable and it conserves the normalization in the discretized level. The memory cost is O⁡(M)O(M) and computational cost is O⁡(M)O(M) per time step, which save significantly from O⁡(Md)O(M^{d}) and O⁡(Md​ln⁡M)O(M^{d}\ln M), respectively, in 2D and 3D when the Cartesian coordinates is used by TSSP.

4.3.2. Cylindrical symmetry in 3D

For 𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, when VV and ψ0\psi_{0} are cylindrically symmetric, i.e., VV and ψ0\psi_{0} are of the form V⁡(r,z)V(r,z) and ψ0​(r,z)\psi_{0}(r,z) (r=x2+y2r=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}), respectively, the Cauchy problem of the GPE (2.1) is reduced to 2D. Due to the symmetry, the GPE (2.1) essentially collapses to the 2D problem (3.57) with r∈(0,+∞)r\in(0,+\infty) and z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R} for ψ:=ψ⁡(r,z,t)\psi:=\psi(r,z,t).

In practice, the GPE (3.57) is truncated on a bounded domain. Choosing R>0R>0 and Z1<Z2Z_{1}<Z_{2} with |Z1||Z_{1}|, |Z2||Z_{2}| and RR sufficiently large, then Eq. (3.57) can be approximated for (r,z)∈(0,R)×(Z1,Z2)(r,z)\in(0,R)\times(Z_{1},Z_{2}) as,

i​∂tψ⁡(r,z,t)=−12​[1r​∂∂r​(r​∂ψ∂r)+∂2ψ∂z2]+(V⁡(r,z)+β​|ψ|2)​ψ,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(r,z,t)=-\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{\partial^{2}\psi}{\partial z^{2}}\right]+\left(V(r,z)+\beta|\psi|^{2}\right)\psi, (4.27)

with boundary condition

∂ψ⁡(0,z,t)∂r=0,ψ⁡(R,z,t)=ψ⁡(r,Z1,t)=ψ⁡(r,Z2,t)=0,z∈[Z1,Z2],r∈[0,R],\displaystyle\frac{\partial\psi(0,z,t)}{\partial r}=0,\;\psi(R,z,t)=\psi(r,Z_{1},t)=\psi(r,Z_{2},t)=0,\quad z\in[Z_{1},Z_{2}],\;r\in[0,R], (4.28)

and initial condition

ψ⁡(r,z,0)=ψ0​(r,z),z∈[Z1,Z2],r∈[0,R].\displaystyle\psi(r,z,0)=\psi_{0}(r,z),\qquad z\in[Z_{1},Z_{2}],\quad r\in[0,R]. (4.29)

Similar to section 3.4, choose time steps as (3.24) and rr- grid points (3.53) for positive integer M>0M>0. For integer N>0N>0, choose mesh size Δ​z=(Z2−Z1)/N\Delta z=(Z_{2}-Z_{1})/N and define zz- grid points zk=Z1+k​Δ​zz_{k}=Z_{1}+k\Delta z for k∈𝒯N0k\in{\mathcal{T}}_{N}^{0}. Let ψj+12​kn\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{n} be the numerical approximation of ψ⁡(rj+12,zk,tn)\psi(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}},z_{k},t_{n}) and ψn\psi^{n} be the solution vector at time t=tnt=t_{n} with components ψj+12​kn\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{n}. Then the time-splitting finite difference (TSFD) discretization for (4.27) reads

ψj+12​k(1)=e−iτ[V(rj+12,zk)+β|ψj+12​kn|2]/2ψj+12​kn,(j,k)∈𝒯M​N0,\displaystyle\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}=e^{-i\tau[V(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}},z_{k})+\beta|\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{n}|^{2}]/2}\;\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{n},\qquad(j,k)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{MN}^{0},
i​ψj+12​k(2)−ψj+12​k(1)τ=−14​(δr2+δz2)​(ψj+12​k(2)+ψj+12​k(1)),(j,k)∈𝒯M​N∗,\displaystyle i\frac{\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{(2)}-\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}}{\tau}=-\frac{1}{4}(\delta_{r}^{2}+\delta_{z}^{2})\left(\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{(2)}+\psi^{(1)}_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}\right),\qquad(j,k)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{MN}^{*},
ψ−12​k(2)=ψ12​k(2),ψM+12​k(2)=ψj+12​ 0(2)=ψj+12​N(2)=0,(j,k)∈𝒯M​N0,\displaystyle\psi_{-\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{(2)}=\psi_{\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{(2)},\ \psi_{M+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{(2)}=\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,0}^{(2)}=\psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,N}^{(2)}=0,\ (j,k)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{MN}^{0},
