with ψj+12​k0=ψ0​(rj+12,zk)\ \psi_{j+\frac{1}{2}\,k}^{0}=\psi_{0}(r_{j+\frac{1}{2}},z_{k}) for (j,k)∈𝒯M​N0(j,k)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{MN}^{0}. This method is second-order accurate in space and time, unconditionally stable and it conserves the normalization in the discretized level. The memory cost is O⁡(M​N)O(MN) and computational cost is O⁡(M​N​ln⁡M)O(MN\ln M) per time step, which save significantly from O⁡(M2​N)O(M^{2}N) and O⁡(M2​N​ln⁡M)O(M^{2}N\ln M), respectively, when the Cartesian coordinates is used by TSSP.

4.4. Error estimates for SIFD and CNFD

In this section, we present the error estimates for CNFD (4.18) and SIFD (4.21). The notations for finite difference operators, related finite dimensional vector space and norms are given in section 3.2. Specially, for real valued nonnegative potential V⁡(x)V(x), we define the corresponding discrete weighted l2l^{2} norm for u=(u0,u1,⋯,uM)T∈XMu=(u_{0},u_{1},\cdots,u_{M})^{T}\in X_{M} as:

‖u‖V2=h​∑j=0M−1Vj​|uj|2.\displaystyle\|u\|_{V}^{2}=h\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}V_{j}|u_{j}|^{2}. (4.31)

In the remaining part of this section, we use the notation p≲qp\lesssim q to represent that there exists a generic constant CC which is independent of time step τ\tau and mesh size hh such that |p|≤C​q|p|\leq C\,q.

To state the error bounds, we define the ‘error’ function en∈XMe^{n}\in X_{M} as

ejn=ψ⁡(xj,tn)−ψjn,j∈𝒯M0,n≥0,\displaystyle e_{j}^{n}=\psi(x_{j},t_{n})-\psi_{j}^{n},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0},\quad n\geq 0, (4.32)

where ψ:=ψ⁡(x,t)\psi:=\psi(x,t) is the exact solution of the GPE (4.1) and ψjn\psi_{j}^{n} is the numerical solution. We make the following assumption on the exact solution ψ\psi, i.e., let 0<T<Tmax0<T<T_{\rm max} with TmaxT_{\rm max} the maximal existing time of the solution [73, 173]:

ψ∈C3​([0,T],W1,∞)∩C2​([0,T],W3,∞)∩C0​([0,T],W5,∞∩H01),\displaystyle\psi\in C^{3}([0,T];W^{1,\infty})\cap C^{2}([0,T];W^{3,\infty})\cap C^{0}([0,T];W^{5,\infty}\cap H_{0}^{1}), (4.33)

where the spatial norms are taken in the interval U=(a,b)U=(a,b).

For the SIFD method, we have [21, 20]

Theorem 4.1.

Assuming that (4.33) holds and that V​(x)∈C1​(U¯)V(x)\in C^{1}({\overline{U}}), there exist h0>0h_{0}>0 and 0<τ0≤140<\tau_{0}\leq\frac{1}{4} sufficiently small, when 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0} and 0<τ≤τ0≤140<\tau\leq\tau_{0}\leq\frac{1}{4}, we have the following error estimates for the SIFD method (4.21) with (4.19), (4.20) and (4.22)

‖en‖2≲h2+τ2,‖δx+​en‖2≲h3/2+τ3/2,‖ψn‖∞≤1+M1,0≤n≤Tτ,\displaystyle\|e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2},\quad\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{3/2}+\tau^{3/2},\quad\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq 1+M_{1},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}, (4.34)

where M1=max0≤t≤T⁡‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(U)M_{1}=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}. In addition, if either ∂nV⁡(x)|Γ=0\partial_{n}V(x)|_{\Gamma}=0 (Γ=∂U\Gamma=\partial U, ∂n\partial_{n} is the outer normal derivative) or ψ∈C0​([0,T],H02​(U))\psi\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{2}_{0}(U)), we have the optimal error estimates

‖en‖2+‖δx+​en‖2≲h2+τ2,‖ψn‖∞≤1+M1,0≤n≤Tτ.\displaystyle\|e^{n}\|_{2}+\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2},\quad\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq 1+M_{1},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}. (4.35)

Similarly, for the CNFD method, we have [21, 20]

Theorem 4.2.

Assuming that (4.33) holds and that V​(x)∈C1​(U¯)V(x)\in C^{1}({\overline{U}}), there exists h0>0h_{0}>0 and τ0>0\tau_{0}>0 sufficiently small, when 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0} and 0<τ≤τ00<\tau\leq\tau_{0}, the CNFD discretization (4.18) with (4.19) and (4.20) admits a unique solution ψn\psi^{n} (0≤n≤Tτ0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}) such that the following error estimates hold,

‖en‖2≲h2+τ2,‖δx+​en‖2≲h3/2+τ3/2,‖ψn‖∞≤1+M1,0≤n≤Tτ.\displaystyle\|e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2},\quad\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{3/2}+\tau^{3/2},\quad\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq 1+M_{1},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}. (4.36)

In addition, if either ∂nV⁡(x)|Γ=0\partial_{n}V(x)|_{\Gamma}=0 or ψ∈C0​([0,T],H02​(U))\psi\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{2}_{0}(U)), we have the optimal error estimates

‖en‖2+‖δx+​en‖2≲h2+τ2,‖ψn‖∞≤1+M1,0≤n≤Tτ.\displaystyle\|e^{n}\|_{2}+\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2},\quad\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq 1+M_{1},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}. (4.37)

Error bounds of conservative CNFD method for NLSE in 1D (without potential V⁡(x)V(x)) was established in [76, 106]. In fact, their proofs for CNFD rely strongly on the conservative property of the method and the discrete version of the Sobolev inequality in 1D

‖f‖L∞2≤‖∇f‖L2⋅‖f‖L2,∀f∈H1​(U)​with​U⊂ℝ,\displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\nabla f\|_{L^{2}}\cdot\|f\|_{L^{2}},\qquad\forall f\in H^{1}(U)\ \hbox{with}\ U\subset{\mathbb{R}}, (4.38)

which immediately implies a priori uniform bound for ‖f‖L∞\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}. However, the extension of the discrete version of the above Sobolev inequality is no longer valid in 2D and 3D. Thus the techniques used in [76, 106] for obtaining error bounds of CNFD for NLSE only work for conservative schemes in 1D and they cannot be extended to either high dimensions or non-conservative finite difference scheme like SIFD.

Here, we are going to use different techniques to establish optimal error bounds of CNFD and SIFD for the GPE (2.1) in 1D which can be directly generalized to 2D and 3D. In the analysis, besides the standard techniques of the energy method, for SIFD, we adopt the mathematical induction; for CNFD, we cut off the nonlinearity.

4.4.1. Convergence rate for SIFD

Firstly, SIFD (4.21) is uniquely solvable [20].

i​δt​ejn=[−12​δx2+Vj]​ejn+1+ejn−12+ξjn+ηjn,j∈𝒯M,n≥1,i\delta_{t}e_{j}^{n}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right]\frac{e_{j}^{n+1}+e_{j}^{n-1}}{2}+\xi_{j}^{n}+\eta^{n}_{j},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\quad n\geq 1, (4.48)

with positive constants C4>0C_{4}>0 and C5>0C_{5}>0 independent of τ\tau and hh. In view of the discrete Gronwall inequality [76, 106, 20] and noticing ‖e0‖2=0\|e^{0}\|_{2}=0 and ‖e1‖2≲h2+τ2\|e^{1}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2}, we immediately obtain ‖en‖2≲h2+τ2\|e^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2} for n=mn=m.

For the semi-H1H^{1} norm, define the discrete linear energy for en∈XMe^{n}\in X_{M} as

ℰ⁡(en)=12​‖δx+​en‖2+‖en‖V2.\displaystyle{{\mathcal{E}}}(e^{n})=\frac{1}{2}\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{n}\|_{2}+\|e^{n}\|_{V}^{2}. (4.52)

Multiplying both sides of (4.48) by ejn+1−ejn−1¯\overline{e_{j}^{n+1}-e_{j}^{n-1}}, summing over index j∈𝒯Mj\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M} and performing summation by parts, taking real part, we have

ℰ⁡(en+1)−ℰ⁡(en−1)=−2​Re​⟨ξn+ηn,en+1−en−1⟩,1≤n≤m−1.\displaystyle{{\mathcal{E}}}(e^{n+1})-{{\mathcal{E}}}(e^{n-1})=-2\;{\rm Re}\left\langle\xi^{n}+\eta^{n},e^{n+1}-e^{n-1}\right\rangle,\qquad 1\leq n\leq m-1. (4.53)

ejn+1−ejn−1=−2​i​τ​[ξjn+ηjn+χjn],j∈𝒯M,\displaystyle e_{j}^{n+1}-e_{j}^{n-1}=-2i\tau\left[\xi_{j}^{n}+\eta_{j}^{n}+\chi_{j}^{n}\right],\qquad j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}, (4.54)

where χn∈XM\chi^{n}\in X_{M} is defined as

χjn=[−12​δx2+Vj]​ejn+1+ejn−12,j∈𝒯M,\displaystyle\chi_{j}^{n}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right]\frac{e_{j}^{n+1}+e_{j}^{n-1}}{2},\qquad j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}, (4.55)

then plugging (4.54) into (4.53), we obtain

ℰ⁡(en+1)−ℰ⁡(en−1)\displaystyle{{\mathcal{E}}}(e^{n+1})-{{\mathcal{E}}}(e^{n-1}) =\displaystyle= −4​τ​Im​⟨ξn+ηn,ξn+ηn+χn⟩\displaystyle-4\tau\,{\rm Im}\left\langle\xi^{n}+\eta^{n},\xi^{n}+\eta^{n}+\chi^{n}\right\rangle (4.56)
=\displaystyle= −4​τ​Im​⟨ξn+ηn,χn⟩,1≤n≤m−1.\displaystyle-4\tau\,{\rm Im}\left\langle\xi^{n}+\eta^{n},\chi^{n}\right\rangle,\quad 1\leq n\leq m-1.

From (4.55), (4.49) and summation by parts, we have

|⟨ξn,χn⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\xi^{n},\chi^{n}\right\rangle\right| =\displaystyle= 12​|⟨ξn,(−12​δx2+V)​(en+1+en−1)⟩|\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left|\left\langle\xi^{n},\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V\right)\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right| (4.57)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim |⟨δx+​ξn,δx+​(en+1+en−1)⟩|+|⟨ξn,V⁡(en+1+en−1)⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\delta_{x}^{+}\xi^{n},\delta_{x}^{+}\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right|+\left|\left\langle\xi^{n},V\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right|
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖δx+​en+1‖22+‖δx+​en‖22+‖δx+​en−1‖22+‖en+1‖22+‖en‖22+‖en−1‖22\displaystyle\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}
+‖δx+​ξn‖22+‖ξn‖22\displaystyle+\|\delta^{+}_{x}\xi^{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\xi^{n}\|_{2}^{2}
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖δx+​en+1‖22+‖δx+​en‖22+‖δx+​en−1‖22,1≤n≤m.\displaystyle\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad 1\leq n\leq m.\qquad

Similarly, noticing (4.50), (4.41) and (4.43), we have

|⟨ηn,χn⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\eta^{n},\chi^{n}\right\rangle\right| =12​|⟨ηn,(−12​δx2+V)​(en+1+en−1)⟩|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left|\left\langle\eta^{n},\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V\right)\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right| (4.58)
≲|⟨δx+​ηn,δx+​(en+1+en−1)⟩|+|⟨ηn,V⁡(en+1+en−1)⟩|\displaystyle\lesssim\left|\left\langle\delta_{x}^{+}\eta^{n},\delta_{x}^{+}\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right|+\left|\left\langle\eta^{n},V\left(e^{n+1}+e^{n-1}\right)\right\rangle\right|
≲‖δx+​en+1‖22+‖δx+​en‖22+‖δx+​en−1‖22+‖en+1‖22+‖en‖22+‖en−1‖22\displaystyle\lesssim\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}
+‖δx+​ηn‖22+‖ηn‖22\displaystyle\quad+\|\delta^{+}_{x}\eta^{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\eta^{n}\|_{2}^{2}
≲‖δx+​en+1‖22+‖δx+​en‖22+‖δx+​en−1‖22+(τ2+h2)2,1≤n≤m.\displaystyle\lesssim\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}+(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2},\quad 1\leq n\leq m.

Plugging (4.57) and (4.58) into (4.56), we get

ℰ⁡(en+1)−ℰ⁡(en−1)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(e^{n+1})-\mathcal{E}(e^{n-1}) ≲τ​(τ2+h2)2+τ⁡[‖δx+​en+1‖22+‖δx+​en‖22+‖δx+​en−1‖22]\displaystyle\lesssim\tau(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2}+\tau\left[\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n}\|^{2}_{2}+\|\delta^{+}_{x}e^{n-1}\|_{2}^{2}\right]
≲τ​(τ2+h2)2+τ⁡[ℰ⁡(en+1)+ℰ⁡(en)+ℰ⁡(en−1)], 1≤n≤m.\displaystyle\lesssim\tau(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2}+\tau\left[\mathcal{E}(e^{n+1})+\mathcal{E}(e^{n})+\mathcal{E}(e^{n-1})\right],\ 1\leq n\leq m.

Summing above inequality for 1≤n≤m−11\leq n\leq m-1, we get

ℰ⁡(en+1)+ℰ⁡(en)≲T​(τ2+h2)2+ℰ⁡(e1)+ℰ⁡(e0)+τ​∑l=1n+1ℰ⁡(el),1≤n≤m−1.\mathcal{E}(e^{n+1})+\mathcal{E}(e^{n})\lesssim T(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2}+\mathcal{E}(e^{1})+\mathcal{E}(e^{0})+\tau\sum_{l=1}^{n+1}\mathcal{E}(e^{l}),\qquad 1\leq n\leq m-1.

Using the discrete Gronwall inequality [20, 76], we have

ℰ⁡(en+1)+ℰ⁡(en)≲(τ2+h2)2+ℰ⁡(e1)+ℰ⁡(e0)≲(τ2+h2)2,1≤n≤m−1.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(e^{n+1})+\mathcal{E}(e^{n})\lesssim(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2}+\mathcal{E}(e^{1})+\mathcal{E}(e^{0})\lesssim(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2},\qquad 1\leq n\leq m-1. (4.59)

Thus ℰ⁡(em)≲(τ2+h2)2{\mathcal{E}}(e^{m})\lesssim(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2} and

‖δx+​em‖22≤ℰ⁡(em)+‖V‖L∞​(U)​‖em‖22≲(τ2+h2)2.\displaystyle\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{m}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\mathcal{E}(e^{m})+\|V\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}\|e^{m}\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim(\tau^{2}+h^{2})^{2}. (4.60)

In view of the discrete Sobolev inequality, we get

‖em‖∞≲‖δx+​em‖2≲τ2+h2.\displaystyle\|e^{m}\|_{\infty}\lesssim\|\delta_{x}^{+}e^{m}\|_{2}\lesssim\tau^{2}+h^{2}. (4.61)

Noticing that in all the above inequalities, the appearing constants are independent of hh and τ\tau. Hence, for sufficiently small τ\tau and hh, we conclude that

‖ψm‖∞≤‖ψ⁡(⋅,tm)‖L∞​(U)+‖em‖∞≤M1+1.\displaystyle\|\psi^{m}\|_{\infty}\leq\|\psi(\cdot,t_{m})\|_{L^{\infty}(U)}+\|e^{m}\|_{\infty}\leq M_{1}+1. (4.62)

This completes the proof of (4.35) at n=mn=m. Therefore the result is proved by mathematical induction.

For the case of assumption (4.33) and V∈C1V\in C^{1} without further assumptions, we will lose half order convergence rate in the semi-H1H^{1} norm because of the boundary (4.42). Notice that the reminder term is O​(h2+τ2)3/2O(h^{2}+\tau^{2})^{3/2} instead of O⁡(h2+τ2)O(h^{2}+\tau^{2}) in (4.58), and that the remaining proof is the same. Hence, we will have the 3/23/2 order convergence rate for discrete semi-H1H^{1} norm. The proof is complete.

Remark 4.2.

Here we emphasis that the above approach can be extended to the higher dimensions, e.g. 2D and 3D, directly. The key point is the discrete Sobolev inequality in 2D and 3D as

∥uh∥∞≤C|lnh|∥uh∥Hs1,∥vh∥∞≤Ch−1/2∥vh∥Hs1,\displaystyle\|u_{h}\|_{\infty}\leq C|\ln h|\,\|u_{h}\|_{H^{1}_{s}},\qquad\|v_{h}\|_{\infty}\leq Ch^{-1/2}\|v_{h}\|_{H^{1}_{s}}, (4.63)

where uhu_{h} and vhv_{h} are 2D and 3D mesh functions with zero at the boundary, respectively, and the discrete semi-H1H^{1} norm ∥⋅∥Hs1\|\cdot\|_{H_{s}^{1}} and l∞l^{\infty} norm ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} can be defined similarly as the discrete semi-H1H^{1} norm and the l∞l^{\infty} norm in (3.27). The same proof works in 2D and 3D, with the above Sobolev inequalities and the additional technical assumption τ=o⁡(1/|ln⁡h|)\tau=o(1/|\ln h|) in 2D and τ=o⁡(h1/3)\tau=o(h^{1/3}) in 3D.

4.4.2. Convergence rate for CNFD

Let ψn∈XM\psi^{n}\in X_{M} be the numerical solution of the CNFD (4.18) and en∈XMe^{n}\in X_{M} be the error function.

Lemma 4.3.

(Conservation of mass and energy) For the CNFD scheme (4.18) with (4.19) and (4.20), for any mesh size h>0h>0, time step τ>0\tau>0 and initial data ψ0\psi_{0}, it conserves the mass and energy in the discretized level, i.e.

∥ψn∥22≡∥ψ0∥22,Eh(ψn)≡Eh(ψ0),n=0,1,2,…,\displaystyle\|\psi^{n}\|_{2}^{2}\equiv\|\psi^{0}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad E_{h}(\psi^{n})\equiv E_{h}(\psi^{0}),\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots\;, (4.64)

where the discrete energy is given by

Eh​(ψn)=12​‖δx+​ψn‖22+‖ψn‖V2+β2​‖ψn‖44.\displaystyle E_{h}(\psi^{n})=\frac{1}{2}\|\delta_{x}^{+}\psi^{n}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\psi^{n}\|_{V}^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\|\psi^{n}\|_{4}^{4}. (4.65)
Proof.

Follow the analogous arguments of the CNFD method for the NLSE [77, 106] and we omit the details here for brevity.

For the solvability, we have

Lemma 4.4.

(Solvability of the difference equations) For any given ψn\psi^{n}, there exists a unique solution ψn+1\psi^{n+1} of the CNFD discretization (4.18) with (4.19).

Proof.

The proof is standard [10, 20]. In higher dimensions (2D and 3D), additional assumption is needed for uniqueness, i.e., time step τ\tau is sufficiently small compared with mesh size.

Denote the local truncation error η~n∈XM\widetilde{\eta}^{n}\in X_{M} (n≥0n\geq 0) of the CNFD scheme (4.18) with (4.19) and (4.20) as

η~jn:\displaystyle\widetilde{\eta}_{j}^{n}: =\displaystyle= i​δt+​ψ​(xj,tn)−[−12​δx2+Vj+β2​(|ψ⁡(xj,tn+1)|2+|ψ⁡(xj,tn)|2)]\displaystyle i\delta_{t}^{+}\psi(x_{j},t_{n})-\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}+\frac{\beta}{2}\left(|\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})|^{2}+|\psi(x_{j},t_{n})|^{2}\right)\right] (4.66)
×ψ⁡(xj,tn)+ψ⁡(xj,tn+1)2,j∈𝒯M.\displaystyle\times\frac{\psi(x_{j},t_{n})+\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})}{2},\qquad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}.

Similar to Lemma 4.2, we have

Lemma 4.5.

(Local truncation error) Assume V⁡(𝐱)∈C⁡(U¯)V(\mathbf{x})\in C({\overline{U}}) and under assumption (4.33), we have

‖η~n‖∞≲τ2+h2,0≤n≤Tτ−1.\displaystyle\|\widetilde{\eta}^{n}\|_{\infty}\lesssim\tau^{2}+h^{2},\qquad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1. (4.67)

In addition, assuming V​(𝐱)∈C1​(U¯)V(\mathbf{x})\in C^{1}({\overline{U}}), we have for 1≤n≤Tτ−11\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1

|δx+​η~jn|≲{τ2+h2,1≤j≤M−2,τ+h,j=0,M−1.\displaystyle|\delta_{x}^{+}\widetilde{\eta}_{j}^{n}|\lesssim\begin{cases}\tau^{2}+h^{2},&1\leq j\leq M-2,\\ \tau+h,&j=0,M-1.\end{cases} (4.68)

In addition, if either ∂nV⁡(x)|Γ=0\partial_{n}V(x)|_{\Gamma}=0 or ψ∈C0​([0,T],H02​(U))\psi\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{2}_{0}(U)), we have

‖δx+​η~n‖∞≲τ2+h2,1≤n≤Tτ−1.\displaystyle\|\delta_{x}^{+}\widetilde{\eta}^{n}\|_{\infty}\lesssim\tau^{2}+h^{2},\qquad 1\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1. (4.69)

One main difficulty in deriving error bounds for CNFD in high dimensions is the l∞l^{\infty} bounds for the finite difference solutions. In [20, 177, 10], this difficulty was overcome by truncating the nonlinearity to a global Lipschitz function with compact support in dd-dimensions (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3). This cutoff would not change ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t) and ψn\psi^{n} if the continuous solution ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t) is bounded and the numerical solution ψn\psi^{n} is close to the continuous solution, i.e., if (4.36) or (4.37) holds.

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

As in the proof of Theorem 4.1, we only prove the optimal convergence under assumptions (4.33) with either ∂nV⁡(x)|Γ=0\partial_{n}V(x)|_{\Gamma}=0 or ψ∈C0​([0,T],H02​(U))\psi\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{2}_{0}(U)). Choose a smooth function ρ​(s)∈C∞​(ℝ)\rho(s)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) such that

ρ⁡(s)={1,0≤|s|≤1,∈[0,1],1≤|s|≤2,0,|s|≥2.\displaystyle\rho(s)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}1,&0\leq|s|\leq 1\,,\\ \in[0,1],&1\leq|s|\leq 2\,,\\ 0,&|s|\geq 2\,.\\ \end{array}\right. (4.70)

Let us denote B=(M1+1)2B=(M_{1}+1)^{2} and denote

fB(s)=ρ(s/B)s,s∈ℝ,\displaystyle f_{{}_{B}}(s)=\rho(s/B)s,\qquad s\in\mathbb{R}, (4.71)

then fB∈C0∞(ℝ)f_{{}_{B}}\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}). Choose ϕ0=ψ0∈XM\phi^{0}=\psi^{0}\in X_{M} and define ϕn∈XM\phi^{n}\in X_{M} (n≥1n\geq 1) as

iδt+ϕjn=[−12δx2+Vj+β2(fB(|ϕjn+1|2)+fB(|ϕjn|2))]ϕjn+1/2,j∈𝒯M,i\delta_{t}^{+}\phi_{j}^{n}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}+\frac{\beta}{2}\left(f_{{}_{B}}(|\phi_{j}^{n+1}|^{2})+f_{{}_{B}}\left(|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2}\right)\right)\right]\phi_{j}^{n+1/2},\quad j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}, (4.72)

where

ϕjn+1/2=12​(ϕjn+1+ϕjn),j∈𝒯M0,n≥0.\displaystyle\phi^{n+1/2}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}(\phi^{n+1}_{j}+\phi^{n}_{j}),\qquad j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}^{0},\quad n\geq 0. (4.73)

In fact, ϕn\phi^{n} can be viewed as another approximation of ψ⁡(x,tn)\psi(x,t_{n}). Define the ‘error’ function e^n∈XM\hat{e}^{n}\in X_{M} (n≥0n\geq 0) with components e^jn=ψ⁡(xj,tn)−ϕjn\hat{e}_{j}^{n}=\psi(x_{j},t_{n})-\phi_{j}^{n} for j∈𝒯M0j\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{M}^{0} and denote the local truncation error η^n∈XM\hat{\eta}^{n}\in X_{M} as

η^jn\displaystyle\hat{\eta}_{j}^{n} :⁣=\displaystyle:= iδt+ψ(xj,tn)−[−12δx2+Vj+β2(fB(|ψ(xj,tn+1)|2)+fB(|ψ(xj,tn)|2))]\displaystyle i\delta_{t}^{+}\psi(x_{j},t_{n})-\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}+\frac{\beta}{2}\left(f_{{}_{B}}(|\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})|^{2})+f_{{}_{B}}(|\psi(x_{j},t_{n})|^{2})\right)\right] (4.74)
×ψ⁡(xj,tn)+ψ⁡(xj,tn+1)2,j∈𝒯M,n≥0.\displaystyle\times\frac{\psi(x_{j},t_{n})+\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})}{2},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\ n\geq 0.

Similar as Lemma 4.5, we can prove

‖η^n‖∞+‖δx+​η^n‖∞≲τ2+h2,0≤n≤Tτ−1.\displaystyle\|\hat{\eta}^{n}\|_{\infty}+\|\delta_{x}^{+}\hat{\eta}^{n}\|_{\infty}\lesssim\tau^{2}+h^{2},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1. (4.75)

Subtracting (4.74) from (4.72), we obtain

i​δt+​e^jn\displaystyle i\delta^{+}_{t}\hat{e}_{j}^{n} =\displaystyle= [−12​δx2+Vj]​e^jn+1/2+ξ^jn+η^jn,j∈𝒯M,n≥0,\displaystyle\left[-\frac{1}{2}\delta_{x}^{2}+V_{j}\right]\hat{e}_{j}^{n+1/2}+\hat{\xi}_{j}^{n}+\hat{\eta}_{j}^{n},\quad j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M},\ n\geq 0, (4.76)

where ξ^n∈XM\hat{\xi}^{n}\in X_{M} defined as

ξ^jn=\displaystyle\hat{\xi}_{j}^{n}= β2​(|ψ⁡(xj,tn+1)|2+|ψ⁡(xj,tn)|2)​ψ⁡(xj,tn+1)+ψ⁡(xj,tn)2\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{2}\left(|\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})|^{2}+|\psi(x_{j},t_{n})|^{2}\right)\frac{\psi(x_{j},t_{n+1})+\psi(x_{j},t_{n})}{2} (4.77)
−β2(fB(|ϕjn+1|2)+fB(|ϕjn|2))ϕjn+1/2,j∈𝒯M0.\displaystyle-\frac{\beta}{2}\left(f_{{}_{B}}(|\phi_{j}^{n+1}|^{2})+f_{{}_{B}}(|\phi_{j}^{n}|^{2})\right)\phi_{j}^{n+1/2},\ j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{M}^{0}. (4.78)

Recalling that fB∈C0∞f_{{}_{B}}\in C_{0}^{\infty}, for 0≤n≤Tτ−10\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1, we can show that [20]

‖ξ^n‖2≲∑k=n,n+1‖e^k‖2,‖δx+​ξ^n‖2≲∑k=n,n+1(‖e^k‖2+‖δx+​e^k‖2).\displaystyle\|\hat{\xi}^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim\sum\limits_{k=n,n+1}\|\hat{e}^{k}\|_{2},\quad\|\delta_{x}^{+}\hat{\xi}^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim\sum\limits_{k=n,n+1}\left(\|\hat{e}^{k}\|_{2}+\|\delta_{x}^{+}\hat{e}^{k}\|_{2}\right). (4.79)

This property is similar to that of the SIFD case (4.50). The same proof for Theorem 4.1 works. However, there is no need to use mathematical induction here, as C0∞C_{0}^{\infty} property of fBf_{{}_{B}} guarantees (4.79). For simplicity, we omit the details here. Finally, we derive the following for sufficiently small hh and τ\tau,

‖e^n‖2+‖δx+​e^n‖2≲h2+τ2,‖ϕn‖∞≤M1+1,0≤n≤Tτ.\displaystyle\|\hat{e}^{n}\|_{2}+\|\delta_{x}^{+}\hat{e}^{n}\|_{2}\lesssim h^{2}+\tau^{2},\quad\|\phi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq M_{1}+1,\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}. (4.80)

From (4.80), we know that (4.72) collapses to CNFD (4.18), i.e., ψn=ϕn\psi^{n}=\phi^{n}. Thus, we prove error estimates (4.37) for CNFD (4.18).

Again, for the case of assumption (4.33) and V∈C1V\in C^{1} without further assumptions, we will lose half order convergence rate in the semi-H1H^{1} norm.

Remark 4.3.

If the cubic nonlinear term β​|ψ|2​ψ\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi in (4.1) is replaced by a general nonlinearity f⁡(|ψ|2)​ψf(|\psi|^{2})\psi, the numerical discretization CNFD and its error estimates in l2l^{2}-norm, l∞l^{\infty}-norm and discrete H1H^{1}-norm are still valid provided that the nonlinear real-valued function f⁡(ρ)∈C3​([0,∞))f(\rho)\in C^{3}([0,\infty)). The higher dimensional case (2D or 3D) is the same as Remark 4.2.

4.5. Error estimates for TSSP

From now on, we investigate the error bounds for time-splitting method. In the last decade, there have been many studies on the analysis of the splitting error for Schrödinger equations [54, 139, 176, 145, 88]. For NLSE, Besse et al. obtained order estimates for the Strang splitting error [54]. Later, Lubich introduced formal Lie derivatives to estimate the Strang splitting error [139]. The formal Lie calculus enables a systematical approach for studying splitting schemes.

In our consideration of the TSSP (4.16) for solving the GPE (4.1), we will restrict ourselves to certain subspaces of H01​(U)H_{0}^{1}(U). Let ϕ⁡(x)∈Hm​(U)∩H01​(U)\phi(x)\in H^{m}(U)\cap H_{0}^{1}(U) be represented in sine series as

ϕ⁡(x)=∑l=1+∞ϕ^l​sin⁡(μl​(x−a)),x∈U=(a,b),\displaystyle\phi(x)=\sum\limits_{l=1}^{+\infty}\widehat{\phi}_{l}\sin(\mu_{l}(x-a)),\qquad x\in U=(a,b), (4.81)

with ϕ^l\widehat{\phi}_{l} given in (3.36), define the subspace Hsinm​(U)⊂Hm∩H01H_{\sin}^{m}(U)\subset H^{m}\cap H_{0}^{1} equipped with the norm

‖ϕ‖Hsinm​(U)=(∑l=1∞μl2​m​|ϕ^l|2)12,\displaystyle\|\phi\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}(U)}=\left(\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\mu_{l}^{2m}|\widehat{\phi}_{l}|^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}, (4.82)

which is equivalent to the HmH^{m} norm in this subspace. We notice that Hsinm(U)={ϕ∈Hm(U)|∂x2​kϕ(a)=∂x2​kϕ(b)=0,0≤2k<m,k∈ℤ}H_{\sin}^{m}(U)=\{\phi\in H^{m}(U)|\partial_{x}^{2k}\phi(a)=\partial_{x}^{2k}\phi(b)=0,\quad 0\leq 2k<m,\,k\in\mathbb{Z}\}. It is easy to see that ei​t​Δe^{it\Delta} will preserve the HsinmH_{\sin}^{m} norm.

The TSSP (4.16) can be thought as the full discretization of the following semi-discretization scheme. Let ψ[n]​(x)\psi^{[n]}(x) be the numerical approximation of ψ⁡(x,tn)\psi(x,t_{n}). From time t=tnt=t_{n} to t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, we use the standard Strang splitting:

ψ{1}(x)=ei​τ​Δ/4ψ[n](x),ψ{2}(x)=e−i⁡(V⁡(x)+β​|ψ{1}​(x)|2)​τψ{1}(x),ψ[n+1](x)=ei​τ​Δ/4ψ{2}(x),x∈U.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\psi^{\{1\}}(x)=e^{i\tau\Delta/4}\psi^{[n]}(x),\quad\psi^{\{2\}}(x)=e^{-i(V(x)+\beta|\psi^{\{1\}}(x)|^{2})\tau}\;\psi^{\{1\}}(x),\\ &\psi^{[n+1]}(x)=e^{i\tau\Delta/4}\psi^{\{2\}}(x),\qquad x\in U.\end{split} (4.83)

In order to guarantee that e−i​τ​(V+β​|ϕ|2)​ϕe^{-i\tau(V+\beta|\phi|^{2})}\phi is a flow in HsinmH_{\sin}^{m}, we make the following assumptions on the potential V⁡(x)V(x)

V⁡(x)∈Hm​(U)and∂xV⁡(x)∈Hsinm−1​(U),m≥1.\displaystyle V(x)\in H^{m}(U)\quad\text{and}\quad\partial_{x}V(x)\in H_{\sin}^{m-1}(U),\quad m\geq 1. (4.84)

To derive the optimal error bounds, we make the following assumption on the exact solution ψ\psi, i.e., let 0<T<Tmax0<T<T_{\rm max} with TmaxT_{\rm max} the maximal existing time of the solution [73, 173]:

ψ∈C⁡([0,T],Hm​(U)∩H01​(U)).\displaystyle\psi\in C\left([0,T];H^{m}(U)\cap H_{0}^{1}(U)\right). (4.85)

It is easy to get that ψ\psi is actually in HsinmH_{\sin}^{m} under assumptions (4.84) and (4.85), by showing that ∂x2​kψ|Γ=0\partial_{x}^{2k}\psi|_{\Gamma}=0 (0≤2​k<m0\leq 2k<m) from the GPE (4.1).

Now, we could state the error estimates for the TSSP (4.16).

Theorem 4.3.

Let ψn∈XM\psi^{n}\in X_{M} be the numerical approximation obtained by the TSSP (4.16). Under assumptions (4.84) and (4.85), there exist constants 0<τ0,h0≤10<\tau_{0},h_{0}\leq 1, such that if 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0}, 0<τ≤τ00<\tau\leq\tau_{0} and m≥5m\geq 5, we have

∥ψ(x,tn)−IM(ψn)(x)∥L2​(U)≲hm+τ2,∥ψn∥∞≤M1+1,∥∇(ψ(x,tn)−IM(ψn)(x))∥L2​(U)≲hm−1+τ2,0≤n≤Tτ,\begin{split}&\|\psi(x,t_{n})-I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x)\|_{L^{2}(U)}\lesssim h^{m}+\tau^{2},\qquad\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq M_{1}+1,\\ &\|\nabla(\psi(x,t_{n})-I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x))\|_{L^{2}(U)}\lesssim h^{m-1}+\tau^{2},\qquad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau},\end{split} (4.86)

where the interpolation operator IMI_{M} is given in (3.30) and M1=maxt∈[0,T]⁡‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞M_{1}=\max_{t\in[0,T]}\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}}.

By Parseval’s identity, we can easily get the following.

Lemma 4.6.

(Conservation of mass) The TSSP (4.16) conserves the total mass, i.e.,

‖ψn‖22=‖ψ0‖22,n≥1.\displaystyle\|\psi^{n}\|_{2}^{2}=\|\psi^{0}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad n\geq 1. (4.87)

The proof of Theorem 4.3 is separated into two steps. The first step is to establish the error estimates for semi-discretization (4.83). Then we analyze the error between the semi-discretization (4.83) and the full discretization TSSP (4.16).

The H1H^{1} error bound for the semi-discretization (4.83) is the following.

Theorem 4.4.

Let ψ[n]​(x)\psi^{[n]}(x) be the solution given by the splitting scheme (4.83). Under assumption (4.84) and (4.85) with m≥5m\geq 5, we have ψ[n]​(x)∈Hsinm\psi^{[n]}(x)\in H_{\sin}^{m} and

‖ψ[n]​(x)−ψ⁡(x,tn)‖L2+‖∇(ψ[n]​(x)−ψ⁡(x,tn))‖L2≲τ2,0≤n≤Tτ.\displaystyle\|\psi^{[n]}(x)-\psi(x,t_{n})\|_{L^{2}}+\|\nabla(\psi^{[n]}(x)-\psi(x,t_{n}))\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\tau^{2},\quad 0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}. (4.88)

The semi-discretization (4.83) can be simplified as

ψ[n+1]​(x)=Sτ​(ψ[n]​(x)).\displaystyle\psi^{[n+1]}(x)=S_{\tau}(\psi^{[n]}(x)). (4.89)

Using the fact L∞​(U)⊂H1​(U)L^{\infty}(U)\subset H^{1}(U) and following [139], we would easily obtain the H01H^{1}_{0} stability of the splitting (4.83).

Lemma 4.7.

(H01H_{0}^{1}-conditional L2L^{2}- and H01H_{0}^{1} stability). If ψ,ϕ∈H01​(U)\psi,\phi\in H_{0}^{1}(U) with

‖ψ‖H01≤M2,‖ϕ‖H10≤M2,\displaystyle\|\psi\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\leq M_{2},\quad\|\phi\|_{H^{0}_{1}}\leq M_{2}, (4.90)

then we have

‖Sτ​(ψ)−Sτ​(ϕ)‖L2≤ec0​τ​‖ψ−ϕ‖L2,‖Sτ​(ψ)−Sτ​(ϕ)‖H01≤ec1​τ​‖ψ−ϕ‖H01,\displaystyle\begin{split}\|S_{\tau}(\psi)-S_{\tau}(\phi)\|_{L^{2}}\leq e^{c_{0}\tau}\|\psi-\phi\|_{L^{2}},\\ \|S_{\tau}(\psi)-S_{\tau}(\phi)\|_{H^{1}_{0}}\leq e^{c_{1}\tau}\|\psi-\phi\|_{H^{1}_{0}},\end{split} (4.91)

where c0c_{0} and c1c_{1} depend on M2M_{2}, V⁡(x)V(x) and β\beta.

To prove Theorem 4.4, we need the local error, which is the key point in analyzing time-splitting methods.

Lemma 4.8.

If ψ0∈Hsin5\psi_{0}\in H_{\sin}^{5}, then the error after one step of (4.83) in H01H^{1}_{0} norm is given by

‖ψ[1]​(x)−ψ⁡(x,τ)‖L2+‖∇(ψ[1]​(x)−ψ⁡(x,τ))‖L2≤C​τ3,\displaystyle\|\psi^{[1]}(x)-\psi(x,\tau)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\nabla(\psi^{[1]}(x)-\psi(x,\tau))\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\tau^{3}, (4.92)

where CC only depends on ‖ψ0‖Hsin5\|\psi_{0}\|_{H_{\sin}^{5}}, V⁡(x)V(x) and β\beta.

We use formal Lie derivative calculus to study the local error in Lemma 4.8. For a general differential equation ϕt=F⁡(ϕ)\phi_{t}=F(\phi) (ϕ∈H01\phi\in H_{0}^{1}), denote the evolution operator φFt​(v)\varphi_{F}^{t}(v) as the solution at time tt with initial value ϕ⁡(0)=v\phi(0)=v. The Lie derivative DFD_{F} is given by [139]

(DF​G)​(v)=dd​t​G​(φFt​(v))|t=0=G′​(v)​F​(v),v∈H01​(U),\displaystyle(D_{F}G)(v)=\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}G(\varphi_{F}^{t}(v))\big|_{t=0}=G^{\prime}(v)F(v),\quad v\in H_{0}^{1}(U), (4.93)

where GG is a vector field on H01H^{1}_{0}. Let T^​(ψ)=i2​Δ​ψ\hat{T}(\psi)=\frac{i}{2}\Delta\psi, V^​(ψ)=−i⁡(V⁡(x)+β​|ψ|2)​ψ\hat{V}(\psi)=-i\left(V(x)+\beta|\psi|^{2}\right)\psi and H^=T^+V^\hat{H}=\hat{T}+\hat{V}, and denote DTD_{T}, DVD_{V} and DHD_{H} as the corresponding Lie derivatives (cf. [139]) for T^\hat{T}, V^\hat{V} and H^\hat{H}, respectively. Similar to [139], one can compute the commutator

[T^,V^]​(ψ)=\displaystyle[\hat{T},\hat{V}](\psi)= T^′​(ψ)​V^​(ψ)−V^′​(ψ)​T^​(ψ)\displaystyle\;\hat{T}^{\prime}(\psi)\hat{V}(\psi)-\hat{V}^{\prime}(\psi)\hat{T}(\psi)
=\displaystyle= i2​(−i)​Δ​(V⁡(x)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​ψ)−[−i​V​Δ​ψ​i2−i​β​(2​|ψ|2​Δ​ψ​i2−ψ2​Δ​ψ¯​i2)]\displaystyle\;\frac{i}{2}(-i)\Delta(V(x)\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi)-\left[-iV\Delta\psi\frac{i}{2}-i\beta\left(2|\psi|^{2}\Delta\psi\frac{i}{2}-\psi^{2}\Delta{\overline{\psi}}\frac{i}{2}\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= 12ψΔV+∇V⋅∇ψ+βψ2Δψ¯+32β|∇ψ|2ψ+β2ψ¯∇ψ⋅∇ψ.\displaystyle\;\frac{1}{2}\psi\Delta V+\nabla V\cdot\nabla\psi+\beta\psi^{2}\Delta{\overline{\psi}}+\frac{3}{2}\beta|\nabla\psi|^{2}\psi+\frac{\beta}{2}{\overline{\psi}}\nabla\psi\cdot\nabla\psi.

Under assumption (4.84) on potential V⁡(x)V(x) with m≥5m\geq 5, following analogous arguments in [139], we have

‖[T^,V^]​(ψ)‖H01≤C​‖ψ‖Hsin3​(1+‖ψ‖Hsin32),\displaystyle\|[\hat{T},\hat{V}](\psi)\|_{H^{1}_{0}}\leq C\|\psi\|_{H_{\sin}^{3}}(1+\|\psi\|_{H_{\sin}^{3}}^{2}), (4.94)
‖[T^,[T^,V^]]​(ψ)‖H01≤C​‖ψ‖Hsin5​(1+‖ψ‖Hsin52).\displaystyle\|[\hat{T},[\hat{T},\hat{V}]](\psi)\|_{H^{1}_{0}}\leq C\|\psi\|_{H_{\sin}^{5}}(1+\|\psi\|_{H_{\sin}^{5}}^{2}). (4.95)

Now, we can prove the local error.

Proof of Lemma 4.8.

The proof is analogous to that in section 5 of [139]. Here, we outline the main part. First of all, by using variation of constant formula (or Duhamel’s principle), one can write the error as

ψ[1]​(x)−ψ⁡(x,τ)=τ​f​(τ2)−∫0τf⁡(s)​𝑑s+r2−r1,\displaystyle\psi^{[1]}(x)-\psi(x,\tau)=\tau f\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right)-\int_{0}^{\tau}f(s)ds+r_{2}-r_{1}, (4.96)

where f⁡(s)=exp⁡((τ−s)​DT)​DV​exp⁡(s​DT)​Id​(ψ0)f(s)=\exp((\tau-s)D_{T})D_{V}\exp(sD_{T}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0}) (Id\rm{Id} the identity operator), and the remainder terms,

r2=τ2​∫01(1−θ)​exp⁡(τ2​DT)​exp⁡(θ​τ​DT)​DV2​exp⁡(τ2​DT)​Id​(ψ0)​𝑑θ.\displaystyle r_{2}=\tau^{2}\int_{0}^{1}(1-\theta)\exp(\frac{\tau}{2}D_{T})\exp(\theta\tau D_{T})D_{V}^{2}\exp(\frac{\tau}{2}D_{T}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0})\,d\theta.

For the principal part, we notice that the midpoint rule quadrature leads to

τ​f​(τ2)−∫0τf⁡(s)​𝑑s=τ3​∫01ker⁡(θ)​f′′​(θ​τ)​𝑑θ,\displaystyle\tau f\left(\frac{\tau}{2}\right)-\int_{0}^{\tau}f(s)ds=\tau^{3}\int_{0}^{1}{\rm ker}(\theta)f^{\prime\prime}(\theta\tau)\,d\theta, (4.97)

where ker⁡(θ){\rm ker}(\theta) is the Peano kernel for midpoint rule and [139]

f′′​(s)=ei​τ2​Δ​[T^,[T^,V^]]​(ei​τ−s2​Δ​ψ0).\displaystyle f^{\prime\prime}(s)=e^{i\frac{\tau}{2}\Delta}[\hat{T},[\hat{T},\hat{V}]](e^{i\frac{\tau-s}{2}\Delta}\psi_{0}). (4.98)

Hence the principal part is of order O⁡(τ3)O(\tau^{3}). For r2−r1r_{2}-r_{1}, denote

g⁡(s,σ)=exp⁡((τ−s−σ)​DT)​DV​exp⁡(σ​DT)​DV​exp⁡(s​DT)​Id​(ψ0),\displaystyle g(s,\sigma)=\exp((\tau-s-\sigma)D_{T})D_{V}\exp(\sigma D_{T})D_{V}\exp(sD_{T}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0}), (4.99)

then we have

r2−r1=τ22​g​(τ2,0)−∫0τ∫0τ−sg⁡(s,σ)​𝑑σ​𝑑s+r~2−r~1,\displaystyle r_{2}-r_{1}=\frac{\tau^{2}}{2}g\left(\frac{\tau}{2},0\right)-\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{0}^{\tau-s}g(s,\sigma)\,d\sigma ds+\tilde{r}_{2}-\tilde{r}_{1}, (4.100)

with

r~2=r2−τ22​g​(τ2,0),r~1=r1−∫0τ∫0τ−sg⁡(s,σ)​𝑑σ​𝑑s.\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{2}=r_{2}-\frac{\tau^{2}}{2}g\left(\frac{\tau}{2},0\right),\quad\tilde{r}_{1}=r_{1}-\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{0}^{\tau-s}g(s,\sigma)\,d\sigma ds. (4.101)

For r~1\tilde{r}_{1}, noticing that

exp⁡(τ​DH)​Id​(ψ0)=exp⁡(τ​DT)​Id​(ψ0)+∫0τexp⁡((τ−s)​DH)​DV​exp⁡(s​DT)​Id​(ψ0),\exp(\tau D_{H}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0})=\exp(\tau D_{T}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0})+\int_{0}^{\tau}\exp((\tau-s)D_{H})D_{V}\exp(sD_{T}){\rm Id}(\psi_{0}),

we can derive from the definition of g⁡(s,σ)g(s,\sigma) and the form of r1r_{1} that

‖r~1‖H01≤C~1​τ3.\displaystyle\|\tilde{r}_{1}\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\leq\tilde{C}_{1}\tau^{3}. (4.102)

Similarly, we get ‖r~2‖H01≤C2~​τ3\|\tilde{r}_{2}\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\leq\tilde{C_{2}}\tau^{3}. Here, C~1\tilde{C}_{1} and C~2\tilde{C}_{2} only depend on ‖ψ0‖Hsin3\|\psi_{0}\|_{H_{\sin}^{3}}, VV and β\beta. The remainder term is also a quadrature rule and it follows that

‖τ22​g​(τ2,0)−∫0τ∫0τ−sg⁡(s,σ)​𝑑σ​𝑑s‖H01≤Cr​τ3,\displaystyle\left\|\frac{\tau^{2}}{2}g\left(\frac{\tau}{2},0\right)-\int_{0}^{\tau}\int_{0}^{\tau-s}g(s,\sigma)\,d\sigma ds\right\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\leq C_{r}\tau^{3}, (4.103)

where CrC_{r} depends on ‖ψ0‖Hsin3\|\psi_{0}\|_{H_{\sin}^{3}}, VV and β\beta. Combining the above results together, we can get Lemma 4.8.

Theorem 4.4 can be proved by a combination of Lemmas 4.7 and 4.8, using induction [139], and we omit this part here.

Proof of Theorem 4.3.

Having Theorem 4.4, we only need to compare the full discretization solution IM​(ψn)​(x)I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x) and the semi-discretization solution ψ[n]​(x)\psi^{[n]}(x) (0≤n≤Tτ0\leq n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}),

IM​(ψn)​(x)−ψ[n]​(x)=IM​(ψn)​(x)−PM​(ψ[n]​(x))+PM​(ψ[n]​(x))−ψ[n]​(x).\displaystyle I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x)-\psi^{[n]}(x)=I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}(x))+P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}(x))-\psi^{[n]}(x). (4.104)

From Theorem 4.4, there exists some M2>0M_{2}>0 such that ‖ψ[n]‖Hsinm≤M2\|\psi^{[n]}\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}}\leq M_{2}. Hence

‖PM​(ψ[n]​(x))−ψ[n]​(x)‖L2≲hm,‖∇[PM​(ψ[n]​(x))−ψ[n]​(x)]‖L2≲hm−1.\displaystyle\|P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}(x))-\psi^{[n]}(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim h^{m},\quad\|\nabla[P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}(x))-\psi^{[n]}(x)]\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim h^{m-1}. (4.105)

Denote eIn​(x)=IM​(ψn)​(x)−PM​(ψ[n]​(x))e^{n}_{I}(x)=I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}(x)), then eI0=IM​(ψ0)​(x)−PM​(ψ[0])​(x)e^{0}_{I}=I_{M}(\psi^{0})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{[0]})(x) and

‖eI0​(x)‖L2≲hm,‖∇eI0​(x)‖L2≲hm−1,‖eI0​(x)‖H2≲hm−2.\displaystyle\|e^{0}_{I}(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim h^{m},\qquad\|\nabla e^{0}_{I}(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim h^{m-1},\quad\|e^{0}_{I}(x)\|_{H^{2}}\lesssim h^{m-2}. (4.106)

From the semi-discretization (4.83), there holds

PM(ψ{1})(x)=ei​τ​Δ/4PM(ψ[n]),PM(ψ{2})(x)=PM(e−i⁡(V⁡(x)+β​|ψ{1}|2)​τψ{1})(x),PM(ψ[n+1])(x)=PM(ei​τ​Δ/4ψ{2})(x),x∈U.\begin{split}&P_{M}(\psi^{\{1\}})(x)=e^{i\tau\Delta/4}P_{M}(\psi^{[n]}),\quad P_{M}(\psi^{\{2\}})(x)=P_{M}(e^{-i(V(x)+\beta|\psi^{\{1\}}|^{2})\tau}\;\psi^{\{1\}})(x),\\ &P_{M}(\psi^{[n+1]})(x)=P_{M}(e^{i\tau\Delta/4}\psi^{\{2\}})(x),\qquad x\in U.\end{split}

Similarly, for the TSSP (4.16), there holds

IM(ψ(1))(x)=ei​τ​Δ/4IM(ψn)(x),IM(ψ(2))(x)=IM(e−i⁡(V⁡(x)+β​|ψ(1)​(x)|2)​τψ(1))(x),IM(ψn+1)(x)=ei​τ​Δ/4IM(ψ(2))(x),x∈U.\begin{split}&I_{M}(\psi^{(1)})(x)=e^{i\tau\Delta/4}I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x),\quad I_{M}(\psi^{(2)})(x)=I_{M}(e^{-i(V(x)+\beta|\psi^{(1)}(x)|^{2})\tau}\;\psi^{(1)})(x),\\ &I_{M}(\psi^{n+1})(x)=e^{i\tau\Delta/4}I_{M}(\psi^{(2)})(x),\qquad x\in U.\end{split}

Noticing that ei​τ​Δe^{i\tau\Delta} preserves HsinmH_{\sin}^{m} norm, we find that

‖eIn​(x)‖Hsinm=‖IM​(ψ(1))​(x)−PM​(ψ{1})​(x)‖Hsinm,\displaystyle\|e_{I}^{n}(x)\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}}=\|I_{M}(\psi^{(1)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{1\}})(x)\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}},
‖eIn+1​(x)‖Hsinm=‖IM​(ψ(2))​(x)−PM​(ψ{2})​(x)‖Hsinm.\displaystyle\|e_{I}^{n+1}(x)\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}}=\|I_{M}(\psi^{(2)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{2\}})(x)\|_{H_{\sin}^{m}}.

Following the analogous mathematical induction for SIFD (Theroem 4.1), we can assume that error estimates (4.86) holds for n≤Tτ−1n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1. For n+1n+1, using the techniques and results in [22], we have

‖IM​(ψ(2))​(x)−PM​(ψ{2})​(x)‖L2≲τ​‖IM​(ψ(1))​(x)−PM​(ψ{1})​(x)‖L2+τ​hm,\displaystyle\|I_{M}(\psi^{(2)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{2\}})(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\tau\|I_{M}(\psi^{(1)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{1\}})(x)\|_{L^{2}}+\tau h^{m},
‖IM​(ψ(2))​(x)−PM​(ψ{2})​(x)‖H01≲τ​‖IM​(ψ(1))​(x)−PM​(ψ{1})​(x)‖H01+τ​hm−1.\displaystyle\|I_{M}(\psi^{(2)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{2\}})(x)\|_{H^{1}_{0}}\lesssim\tau\|I_{M}(\psi^{(1)})(x)-P_{M}(\psi^{\{1\}})(x)\|_{H^{1}_{0}}+\tau h^{m-1}.

Hence for n≤Tτ−1n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1,

‖eIn+1​(x)‖L2≲τ​‖eIn​(x)‖L2+τ​hm,‖eIn+1​(x)‖H01≲τ​‖eIn​(x)‖H01+τ​hm−1.\displaystyle\|e_{I}^{n+1}(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\tau\|e^{n}_{I}(x)\|_{L^{2}}+\tau h^{m},\quad\|e_{I}^{n+1}(x)\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\lesssim\tau\|e^{n}_{I}(x)\|_{H_{0}^{1}}+\tau h^{m-1}. (4.107)

Then, mathematical induction and discrete Gronwall inequality would imply that for all n≤Tτ−1n\leq\frac{T}{\tau}-1 and small τ\tau,

‖eIn+1​(x)‖L2≲hm+τ2,‖eIn+1​(x)‖H01≲hm−1+τ2.\displaystyle\|e_{I}^{n+1}(x)\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim h^{m}+\tau^{2},\quad\|e_{I}^{n+1}(x)\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\lesssim h^{m-1}+\tau^{2}. (4.108)

Hence ‖IM​(ψn)​(x)−ψ[n]​(x)‖H01≲hm−1+τ2\|I_{M}(\psi^{n})(x)-\psi^{[n]}(x)\|_{H_{0}^{1}}\lesssim h^{m-1}+\tau^{2}, and discrete Sobolev inequality gives that ‖ψn‖∞≤M1+1\|\psi^{n}\|_{\infty}\leq M_{1}+1 (n≤Tτn\leq\frac{T}{\tau}) (cf. proof of Theorem 4.1). This would complete the proof of Theorem 4.3.

Remark 4.4.

Similar as Remark 4.2, results in Theorem 4.3 can be extended to higher dimensions (2D and 3D) and the proof presented in this section is still valid with small modification of Lemma 4.7, by using the fact that H2​(ℝd)⊂L∞​(ℝd)H^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\subset L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d=2,3d=2,3).

For time splitting Fourier pseudospectral method and time splitting finite difference method (4.17), similar error estimates to Theorem 4.3 can be established.

4.6. Numerical results

In this section, we report numerical results of the proposed numerical methods.

Example 4.1.

1D defocusing condensate, i.e. we choose d=1d=1 and consider GPE

i∂tψ=−12∂x​xψ+x22ψ+β|ψ|2ψ,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}\psi+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi, (4.109)

with positive β=50\beta=50. The initial condition is taken as

ψ(x,0)=1π1/4e−x2/2,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle\psi(x,0)=\frac{1}{\pi^{1/4}}e^{-x^{2}/2},\qquad x\in{\mathbb{R}}. (4.110)

We solve this problem on [−16,16][-16,16], i.e. a=−16a=-16 and b=16b=16 with homogenous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Let ψ\psi be the ‘exact’ solution which is obtained numerically by using TSSP4 (fourth order time-splitting sine pseudospectral method (4.10)) with a very fine mesh and time step, e.g., h=11024h=\frac{1}{1024} and τ=0.0001\tau=0.0001, and ψh,τ\psi_{h,\tau} be the numerical solution obtained by using a method with mesh size hh and time step τ\tau.

First we compare the discretization error in space. We choose a very small time step, e.g., τ=0.0001\tau=0.0001 for CNFD, TSSP4 and TSFD, τ=0.00001\tau=0.00001 for TSSP2 such that the error from the time discretization is negligible compared to the spatial discretization error, and solve the GPE using different methods and various spatial mesh sizes hh. Tab. 4.1 lists the numerical errors ‖ψ⁡(t)−ψh,τ​(t)‖l2\|\psi(t)-\psi_{h,\tau}(t)\|_{l^{2}} at t=1t=1 for various spatial mesh sizes hh.

Secondly, we test the discretization error in time. Tab. 4.2 shows the numerical errors ‖ψ⁡(t)−ψh,τ​(t)‖l2\|\psi(t)-\psi_{h,\tau}(t)\|_{l^{2}} at t=1t=1 with a very small mesh size h=11024h=\frac{1}{1024} for different time steps τ\tau and different numerical methods.

From Tabs. 4.1-4.2, one can make the following observations: (i) Both TSSP2 and TSSP4 are spectral accurate in space and they share the same accuracy for fixed mesh size hh, and resp., TSFD and CNFD are second-order in space and they share the same accuracy for fixed mesh size hh. (ii) TSSP2, TSFD and CNFD are second-order in time and TSSP4 is fourth-order in time. In general, for fixed time step τ\tau, the error from time discretization of TSSP2 is much smaller than that of TSFD and CNFD, and the error from time discretization of TSFD is much smaller than that of CNFD. From our computations, the error bounds for SIFD are similar to CNFD and we omit it here (cf. [21, 20]). For more comparisons, we refer to [42] and references therein.

Among the above numerical methods: (i) TSSP is explicit with computational cost per time step at O⁡(M​ln⁡M)O(M\ln M) with MM the total number of unknowns in 1D, 2D and 3D, TSFD and SIFD are implicit with computational cost per time step O⁡(M)O(M) and O⁡(M​ln⁡M)O(M\ln M) in 1D and 2D/3D, respectively, CNFD is implicit which is the most expensive one since it needs to solve a fully coupled nonlinear system per time step. (ii) The storage requirement of TSSP is little less than those of TSFD, CNFD and SIFD. (iii) TSSP, TSFD and CNFD are unconditionally stable and SIFD is conditionally stable. (iv) TSSP and TSFD are time transverse invariant, where CNFD and SIFD are not. (v) TSSP, TSFD and CNFD conserve the mass in the discretized level, where SIFD doesn’t. (vi) CNFD conserves the energy in the discretized level, where TSSP, TSFD and SIFD don’t. However, when the time step is small, TSSP, TSFD and SIFD conserve the energy very well in practical computation. (vii) Extension of all the numerical methods to 2D and 3D cases is straightforward without additional numerical difficulty. Based on these comparisons, in order to solve the GPE numerically for computing the dynamics of BEC, when the solution is smooth, we recommend to use TSSP method, and resp., when the solution is not very smooth, e.g. with random potential, we recommend to use TSFD.

4.7. Extension to damped Gross-Pitaevskii equations

In section 2.2.3, a damping term is introduced in GPE to describe the collapse of focusing BEC. Our numerical methods can be generalized to this damped GPE easily. For simplicity, we will only consider 1D case and extensions to 2D and 3D are straightforward. For d=1d=1, the general damped NLSE becomes [30, 32]

i​ψt=−12​ψx​x+V⁡(x)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​σ​ψ−i​f​(|ψ|2)​ψ,a<x<b,t>0,\displaystyle i\psi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{xx}+V(x)\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2\sigma}\psi-i\,f(|\psi|^{2})\psi,\quad a<x<b,\quad t>0, (4.111)
ψ⁡(x,t=0)=ψ0​(x),a≤x≤b,ψ⁡(a,t)=ψ⁡(b,t)=0,t≥0.\displaystyle\psi(x,t=0)=\psi_{0}(x),\quad a\leq x\leq b,\qquad\psi(a,t)=\psi(b,t)={0},\quad t\geq 0. (4.112)

Due to the high performance of TSSP (4.16), we will extend it to solve damped GPE and adopt the same notations and mesh strategy. From time t=tnt=t_{n} to time t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, the damped GPE (4.111) is solved in two steps. One solves

i​ψt=−12​ψx​x,i\;\psi_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{xx}, (4.113)

for one time step, followed by solving

i​ψt​(x,t)=V⁡(x)​ψ​(x,t)+β​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2​σ​ψ​(x,t)−i​f​(|ψ⁡(x,t)|2)​ψ​(x,t),i\;\psi_{t}(x,t)=V(x)\psi(x,t)+\beta|\psi(x,t)|^{2\sigma}\psi(x,t)-i\,f(|\psi(x,t)|^{2})\psi(x,t), (4.114)

again for the same time step. Equation (4.113) is discretized in space by the sine-spectral method and integrated in time exactly. For t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}], multiplying the ODE (4.114) by ψ⁡(x,t)¯\overline{\psi(x,t)}, the conjugate of ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t), one obtains

i​ψt​(x,t)​ψ⁡(x,t)¯=V⁡(x)​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2+β​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2​σ+2−i​f​(|ψ⁡(x,t)|2)​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2.i\;\psi_{t}(x,t)\overline{\psi(x,t)}=V(x)|\psi(x,t)|^{2}+\beta|\psi(x,t)|^{2\sigma+2}-i\,f(|\psi(x,t)|^{2})|\psi(x,t)|^{2}. (4.115)

Subtracting the conjugate of Eq. (4.115) from Eq. (4.115) and multiplying by −i-i one obtains

dd​t​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2=ψt​(x,t)¯​ψ​(x,t)+ψt​(x,t)​ψ⁡(x,t)¯=−2​f​(|ψ⁡(x,t)|2)​|ψ⁡(x,t)|2.\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}|\psi(x,t)|^{2}=\overline{\psi_{t}(x,t)}\psi(x,t)+\psi_{t}(x,t)\overline{\psi(x,t)}=-2f(|\psi(x,t)|^{2})|\psi(x,t)|^{2}. (4.116)

Let

g⁡(s)=∫1s​f​(s)​𝑑s,h⁡(s,s′)={g−1​(g⁡(s)−2​s′),s>0,s′≥0,0,s=0,s′≥0.g(s)=\int\frac{1}{s\;f(s)}\;ds,\qquad h(s,s^{\prime})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}g^{-1}\left(g(s)-2s^{\prime}\right),&s>0,\ s^{\prime}\geq 0,\\ 0,&s=0,\ s^{\prime}\geq 0.\end{array}\right.\\ (4.117)

Then, if f⁡(s)≥0f(s)\geq 0 for s≥0s\geq 0, we find

0≤h⁡(s,s′)≤s,fors≥0,s′≥0,0\leq h(s,s^{\prime})\leq s,\qquad\hbox{for}\quad s\geq 0,\quad s^{\prime}\geq 0, (4.118)

0≤ρ⁡(t)\displaystyle 0\leq\rho(t) =\displaystyle= ρ⁡(tn+s′):=|ψ⁡(x,t)|2=h⁡(|ψ⁡(x,tn)|2,t−tn):=h⁡(ρ⁡(tn),s′)\displaystyle\rho(t_{n}+s^{\prime}):=|\psi(x,t)|^{2}=h\left(|\psi(x,t_{n})|^{2},t-t_{n}\right):=h\left(\rho(t_{n}),s^{\prime}\right) (4.119)

For some frequently used damping terms, the integrals in (4.117) and (4.122) can be evaluated analytically (cf. [30]).

5. Theory for rotational BEC

In view of potential applications, the study of quantized vortices, which are related to superfluid properties, is one of the key issues. In fact, bulk superfluids are distinguished from normal fluids by their ability to support dissipationless flow. Such persistent currents are intimately related to the existence of quantized vortices, which are localized phase singularities with integer topological charge [97]. The superfluid vortex is an example of a topological defect that is well known in superconductors and in liquid helium. Currently, one of the most popular ways to generate quantized vortices from BEC ground state is the following: impose a laser beam rotating with an angular velocity on the magnetic trap holding the atoms to create a harmonic anisotropic potential. Various experiments have confirmed the observation of quantized vortices in BEC under a rotational frame [1, 140, 68].

5.1. GPE with an angular momentum rotation term

At temperatures TT much smaller than the critical temperature TcT_{c}, following the mean field theory (cf. section 1.2), BEC in a rotational frame is well described by the macroscopic wave function ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(\mathbf{x},t), whose evolution is governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE) with an angular momentum rotation term [40, 41, 44, 97, 5], (w.l.o.g.) assuming the rotation being around the zz-axis:

i​ℏ​∂ψ⁡(𝐱,t)∂t=(−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+N​g​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2−Ω​Lz)​ψ​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\left(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+Ng|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}-\Omega L_{z}\right)\psi(\mathbf{x},t), (5.1)

where 𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is the spatial coordinate vector,  and

Lz=−iℏ(x∂y−y∂x)\displaystyle L_{z}=-i\hbar\left(x\partial_{y}-y\partial_{x}\right) (5.2)

is the zz-component of the angular momentum operator L=(Lx,Ly,Lz)TL=(L_{x},L_{y},L_{z})^{T} given by L=−i​ℏ​(𝐱∧∇)L=-i\hbar(\mathbf{x}\wedge\nabla). The appearance of the angular momentum term means that we are using a reference frame where the trap is at rest. The energy functional per particle E⁡(ψ)E(\psi) is defined as

E⁡(ψ)=∫ℝ3[ℏ22​m​|∇ψ|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ|2+N​g2​|ψ|4−Ω​ψ¯​Lz​ψ]​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle E(\psi)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\left|\nabla\psi\right|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi|^{2}+\frac{Ng}{2}|\psi|^{4}-\Omega{\overline{\psi}}L_{z}\psi\right]\;d\mathbf{x}, (5.3)

and wave function is normalized as

∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=1.\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\;|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=1. (5.4)

5.1.1. Dimensionless form

For the conventional harmonic potential case, by introducing the dimensionless variables: t→t/ω0t\to t/\omega_{0} with ω0=min⁡{ωx,ωy,ωz}\omega_{0}=\min\{\omega_{x},\omega_{y},\omega_{z}\}, 𝐱→𝐱​xs\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{x}x_{s} with xs=ℏ/m​ω0x_{s}=\sqrt{\hbar/m\omega_{0}}, ψ→ψ/xs3/2\psi\to\psi/x_{s}^{3/2}, Ω→Ω​ω0\Omega\to\Omega\omega_{0} and E⁡(⋅)→ℏ​ω0​Eβ,Ω​(⋅)E(\cdot)\to\hbar\omega_{0}E_{\beta,\Omega}(\cdot), we get the dimensionless GPE

i​∂ψ⁡(𝐱,t)∂t=(−12​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+κ​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2−Ω​Lz)​ψ​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle i\;\frac{\partial\psi(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+\kappa\;|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}-\Omega L_{z}\right)\psi(\mathbf{x},t), (5.5)

where κ=g​Nxs3​ℏ​ω0=4​π​as​Nxs\kappa=\frac{gN}{x_{s}^{3}\hbar\omega_{0}}=\frac{4\pi a_{s}N}{x_{s}}, Lz=−i(x∂y−y∂x)L_{z}=-i(x\partial_{y}-y\partial_{x}) (L=−i⁡(𝐱∧∇)L=-i(\mathbf{x}\wedge\nabla)), V⁡(𝐱)=12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2)V(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right) with γx=ωxω0\gamma_{x}=\frac{\omega_{x}}{\omega_{0}}, γy=ωyω0\gamma_{y}=\frac{\omega_{y}}{\omega_{0}} and γz=ωzω0\gamma_{z}=\frac{\omega_{z}}{\omega_{0}}.

In a disk-shaped condensate with parameters ωx≈ωy\omega_{x}\approx\omega_{y} and ωz≫ωx\omega_{z}\gg\omega_{x} (⟺\Longleftrightarrow γx=1\gamma_{x}=1, γy≈1\gamma_{y}\approx 1 and γz≫1\gamma_{z}\gg 1 with choosing ω0=ωx\omega_{0}=\omega_{x}), the 3D GPE (5.5) can be reduced to a 2D GPE with 𝐱=(x,y)T\mathbf{x}=(x,y)^{T} (cf. section 1.3.3):

i​∂ψ⁡(𝐱,t)∂t=−12​∇2ψ+V2​(x,y)​ψ+c2​κ​|ψ|2​ψ−Ω​Lz​ψ,\displaystyle i\;\frac{\partial\psi(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi+V_{2}(x,y)\psi+c_{2}\kappa|\psi|^{2}\psi-\Omega L_{z}\psi, (5.6)

where c2=γz/2​πc_{2}=\sqrt{\gamma_{z}/2\pi} and V2​(x,y)=12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2)V_{2}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}\right) [44, 46, 20, 97].

Thus here we consider the dimensionless GPE under a rotational frame in dd-dimensions (d=2,3d=2,3):

i​∂ψ⁡(𝐱,t)∂t=−12​∇2ψ+V⁡(𝐱)​ψ+β​|ψ|2​ψ−Ω​Lz​ψ,𝐱∈ℝd,t>0,\displaystyle i\;\frac{\partial\psi(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi+V(\mathbf{x})\psi+\beta|\psi|^{2}\psi-\Omega L_{z}\psi,\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\quad t>0, (5.7)

where

β=κ​{γz/2​π,1,​V​(𝐱)={12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2),d=2,12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2),d=3.\displaystyle\beta=\kappa\begin{cases}\sqrt{\gamma_{z}/2\pi},\\ 1,\end{cases}\,V(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}\right),&d=2,\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}\right),&d=3.\end{cases} (5.8)

Then the dimensionless energy functional per particle Eβ,Ω​(ψ)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\psi) is defined as

Eβ,Ω​(ψ)=∫ℝd[12​|∇ψ​(𝐱,t)|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ|2+β2​|ψ|4−Ω​ψ¯​Lz​ψ]​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle E_{\beta,\Omega}(\psi)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left|\nabla\psi(\mathbf{x},t)\right|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\;|\psi|^{4}-\Omega{\overline{\psi}}\,L_{z}\psi\right]d\mathbf{x}, (5.9)

and the normalization is given by

‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(ℝd)2=‖ψ⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(ℝd)2=1.\displaystyle\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}=\|\psi(\cdot,0)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}^{2}=1. (5.10)

The vortex structure of rotating BEC in 3D is very complicated [4, 97] due to the presence of vortex lines, while in 2D, the structure is relatively simple as the vortex center is only a point. As a result, most investigations start from the 2D case.

5.2. Theory for ground states

Similar to section 2, the ground state wave function ϕg:=ϕg​(𝐱)\phi_{g}:=\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x}) of a rotating BEC satisfies the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (Euler-Lagrange equation)

μϕ(𝐱)=[−12∇2+V(𝐱)+β|ϕ|2−ΩLz]ϕ(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd,d=2,3,\displaystyle\mu\;\phi(\mathbf{x})=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+\beta|\phi|^{2}-\Omega L_{z}\right]\phi(\mathbf{x}),\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\quad d=2,3, (5.11)

under the normalization condition

‖ϕ‖22=∫ℝd|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=1,\displaystyle\|\phi\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\;|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=1, (5.12)

with eigenvalue (or chemical potential) μ\mu given by

μ=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)+β2​∫ℝd|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4​𝑑𝐱.\mu=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi)+\frac{\beta}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left|\phi(\mathbf{x})\right|^{4}\;d\mathbf{x}. (5.13)

The eigenfunction ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi(\mathbf{x}) of (5.11) under the constraint (5.12) with least energy is called ground state. The ground state can be found by minimizing the energy functional Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi) (5.9) over the unit sphere S={ϕ|∥ϕ∥2=1,Eβ,Ω(ϕ)<∞}S=\{\phi\ |\ \|\phi\|_{2}=1,\ E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi)<\infty\}:

(I) Find (μβ,Ωg,ϕg∈S)(\mu_{\beta,\Omega}^{g},\phi_{g}\in S) such that

Eβ,Ωg:=Eβ,Ωg​(ϕg)=minϕ∈S⁡Eβ,Ω​(ϕ),μβ,Ωg:=μβ,Ωg​(ϕg).\displaystyle E^{g}_{\beta,\Omega}:=E_{\beta,\Omega}^{g}(\phi_{g})=\min_{\phi\in S}\;E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi),\quad\mu^{g}_{\beta,\Omega}:=\mu^{g}_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi_{g}). (5.14)

Any eigenfunction ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi(\mathbf{x}) of (5.11) under constraint (5.12) whose energy Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)>Eβ,Ω​(ϕg)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi)>E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi_{g}) is usually called as an excited state in the physics literature.

Existence/nonexistence results of ground state depend on the magnitude |Ω||\Omega| of the angular velocity relative to the trapping frequencies [162, 46, 64].

For the existence and simple properties of ground state for rotating BEC, we have the following [46, 162].

Theorem 5.1.

Suppose that V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is given in (5.8), then we have the conclusions below.

i) In 2D, if ϕβ,Ω​(x,y)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(x,y)\in S is a ground state of the energy functional Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi), then ϕβ,Ω​(x,−y)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(x,-y)\in S and ϕβ,Ω​(−x,y)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(-x,y)\in S are ground states of the energy functional Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi). Furthermore

Eβ,Ωg=Eβ,−Ωg,μβ,Ωg=μβ,−Ωg.\displaystyle E_{\beta,\Omega}^{g}=E_{\beta,-\Omega}^{g},\qquad\mu_{\beta,\Omega}^{g}=\mu_{\beta,-\Omega}^{g}. (5.15)

ii) In 3D, if ϕβ,Ω​(x,y,z)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(x,y,z)\in S is a ground state of the energy functional Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi), then ϕβ,Ω​(x,−y,z)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(x,-y,z)\in S and ϕβ,Ω​(−x,y,z)∈S\phi_{\beta,\Omega}(-x,y,z)\in S are ground states of the energy functional Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi), and (5.15) is also valid.

iii) When |Ω|<min⁡{γx,γy}|\Omega|<\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\} and β≥0\beta\geq 0 in 3D or β>−Cb\beta>-C_{b} in 2D (CbC_{b} given in (2.12)), there exists a minimizer for the minimization problem (5.14), i.e. there exist ground state.

Theorem 5.1 is a direct consequence of the below observation and the theory for non-rotating BEC (cf. section 2).

Lemma 5.1.

Under the conditions of Theorem 5.1, the following results hold.

i) In 2D, we have

Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,−y))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,y)),Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ⁡(−x,y))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,y)),ϕ∈S.E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi(x,-y))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(x,y)),\quad E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi(-x,y))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(x,y)),\quad\phi\in S.

ii) In 3D, we have

Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,−y,z))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,y,z)),Eβ,−Ω​(ϕ⁡(−x,y,z))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(x,y,z)),ϕ∈S.E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi(x,-y,z))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(x,y,z)),\ E_{\beta,-\Omega}(\phi(-x,y,z))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(x,y,z)),\ \phi\in S.

iii) In 2D and 3D, we have

∫ℝd[1−|Ω|2​|∇ϕ​(𝐱)|2+(V⁡(𝐱)−|Ω|2​(x2+y2))​|ϕ|2+β2​|ϕ|4]​𝑑𝐱≤Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left[\frac{1-|\Omega|}{2}\left|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}+\left(V(\mathbf{x})-\frac{|\Omega|}{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})\right)|\phi|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\;|\phi|^{4}\right]d\mathbf{x}\leq E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi) (5.16)
≤\displaystyle\leq ∫ℝd[1+|Ω|2​|∇ϕ​(𝐱)|2+(V⁡(𝐱)+|Ω|2​(x2+y2))​|ϕ|2+β2​|ϕ|4]​𝑑𝐱.\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left[\frac{1+|\Omega|}{2}\left|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x})\right|^{2}+\left(V(\mathbf{x})+\frac{|\Omega|}{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})\right)|\phi|^{2}+\frac{\beta}{2}\;|\phi|^{4}\right]d\mathbf{x}.\qquad

For understanding the uniqueness question, note that Eβ,Ω​(α​ϕβ,Ωg)=Eβ,Ω​(ϕβ,Ωg)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\alpha\phi_{\beta,\Omega}^{g})=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi_{\beta,\Omega}^{g}) for all α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}} with |α|=1|\alpha|=1. Thus an additional constraint has to be introduced to show uniqueness. For non-rotating BEC, i.e. Ω=0\Omega=0, the unique positive minimizer is usually taken as the ground state. In fact, the ground state is unique up to a constant α\alpha with |α|=1|\alpha|=1, i.e. density of the ground state is unique, when Ω=0\Omega=0. For rotating BEC under |Ω|<min⁡{γx,γy}|\Omega|<\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}, the density of the ground state may be no longer unique when |Ω|>Ωc|\Omega|>\Omega^{c} with Ωc\Omega^{c} a critical angular rotation speed.

When rotational speed exceeds the trap frequency in xx- or yy- direction, i.e. Ω>min⁡{γx,γy}\Omega>\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}, there will be no ground state [64, 46].

Theorem 5.2.

(nonexistence) Suppose that V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is given in (5.8), then there exists no minimizer for problem (5.14) if one of the following holds:

(i) β<0\beta<0 in 3D or β<−Cb\beta<-C_{b} (CbC_{b} given in (2.12)) in 2D;

(ii) |Ω|>min⁡{γx,γy}|\Omega|>\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}.

5.3. Critical speeds for quantized vortices

From Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, only the case of 0≤Ω<min⁡{γx,γy}0\leq\Omega<\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\} is interesting for considering the ground state of a rotating BEC and we will assume Ω≥0\Omega\geq 0 in the subsequent discussions. In particular, the vortex appears in the ground state only if the rotational speed exceeds certain critical value. Various experiments and mathematical studies confirm the existence of such critical speeds.

In [162], for a radially symmetric potential in 2D, Seiringer proved that there exists critical velocity Ω0>0\Omega_{0}>0 that a state containing vortices is energetically favorable for Ω>Ω0\Omega>\Omega_{0}. The point is that, as Ω\Omega increases from 0 to min⁡{γx,γy}\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}, the first ground state with vortex should be the central vortex state, i.e., a state containing central vortex (vortex line) in the rotational center (axis).

In 2D with radially symmetric potential V⁡(r)V(r) (r=|𝐱|r=|\mathbf{x}|, 𝐱∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}), the symmetric state (m=0m=0) and central vortex state with index (or winding number or circulation) 0≠m∈ℤ0\neq m\in\mathbb{Z} is the solution of the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (5.11)-(5.13) with the form

ϕ⁡(𝐱)=ϕm​(r)​ei​m​θ,where(r,θ)is the polar coordinate.\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x})=\phi_{m}(r)e^{im\theta},\quad\text{where}\quad(r,\theta)\quad\text{is the polar coordinate}. (5.17)

In polar coordinate, the angular momentum term (5.2) becomes Lz=−i​∂∂θL_{z}=-i\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}. In order to find the above central vortex states with index mm (m≠0m\neq 0), ϕ⁡(𝐱)=ϕm​(r)​ei​m​θ\phi(\mathbf{x})=\phi_{m}(r)e^{im\theta}, we need to find a real nonnegative function ϕm​(r):=ϕβ,Ωm​(r)\phi_{m}(r):=\phi_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(r) which minimizes the energy functional

Eβ,Ωm​(ϕ⁡(r))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(r)​ei​m​θ)\displaystyle E_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(\phi(r))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(r)e^{im\theta}) (5.18)
=\displaystyle= π​∫0∞[|ϕ′​(r)|2+(2​V​(r)+m2r2)​|ϕ⁡(r)|2+β​|ϕ⁡(r)|4−2​m​Ω​|ϕ⁡(r)|2]​r​𝑑r\displaystyle\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\left[|\phi^{\prime}(r)|^{2}+\left(2V(r)+\frac{m^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)|\phi(r)|^{2}+\beta|\phi(r)|^{4}-2m\Omega|\phi(r)|^{2}\right]r\;dr
=\displaystyle= Eβ,0n​(ϕ⁡(r))−m​Ω,Ω≥0,m≥0,\displaystyle E_{\beta,0}^{n}(\phi(r))-m\Omega,\qquad\Omega\geq 0,\quad m\geq 0,

over the set Sr={ϕ(r)∈ℝ| 2π∫0∞|ϕ(r)|2rdr=1,Eβ,0m(ϕ)<∞,ϕ′(0)=0(m=0),and resp.ϕ(0)=0(m≠0)}S_{r}=\{\phi(r)\in{\mathbb{R}}\ |\ 2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}|\phi(r)|^{2}r\;dr=1,\ E_{\beta,0}^{m}(\phi)<\infty,\ \phi^{\prime}(0)=0\ (m=0),\ \hbox{and resp.}\ \phi(0)=0(m\neq 0)\}. The existence and uniqueness of nonnegative minimizer for this minimization problem can be obtained similarly as for the ground state when Ω=0\Omega=0 [133, 162]. It is clear from (5.18) that contribution of rotation in the energy (5.18) is fixed with index mm and the central vortex state with index mm is independent of Ω\Omega. In fact, let us denote

Em​(ϕ⁡(r))=Eβ,Ωm​(ϕ⁡(r))+m​Ω,\displaystyle E^{m}(\phi(r))=E_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(\phi(r))+m\Omega, (5.19)

and the central vortex state can be found as the minimizer of energy Em​(ϕ)E^{m}(\phi) which is independent of Ω\Omega.

Similarly, in order to find the cylindrically symmetric state (m=0m=0), and resp. central vortex line states (m≠0m\neq 0), in 3D with cylindrical symmetry, i.e. d=3d=3 and V⁡(𝐱)=V⁡(r,z)V(\mathbf{x})=V(r,z) in (5.7), we solve the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (5.11)-(5.13) with the special form of wave function as

ϕ⁡(𝐱)=ϕm​(x,y,z)=ϕm​(r,z)​ei​m​θ,\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x})=\phi_{m}(x,y,z)=\phi_{m}(r,z)e^{im\theta}, (5.20)

where (r,θ,z)(r,\theta,z) is the cylindrical coordinate, mm is an integer and called as index when m≠0m\neq 0. ϕm​(r,z)\phi_{m}(r,z) is a real function independent of angle. It is equivalent to computing a real nonnegative function ϕm​(r,z):=ϕβ,Ωm​(r,z)\phi_{m}(r,z):=\phi_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(r,z) which minimizes the energy functional

Eβ,Ωm​(ϕ⁡(r,z))=Eβ,Ω​(ϕ⁡(r,z)​ei​m​θ)\displaystyle E_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(\phi(r,z))=E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi(r,z)e^{im\theta}) (5.21)
=\displaystyle= π​∫0∞∫−∞∞[|∂rϕ|2+|∂zϕ|2+(2​V​(r,z)+m2r2−2​m​Ω)​|ϕ|2+β​|ϕ|4]​r​𝑑z​𝑑r,\displaystyle\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[|\partial_{r}\phi|^{2}+|\partial_{z}\phi|^{2}+\left(2V(r,z)+\frac{m^{2}}{r^{2}}-2m\Omega\right)|\phi|^{2}+\beta|\phi|^{4}\right]r\;dzdr,

over the set Sc={ϕ∈ℝ| 2π∫0∞∫−∞∞|ϕ(r,z)|2rdzdr=1,Eβ,0m(ϕ)<∞,∂rϕ(0,r)=0(m=0),and resp.ϕ(0,z)=0(m≠0),−∞<z<∞}S_{c}=\{\phi\in{\mathbb{R}}\ |\ 2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\phi(r,z)|^{2}r\;dzdr=1,\ E_{\beta,0}^{m}(\phi)<\infty,\ \ \partial_{r}\phi(0,r)=0\ (m=0),\hbox{and resp.}\ \phi(0,z)=0\ (m\neq 0),\;-\infty<z<\infty\}.

For 2D case, by carefully studying the energy functional (5.18), Seiringer [162] established the estimates of critical velocity Ωm\Omega_{m} (m≥0m\geq 0) when a central vortex ϕ⁡(r)\phi(r) with index m+1m+1 is energetically favorable to a central vortex state with index mm for Ω>Ωm\Omega>\Omega_{m}, i.e., Eβ,Ωm+1​(ϕ⁡(r))<Eβ,Ωm​(ϕ⁡(r))E_{\beta,\Omega}^{m+1}(\phi(r))<E_{\beta,\Omega}^{m}(\phi(r)). The critical speed is given by

Ωm=minϕ∈Sr⁡Em+1​(ϕ⁡(r))−minϕ∈Sr⁡Em​(ϕ⁡(r))>0.\displaystyle\Omega_{m}=\min_{\phi\in S_{r}}{E^{m+1}(\phi(r))}-\min_{\phi\in S_{r}}{E^{m}(\phi(r))}>0. (5.22)

The estimates for Ωm\Omega_{m} is the following.

Theorem 5.3.

(cf. [162]) In 2D, assume potential V⁡(r)=12​r2V(r)=\frac{1}{2}r^{2} (r=|𝐱|r=|\mathbf{x}|, 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), for positive β>0\beta>0 and m≥0m\geq 0, then the following bounds on Ωm\Omega_{m} hold,

Ωm≤(2​m+1)​2​π​eβ​(1+2​βπ)​(3+[ln⁡(β/(2​π​e2))]),\displaystyle\Omega_{m}\leq(2m+1)\frac{2\pi e}{\beta}\left(1+\sqrt{\frac{2\beta}{\pi}}\right)\left(3+\left[\ln(\beta/(2\pi e^{2}))\right]\right), (5.23)
Ωm≥2​m+1(m+2)​1+βbm+1​(m+2),\displaystyle\Omega_{m}\geq\frac{2m+1}{(m+2)\sqrt{1+\frac{\beta}{b_{m+1}(m+2)}}}, (5.24)

where bm=2×4m​π​(m!)2(2​m)!b_{m}=\frac{2\times 4^{m}\pi(m!)^{2}}{(2m)!}. In addition, there is a relation between the critical velocities as Ωm+1≤2​m+32​m+1​Ωm\Omega_{m+1}\leq\frac{2m+3}{2m+1}\Omega_{m}.

In particular, we notice that Ω0\Omega_{0} is the critical velocity for the appearance of vortex in the ground state. For large Ω\Omega, the central vortex state (5.17) will no longer be the right ansatz for ground state due to the symmetry breaking [162].

Theorem 5.4.

(cf. [162]) In 2D, assume potential V⁡(r)=12​γr2​r2V(r)=\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{r}^{2}r^{2} (r=|𝐱|r=|\mathbf{x}|, 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), for fixed rotational speed 0<Ω<γr0<\Omega<\gamma_{r}, there exists a constant βΩ\beta_{\Omega}, such that if β≥βΩ\beta\geq\beta_{\Omega}, no ground state of problem (5.14) is an eigenfunction of the angular momentum operator LzL_{z} (5.2). Let ϕg\phi_{g} be the ground state of (5.14) when β≥βΩ\beta\geq\beta_{\Omega}, then |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is not radially symmetric.

For small rotational speed Ω\Omega with radial potential V⁡(r)V(r), the minimizer of problem (5.14) remains the same as the ground state of the non-rotating case, i.e., the ground state of small Ω\Omega is the same as that of Ω=0\Omega=0. This observation is recently proved rigourously by Aftalion et al. [7].

Theorem 5.5.

(cf. [7]) In 2D, assuming potential V⁡(r)=12​γr2​r2V(r)=\frac{1}{2}\gamma_{r}^{2}r^{2} (r=|𝐱|r=|\mathbf{x}|, 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), let ϕβ,Ωg​(𝐱)\phi^{g}_{\beta,\Omega}(\mathbf{x}) be the solution of the minimization problem (5.14) with rotational speed Ω\Omega and ϕβ,0g​(r)\phi^{g}_{\beta,0}(r) be the unique positive minimizer for (5.14) with Ω=0\Omega=0 (see section 2). There exists β0≥0\beta_{0}\geq 0, such that when β≥β0\beta\geq\beta_{0}, for 0≤Ω≤Ωβ0\leq\Omega\leq\Omega_{\beta} (constant Ωβ\Omega_{\beta} depends on β\beta), ϕβ,Ωg=ei​θ​ϕβ,0g\phi^{g}_{\beta,\Omega}=e^{i\theta}\phi^{g}_{\beta,0} for some constant θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}.

All these results are valid for general potential V⁡(r)V(r) [162, 7].

When Ω\Omega increases, the number of vortices in the ground state will also increase and the vortices interact. At high rotational speed, vortices will form a lattice, known as an Abrikosov lattice [5, 97, 4]. For the fast rotational speeds, Correggi [83] studied the expansion of energy (5.9) and proved that the vortices will be asymptotically equidistributed, which means that the vortices will form a triangle lattice. For general harmonic potentials in 2D, i.e., γx≠γy\gamma_{x}\neq\gamma_{y}, Ignat et al. estimated the critical angular velocity for the existence of nn vortices in the ground state as well as the location of the vortex centers [119, 120].

If an anharmonic potential, i.e. V⁡(𝐱)=V⁡(r)=O⁡(r4)V(\mathbf{x})=V(r)=O(r^{4}) when r→∞r\to\infty, is considered instead of harmonic potentials, there exists another phase transition [81, 82]. When Ω\Omega increases, the ground state of a rotating BEC with anharmonic potential will first undergo a phase transition to the vortex state, and then become a vortex lattice. If the velocity Ω\Omega keeps increasing, the vortex lattice will disappear, and the density will be depleted near the trap center. Then all the vortices will be pushed away from the center and form a giant vortex (or vortex ring) [156]. Thus, there are three typical critical speeds that can be identified with these kinds of phase transitions in rotating BEC [81]. In the study of the critical speeds, a more widely used scaling is different from the one adopted here [5] (cf. section 7).

5.4. Well-posedness of Cauchy problem

This section is devoted to the well-posedness of Cauchy problem for the rotating GPE (5.7). We use the same notations for function spaces as those in section 2.

Like the non-rotating case (Ω=0\Omega=0) (cf. section 2), the key part is to establish the dispersive estimates like Lemma 2.4 for the evolutionary operator ei​t​LRe^{itL_{R}} generated by the linear operator

LR=−12∇2+V(𝐱)−ΩLz,𝐱∈ℝd,d=2,3.\displaystyle L_{R}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})-\Omega L_{z},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad d=2,3. (5.25)

For the special case V⁡(𝐱)=ω22​|𝐱|2V(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\omega^{2}}{2}|\mathbf{x}|^{2} and Ω=ω\Omega=\omega, Hao et al. obtained the dispersive estimates for ei​t​LRe^{itL_{R}} using a generalization of Mehler’s formula for the kernel of ei​t​LRe^{itL_{R}} [111, 112, 73]. Later, Antonelli et al. found another approach to establish the dispersive estimates for ei​t​LRe^{itL_{R}} without those assumptions on Ω\Omega and VV in [111, 112]. It turns out that the rotational term LzL_{z} does not affect the dispersive behavior (in short time), and the dispersive estimates for ei​t​LRe^{itL_{R}} are then analogous to those in Lemma 2.4 for harmonic potentials. Then the well-posedness of the rotational GPE (5.7) follows from the classical arguments [73, 173].

Theorem 5.6.

(cf. [13]) Assume that V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is given by (5.8) and denote γmin=min⁡{γα}\gamma_{\min}=\min\{\gamma_{\alpha}\} (γα>0\gamma_{\alpha}>0; α=x,y\alpha=x,y for d=2d=2, and α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z for d=3d=3), then we have the following results.

(i) For any initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱)∈X⁡(ℝd)\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\in X(\mathbb{R}^{d}) (d=2,3d=2,3), there exists a Tmax∈(0,+∞]T_{{\rm max}}\in(0,+\infty] such that the Cauchy problem of (5.7) has a unique maximal solution ψ∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X)\psi\in C\left([0,T_{{\rm max}}),X\right). It is maximal in the sense that if Tmax<∞T_{{\rm max}}<\infty, then ‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖X→∞\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{X}\to\infty when t→Tmax−t\to T^{-}_{{\rm max}}.

(ii) As long as the solution ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(\mathbf{x},t) remains in the energy space XX, the L2L^{2}-norm ‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖2\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{2} and energy Eβ,Ω​(ψ​(⋅,t))E_{\beta,\Omega}(\psi(\cdot,t)) in (5.9) are conserved for t∈[0,Tmax)t\in[0,T_{\rm max}).

(iii) The solution of the Cauchy problem for (5.7) is global in time, i.e., Tmax=∞T_{\rm max}=\infty, if β≥0\beta\geq 0.

(iv) If β<0\beta<0 in 2D and 3D, and if either:

  1. (1)

    V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is axially symmetric, i.e., Ω​Lz​V​(𝐱)=0\Omega\,L_{z}V(\mathbf{x})=0;

  2. (2)

    Ω​Lz​V​(𝐱)≠0\Omega\,L_{z}V(\mathbf{x})\neq 0 and d​(1−(Ω/γmin)2CLOSE≥1d\sqrt{(1-(\Omega/\gamma_{\min})^{2}}\geq 1 with |Ω|≤γmin|\Omega|\leq\gamma_{\min} (d=2,3d=2,3).

Then there exists ψ0∈X⁡(ℝd)\psi_{0}\in X(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that finite time blow-up happens for the solution of the corresponding Cauchy problem (5.7).

In this section, we present results on the dynamical properties of rotating BEC governed by GPE with an angular momentum term (5.7).

For the dynamics of angular momentum expectation in rotating BEC, we have the following lemmas [28]:

If the initial data ψ0​(𝐱)\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}) for the Cauchy problem of (5.7) is chosen as a stationary state with a shift in its center, one can construct an exact solution of the GPE with an angular momentum term (5.7), which is similar to Lemma 2.9 [28].

Suppose V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is given by (5.8), if the initial data ψ0​(𝐱)\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x}) for the Cauchy problem of (5.7) is chosen as

and 𝐱c​(t)=(xc​(t),yc​(t))T\mathbf{x}_{c}(t)=(x_{c}(t),y_{c}(t))^{T} in 2D, and resp., 𝐱c​(t)=(xc​(t),yc​(t),zc​(t))T\mathbf{x}_{c}(t)=(x_{c}(t),y_{c}(t),z_{c}(t))^{T} in 3D, satisfies the following second-order ODE system:

x¨c​(t)−2​Ω​y˙c​(t)+(γx2−Ω2)​xc​(t)=0,\displaystyle\ddot{x}_{c}(t)-2\Omega\dot{y}_{c}(t)+\left(\gamma_{x}^{2}-\Omega^{2}\right)x_{c}(t)=0, (5.39)

We note that the above ODE system (5.39)-(5.41) can be solved analytically [28].

6. Numerical methods for rotational BEC

In this section, we first present efficient and accurate numerical methods for computing ground states, as well as the central vortex states (5.17) of rotating BEC modeled by the GPE with an angular momentum term (5.7). To compute the dynamics of rotating BEC based on GPE (5.7), there are new difficulties due to the angular momentum term LzL_{z} in (5.7). We will show how to design efficient numerical methods for simulating the dynamics of the rotational GPE (5.7). In most cases, we consider the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) given as (5.8) if no further clarification.

6.1. Computing ground states

In order to find the ground state for rotational GPE (5.7), we need to solve the minimization problem (5.14). Analogous to the non-rotating case (cf. section 3), we adopt the gradient flow with discrete normalization (GFDN) method (or imaginary time method) [45].

ϕt=−δ​Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)δ​ϕ¯=12​∇2ϕ−V⁡(𝐱)​ϕ−β​|ϕ|2​ϕ+Ω​Lz​ϕ,tn<t<tn+1,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=-\frac{\delta E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi)}{\delta\overline{\phi}}=\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\phi-V(\mathbf{x})\phi-\beta\;|\phi|^{2}\phi+\Omega\;L_{z}\phi,\quad t_{n}<t<t_{n+1},\qquad (6.1)
ϕ(𝐱,tn+1)=△ϕ(𝐱,tn+1+)=ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1−)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖2,𝐱∈ℝd,d=2,3,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\triangle}}{{=}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{+})=\frac{\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{-})}{\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}},\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\quad d=2,3,\quad n\geq 0, (6.2)
ϕ(𝐱,0)=ϕ0(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝdwith∥ϕ0∥2=1;\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\qquad\hbox{with}\quad\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}=1; (6.3)

where 0=t0<t1<t2<⋯<tn<⋯0=t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{n}<\cdots with τn=tn+1−tn>0\tau_{n}=t_{n+1}-t_{n}>0 and τ=maxn≥0⁡τn\tau=\max_{n\geq 0}\;\tau_{n}, and ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn±)=limt→tn±ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n}^{\pm})=\lim_{t\to t_{n}^{\pm}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t). As stated in section 3, the gradient flow (6.1) can be viewed as applying the steepest descent method to the energy functional Eβ,Ω​(ϕ)E_{\beta,\Omega}(\phi) (5.9) without constraint and (6.2) then projects the solution back to the unit sphere in order to satisfy the constraint (5.12).

In non-rotating BEC, i.e. Ω=0\Omega=0, the unique real valued nonnegative ground state solution ϕg​(𝐱)≥0\phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for all 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is obtained by choosing a positive initial datum ϕ0​(𝐱)≥0\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, e.g., the ground state solution of linear Schrödinger equation with a harmonic oscillator potential [15, 27]. For rotating BEC, e.g., |Ω|<min⁡{γx,γy}|\Omega|<\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}, our numerical experiences suggest that the initial data can be chosen as a linear combination of the ground state and central vortex ground state with index m=1m=1 of (5.7) when β=0\beta=0 and Ω=0\Omega=0, which are given explicitly in section 6.5.

6.1.1. Backward Euler finite difference method

In order to derive a full discretization of the GFDN (6.1)-(6.3), we first truncate the physical domain of the problem to a rectangle in 2D or a box in 3D with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition, and then apply backward Euler for time discretization and second-order centered finite difference for spatial derivatives. The backward Euler finite difference method is similar to the BEFD discretization for non-rotating BEC in section 3.2 and we omit the details here for brevity [45].

6.1.2. Backward Euler Fourier pseudospectral method

Computing the ground state of rotating BEC is a very challenging problem, especially for fast rotational speed Ω\Omega close to min⁡{γx,γy}\min\{\gamma_{x},\gamma_{y}\}, where many vortices exist in the ground state. In order to achieve high resolution for the vortex structure, a very fine mesh must be used if BEFD is used for discretizing the GFDN (6.1)-(6.3), when Ω\Omega is large. Here, we propose a Fourier pseudospectral discretization in space for the GFDN (6.1)-(6.3) to maintain the accuracy for high rotational speed Ω\Omega with less computational cost.

We first truncate the problem (6.1)-(6.3) in 2D on a rectangle U=[a,b]×[c,d]U=[a,b]\times[c,d], and resp. in 3D on a box U=[a,b]×[c,d]×[e,f]U=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f] with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition:

ϕt=[12​∇2−V⁡(𝐱)−β​|ϕ|2+Ω​Lz]​ϕ,tn<t<tn+1,𝐱∈U,\displaystyle\phi_{t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-\beta|\phi|^{2}+\Omega\;L_{z}\right]\phi,\qquad t_{n}<t<t_{n+1},\quad\mathbf{x}\in U, (6.4)
ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1)=△ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1+)=ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn+1−)‖ϕ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖L2​(U),𝐱∈U,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\triangle}}{{=}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{+})=\frac{\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{-})}{\|\phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{L^{2}(U)}},\quad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad n\geq 0, (6.5)
ϕ(𝐱,⋅)|∂U=0,ϕ(𝐱,0)=ϕ0(𝐱),𝐱∈Uwith∥ϕ0∥L2​(U)=1;\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{x},\cdot)|_{\partial U}=0,\quad\phi(\mathbf{x},0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}),\quad\mathbf{x}\in U\quad\hbox{with}\quad\|\phi_{0}\|_{L^{2}(U)}=1; (6.6)

where ϕ⁡(𝐱,tn±)=limt→tn±ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)\phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n}^{\pm})=\lim_{t\to t_{n}^{\pm}}\phi(\mathbf{x},t).

For the simplicity of notation, we only present the methods in 2D. Generalizations to d=3d=3 are straightforward for tensor product grids and the results remain valid without modifications. Choose mesh sizes Δ​x:=b−aM\Delta x:=\frac{b-a}{M} and Δ​y:=d−cN\Delta y:=\frac{d-c}{N} with MM and NN two even positive integers and denote the grid points as

xj:=a+jΔx,j=0,1,…,M;yk:=c+kΔy,k=0,1,…,N.\displaystyle x_{j}:=a+j\,\Delta x,\quad j=0,1,\ldots,M;\qquad y_{k}:=c+k\,\Delta y,\quad k=0,1,\ldots,N. (6.7)

𝒯M​N0={(j,k)|j=0,1,2…,M,k=0,1,2…,N}.\displaystyle{{\mathcal{T}}}_{MN}^{0}=\{(j,k)\ |\ j=0,1,2\ldots,M,\ k=0,1,2\ldots,N\}.
