7.3. Semiclassical limits and geometric optics

Suppose Vε​(𝐱)=V0​(𝐱)+Wε​(𝐱)V^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})=V_{0}(\mathbf{x})+W^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}) in (7.7), and we set

ψε​(𝐱,t)=ρε​(𝐱,t)​exp⁡(iε​Sε​(𝐱,t)),\displaystyle\psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},t)=\sqrt{\rho^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},t)}\exp\left(\frac{i}{\varepsilon}S^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},t)\right), (7.17)

where ρε=|ψε|2\rho^{\varepsilon}=|\psi^{\varepsilon}|^{2} and SεS^{\varepsilon} are the density and phase of the wave function, respectively. Inserting (7.17) into the GPE (7.7) and separating real and imaginary parts give [104, 103, 28, 69, 192]

ρtε+div(ρε∇Sε)+ΩL^zρε=0,\displaystyle\rho_{t}^{\varepsilon}+{\rm div}\,(\rho^{\varepsilon}\;\nabla S^{\varepsilon})+\Omega\hat{L}_{z}\rho^{\varepsilon}=0, (7.18)
Stε+12​|∇Sε|2+ρε+Vε​(𝐱)+Ω​L^z​Sε=ε22​1ρε​Δ​ρε,\displaystyle S_{t}^{\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla S^{\varepsilon}|^{2}+\rho^{\varepsilon}+V^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})+\Omega\hat{L}_{z}S^{\varepsilon}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^{\varepsilon}}}\ \Delta\sqrt{\rho^{\varepsilon}}, (7.19)

where L^z=(x∂y−y∂x)\hat{L}_{z}=(x\partial_{y}-y\partial_{x}). The equation (7.18) is the transport equation for the atom density and (7.19) the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the phase.

By formally passing to the limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 (cf. [102]), we obtain the system

ρt0+div(ρ0∇S0)+ΩL^zρ0=0,\displaystyle\rho^{0}_{t}+{\rm div}\,(\rho^{0}\;\nabla S^{0})+\Omega\hat{L}_{z}\rho^{0}=0, (7.20)
St0+12​|∇S0|2+ρ0+V0​(𝐱)+Ω​L^z​S0=0.\displaystyle S^{0}_{t}+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla S^{0}|^{2}+\rho^{0}+V_{0}(\mathbf{x})+\Omega\hat{L}_{z}S^{0}=0. (7.21)

It is well known that this limit process is only correct in the defocusing case β>0\beta>0 before caustic onset, i.e. in time-intervals where the solution of the Hamilton-Jacobian equation (7.19) coupled with the atom-number conservation equation (7.18) is smooth. After the breakdown of regularity, oscillations occur, which make the term ε22​1ρε​Δ​ρε\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{\rho^{\varepsilon}}}\ \Delta\sqrt{\rho^{\varepsilon}} at least O⁡(1)O(1) such that the validity of the formal limit process is destroyed. The limiting behavior after caustics onset is not understood yet except in 1D case without confinement, see [122]. Also, the focusing case β<0\beta<0 is not fully understood yet.

Furthermore, by defining the current densities

𝐉ε(𝐱,t)=ρε∇Sε=εIm[ψε¯∇ψε],\displaystyle{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x},t)=\rho^{\varepsilon}\nabla S^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\,{\rm Im}\left[\overline{\psi^{\varepsilon}}\nabla\psi^{\varepsilon}\right], (7.22)

we can rewrite (7.18)-(7.19) as a coupled Euler system with third-order dispersion terms [104, 103, 28, 69, 192]

∂tρε+div​𝐉ε+Ω​L^z​ρε=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho^{\varepsilon}+{\rm div}{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}+\Omega\widehat{L}_{z}\rho^{\varepsilon}=0, (7.23)
∂t𝐉ε+div(𝐉ε⊗𝐉ερε)+ρε∇Vε(𝐱)+12∇(ρε)2+ΩL^z𝐉ε=ε24∇(ρε∇2lnρε).\displaystyle\partial_{t}{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}+{\rm div}\left(\frac{{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}\otimes{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}}{\rho^{\varepsilon}}\right)+\rho^{\varepsilon}\nabla V^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{2}\nabla\left(\rho^{\varepsilon}\right)^{2}+\Omega\widehat{L}_{z}{\bf J}^{\varepsilon}=\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{4}\nabla\left(\rho^{\varepsilon}\nabla^{2}\ln\rho^{\varepsilon}\right).\hskip 9.24994pt (7.24)

Letting ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+} in (7.23)-(7.24), formally we get an Euler system coupling through the pressures [104, 103, 28, 69, 192]

∂tρ0+div​𝐉0+Ω​L^z​ρ0=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\rho^{0}+{\rm div}{\bf J}^{0}+\Omega\widehat{L}_{z}\rho^{0}=0, (7.25)
∂t𝐉0+div(𝐉0⊗𝐉0ρ0)+ρ0∇V0(𝐱)+12∇(ρ0)2+ΩL^z𝐉0=0,\displaystyle\partial_{t}{\bf J}^{0}+{\rm div}\left(\frac{{\bf J}^{0}\otimes{\bf J}^{0}}{\rho^{0}}\right)+\rho^{0}\nabla V_{0}(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{2}\nabla\left(\rho^{0}\right)^{2}+\Omega\widehat{L}_{z}{\bf J}^{0}=0,\qquad\quad (7.26)

where 𝐉0(𝐱,t)=ρ0∇S0{\bf J}^{0}(\mathbf{x},t)=\rho^{0}\nabla S^{0}. The system (7.25)-(7.26) is a coupled isotropic Euler system with quadratic pressure-density constitutive relations in the rotational frame. The formal asymptotics is supposed to hold up to caustic onset time [103, 104].

8. Mathematical theory and numerical methods for dipolar BEC

In the last several years, there has been a quest for realizing a novel kind of quantum gases with the dipolar interaction, acting between particles having a permanent magnetic or electric dipole moment. In 2005, the first dipolar BEC with 52Cr atoms was successfully realized in experiments at the Stuttgart University [107]. Later in 2011, a dipolar BEC with 164Dy atoms, whose dipole-dipole interaction is much stronger than that of 52Cr, was achieved in experiments at the Stanford University [138]. Very recently in 2012, a dipolar BEC of 168Er atoms has been produced in Innsbruck University [8]. These successes of experiments have renewed interests in theoretically studying dipolar BECs.

8.1. GPE with dipole-dipole interaction

At temperature TT much smaller than the critical temperature TcT_{c}, a dipolar BEC is well described by the macroscopic wave function ψ=ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi=\psi(\mathbf{x},t) whose evolution is governed by the 3D Gross-Pitaevskii equation (GPE) [187, 161, 49]

i​ℏ​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+g​|ψ|2+(Vdip∗|ψ|2)]​ψ,𝐱∈ℝ3,t>0,\displaystyle i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+g|\psi|^{2}+\left(V_{\rm dip}\ast|\psi|^{2}\right)\right]\psi,\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3},\ t>0, (8.1)

where 𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}^{3}} is the Cartesian coordinate and a harmonic trap potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is considered here. g=4​π​ℏ2​asmg=\frac{4\pi\hbar^{2}a_{s}}{m} describes local (or short-range) interaction between dipoles in the condensate with asa_{s} the ss-wave scattering length. The long-range dipolar interaction potential between two dipoles is given by

Vdip​(𝐱)=μ0​μdip24​π​1−3​(𝐱⋅𝐧)𝟐/|𝐱|𝟐|𝐱|3=μ0​μdip24​π​1−3​cos2⁡(θ)|𝐱|3,𝐱∈ℝ3,\displaystyle V_{\rm dip}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\mu_{0}\mu_{\rm dip}^{2}}{4\pi}\,\frac{1-3(\mathbf{x}\cdot\bf n)^{2}/|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}{|\mathbf{x}|^{3}}=\frac{\mu_{0}\mu_{\rm dip}^{2}}{4\pi}\,\frac{1-3\cos^{2}(\theta)}{|\mathbf{x}|^{3}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, (8.2)

where μ0\mu_{0} is the vacuum magnetic permeability, μdip\mu_{\rm dip} is permanent magnetic dipole moment (e.g. μdip=6μB\mu_{\rm dip}=6\mu_{{}_{B}} for 52Cr with μB\mu_{{}_{B}} being the Bohr magneton), 𝐧=(n1,n2,n3)T∈ℝ3{\bf n}=(n_{1},n_{2},n_{3})^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is the dipole axis (or dipole moment) which is a given unit vector, i.e. |𝐧|=n12+n22+n33=1|{\bf n}|=\sqrt{n_{1}^{2}+n_{2}^{2}+n_{3}^{3}}=1, and θ\theta is the angle between the dipole axis 𝐧{\bf n} and the vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The wave function is normalized according to

‖ψ‖22:=∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=N,\displaystyle\|\psi\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=N, (8.3)

where NN is the total number of dipolar particles in the dipolar BEC.

By introducing the dimensionless variables, t→tω0t\to\frac{t}{\omega_{0}} with ω0=min⁡{ωx,ωy,ωz}\omega_{0}=\min\{\omega_{x},\omega_{y},\omega_{z}\}, 𝐱→xs​𝐱\mathbf{x}\to x_{s}\mathbf{x} with xs=ℏm​ω0x_{s}=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega_{0}}}, ψ→N​ψxs3/2\psi\to\frac{\sqrt{N}\psi}{x_{s}^{3/2}}, we obtain the dimensionless GPE in 3D from (8.1) as :

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[−12​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+β​|ψ|2+λ⁡(Udip∗|ψ|2)]​ψ,𝐱∈ℝ3,t>0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+\beta|\psi|^{2}+\lambda\left(U_{\rm dip}\ast|\psi|^{2}\right)\right]\psi,\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3},\;t>0, (8.4)

where β=N​gℏ​ω0​xs3=4​π​as​Nxs\beta=\frac{Ng}{\hbar\omega_{0}x_{s}^{3}}=\frac{4\pi a_{s}N}{x_{s}}, λ=m​N​μ0​μdip23​ℏ2​xs\lambda=\frac{mN\mu_{0}\mu_{\rm dip}^{2}}{3\hbar^{2}x_{s}}, V⁡(𝐱)=12​(γx2​x2+γy2​y2+γz2​z2)V(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{2}(\gamma_{x}^{2}x^{2}+\gamma_{y}^{2}y^{2}+\gamma_{z}^{2}z^{2}) is the dimensionless harmonic trapping potential with γx=ωxω0\gamma_{x}=\frac{\omega_{x}}{\omega_{0}}, γy=ωyω0\gamma_{y}=\frac{\omega_{y}}{\omega_{0}} and γz=ωzω0\gamma_{z}=\frac{\omega_{z}}{\omega_{0}}, and the dimensionless long-range dipolar interaction potential Udip​(𝐱)U_{\rm dip}(\mathbf{x}) is given as

Udip​(𝐱)=34​π​1−3​(𝐱⋅𝐧)𝟐/|𝐱|𝟐|𝐱|3=34​π​1−3​cos2⁡(θ)|𝐱|3,𝐱∈ℝ3.\displaystyle U_{\rm dip}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{3}{4\pi}\,\frac{1-3(\mathbf{x}\cdot\bf n)^{2}/|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}{|\mathbf{x}|^{3}}=\frac{3}{4\pi}\,\frac{1-3\cos^{2}(\theta)}{|\mathbf{x}|^{3}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. (8.5)

Although the kernel UdipU_{\rm dip} is highly singular near the origin, the convolution is well-defined for ρ∈Lp​(ℝ3)\rho\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) with Udip∗ρ∈Lp​(ℝ3)U_{\rm dip}*\rho\in L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) for p∈(1,∞)p\in(1,\infty) [70].

Denote the differential operators ∂𝐧=𝐧⋅∇\partial_{{\bf n}}={\bf n}\cdot\nabla and ∂𝐧𝐧=∂𝐧∂𝐧\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}=\partial_{{\bf n}}\partial_{{\bf n}}, and notice the identity [23]

Udip​(𝐱)=34​π​|𝐱|3​(1−3​(𝐱⋅𝐧)2|𝐱|2)=−δ⁡(𝐫)−3​∂𝐧𝐧(14​π​|𝐱|),𝐱∈ℝ3,\displaystyle U_{\rm dip}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{3}{4\pi|\mathbf{x}|^{3}}\left(1-\frac{3(\mathbf{x}\cdot{\bf n})^{2}}{|\mathbf{x}|^{2}}\right)=-\delta({\bf r})-3\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\left(\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf{x}|}\right),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, (8.6)

we can re-formulate the GPE (8.4) as the following Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson system (GPPS) [23, 18, 65]

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[−12​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+(β−λ)​|ψ|2−3​λ​∂𝐧𝐧φ]​ψ,𝐱∈ℝ3,t>0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+(\beta-\lambda)|\psi|^{2}-3\lambda\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\varphi\right]\psi,\quad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3},\quad t>0, (8.7)
∇2φ​(𝐱,t)=−|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2,𝐱∈ℝ3,lim|𝐱|→∞φ⁡(𝐱,t)=0,t≥0.\displaystyle\qquad\nabla^{2}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)=-|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3},\qquad\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)=0,\qquad t\geq 0. (8.8)

The above GPPS in 3D conserves the mass, or the normalization condition,

N⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t)):=‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖22=∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱≡∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,0)|2​𝑑𝐱=1,t≥0,\displaystyle N(\psi(\cdot,t)):=\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}\equiv\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},0)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=1,\quad t\geq 0, (8.9)

and energy per particle with φ=14​π​|𝐱|∗|ψ|2\varphi=\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf{x}|}*|\psi|^{2},

E3​D​(ψ)=∫ℝ3[12​|∇ψ|2+V⁡(𝐱)​|ψ|2+β−λ2​|ψ|4+3​λ2​|∂𝐧∇φ|2]​𝑑𝐱.\displaystyle E_{\rm 3D}(\psi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\psi|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi|^{2}+\frac{\beta-\lambda}{2}|\psi|^{4}+\frac{3\lambda}{2}\left|\partial_{{\bf n}}\nabla\varphi\right|^{2}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}. (8.10)

From (8.6), it is straightforward to get the Fourier transform of Udip​(𝐱)U_{\rm dip}(\mathbf{x}) as

(Udip)^​(ξ)=−1+3​(𝐧⋅ξ)2|ξ|2,ξ∈ℝ3.\displaystyle\widehat{(U_{\rm dip})}(\xi)=-1+\frac{3\left({\bf n}\cdot\xi\right)^{2}}{|\xi|^{2}},\qquad\xi\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. (8.11)

8.2. Dimension reduction

In many physical experiments of dipolar BECs, the condensates are confined with strong harmonic trap in one or two axis directions, resulting in a disk- or cigar-shaped dipolar BEC, respectively. Mathematically speaking, this corresponds to the anisotropic potentials V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) of the form:

Case I (disk-shaped), potential is strongly confined in vertical zz direction with

V⁡(𝐱)=V2​(x,y)+z22​ε4,𝐱∈ℝ3,\displaystyle V(\mathbf{x})=V_{2}(x,y)+\frac{z^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{4}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, (8.12)

Case II (cigar-shaped), potential is strongly confined in horizontal 𝐱⟂=(x,y)T∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}_{\perp}=(x,y)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} plane with

V⁡(𝐱)=V1​(z)+x2+y22​ε4,𝐱∈ℝ3,\displaystyle V(\mathbf{x})=V_{1}(z)+\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{4}},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, (8.13)

where 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1 (ε=1/γz\varepsilon=1/\gamma_{z} in Case I and ε=1/γr\varepsilon=1/\gamma_{r} with γx=γy=γr\gamma_{x}=\gamma_{y}=\gamma_{r} in Case II) is a small parameter describing the strength of confinement. In such cases, the above GPPS in 3D can be formally reduced to 2D and 1D, respectively [65].

In Case I, when ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}, evolution of the solution ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(\mathbf{x},t) of GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) in zz-direction would essentially occur in the ground state mode of −12∂z​z+z22​ε4-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{zz}+\frac{z^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{4}}, which is spanned by wε(z)=ε−1/2π−1/4e−z22​ε2w_{\varepsilon}(z)=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\pi^{-1/4}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}} [65, 18]. By taking the ansatz

ψ(𝐱⟂,z,t)=e−it/2ε2ϕ(𝐱⟂,t)wε(z),(𝐱⟂,z)T=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3,t≥0,\displaystyle\psi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},z,t)=e^{-it/2\varepsilon^{2}}\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t)w_{\varepsilon}(z),\qquad(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},z)^{T}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3},\quad t\geq 0, (8.14)

the 3D GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) can be formally reduced to a quasi-2D equation I [65, 18]:

i∂tϕ=[−12∇2+V2+β2​D|ϕ|2−3​λ2(∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂−n32∇2)φ2​D]ϕ,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\phi=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V_{2}+\beta_{2D}|\phi|^{2}-\frac{3\lambda}{2}(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}-n_{3}^{2}\nabla^{2})\varphi^{2D}\right]\phi, (8.15)

where β2​D=β−λ+3​λ​n322​π​ε\beta_{2D}=\frac{\beta-\lambda+3\lambda n_{3}^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}, 𝐧⟂=(n1,n2)T{\bf n}_{\perp}=(n_{1},n_{2})^{T}, ∂𝐧⟂=𝐧⟂⋅∇=𝐧⟂⋅(∂x,∂y)T\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}}={\bf n}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla={\bf n}_{\perp}\cdot(\partial_{x},\partial_{y})^{T}, ∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂=∂𝐧⟂(∂𝐧⟂)\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}=\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}}(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}}), ∇2=∂x​x+∂y​y\nabla^{2}=\partial_{xx}+\partial_{yy} and

φ2​D​(x,y,t)=Uε2​D∗|ϕ|2,Uε2​D​(x,y)=12​2​π3/2​∫ℝe−s2/2x2+y2+ε2​s2​𝑑s.\displaystyle\varphi^{2D}(x,y,t)=U^{2D}_{\varepsilon}*|\phi|^{2},\quad U^{2D}_{\varepsilon}(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}\pi^{3/2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{-s^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}s^{2}}}\,ds. (8.16)

In addition, as ε→0+\varepsilon\to 0^{+}, φ2​D\varphi^{2D} can be approximated by φ∞2​D\varphi^{2D}_{\infty} [65] as :

φ∞2​D​(𝐱⟂,t)=Udip2​D∗|ϕ|2,withUdip2​D​(𝐱⟂)=12​π​|𝐱⟂|,\displaystyle\varphi^{2D}_{\infty}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t)=U_{\rm dip}^{2D}*|\phi|^{2},\quad\hbox{with}\quad U_{\rm dip}^{2D}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})=\frac{1}{2\pi|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|}, (8.17)

which can be re-written as a fractional Poisson equation

(−∇2)1/2​φ∞2​D​(𝐱⟂​t)=|ϕ⁡(𝐱⟂,t)|2,lim|𝐱⟂|→∞φ∞2​D​(𝐱⟂,t)=0,t≥0.\displaystyle(-\nabla^{2})^{1/2}\varphi^{2D}_{\infty}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}t)=|\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t)|^{2},\quad\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|\to\infty}\varphi^{2D}_{\infty}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t)=0,\qquad t\geq 0. (8.18)

Thus an alternative quasi-2D equation II can be obtained as:

i∂tϕ=(−12∇2+V2+β2​D|ϕ|2−3​λ2(∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂−n32∇2)(−∇2)−12(|ϕ|2))ϕ.\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\phi=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V_{2}+\beta_{2D}|\phi|^{2}-\frac{3\lambda}{2}(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}-n_{3}^{2}\nabla^{2})(-\nabla^{2})^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|\phi|^{2})\right)\phi. (8.19)

Similarly, in Case II, evolution of the solution ψ⁡(x,y,z,t)\psi(x,y,z,t) of GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) in (x,y)(x,y) plane would essentially occur in the ground state mode of −12(∂x​x+∂y​y)+x2+y22​ε4-\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{xx}+\partial_{yy})+\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{4}}, which is spanned by wε(x,y)=ε−1π−1/2e−x2+y22​ε2w_{\varepsilon}(x,y)=\varepsilon^{-1}\pi^{-1/2}e^{-\frac{x^{2}+y^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}} [18, 65]. Again, by taking the ansatz

ψ(x,y,z,t)=e−it/ε2ϕ(z,t)wε(x,y),t≥0,\displaystyle\psi(x,y,z,t)=e^{-it/\varepsilon^{2}}\phi(z,t)w_{\varepsilon}(x,y),\quad t\geq 0, (8.20)

the 3D GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) can be formally reduced to a quasi-1D equation:

i∂tϕ=[−12∂z​z+V1+β1​D|ϕ|2−3​λ​(3​n32−1)8​2​π​ε∂z​zφ1​D]ϕ,z∈ℝ,t>0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\phi=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{zz}+V_{1}+\beta_{1D}|\phi|^{2}-\frac{3\lambda(3n_{3}^{2}-1)}{8\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}\partial_{zz}\varphi^{1D}\right]\phi,\quad z\in{\mathbb{R}},\ t>0, (8.21)

where β1​D=β+12​λ​(1−3​n32)2​π​ε2\beta_{1D}=\frac{\beta+\frac{1}{2}\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})}{2\pi\varepsilon^{2}} and

φ1​D(z,t)=Uε1​D∗|ϕ|2,Uε1​D(z)=2​ez2/2​ε2π​ε∫|z|∞e−s2/2ε2ds.\displaystyle\varphi^{1D}(z,t)=U_{\varepsilon}^{1D}*|\phi|^{2},\qquad U^{1D}_{\varepsilon}(z)=\frac{\sqrt{2}e^{z^{2}/2\varepsilon^{2}}}{\sqrt{\pi}\,\varepsilon}\int_{|z|}^{\infty}e^{-s^{2}/2\varepsilon^{2}}\,ds. (8.22)
Remark 8.1.

To describe a rotating dipolar BEC, we only need to include the angular momentum term (5.2) in the dipolar GPE (8.1). Therefore, dimensionless rotating dipolar GPEs in 3D and quasi-2D regime are straightforward.

8.3. Theory for ground states

In this section, we report results for ground state of dipolar BECs. Denote unit sphere

S=X∩{u∈L2​(ℝd)|‖u‖L2​(ℝd)=1},\displaystyle S=X\cap\left\{u\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\big|\,\|u\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=1\right\}, (8.23)

where XX is the energy space associated with corresponding potential (2.6).

8.3.1. 3D case

In 3D, the ground state of GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) is the minimizer of energy E3​DE_{3D} (8.10) over the nonconvex set SS [23].

Theorem 8.1.

Assume V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for 𝐱∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} and lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty (i.e., confining potential) in GPPS (8.7)-(8.8), then we have:

(i) If β≥0\beta\geq 0 and −12​β≤λ≤β-\frac{1}{2}\beta\leq\lambda\leq\beta, there exists a ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S, and the positive ground state |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is unique. Moreover, ϕg=ei​θ0​|ϕg|\phi_{g}=e^{i\theta_{0}}|\phi_{g}| for some constant θ0∈ℝ\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

(ii) If β<0\beta<0, or β≥0\beta\geq 0 and λ<−12​β\lambda<-\frac{1}{2}\beta or λ>β\lambda>\beta, there exists no ground state, i.e., infϕ∈SE3​D​(ϕ)=−∞\inf\limits_{\phi\in S}E_{\rm 3D}(\phi)=-\infty.

By splitting the total energy E3​D​(⋅)E_{\rm 3D}(\cdot) in (8.10) into kinetic, potential, interaction and dipolar energies, i.e.

E3​D​(ϕ)=Ekin​(ϕ)+Epot​(ϕ)+Eint​(ϕ)+Edip​(ϕ),\displaystyle E_{3D}(\phi)=E_{\rm kin}(\phi)+E_{\rm pot}(\phi)+E_{\rm int}(\phi)+E_{\rm dip}(\phi), (8.24)

where

Ekin​(ϕ)=\displaystyle E_{\rm kin}(\phi)= 12​∫ℝ3|∇ϕ​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱,Epot​(ϕ)=∫ℝ3V⁡(𝐱)​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱,Eint​(ϕ)=β2​∫ℝ3|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\nabla\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}d\mathbf{x},\ E_{\rm pot}(\phi)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}V(\mathbf{x})|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}d\mathbf{x},\ E_{\rm int}(\phi)=\frac{\beta}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{4}d\mathbf{x},
Edip​(ϕ)=\displaystyle E_{\rm dip}(\phi)= λ2​∫ℝ3(Udip∗|ϕ|2)​|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=λ2​∫ℝ3|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2​[−|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|2−3​∂𝐧𝐧φ]​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left(U_{\rm dip}\ast|\phi|^{2}\right)|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}d\mathbf{x}=\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\left[-|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{2}-3\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\varphi\right]d\mathbf{x} (8.25)
=\displaystyle= λ2​∫ℝ3[−|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4+3​(∇2φ)​(∂𝐧𝐧φ)]​𝑑𝐱=λ2​∫ℝ3[−|ϕ⁡(𝐱)|4+3​|∂𝐧∇φ|2]​𝑑𝐱,\displaystyle\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[-|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{4}+3(\nabla^{2}\varphi)(\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\varphi)\right]d\mathbf{x}=\frac{\lambda}{2}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[-|\phi(\mathbf{x})|^{4}+3\left|\partial_{\bf n}\nabla\varphi\right|^{2}\right]d\mathbf{x},

with φ=14​π​|𝐱|∗|ϕ|2\varphi=\frac{1}{4\pi|\mathbf{x}|}*|\phi|^{2}, we have the following Viral identity [23]:

Proposition 8.1.

Suppose V⁡(λ​𝐱)=λ2​V​(𝐱)V(\lambda\mathbf{x})=\lambda^{2}V(\mathbf{x}) for all λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and ϕg\phi_{g} is the ground state of a dipolar BEC, i.e., the minimizer of energy (8.10) under the normalization constraint (8.9), then we have

2​Ekin​(ϕe)−2​Epot​(ϕe)+3​Eint​(ϕe)+3​Edip​(ϕe)=0.\displaystyle 2E_{\rm kin}(\phi_{e})-2E_{\rm pot}(\phi_{e})+3E_{\rm int}(\phi_{e})+3E_{\rm dip}(\phi_{e})=0. (8.26)

8.3.2. Quasi-2D case I

Associated to the quasi-2D equation I (8.15)-(8.16), the energy is

E2​D​(ϕ)=∫ℝ2[12​|∇ϕ|2+V2​(𝐱⟂)​|ϕ|2+β2​D​|ϕ|4−3​λ4​|ϕ|2​φ2​D~]​d​𝐱⟂,ϕ∈X,\displaystyle E_{\rm 2D}(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}+V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})|\phi|^{2}+\beta_{2D}|\phi|^{4}-\frac{3\lambda}{4}|\phi|^{2}\widetilde{\varphi^{2D}}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}_{\perp},\quad\phi\in X, (8.27)

where β2​D=β−λ+3​λ​n322​π​ε\beta_{2D}=\frac{\beta-\lambda+3\lambda n_{3}^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon} and

φ2​D~=(∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂−n32∇2)φ2​D,φ2​D=Uε2​D∗|ϕ|2.\displaystyle\widetilde{\varphi^{2D}}=\left(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}-n_{3}^{2}\nabla^{2}\right)\varphi^{2D},\qquad\varphi^{2D}=U_{\varepsilon}^{2D}*|\phi|^{2}. (8.28)

The ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of (8.15) is the minimizer of the nonconvex minimization problem [18]:

Find ​ϕg∈S,such that ​E2​D​(ϕg)=minϕ∈S⁡E2​D​(ϕ).\displaystyle\mbox{Find }\phi_{g}\in S,\quad\mbox{such that }E_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{g})=\min\limits_{\phi\in S}E_{\rm 2D}(\phi). (8.29)
Theorem 8.2.

Assume 0≤V2​(𝐱⟂)0\leq V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}) and lim|𝐱⟂|→∞V2​(𝐱⟂)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|\to\infty}V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})=\infty, then we have

(i) There exists a ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of the system (8.15)-(8.16) if one of the following conditions holds

(A11) λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and β−λ>−2​π​Cb​ε\beta-\lambda>-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon;
(A22) λ<0\lambda<0 and β+12​(1+3​|2​n32−1|)​λ>−2​π​Cb​ε\beta+\frac{1}{2}(1+3|2n_{3}^{2}-1|)\lambda>-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon,

where CbC_{b} is given in (2.12).

(ii) The positive ground state |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is unique under one of the following conditions:

(A1′) λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and β−λ≥0\beta-\lambda\geq 0;
(A2′) λ<0\lambda<0 and β+12​(1+3​|2​n32−1|)​λ≥0\beta+\frac{1}{2}(1+3|2n_{3}^{2}-1|)\lambda\geq 0.

Moreover, any ground state is of the form ϕg=ei​θ0​|ϕg|\phi_{g}=e^{i\theta_{0}}|\phi_{g}| for some constant θ0∈ℝ\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

(iii) If β+12​λ​(1−3​n32)<−2​π​Cb​ε\beta+\frac{1}{2}\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})<-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon, there exists no ground state of Eq. (8.15).

8.3.3. Quasi-2D case II

Associated to the quasi-2D equation II (8.19), the energy is

E~2​D​(ϕ)=∫ℝ2[12​|∇ϕ|2+V2​(𝐱⟂)​|ϕ|2+β2​D​|ϕ|4−3​λ4​|ϕ|2​φ]​𝑑𝐱,ϕ∈X,\displaystyle\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}+V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})|\phi|^{2}+\beta_{2D}|\phi|^{4}-\frac{3\lambda}{4}|\phi|^{2}\varphi\right]\,d\mathbf{x},\;\phi\in X, (8.30)

where

φ(𝐱⟂)=(∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂−n32∇2)((−∇2)−1/2|ϕ|2).\displaystyle\varphi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})=\left(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}-n_{3}^{2}\nabla^{2}\right)((-\nabla^{2})^{-1/2}|\phi|^{2}). (8.31)

The ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of the equation (8.19) is defined as the minimizer of the nonconvex minimization problem:

Find ϕg∈S,such that E~2​D(ϕg)=minϕ∈SE~2​D(ϕ).\displaystyle\mbox{Find }\phi_{g}\in S,\quad\mbox{such that }\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{g})=\min\limits_{\phi\in S}\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi). (8.32)

For the above ground state, we have the following results [18].

Theorem 8.3.

Assume 0≤V2​(𝐱⟂)0\leq V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}) and lim|𝐱⟂|→∞V2​(𝐱⟂)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|\to\infty}V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})=\infty, then we have

(i) There exists a ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of the equation (8.19) if one of the following conditions holds

(B1) λ=0\lambda=0 and β>−2​π​Cb​ε\beta>-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon;
(B2) λ>0\lambda>0, n3=0n_{3}=0 and β−λ>−2​π​Cb​ε\beta-\lambda>-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon;
(B3) λ<0\lambda<0, n32≥12n_{3}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2} and β−(1−3​n32)​λ>−2​π​Cb​ε\beta-(1-3n_{3}^{2})\lambda>-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon.

(ii) The positive ground state |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is unique under one of the following conditions

(B1′) λ=0\lambda=0 and β≥0\beta\geq 0;
(B2′) λ>0\lambda>0, n3=0n_{3}=0 and β≥λ\beta\geq\lambda;
(B3′) λ<0\lambda<0, n32≥12n_{3}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2} and β−(1−3​n32)​λ≥0\beta-(1-3n_{3}^{2})\lambda\geq 0.

Moreover, any ground state ϕg=ei​θ0​|ϕg|\phi_{g}=e^{i\theta_{0}}|\phi_{g}| for some constant θ0∈ℝ\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

(iii) There exists no ground state of the equation (8.19) if one of the following conditions holds

(B1′′) λ>0\lambda>0 and n3≠0n_{3}\neq 0;
(B2′′) λ<0\lambda<0 and n32<12n_{3}^{2}<\frac{1}{2};
(B3′′) λ=0\lambda=0 and β<−2​π​Cb​ε\beta<-\sqrt{2\pi}C_{b}\,\varepsilon.

8.3.4. Quasi-1D case

Associated to the quasi-1D equation (8.21), the energy is

E1​D​(ϕ)=∫ℝ[12​|∂zϕ|2+V1​(z)​|ϕ|2+12​β1​D​|ϕ|4+3​λ​(1−3​n32)16​2​π​ε​|ϕ|2​φ]​𝑑z,\displaystyle E_{\rm 1D}(\phi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\partial_{z}\phi|^{2}+V_{1}(z)|\phi|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{1D}|\phi|^{4}+\frac{3\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})}{16\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}|\phi|^{2}\varphi\right]\,dz, (8.33)

where β1​D=β+12​λ​(1−3​n32)2​π​ε2\beta_{1D}=\frac{\beta+\frac{1}{2}\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})}{2\pi\varepsilon^{2}} and

φ⁡(z)=∂z​z(Uε1​D∗|ϕ|2),Uε1​D​(z)=2​ez22​ε2π​∫|z|∞e−s22​ε2​𝑑s.\displaystyle\varphi(z)=\partial_{zz}(U_{\varepsilon}^{1D}*|\phi|^{2}),\quad U_{\varepsilon}^{1D}(z)=\frac{2e^{\frac{z^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{|z|}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{s^{2}}{2\varepsilon^{2}}}\,ds. (8.34)

Again, the ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of the equation (8.21) is defined as the minimizer of the nonconvex minimization problem:

For the above ground state, we have the following results [18].

Theorem 8.4.

(Existence and uniqueness of ground state) Assume 0≤V1​(z)0\leq V_{1}(z) and lim|z|→∞V1​(z)=∞\lim_{|z|\to\infty}V_{1}(z)=\infty, for any parameter β\beta, λ\lambda and ε\varepsilon, there exists a ground state ϕg∈S\phi_{g}\in S of the quasi-1D equation (8.21)-(8.22), and the positive ground state |ϕg||\phi_{g}| is unique under one of the following conditions:

(C1) λ⁡(1−3​n32)≥0\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})\geq 0 and β−(1−3​n32)​λ≥0\beta-(1-3n_{3}^{2})\lambda\geq 0;

(C2) λ⁡(1−3​n32)<0\lambda(1-3n_{3}^{2})<0 and β+λ2​(1−3​n32)≥0\beta+\frac{\lambda}{2}(1-3n_{3}^{2})\geq 0.

Moreover, ϕg=ei​θ0​|ϕg|\phi_{g}=e^{i\theta_{0}}|\phi_{g}| for some constant θ0∈ℝ\theta_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

8.4. Well-posedness for dynamics

In this section, we study the well-posedness for dynamics of dipolar BECs.

8.4.1. 3D case

In 3D, we have the following results for GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) [23].

Theorem 8.5.

(Well-posedness) Suppose the real-valued trap potential V⁡(𝐱)∈C∞​(ℝ3)V(\mathbf{x})\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) such that V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for 𝐱∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3} and Dα​V​(𝐱)∈L∞​(ℝ3)D^{\alpha}V(\mathbf{x})\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) for all α∈ℕ03\alpha\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{3} with |α|≥2|\alpha|\geq 2. For any initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱)∈X\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\in X, there exists Tmax∈(0,+∞]T_{\mbox{\rm max}}\in(0,+\infty] such that the problem (8.7)-(8.8) has a unique maximal solution ψ∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X)\psi\in C\left([0,T_{\rm max}),X\right). It is maximal in the sense that if Tmax<∞T_{\rm max}<\infty, then ‖ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖X→∞\|\psi(\cdot,t)\|_{X}\to\infty when t→Tmax−t\to T^{-}_{\rm max}. Moreover, the mass N⁡(ψ⁡(⋅,t))N(\psi(\cdot,t)) and energy E3​D​(ψ​(⋅,t))E_{\rm 3D}(\psi(\cdot,t)) defined in (8.9) and (8.10), respectively, are conserved for t∈[0,Tmax)t\in[0,T_{\rm max}). Specifically, if β≥0\beta\geq 0 and −12​β≤λ≤β-\frac{1}{2}\beta\leq\lambda\leq\beta, the solution to (8.7)-(8.8) is global in time, i.e., Tmax=∞T_{\rm max}=\infty.

Theorem 8.6.

(Finite time blow-up) If β<0\beta<0, or β≥0\beta\geq 0 and λ<−12​β\lambda<-\frac{1}{2}\beta or λ>β\lambda>\beta, and assume V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) satisfies 3​V​(𝐱)+𝐱⋅∇V​(𝐱)≥03V(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{x}\cdot\nabla V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 for 𝐱∈ℝ3\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. For any initial data ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=ψ0​(𝐱)∈X\psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x})\in X to the problem (8.7)-(8.8), there exists finite time blow-up, i.e., Tmax<∞T_{\rm max}<\infty, if one of the following holds:

V2(𝐱⟂)∈C∞(ℝ2) and D𝐤V2(𝐱⟂)∈L∞(ℝ2),for all 𝐤∈ℕ02with|𝐤|≥2,\displaystyle V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})\hbox{ and }D^{{\bf k}}V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),\qquad\hbox{for all }{\bf k}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{2}\ \hbox{with}\ |{\bf k}|\geq 2, (8.36)

8.4.3. Quasi-2D case II

For quasi-2D equation II (8.19), noticing the nonlinearity ϕ(∂𝐧⟂​𝐧⟂−n32∇2)((−∇2)−1/2|ϕ|2)\phi(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\perp}{\bf n}_{\perp}}-n_{3}^{2}\nabla^{2})((-\nabla^{2})^{-1/2}|\phi|^{2}) is actually a derivative nonlinearity, it would bring significant difficulty in analyzing the dynamic behavior. The Cauchy problem of the Schrödinger equation with derivative nonlinearity has been investigated extensively in the literatures [115, 125]. We are able to prove the existence results in the energy space with the special structure of our nonlinearity [18].

Theorem 8.9.

(Existence for Cauchy problem) Suppose the real potential V2​(𝐱⟂)V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}) satisfies (8.36) and lim|𝐱⟂|→∞V2​(𝐱⟂)=∞\lim_{|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|\to\infty}V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})=\infty, and initial value ϕ0​(𝐱⟂)∈X\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\in X, either condition (B2) or (B3) in Theorem 8.3 holds with constant CbC_{b} being replaced by Cb/‖ϕ0‖22C_{b}/\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}^{2}, then there exists a solution ϕ∈L∞​([0,∞),X)∩W1,∞​([0,∞),X∗)\phi\in L^{\infty}([0,\infty);X)\cap W^{1,\infty}([0,\infty);X^{\ast}) for the Cauchy problem of (8.19). Here X∗X^{\ast} denotes the dual space of XX. Moreover, there holds for L2L^{2} norm and energy E~2​D\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D} (8.30) conservation, i.e.

‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(ℝ2)=‖ϕ0‖L2​(ℝ2),E~2​D​(ϕ⁡(⋅,t))≤E~2​D​(ϕ0),∀t≥0.\displaystyle\|\phi(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=\|\phi_{0}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2})},\quad\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi(\cdot,t))\leq\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{0}),\quad\forall t\geq 0. (8.37)

Next, we discuss possible finite time blow-up for the continuous solutions of the quasi-2D equation II (8.19). To this purpose, the following assumptions are introduced:

(A) Assumption on the trap and coefficient of the cubic term, i.e. V2​(𝐱⟂)V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}) satisfies 3​V2​(𝐱⟂)+𝐱⟂⋅∇V2​(𝐱⟂)≥03V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})+\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\geq 0, β−λ+3​λ​n322​π​ε≥−Cb‖ϕ0‖22\frac{\beta-\lambda+3\lambda n_{3}^{2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon}\geq-\frac{C_{b}}{\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}^{2}}, with ϕ0\phi_{0} being the initial data of equation (8.19);

(B) Assumption on the trap and coefficient of the nonlocal term, i.e. V2​(𝐱⟂)V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}) satisfies 2​V2​(𝐱⟂)+𝐱⟂⋅∇V2​(𝐱⟂)≥02V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})+\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla V_{2}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\geq 0, λ=0\lambda=0 or λ>0\lambda>0 and n32≥12n_{3}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}.

Theorem 8.10.

(Finite time blow-up) For any initial data ϕ⁡(𝐱⟂,t=0)=ϕ0​(𝐱⟂)∈X\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t=0)=\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\in X with finite variance δV0=∫ℝ2|𝐱⟂|2​|ϕ0​(𝐱⟂)|2​d​𝐱⟂<∞\delta_{V}^{0}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|\mathbf{x}_{\perp}|^{2}|\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}_{\perp}<\infty, if conditions (B1), (B2) and (B3) with constant CbC_{b} being replaced by Cb/‖ϕ0‖22C_{b}/\|\phi_{0}\|_{2}^{2} are not satisfied, let ϕ:=ϕ⁡(𝐱⟂,t)∈C⁡([0,Tmax),X)\phi:=\phi(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},t)\in C([0,T_{\rm max}),X) solution of the problem (8.19) with L2L^{2} norm and energy conservation, then there exists finite time blow-up, i.e., Tmax<∞T_{\rm max}<\infty, if one of the following condition holds:

(i) E~2​D​(ϕ0)<0\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{0})<0, and either Assumption (A) or (B) holds;

(ii) E~2​D​(ϕ0)=0\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{0})=0 and Im⁡(∫ℝ2ϕ¯0​(𝐱⟂)​(𝐱⟂⋅∇ϕ0​(𝐱⟂))​d​𝐱⟂)<0{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\overline{\phi}}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\ (\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}))\,d\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\right)<0, and either Assumption (A) or (B) holds;

(iii) E~2​D​(ϕ0)>0\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{0})>0, and Im⁡(∫ℝ2ϕ¯0​(𝐱⟂)​(𝐱⟂⋅∇ϕ0​(𝐱⟂))​d​𝐱⟂)<−(3​E~2​D0)1/2​δV0{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\overline{\phi}}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\ (\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}))\,d\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\right)<-(3\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}^{0})^{1/2}\delta_{V}^{0} if Assumption (A) holds, or Im⁡(∫ℝ2ϕ¯0​(𝐱⟂)​(𝐱⟂⋅∇ϕ0​(𝐱⟂))​d​𝐱⟂)<−(2​E~2​D0)1/2​δV0{\rm Im}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\overline{\phi}}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp})\ (\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\cdot\nabla\phi_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp}))\,d\mathbf{x}_{\perp}\right)<-(2\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}^{0})^{1/2}\delta_{V}^{0} if Assumption (B) holds. Here E~2​D0=E~2​D​(ϕ0)\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}^{0}=\tilde{E}_{\rm 2D}(\phi_{0}).

8.4.4. Quasi-1D case

Concerning the Cauchy problem, similar results as Theorem 8.7 can be obtained for the equation (8.21) [18].

Theorem 8.11.

(Well-posedness for Cauchy problem) Suppose the real-valued trap potential satisfies V1​(z)≥0V_{1}(z)\geq 0 for z∈ℝz\in{\mathbb{R}} and V1​(z)∈C∞​(ℝ)V_{1}(z)\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), Dk​V1​(z)∈L∞​(ℝ)D^{k}V_{1}(z)\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) for all integers k≥2k\geq 2, for any initial data ϕ⁡(z,t=0)=ϕ0​(z)∈X\phi(z,t=0)=\phi_{0}(z)\in X, there exists a unique solution ϕ∈C⁡([0,∞),X)∩C1​([0,∞),X∗)\phi\in C\left([0,\infty),X\right)\cap C^{1}\left([0,\infty),X^{\ast}\right) to the Cauchy problem of equation (8.21).

8.5. Convergence rate of dimension reduction

In this section, we discuss the dimension reduction of 3D GPPS to lower dimensions. In lower dimensions, we require that in the quasi-2D case, β=O⁡(ε)\beta=O(\varepsilon), λ=O⁡(ε)\lambda=O(\varepsilon), and in the quasi-1D case, β=O⁡(ε2)\beta=O(\varepsilon^{2}), λ=O⁡(ε2)\lambda=O(\varepsilon^{2}), i.e. we are considering the weak interaction regime, then we would get an ε\varepsilon-independent limiting equation. In this regime, we will see that GPPS will reduce to a regular GPE in lower dimensions [18].

8.5.1. Reduction to 2D

We consider the weak interaction regime, i.e., β→ε​β\beta\to\varepsilon\beta, λ→ε​λ\lambda\to\varepsilon\lambda. In Case I (8.12), for full 3D GPPS (8.7)-(8.8), introduce the re-scaling z→ε​zz\to\varepsilon z, ψ→ε−1/2ψε\psi\to\varepsilon^{-1/2}\psi^{\varepsilon} which preserves the normalization, then

i​∂tψε​(𝐱⟂,z,t)=[𝐇𝐱⟂V+1ε2​𝐇z+(β−λ)​|ψε|2−3​ε​λ​∂𝐧ε​𝐧εφε]​ψε,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi^{\varepsilon}(\mathbf{x}_{\perp},z,t)=\left[\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}_{\perp}}^{V}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{2}}\mathbf{H}_{z}+(\beta-\lambda)|\psi^{\varepsilon}|^{2}-3\varepsilon\lambda\partial_{{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}}\varphi^{\varepsilon}\right]\psi^{\varepsilon}, (8.38)

where 𝐱⟂=(x,y)∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}_{\perp}=(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and

𝐇𝐱⟂V=−12(∂x​x+∂y​y)+V2(x,y),𝐇z=−12∂z​z+z22,\displaystyle\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{x}_{\perp}}^{V}=-\frac{1}{2}(\partial_{xx}+\partial_{yy})+V_{2}(x,y),\qquad\mathbf{H}_{z}=-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{zz}+\frac{z^{2}}{2}, (8.39)
𝐧ε=(n1,n2,n3/ε),∂𝐧ε=𝐧ε⋅∇,∂𝐧ε​𝐧ε=∂𝐧ε(∂𝐧ε),\displaystyle{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}=(n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}/\varepsilon),\qquad\partial_{{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}}={\bf n}_{\varepsilon}\cdot\nabla,\qquad\partial_{{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}}=\partial_{{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}}(\partial_{{\bf n}_{\varepsilon}}), (8.40)

8.6. Numerical methods for computing ground states

In this section, we present efficient and accurate numerical methods for computing ground states of dipolar BECs, based on the new formulation GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) of dipolar GPE (8.4) in 3D.

The difficulty of computing dipolar GPE mainly comes from the dipolar term. In most of the numerical methods used in the literatures for theoretically and/or numerically studying the ground states of dipolar BECs, the way to deal with the convolution in (8.4) is usually to use the Fourier transform [154, 186]. However, due to the high singularity in the dipolar interaction potential (8.5), there are two drawbacks in these numerical methods: (i) the Fourier transforms of the dipolar interaction potential (8.5) and the density function |ψ|2|\psi|^{2} are usually carried out in the continuous level on the whole space ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} and in the discrete level on a bounded computational domain UU, respectively, and due to this mismatch, there is a locking phenomena in practical computation as observed in [154]; (ii) the second term in the Fourier transform of the dipolar interaction potential is 00\frac{0}{0}-type for 00-mode, i.e when ξ=0\xi=0 (see (8.11) for details), and it is artificially omitted when ξ=0\xi=0 in practical computation [154, 188, 186] thus this may cause some numerical problems too. With formulation (8.7)-(8.8), new numerical methods for computing ground states and dynamics of dipolar BECs can be constructed, which can avoid the above two drawbacks and thus they are more accurate than those currently used in the literatures.

Based on the new mathematical formulation for the energy associated with GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) in (8.10), we will present an efficient and accurate backward Euler sine pseudospectral (BESP) method for computing the ground states of a dipolar BEC.

In practice, the whole space problem is usually truncated into a bounded computational domain U=[a,b]×[c,d]×[e,f]U=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f] with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition. We adopt the method of gradient flow with discrete normalization (GFDN) as in section 3: choose a time step τ>0\tau>0 and set tn=n​τt_{n}=n\;\tau for n=0,1,…n=0,1,\ldots Applying the steepest decent method to the energy functional E3​D​(ϕ)E_{\rm 3D}(\phi) in (8.10) without the normalization constraint (8.9), and then projecting the solution back to the unit sphere SS at the end of each time interval [tn,tn+1][t_{n},t_{n+1}] in order to satisfy the constraint (8.9). Then GFDN for computing ground state of the GPPS (8.7)-(8.8) is [23]:

∂tϕ⁡(𝐱,t)=[12​∇2−V⁡(𝐱)−(β−λ)​|ϕ⁡(𝐱,t)|2+3​λ​∂𝐧𝐧φ⁡(𝐱,t)]​ϕ​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\phi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-(\beta-\lambda)|\phi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+3\lambda\partial_{\bf{nn}}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)\right]\phi(\mathbf{x},t),\qquad (8.52)

and the discrete norm is defined as

‖ϕ+‖22=hx​hy​hz​∑j=1M−1∑k=1N−1∑l=1L−1|ϕj​k​l+|2.\|\phi^{+}\|_{2}^{2}=h_{x}h_{y}h_{z}\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}|\phi_{jkl}^{+}|^{2}.

Similar as those in section 3.3 (cf. [25]), the linear system (8.61)-(8.64) can be iteratively solved in phase space very efficiently via discrete sine transform and we omit the details here for brevity.

8.7. Time splitting scheme for dynamics

Similarly, based on the new Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson type system (8.7)-(8.8), we will present an efficient and accurate time-splitting sine pseudospectral (TSSP) method for computing the dynamics of a dipolar BEC.

Again, in practice, the whole space problem is truncated into a bounded computational domain U=[a,b]×[c,d]×[e,f]U=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[e,f] with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition. From time t=tnt=t_{n} to time t=tn+1t=t_{n+1}, the Gross-Pitaevskii-Poisson type system (8.7)-(8.8) is solved in two steps. One solves first

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=−12​∇2ψ​(𝐱,t),𝐱∈U,ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|𝐱∈∂U=0,tn≤t≤tn+1,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi(\mathbf{x},t),\quad\mathbf{x}\in U,\quad\left.\psi(\mathbf{x},t)\right|_{\mathbf{x}\in\partial U}=0,\quad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}, (8.67)

for the time step of length τ\tau, followed by solving

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[V⁡(𝐱)+(β−λ)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2−3​λ​∂𝐧𝐧φ⁡(𝐱,t)]​ψ​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[V(\mathbf{x})+(\beta-\lambda)|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}-3\lambda\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)\right]\psi(\mathbf{x},t), (8.68)
∇2φ​(𝐱,t)=−|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2,𝐱∈U,tn≤t≤tn+1;\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)=-|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in U,\qquad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}; (8.69)
φ⁡(𝐱,t)|𝐱∈∂U=0,ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|𝐱∈∂U=0,tn≤t≤tn+1;\displaystyle\left.\varphi(\mathbf{x},t)\right|_{\mathbf{x}\in\partial U}=0,\qquad\left.\psi(\mathbf{x},t)\right|_{\mathbf{x}\in\partial U}=0,\qquad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}; (8.70)

for the same time step. Eq. (8.67) will be discretized in space by sine pseudospectral method and integrated in time exactly. For t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}], the equations (8.68)-(8.70) leave |ψ||\psi| and φ\varphi invariant in tt and therefore they collapses to

i​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[V⁡(𝐱)+(β−λ)​|ψ⁡(𝐱,tn)|2−3​λ​∂𝐧𝐧φ⁡(𝐱,tn)]​ψ​(𝐱,t),tn≤t≤tn+1,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[V(\mathbf{x})+(\beta-\lambda)|\psi(\mathbf{x},t_{n})|^{2}-3\lambda\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t_{n})\right]\psi(\mathbf{x},t),\ t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}, (8.71)
∇2φ​(𝐱,tn)=−|ψ⁡(𝐱,tn)|2,𝐱∈U.\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\varphi(\mathbf{x},t_{n})=-|\psi(\mathbf{x},t_{n})|^{2},\hskip 18.49988pt\mathbf{x}\in U. (8.72)

Again, equation (8.72) will be discretized in space by sine pseudospectral method [47, 164, 165, 23] and the linear ODE (8.71) can be integrated in time exactly.

Let ψj​k​ln\psi_{jkl}^{n} and φj​k​ln\varphi_{jkl}^{n} be the approximations of ψ⁡(xj,yk,zl,tn)\psi(x_{j},y_{k},z_{l},t_{n}) and φ⁡(xj,yk,zl,tn)\varphi(x_{j},y_{k},z_{l},t_{n}), respectively, which are the solutions of (8.7)-(8.8); and choose ψj​k​l0=ψ0​(xj,yk,zl)\psi^{0}_{jkl}=\psi_{0}(x_{j},y_{k},z_{l}) for (j,k,l)∈𝒯M​K​L0(j,k,l)\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{MKL}^{0}. For n=0,1,…n=0,1,\ldots, a second-order TSSP method for solving (8.7)-(8.8) via the standard Strang splitting is [23]

ψj​k​l(1)=∑p=1M−1∑q=1K−1∑s=1L−1e−i​τ​(μpx)2+(μqy)2+(μrz)24​(ψn)~p​q​s​sin⁡(j​p​πM)​sin⁡(k​q​πK)​sin⁡(l​s​πL),\displaystyle\psi^{(1)}_{jkl}=\sum_{p=1}^{M-1}\sum_{q=1}^{K-1}\sum_{s=1}^{L-1}e^{-i\tau\frac{(\mu_{p}^{x})^{2}+(\mu_{q}^{y})^{2}+(\mu_{r}^{z})^{2}}{4}}\;\widetilde{(\psi^{n})}_{pqs}\sin\left(\frac{jp\pi}{M}\right)\sin\left(\frac{kq\pi}{K}\right)\sin\left(\frac{ls\pi}{L}\right),
ψj​k​l(2)=e−i​τ​[V⁡(xj,yk,zl)+(β−λ)​|ψj​k​l(1)|2−3​λ​(∂𝐧𝐧sφ(1))|j​k​l]​ψj​k​l(1),(j,k,l)∈𝒯M​K​L0,\displaystyle\psi^{(2)}_{jkl}=e^{-i\tau\left[V(x_{j},y_{k},z_{l})+(\beta-\lambda)|\psi_{jkl}^{(1)}|^{2}-3\lambda\left.\left(\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}^{s}\varphi^{(1)}\right)\right|_{jkl}\right]}\;\psi_{jkl}^{(1)},\hskip 9.24994pt(j,k,l)\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{MKL}^{0}, (8.73)
ψj​k​ln+1=∑p=1M−1∑q=1K−1∑s=1L−1e−i​τ​(μpx)2+(μqy)2+(μrz)24​(ψ(2))~p​q​s​sin⁡(j​p​πM)​sin⁡(k​q​πK)​sin⁡(l​s​πL);\displaystyle\psi^{n+1}_{jkl}=\sum_{p=1}^{M-1}\sum_{q=1}^{K-1}\sum_{s=1}^{L-1}e^{-i\tau\frac{(\mu_{p}^{x})^{2}+(\mu_{q}^{y})^{2}+(\mu_{r}^{z})^{2}}{4}}\;\widetilde{(\psi^{(2)})}_{pqs}\sin\left(\frac{jp\pi}{M}\right)\sin\left(\frac{kq\pi}{K}\right)\sin\left(\frac{ls\pi}{L}\right);

where (ψn)~p​q​s\widetilde{(\psi^{n})}_{pqs} and (ψ(2))~p​q​s\widetilde{(\psi^{(2)})}_{pqs} ((p,q,s)∈𝒯M​K​L(p,q,s)\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{MKL}) are the discrete sine transform coefficients of the vectors ψn\psi^{n} and ψ(2)\psi^{(2)}, respectively (defined similarly as those in (8.66)); and (∂𝐧𝐧sφ(1))|j​k​l\left.\left(\partial_{{\bf n}{\bf n}}^{s}\varphi^{(1)}\right)\right|_{jkl} can be computed as in (8.65) with ρj​k​ln=ρj​k​l(1):=|ψj​k​l(1)|2\rho^{n}_{jkl}=\rho^{(1)}_{jkl}:=|\psi^{(1)}_{jkl}|^{2} for (j,k,l)∈𝒯M​K​L0(j,k,l)\in{{\mathcal{T}}}_{MKL}^{0}.

The above method is explicit and unconditionally stable. The memory cost is O⁡(M​K​L)O(MKL) and the computational cost per time step is O⁡(M​K​L​ln⁡(M​K​L))O\left(MKL\ln(MKL)\right).

In this section, we first compare our new methods and the standard method used in the literatures [188, 186] to evaluate numerically the dipolar energy and then report ground states and dynamics of dipolar BECs by using our new numerical methods.

8.9. Extensions in lower dimensions

Here, we consider the numerical methods for computing ground states and dynamics for dipolar BECs in 2D and 1D. The difficulties arise from the nonlocal terms, i.e., the dipolar terms in quasi-2D equation I (8.15), quasi-2D equation II (8.19) and quasi-1D equation (8.21). It is obvious that those methods introduced in sections 3 and 4 can be extended here, provided that the nonlocal terms can be computed properly.

We propose to compute the convolution terms in (8.15), (8.19) and (8.21) by Fourier transform. Unlike the 3D case, there are no singularities for convolution kernels at origin, thus discrete Fourier transform is accurate in these cases.

Lemma 8.1.

(Kernels Uε2​DU_{\varepsilon}^{2D} in (8.16) and Uε1​DU_{\varepsilon}^{1D}(8.22) ) For any real function f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) in the Schwartz space 𝒮⁡(ℝ2){\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), we have

Uε2​D∗f^​(ξ)=f^​(ξ)​Uε2​D^​(ξ)=f^​(ξ)π​∫ℝe−ε2s2/2|ξ|2+s2​𝑑s,f∈𝒮⁡(ℝ2).\displaystyle\widehat{U_{\varepsilon}^{2D}*f}(\xi)=\hat{f}(\xi)\,\widehat{U_{\varepsilon}^{2D}}(\xi)=\frac{\hat{f}(\xi)}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon^{2}s^{2}/2}}{|\xi|^{2}+s^{2}}ds,\qquad f\in{\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). (8.76)

For any g⁡(z)g(z) in the Schwartz space 𝒮⁡(ℝ){\mathcal{S}}(\mathbb{R}), we have

Uε1​D∗g^​(ξ)=g^​(ξ)​Uε1​D^​(ξ)=2​ε​g^​(ξ)π​∫0∞e−ε2s/2|ξ|2+s​𝑑s,ξ∈ℝ.\displaystyle\widehat{U_{\varepsilon}^{1D}*g}(\xi)=\hat{g}(\xi)\widehat{U_{\varepsilon}^{1D}}(\xi)=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,\varepsilon\hat{g}(\xi)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon^{2}s/2}}{|\xi|^{2}+s}ds,\quad\xi\in{\mathbb{R}}. (8.77)

Here f^\widehat{f} and g^\widehat{g} denote the Fourier transforms of ff and gg, respectively.

The Fourier transforms of Uε2​DU_{\varepsilon}^{2D} and Uε1​DU_{\varepsilon}^{1D} can be written in terms of the second kind Bessel functions [65].

9. Mathematical theory and numerical methods for two component BEC

In view of potential applications, such as the generation of bright beams of coherent matter waves (atom laser), a central goal in the study of BEC has been the formation of condensate with the number of atoms being as large as possible. It is thus of particular interest to study a scenario where this goal is achieved by uniting two (or more) independently grown condensates to form one large single condensate. The first experiment involving the uniting of multiple-component BEC was performed with atoms evaporatively cooled in the |F=2,mf=2⟩|F=2,m_{f}=2\rangle and |1,−1⟩|1,-1\rangle spin states of 87Rb [142]. It demonstrated the possibility of producing long-lived multiple condensate systems, and that the condensate wave function is dramatically affected by the presence of inter-component interactions.

9.1. Coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations

At temperatures TT much smaller than the critical temperature TcT_{c} [150], a two-component BEC with an internal atomic Josephson junction (or an external driving field) can be well described by the coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations (CGPEs) [134, 131, 185, 195, 19],

i​ℏ​∂tψ1=[−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+ℏ​δ+g11​|ψ1|2+g12​|ψ2|2]​ψ1+λ​ℏ​ψ2,iℏ∂tψ2=[−ℏ22​m∇2+V(𝐱)+g21|ψ1|2+g22|ψ2|2]ψ2+λℏψ1,𝐱∈ℝ3.\displaystyle\begin{split}&i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi_{1}=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+\hbar\delta+g_{11}|\psi_{1}|^{2}+g_{12}|\psi_{2}|^{2}\right]\psi_{1}+\lambda\hbar\psi_{2},\\ &i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi_{2}=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+g_{21}|\psi_{1}|^{2}+g_{22}|\psi_{2}|^{2}\right]\psi_{2}+\lambda\hbar\psi_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}.\end{split} (9.1)

Here Ψ:=Ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=(ψ1​(𝐱,t),ψ2​(𝐱,t))T\Psi:=\Psi(\mathbf{x},t)=(\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t),\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t))^{T} is the complex-valued macroscopic wave function, V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is the real-valued external trapping potential, λ\lambda is the effective Rabi frequency describing the strength to realize the internal atomic Josephson junction (JJ) by a Raman transition, δ\delta is the Raman transition constant. The interactions of particles are described by gj​l=4​π​ℏ2​aj​lmg_{jl}=\frac{4\pi\hbar^{2}a_{jl}}{m} with aj​l=al​ja_{jl}=a_{lj} (j,l=1,2j,l=1,2) being the ss-wave scattering lengths between the jjth and llth component (positive for repulsive interaction and negative for attractive interaction). It is necessary to ensure that the wave function is properly normalized. Especially, we require

∫ℝ3[|ψ1​(𝐱,t)|2+|ψ2​(𝐱,t)|2]​𝑑𝐱=N=N10+N20,\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[|\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+|\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}=N=N_{1}^{0}+N_{2}^{0}, (9.2)

where

Nj0=∫ℝ3|ψj​(𝐱,0)|2​𝑑𝐱,N_{j}^{0}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\psi_{j}(\mathbf{x},0)|^{2}d\mathbf{x},

is the particle number of the jjth (j=1,2j=1,2) component at time t=0t=0 and NN the total number of particle in the two-component BEC.

By properly nondimensionalization and dimension reduction, we can obtain the following dimensionless CGPEs in dd-dimensions (d=1,2,3d=1,2,3) for a two-component BEC [195, 19]

i∂tψ1=[−12∇2+V(𝐱)+δ+(β11|ψ1|2+β12|ψ2|2)]ψ1+λψ2,𝐱∈ℝd,i∂tψ2=[−12∇2+V(𝐱)+(β12|ψ1|2+β22|ψ2|2)]ψ2+λψ1,𝐱∈ℝd.\displaystyle\begin{split}&i\partial_{t}\psi_{1}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+\delta+(\beta_{11}|\psi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{12}|\psi_{2}|^{2})\right]\psi_{1}+\lambda\psi_{2},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\\ &i\partial_{t}\psi_{2}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+(\beta_{12}|\psi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{22}|\psi_{2}|^{2})\right]\psi_{2}+\lambda\psi_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.\end{split} (9.3)

Here Ψ:=Ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=(ψ1​(𝐱,t),ψ2​(𝐱,t))T\Psi:=\Psi(\mathbf{x},t)=(\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t),\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t))^{T} is the dimensionless complex-valued macroscopic wave function, V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is the dimensionless real-valued external trapping potential, β11\beta_{11}, β12=β21\beta_{12}=\beta_{21}, β22\beta_{22} are dimensionless interaction constants, δ\delta and λ\lambda are dimensionless constants. In addition, the wave function is normalized as

‖Ψ‖22:=∫ℝd[|ψ1​(𝐱,t)|2+|ψ2​(𝐱,t)|2]​𝑑𝐱=1.\displaystyle\|\Psi\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left[|\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}+|\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}=1. (9.4)

The dimensionless CGPEs (9.3) conserves the total mass or normalization, i.e.

N⁡(t):=‖Ψ⁡(⋅,t)‖2=N1​(t)+N2​(t)≡‖Ψ⁡(⋅,0)‖2=1,t≥0,\displaystyle N(t):=\|\Psi(\cdot,t)\|^{2}=N_{1}(t)+N_{2}(t)\equiv\|\Psi(\cdot,0)\|^{2}=1,\quad t\geq 0, (9.5)

with

Nj(t)=∥ψj(𝐱,t)∥22:=∥ψj(𝐱,t)∥22=∫ℝd|ψj(𝐱,t)|2d𝐱,t≥0,j=1,2,\displaystyle N_{j}(t)=\|\psi_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)\|_{2}^{2}:=\|\psi_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\psi_{j}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x},\quad t\geq 0,\quad j=1,2, (9.6)

and the energy

E⁡(Ψ)\displaystyle E(\Psi) =\displaystyle= ∫ℝd[12(|∇ψ1|2+|∇ψ2|2)+V(𝐱)(|ψ1|2+|ψ2|2)+δ|ψ1|2+12β11|ψ1|4\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\left(|\nabla\psi_{1}|^{2}+|\nabla\psi_{2}|^{2}\right)+V(\mathbf{x})(|\psi_{1}|^{2}+|\psi_{2}|^{2})+\delta|\psi_{1}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{11}|\psi_{1}|^{4} (9.7)
+12β22|ψ2|4+β12|ψ1|2|ψ2|2+2λ⋅Re(ψ1ψ¯2)]d𝐱.\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{22}|\psi_{2}|^{4}+\beta_{12}|\psi_{1}|^{2}|\psi_{2}|^{2}+2\lambda\cdot\text{Re}(\psi_{1}{\overline{\psi}}_{2})\biggl]d\mathbf{x}.

In addition, if there is no internal Josephson junction in (9.3), i.e. λ=0\lambda=0, the mass of each component is also conserved, i.e.

N1​(t)≡∫ℝd|ψ1​(𝐱,0)|2​𝑑𝐱:=α,N2​(t)≡∫ℝd|ψ2​(𝐱,0)|2​𝑑𝐱:=1−α,\displaystyle N_{1}(t)\equiv\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},0)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}:=\alpha,\quad N_{2}(t)\equiv\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},0)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}:=1-\alpha, (9.8)

with 0≤α≤10\leq\alpha\leq 1 a given constant.

9.2. Ground states for the case without Josephson junction

If there is no external driving field in (9.3), i.e. λ=0\lambda=0, for any given α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], the ground state Φgα​(𝐱)=(ϕ1α​(𝐱),ϕ2α​(𝐱))T\Phi_{g}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x})=(\phi_{1}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}),\phi_{2}^{\alpha}(\mathbf{x}))^{T} of the two-component BEC is defined as the minimizer of the following nonconvex minimization problem:
Find (Φgα∈Sα)\left(\Phi_{g}^{\alpha}\in S_{\alpha}\right), such that

Egα:=E0​(Φgα)=minΦ∈Sα⁡E0​(Φ),E_{g}^{\alpha}:=E_{0}\left(\Phi_{g}^{\alpha}\right)=\min_{\Phi\in S_{\alpha}}E_{0}\left(\Phi\right), (9.9)

where SαS_{\alpha} is a nonconvex set defined as

Sα:={Φ=(ϕ1,ϕ2)T|∥ϕ1∥22=α,∥ϕ2∥22=1−α,E0(Φ)<∞},\displaystyle S_{\alpha}:=\left\{\Phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})^{T}\ |\ \|\phi_{1}\|_{2}^{2}=\alpha,\ \|\phi_{2}\|_{2}^{2}=1-\alpha,\ E_{0}(\Phi)<\infty\right\}, (9.10)

and the energy functional E0​(Φ)E_{0}(\Phi) is defined as

E0​(Φ)\displaystyle E_{0}(\Phi) =\displaystyle= ∫ℝd[12(|∇ϕ1|2+|∇ϕ2|2)+V(𝐱)(|ϕ1|2+|ϕ2|2)+δ|ϕ1|2+12β11|ϕ1|4\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\left(|\nabla\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\nabla\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)+V(\mathbf{x})(|\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\phi_{2}|^{2})+\delta|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{4} (9.11)
+12β22|ϕ2|4+β12|ϕ1|2|ϕ2|2]d𝐱.\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{4}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}|\phi_{2}|^{2}\biggl]d\mathbf{x}.

Again, it is easy to see that the ground state Φgα\Phi_{g}^{\alpha} satisfies the following Euler-Lagrange equations,

μ1ϕ1=[−12∇2+V(𝕩)+δ+(β11|ϕ1|2+β12|ϕ2|2)]ϕ1,𝐱∈ℝd,μ2ϕ2=[−12∇2+V(𝕩)+(β12|ϕ1|2+β22|ϕ2|2)]ϕ2,𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\mu_{1}\,\phi_{1}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbb{x})+\delta+(\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\\ &\mu_{2}\,\phi_{2}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbb{x})+(\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{2},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\end{split} (9.12)

under the two constraints

‖ϕ1‖22:=∫ℝd|ϕ1​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=α,‖ϕ2‖22:=∫ℝd|ϕ2​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=1−α,\displaystyle\|\phi_{1}\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}=\alpha,\qquad\|\phi_{2}\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x}=1-\alpha, (9.13)

with μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} being the Lagrange multipliers or chemical potentials corresponding to the two constraints (9.13). Again, the above time-independent CGPEs (9.12) can also be obtained from the CGPEs (9.3) with λ=0\lambda=0 by substituting the ansatz

ψ1​(𝐱,t)=e−i​μ1​t​ϕ1​(𝐱),ψ2​(𝐱,t)=e−i​μ2​t​ϕ2​(𝐱).\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{-i\mu_{1}t}\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{-i\mu_{2}t}\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x}). (9.14)

Considering the case α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) in minimization problem (9.9), denote

β11′:=α​β11,β22′:=(1−α)​β22,β12′:=α⁡(1−α)​β12,α′:=α⁡(1−α),\beta_{11}^{\prime}:=\alpha\beta_{11},\quad\beta_{22}^{\prime}:=(1-\alpha)\beta_{22},\quad\beta_{12}^{\prime}:=\sqrt{\alpha(1-\alpha)}\beta_{12},\quad\alpha^{\prime}:=\alpha(1-\alpha),

and

B=(β11β12β21β22),B′=(β11′β12′β21′β22′).B=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\beta_{11}&\beta_{12}\\ \beta_{21}&\beta_{22}\\ \end{array}\right),\qquad B^{\prime}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\beta_{11}^{\prime}&\beta_{12}^{\prime}\\ \beta_{21}^{\prime}&\beta_{22}^{\prime}\\ \end{array}\right).

Then the following conclusions can be drawn [19].

Theorem 9.1.

(Existence and uniqueness of (9.9)) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 satisfying lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty and at least one of the following condition holds,

  1. (i)

    d=1d=1;

  2. (ii)

    d=2d=2 and β11′≥−Cb\beta^{\prime}_{11}\geq-C_{b}, β22′≥−Cb\beta^{\prime}_{22}\geq-C_{b}, and β12′≥−(Cb+β11′)​(Cb+β22′)\beta^{\prime}_{12}\geq-\sqrt{(C_{b}+\beta^{\prime}_{11})(C_{b}+\beta_{22}^{\prime})};

  3. (iii)

    d=3d=3 and BB is either positive semi-definite or nonnegative,

then there exists a ground state Φg=(ϕ1g,ϕ2g)T\Phi_{g}=(\phi_{1}^{g},\phi_{2}^{g})^{T} of (9.9). In addition, Φ~g:=(ei​θ1​|ϕ1g|,ei​θ2​|ϕ2g|)\widetilde{\Phi}_{g}:=(e^{i\theta_{1}}|\phi_{1}^{g}|,e^{i\theta_{2}}|\phi_{2}^{g}|) is also a ground state of (9.9) with two constants θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2}. Furthermore, if the matrix B′B^{\prime} is positive semi-definite, the ground state (|ϕ1g|,|ϕ2g|)T(|\phi_{1}^{g}|,|\phi_{2}^{g}|)^{T} of (9.9) is unique. In contrast, if one of the following conditions holds,

  1. (i)

    d=2d=2 and β11′<−Cb\beta_{11}^{\prime}<-C_{b} or β22′<−Cb\beta_{22}^{\prime}<-C_{b} or β12′<−12​α′​(α​β11′+(1−α)​β22′+Cb)\beta^{\prime}_{12}<-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\alpha^{\prime}}}\left(\alpha\beta^{\prime}_{11}+(1-\alpha)\beta_{22}^{\prime}+C_{b}\right);

  2. (ii)

    d=3d=3 and β11<0\beta_{11}<0 or β22<0\beta_{22}<0 or β12<−12​α′​(α2​β11+(1−α)2​β22)\beta_{12}<-\frac{1}{2\alpha^{\prime}}(\alpha^{2}\beta_{11}+(1-\alpha)^{2}\beta_{22}).

there exists no ground states of (9.9).

9.3. Ground states for the case with Josephson junction

The ground state Φg​(𝐱)=(ϕ1g​(𝐱),ϕ2g​(𝐱))T\Phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})=(\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x}),\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x}))^{T} of the two-component BEC with an internal Josephson junction (9.3) is defined as the minimizer of the following nonconvex minimization problem:
Find (Φg∈S)\left(\Phi_{g}\in S\right), such that

Eg:=E⁡(Φg)=minΦ∈S⁡E⁡(Φ),E_{g}:=E\left(\Phi_{g}\right)=\min_{\Phi\in S}E\left(\Phi\right), (9.15)

where SS is a nonconvex set defined as

S:={Φ=(ϕ1,ϕ2)T|∫ℝd(|ϕ1(𝐱)|2+|ϕ2(𝐱)|2)d𝐱=1,E(Φ)<∞}.\displaystyle S:=\left\{\Phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})^{T}\big|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left(|\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}+|\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\right)d\mathbf{x}=1,\ E(\Phi)<\infty\right\}. (9.16)

It is easy to see that the ground state Φg\Phi_{g} satisfies the following Euler-Lagrange equations,

μϕ1=[−12∇2+V(𝕩)+δ+(β11|ϕ1|2+β12|ϕ2|2)]ϕ1+λϕ2,𝐱∈ℝd,μϕ2=[−12∇2+V(𝕩)+(β12|ϕ1|2+β22|ϕ2|2)]ϕ2+λϕ1,𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\mu\,\phi_{1}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbb{x})+\delta+(\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{1}+\lambda\phi_{2},\quad\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\\ &\mu\,\phi_{2}=\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbb{x})+(\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{2}+\lambda\phi_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d},\end{split} (9.17)

under the constraint

‖Φ‖22:=‖Φ‖22=∫ℝd[|ϕ1​(𝐱)|2+|ϕ2​(𝐱)|2]​𝑑𝐱=1,\displaystyle\|\Phi\|_{2}^{2}:=\|\Phi\|_{2}^{2}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left[|\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}+|\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\right]\,d\mathbf{x}=1, (9.18)

with the eigenvalue μ\mu being the Lagrange multiplier or chemical potential corresponding to the constraint (9.18), which can be computed as

μ\displaystyle\mu =\displaystyle= μ(Φ)=∫ℝd[12(|∇ϕ1|2+|∇ϕ2|2)+V(𝐱)(|ϕ1|2+|ϕ2|2)+δ|ϕ1|2+β11|ϕ1|4\displaystyle\mu(\Phi)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\left(|\nabla\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\nabla\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)+V(\mathbf{x})(|\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\phi_{2}|^{2})+\delta|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{4} (9.19)
+β22|ϕ2|4+2β12|ϕ1|2|ϕ2|2+2λ⋅Re(ϕ1ϕ¯2)]d𝐱.\displaystyle\qquad+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{4}+2\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}|\phi_{2}|^{2}+2\lambda\cdot\text{Re}(\phi_{1}{\overline{\phi}}_{2})\biggl]d\mathbf{x}.

In fact, the above time-independent CGPEs (9.17) can also be obtained from the CGPEs (9.3) by substituting the ansatz

ψ1​(𝐱,t)=e−i​μ​t​ϕ1​(𝐱),ψ2​(𝐱,t)=e−i​μ​t​ϕ2​(𝐱).\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{-i\mu t}\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\psi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{-i\mu t}\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x}). (9.20)

The eigenfunctions of the nonlinear eigenvalue problem (9.17) under the normalization (9.18) are usually called as stationary states of the two-component BEC (9.3). Among them, the eigenfunction with minimum energy is the ground state and those whose energy are larger than that of the ground state are usually called as excited states.

It is easy to see that the ground state Φg\Phi_{g} defined in (9.15) is equivalent to the following:
Find (Φg∈S)\left(\Phi_{g}\in S\right), such that

E⁡(Φg)=minΦ∈S⁡E⁡(Φ)=minα∈[0,1]⁡E⁡(α),E⁡(α)=minΦ∈Sα⁡E⁡(Φ).\displaystyle E\left(\Phi_{g}\right)=\min_{\Phi\in S}E\left(\Phi\right)=\min_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\;E(\alpha),\qquad E(\alpha)=\min_{\Phi\in S_{\alpha}}\;E(\Phi). (9.21)

Denote

𝒟={Φ=(ϕ1,ϕ2)T|V|ϕj|2∈L1(ℝd),ϕj∈H1(ℝd)∩L4(ℝd),j=1,2},\mathcal{D}=\left\{\Phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})^{T}\ |\,V\,|\phi_{j}|^{2}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ \phi_{j}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\ j=1,2\right\}, (9.22)

then the ground state Φg\Phi_{g} of (9.15) is also given by the following:
Find (Φg∈𝒟1)\left(\Phi_{g}\in\mathcal{D}_{1}\right), such that

Eg:=E⁡(Φg)=minΦ∈𝒟1⁡E⁡(Φ),E_{g}:=E\left(\Phi_{g}\right)=\min_{\Phi\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}E\left(\Phi\right), (9.23)

where

𝒟1=𝒟∩{Φ=(ϕ1,ϕ2)T|‖Φ‖2=∫ℝd(|ϕ1​(𝐱)|2+|ϕ2​(𝐱)|2)​𝑑𝐱=1}.\mathcal{D}_{1}=\mathcal{D}\cap\left\{\Phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})^{T}\ |\ \|\Phi\|^{2}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(|\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}+|\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x})|^{2})\,d\mathbf{x}=1\right\}. (9.24)

In addition, we introduce the auxiliary energy functional

E~​(Φ)=\displaystyle\widetilde{E}(\Phi)= ∫ℝd{12(|∇ϕ1|2+|∇ϕ2|2)+[V(𝐱)(|ϕ1|2+|ϕ2|2)+δ|ϕ1|2]\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\bigg\{\frac{1}{2}\left(|\nabla\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\nabla\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)+\left[V(\mathbf{x})\left(|\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)+\delta|\phi_{1}|^{2}\right] (9.25)
+(12β11|ϕ1|4+12β22|ϕ2|4+β12|ϕ1|2|ϕ2|2)−2|λ|⋅|ϕ1|⋅|ϕ2|}d𝐱,\displaystyle+\left(\frac{1}{2}\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{4}+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{4}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}|\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)-2|\lambda|\cdot|\phi_{1}|\cdot|\phi_{2}|\,\bigg\}\,d\mathbf{x},

and the auxiliary nonconvex minimization problem:
Find (Φg∈𝒟1)\left(\Phi_{g}\in\mathcal{D}_{1}\right), such that

E~​(Φg)=minΦ∈𝒟1⁡E~​(Φ).\widetilde{E}\left(\Phi_{g}\right)=\min_{\Phi\in\mathcal{D}_{1}}\widetilde{E}\left(\Phi\right). (9.26)

For Φ=(ϕ1,ϕ2)T\Phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})^{T}, we write E⁡(ϕ1,ϕ2)=E⁡(Φ)E(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})=E(\Phi) and E~​(ϕ1,ϕ2)=E~​(Φ)\widetilde{E}(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})=\widetilde{E}(\Phi). Then we have the following lemmas [19]:

Lemma 9.1.

For the minimizers Φg​(𝐱)=(ϕ1g​(𝐱),ϕ2g​(𝐱))T\Phi_{g}(\mathbf{x})=(\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x}),\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x}))^{T} of the nonconvex minimization problems (9.23) and (9.26), we have

(i). If Φg\Phi_{g} is a minimizer of (9.23), then ϕ1g​(𝐱)=ei​θ1​|ϕ1g​(𝐱)|\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x})=e^{i\theta_{1}}|\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x})| and ϕ2g​(𝐱)=ei​θ2​|ϕ2g​(𝐱)|\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x})=e^{i\theta_{2}}|\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x})| with θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} two constants satisfying θ1=θ2\theta_{1}=\theta_{2} if λ<0\lambda<0; and θ1=θ2±π\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}\pm\pi if λ>0\lambda>0. In addition, Φ~g=(ei​θ3​ϕ1g,ei​θ4​ϕ2g)T\widetilde{\Phi}_{g}=\left(e^{i\theta_{3}}\phi_{1}^{g},e^{i\theta_{4}}\phi_{2}^{g}\right)^{T} with θ3\theta_{3} and θ4\theta_{4} two constants satisfying θ3=θ4\theta_{3}=\theta_{4} if λ<0\lambda<0; and θ3=θ4±π\theta_{3}=\theta_{4}\pm\pi if λ>0\lambda>0 is also a minimizer of (9.23).

(ii). If Φg\Phi_{g} is a minimizer of (9.26), then ϕ1g​(𝐱)=ei​θ1​|ϕ1g​(𝐱)|\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x})=e^{i\theta_{1}}|\phi_{1}^{g}(\mathbf{x})| and ϕ2g​(𝐱)=ei​θ2​|ϕ2g​(𝐱)|\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x})=e^{i\theta_{2}}|\phi_{2}^{g}(\mathbf{x})| with θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} two constants. In addition, Φ~g=(ei​θ3​ϕ1g,ei​θ4​ϕ2g)T\widetilde{\Phi}_{g}=\left(e^{i\theta_{3}}\phi_{1}^{g},e^{i\theta_{4}}\phi_{2}^{g}\right)^{T} with θ3\theta_{3} and θ4\theta_{4} two constants is also a minimizer of (9.26).

(iii). If Φg\Phi_{g} is a minimizer of (9.23), then Φg\Phi_{g} is also a minimizer of (9.26).

(iv). If Φg\Phi_{g} is a minimizer of (9.26), then Φ~g=(|ϕ1g|,−sign​(λ)​|ϕ2g|)T\widetilde{\Phi}_{g}=\left(|\phi_{1}^{g}|,-\text{sign}(\lambda)|\phi_{2}^{g}|\right)^{T} is a minimizer of (9.23).

For the auxiliary minimization problem (9.26), we have the following results generalizing the single component BEC case in section 2.

Theorem 9.2.

(Existence and uniqueness of (9.26) [19]) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 satisfying lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty, then there exists a minimizer Φ∞=(ϕ1∞,ϕ2∞)T∈𝒟1\Phi^{\infty}=(\phi_{1}^{\infty},\phi_{2}^{\infty})^{T}\in\mathcal{D}_{1} of (9.26) if one of the following conditions holds,

  1. (i)

    d=1d=1;

  2. (ii)

    d=2d=2 and β11≥−Cb,β22≥−Cb\beta_{11}\geq-C_{b},\beta_{22}\geq-C_{b}, β12≥−Cb−Cb+β11​Cb+β22\beta_{12}\geq-C_{b}-\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{11}}\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{22}};

  3. (iii)

    d=3d=3 and BB is either positive semi-definite or nonnegative,

where CbC_{b} is given in (2.12). In addition, if the matrix BB is positive semi-definite and at least one of the parameters δ\delta, λ\lambda, γ1\gamma_{1} and γ2\gamma_{2} are nonzero, then the minimizer (|ϕ1∞|,|ϕ2∞|)T(|\phi_{1}^{\infty}|,|\phi_{2}^{\infty}|)^{T} is unique.

Combining Theorem 9.2 and Lemma 9.1, we draw the conclusions [19]:

Theorem 9.3.

(Existence and uniqueness of (9.15)) Suppose V⁡(𝐱)≥0V(\mathbf{x})\geq 0 satisfying lim|𝐱|→∞V⁡(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V(\mathbf{x})=\infty and at least one of the following condition holds,

  1. (i)

    d=1d=1;

  2. (ii)

    d=2d=2 and β11≥−Cb\beta_{11}\geq-C_{b}, β22≥−Cb\beta_{22}\geq-C_{b}, and β12≥−Cb−Cb+β11​Cb+β22\beta_{12}\geq-C_{b}-\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{11}}\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{22}};

  3. (iii)

    d=3d=3 and BB is either positive semi-definite or nonnegative,

there exists a ground state Φg=(ϕ1g,ϕ2g)T\Phi_{g}=(\phi_{1}^{g},\phi_{2}^{g})^{T} of (9.15). In addition, Φ~g:=(ei​θ1​|ϕ1g|,ei​θ2​|ϕ2g|)\widetilde{\Phi}_{g}:=(e^{i\theta_{1}}|\phi_{1}^{g}|,e^{i\theta_{2}}|\phi_{2}^{g}|) is also a ground state of (9.15) with θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2} two constants satisfying θ1−θ2=±π\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}=\pm\pi when λ>0\lambda>0 and θ1−θ2=0\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}=0 when λ<0\lambda<0, respectively. Furthermore, if the matrix BB is positive semi-definite and at least one of the parameters δ\delta, λ\lambda, γ1\gamma_{1} and γ2\gamma_{2} are nonzero, then the ground state (|ϕ1g|,−sign⁡(λ)​|ϕ2g|)T(|\phi_{1}^{g}|,-{\rm sign}(\lambda)|\phi_{2}^{g}|)^{T} is unique. In contrast, if one of the following conditions holds,

  1. (i)

    d=2d=2 and β11<−Cb\beta_{11}<-C_{b} or β22<−Cb\beta_{22}<-C_{b} or β12<−Cb−Cb+β11​Cb+β22\beta_{12}<-C_{b}-\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{11}}\sqrt{C_{b}+\beta_{22}} ;

  2. (ii)

    d=3d=3 and β11<0\beta_{11}<0 or β22<0\beta_{22}<0 or β12<0\beta_{12}<0 with β122>β11​β22\beta_{12}^{2}>\beta_{11}\beta_{22};

there exists no ground state of (9.15).

When either |δ||\delta| or |λ||\lambda| goes to infinity, the two component ground state problem (9.15) will collapse to a single component ground state problem in section 2 [19].

For fixed β11≥0\beta_{11}\geq 0 and β22≥0\beta_{22}\geq 0, when β12→∞\beta_{12}\to\infty, the phase of two components of the ground state Φg=(ϕ1g,ϕ2g)T\Phi_{g}=(\phi_{1}^{g},\phi_{2}^{g})^{T} will be segregated [63, 66, 92], i.e. Φg\Phi_{g} will converge to a state such that ϕ1g⋅ϕ2g=0\phi_{1}^{g}\cdot\phi_{2}^{g}=0.

Remark 9.1.

If the potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) in the two equations in (9.3) is chosen to be different in different equations, i.e. Vj​(𝐱)V_{j}(\mathbf{x}) in the jjth (j=1,2j=1,2) equation, and they satisfy Vj​(𝐱)≥0V_{j}(\mathbf{x})\geq 0, lim|𝐱|→∞Vj​(𝐱)=∞\lim\limits_{|\mathbf{x}|\to\infty}V_{j}(\mathbf{x})=\infty (j=1,2j=1,2), then the conclusions in the above Lemmas and Theorems 9.2-9.3 are still valid under the similar conditions.

9.4. Dynamical properties

Well-posedness of Cauchy problem of the CGPEs (9.3) in energy space is quite similar to that of single GPE (cf. section 2), and we omit the results here. If there is no internal Josephson junction, i.e. λ=0\lambda=0, the density of each component is conserved. With an internal Josephson junction, we have the following lemmas for the dynamics of the density of each component [195]:

Lemma 9.2.

Suppose (ψ1​(𝐱,t),ψ2​(𝐱,t))(\psi_{1}({\mathbf{x}},t),\psi_{2}({\mathbf{x}},t)) is the solution of the CGPEs (9.3) with potential V⁡(𝐱)+δV(\mathbf{x})+\delta for the first component ψ1\psi_{1} replaced by V1​(𝐱)V_{1}(\mathbf{x}) and potential V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) for the second component ψ2\psi_{2} replaced by V2​(𝐱)V_{2}(\mathbf{x}); then we have, for j=1,2j=1,2

N¨j​(t)=−2​λ2​[2​Nj​(t)−1]+Fj​(t),t≥0,\displaystyle\ddot{N}_{j}(t)=-2\lambda^{2}\left[2N_{j}(t)-1\right]+F_{j}(t),\qquad t\geq 0, (9.27)

with initial conditions

Nj​(0)=Nj(0)=∫ℝd|ψj0​(𝐱)|2​𝑑𝐱=Nj0N,\displaystyle N_{j}(0)=N_{j}^{(0)}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}|\psi_{j}^{0}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}\;d{\mathbf{x}}=\frac{N_{j}^{0}}{N}, (9.28)
N˙j​(0)=Nj(1)=2​λ​∫ℝdIm⁡[ψj0​(𝐱)​(ψkj0​(𝐱)¯)]​𝑑𝐱;\displaystyle\dot{N}_{j}(0)=N_{j}^{(1)}=2\lambda\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\rm Im}\left[\psi_{j}^{0}(\mathbf{x})\left(\overline{\psi_{k_{j}}^{0}(\mathbf{x})}\right)\right]\;d{\mathbf{x}}; (9.29)

where k1=2k_{1}=2, k2=1k_{2}=1 and for t≥0t\geq 0,

Fj(t)=λ∫ℝd(ψj¯ψkj+ψjψkj¯)[Vkj(𝐱)−Vj(𝐱)\displaystyle F_{j}(t)=\lambda\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\left(\overline{\psi_{j}}\psi_{k_{j}}+\psi_{j}\overline{\psi_{k_{j}}}\right)\bigg[V_{k_{j}}({\mathbf{x}})-V_{j}({\mathbf{x}})
−(βj​j−βkj​j)|ψj|2+(βkj​kj−βj​kj)|ψkj|2]d𝐱,t≥0.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad-(\beta_{jj}-\beta_{k_{j}j})|\psi_{j}|^{2}+(\beta_{k_{j}k_{j}}-\beta_{jk_{j}})|\psi_{k_{j}}|^{2}\bigg]d\mathbf{x},\quad t\geq 0.\qquad\qquad

From this lemma, we have [195]

Lemma 9.3.

If δ=0\delta=0 and β11=β12=β21=β22\beta_{11}=\beta_{12}=\beta_{21}=\beta_{22} in (9.3), for any initial data Ψ⁡(𝐱,t=0)=(ψ10​(𝐱),ψ20​(𝐱))T\Psi(\mathbf{x},t=0)=(\psi_{1}^{0}(\mathbf{x}),\psi_{2}^{0}(\mathbf{x}))^{T}, we have, for t≥0t\geq 0,

Nj(t)=‖ψj(⋅,t)‖22=(Nj(0)−12)cos(2λt)+Nj(1)2​λsin(2λt)+12,j=1,2.\displaystyle N_{j}(t)=\left\|\psi_{j}(\cdot,t)\right\|_{2}^{2}=\left(N_{j}^{(0)}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\cos(2\lambda t)+\frac{N_{j}^{(1)}}{2\lambda}\sin(2\lambda t)+\frac{1}{2},\quad j=1,2. (9.30)

Thus in this case, the density of each component is a periodic function with period T=π/|λ|T=\pi/|\lambda| depending only on λ\lambda.

9.5. Numerical methods for computing ground states

To find the ground state, we first present a continuous normalized gradient flow (CNGF) method discussed in section 3.1 and then propose a GFDN method based on discretization of CNGF.

9.5.1. Continuous normalized gradient flow and its discretization

In order to compute the ground state of two-component BEC with an internal Josephson junction (9.15), we construct the following CNGF [19]:

∂ϕ1​(𝐱,t)∂t=[12​∇2−V⁡(𝐱)−δ−(β11​|ϕ1|2+β12​|ϕ2|2)]​ϕ1−λ​ϕ2+μΦ​(t)​ϕ1,∂ϕ2​(𝐱,t)∂t=[12​∇2−V⁡(𝐱)−(β12​|ϕ1|2+β22​|ϕ2|2)]​ϕ2−λ​ϕ1+μΦ​(t)​ϕ2,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\qquad\frac{\partial\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-\delta-(\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{1}-\lambda\phi_{2}+\mu_{\Phi}(t)\phi_{1},\\ &\qquad\frac{\partial\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-(\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{2}-\lambda\phi_{1}+\mu_{\Phi}(t)\phi_{2},\end{split} (9.31)

where Φ⁡(𝐱,t)=(ϕ1​(𝐱,t),ϕ2​(𝐱,t))T\Phi(\mathbf{x},t)=(\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t),\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t))^{T} and μΦ​(t)\mu_{\Phi}(t) is chosen such that the above CNGF is mass or normalization conservative and it is given as

μΦ​(t)\displaystyle\mu_{\Phi}(t) =\displaystyle= 1‖Φ⁡(⋅,t)‖22∫ℝd[12(|∇ϕ1|2+|∇ϕ2|2)+V(𝐱)(|ϕ1|2+|ϕ2|2)+δ|ϕ1|2\displaystyle\frac{1}{\|\Phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\biggl[\frac{1}{2}\left(|\nabla\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\nabla\phi_{2}|^{2}\right)+V(\mathbf{x})(|\phi_{1}|^{2}+|\phi_{2}|^{2})+\delta|\phi_{1}|^{2} (9.32)
+β11|ϕ1|4+β22|ϕ2|4+2β12|ϕ1|2|ϕ2|2+2λRe(ϕ1ϕ¯2)]d𝐱\displaystyle\qquad+\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{4}+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{4}+2\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}|\phi_{2}|^{2}+2\lambda\ \text{Re}(\phi_{1}{\overline{\phi}}_{2})\biggr]\,d\mathbf{x}
=\displaystyle= μ⁡(Φ⁡(⋅,t))‖Φ⁡(⋅,t)‖22,t≥0.\displaystyle\frac{\mu(\Phi(\cdot,t))}{\|\Phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad t\geq 0.

For the above CNGF, we have [19]

Theorem 9.4.

For any given initial data

Φ⁡(𝐱,0)=(ϕ10​(𝐱),ϕ20​(𝐱))T:=Φ(0)​(𝐱),𝐱∈ℝd,\displaystyle\Phi(\mathbf{x},0)=(\phi_{1}^{0}(\mathbf{x}),\phi_{2}^{0}(\mathbf{x}))^{T}:=\Phi^{(0)}(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\mathbf{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, (9.33)

satisfying ‖Φ(0)‖22=1\|\Phi^{(0)}\|_{2}^{2}=1, the CNGF (9.31) is mass or normalization conservative and energy diminishing, i.e.

‖Φ⁡(⋅,t)‖22≡‖Φ(0)‖22=1,E⁡(Φ⁡(⋅,t))≤E⁡(Φ⁡(⋅,s)),0≤s≤t.\|\Phi(\cdot,t)\|_{2}^{2}\equiv\|\Phi^{(0)}\|_{2}^{2}=1,\qquad E(\Phi(\cdot,t))\leq E(\Phi(\cdot,s)),\qquad 0\leq s\leq t. (9.34)

For practical computation, here we also present a second-order in both space and time full discretization for the above CNGF (9.31). For simplicity of notation, we introduce the method for the case of one spatial dimension (1D) in a bounded domain U=(a,b)U=(a,b) with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition

Φ⁡(a,t)=Φ⁡(b,t)=𝟎,t≥0.\displaystyle\Phi(a,t)=\Phi(b,t)={\bf 0},\qquad t\geq 0. (9.35)

Generalizations to higher dimensions are straightforward for tensor product grids.

Let Φjn=(ϕ1,jn,ϕ2,jn)T\Phi_{j}^{n}=(\phi_{1,j}^{n},\phi_{2,j}^{n})^{T} be the numerical approximation of Φ⁡(xj,tn)\Phi(x_{j},t_{n}) and Φn\Phi^{n} be the solution vector with component Φjn\Phi_{j}^{n}. In addition, denote Φjn+1/2=(ϕ1,jn+1/2,ϕ2,jn+1/2)T\Phi_{j}^{n+1/2}=(\phi_{1,j}^{n+1/2},\phi_{2,j}^{n+1/2})^{T} with

ϕl,jn+1/2=12(ϕl,jn+1+ϕl,jn),j=0,1,2,…,M,l=1,2.\displaystyle\phi_{l,j}^{n+1/2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\phi_{l,j}^{n+1}+\phi_{l,j}^{n}\right),\qquad j=0,1,2,\ldots,M,\qquad l=1,2. (9.36)

where

with

DΦ,hn+1/2\displaystyle D_{\Phi,h}^{n+1/2} =\displaystyle= h∑j=0M−1{∑l=12(12​h2|ϕl,j+1n+1/2−ϕl,jn+1/2|2+V(xj)|ϕl,jn+1/2|2)+δ|ϕ1,jn+1/2|2\displaystyle h\sum\limits_{j=0}^{M-1}\biggl\{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{2h^{2}}|\phi_{l,j+1}^{n+1/2}-\phi_{l,j}^{n+1/2}|^{2}+V(x_{j})|\phi_{l,j}^{n+1/2}|^{2}\right)+\delta|\phi_{1,j}^{n+1/2}|^{2} (9.38)

+12​β12​[(|ϕ2,jn+1|2+|ϕ2,jn|2)​|ϕ1,jn+1/2|2+(|ϕ1,jn+1|2|+|ϕ1,jn|2)​|ϕ2,jn+1/2|2]\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\beta_{12}\left[(|\phi_{2,j}^{n+1}|^{2}+|\phi_{2,j}^{n}|^{2})|\phi_{1,j}^{n+1/2}|^{2}+(|\phi_{1,j}^{n+1}|^{2}|+|\phi_{1,j}^{n}|^{2})|\phi_{2,j}^{n+1/2}|^{2}\right]

The boundary condition (9.35) is discretized as

ϕ1,0n+1=ϕ1,Mn+1=ϕ2,0n+1=ϕ2,Mn+1=0,n=0,1,2,….\displaystyle\phi_{1,0}^{n+1}=\phi_{1,M}^{n+1}=\phi_{2,0}^{n+1}=\phi_{2,M}^{n+1}=0,\quad n=0,1,2,\ldots. (9.39)

ϕ1,j0=ϕ10(xj),ϕ2,j0=ϕ20(xj),j=0,1,…,M.\displaystyle\phi_{1,j}^{0}=\phi_{1}^{0}(x_{j}),\qquad\phi_{2,j}^{0}=\phi_{2}^{0}(x_{j}),\qquad j=0,1,\ldots,M. (9.40)

In the above full discretization, at every time step, we need to solve a fully nonlinear system which is very tedious in practical computation. Below we present a more efficient discretization for the CNGF (9.31) for computing the ground states.

9.5.2. Gradient flow with discrete normalization

Another more efficient way to discretize the CNGF (9.31) is through the construction of the following GFDN [19]:

∂ϕ1∂t=[12​∇2−V⁡(𝐱)−δ−(β11​|ϕ1|2+β12​|ϕ2|2)]​ϕ1−λ​ϕ2,∂ϕ2∂t=[12∇2−V(𝐱)−(β12|ϕ1|2+β22|ϕ2|2)]ϕ2−λϕ1,t∈(tn,tn+1),\displaystyle\begin{split}\frac{\partial\phi_{1}}{\partial t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-\delta-(\beta_{11}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{12}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{1}-\lambda\phi_{2},\qquad\qquad\quad\\ \frac{\partial\phi_{2}}{\partial t}=\left[\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}-V(\mathbf{x})-(\beta_{12}|\phi_{1}|^{2}+\beta_{22}|\phi_{2}|^{2})\right]\phi_{2}-\lambda\phi_{1},\quad t\in(t_{n},t_{n+1}),\end{split} (9.41)

followed by a projection step as

ϕl(𝐱,tn+1):=ϕl(𝐱,tn+1+)=σln+1ϕl(𝐱,tn+1−),l=1,2,n≥0,\displaystyle\phi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}):=\phi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{+})=\sigma_{l}^{n+1}\;\phi_{l}(\mathbf{x}\,,t_{n+1}^{-}),\qquad l=1,2,\quad n\geq 0, (9.42)

where ϕl​(𝐱,tn+1±)=limt→tn+1±ϕl​(𝐱,t)\phi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1}^{\pm})=\lim\limits_{t\to t_{n+1}^{\pm}}\phi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t) (l=1,2l=1,2) and σln+1\sigma_{l}^{n+1} (l=1,2l=1,2) are chosen such that

‖Φ⁡(𝐱,tn+1)‖2=‖ϕ1​(𝐱,tn+1)‖22+‖ϕ2​(𝐱,tn+1)‖22=1,n≥0.\displaystyle\|\Phi(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\|^{2}=\|\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\|_{2}^{2}+\|\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t_{n+1})\|_{2}^{2}=1,\qquad n\geq 0. (9.43)

The above GFDN (9.41)-(9.42) can be viewed as applying the first-order splitting method to the CNGF (9.31) and the projection step (9.42) is equivalent to solving the following ordinary differential equations (ODEs)

∂ϕ1​(𝐱,t)∂t=μΦ​(t)​ϕ1,∂ϕ2​(𝐱,t)∂t=μΦ​(t)​ϕ2,tn≤t≤tn+1,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\phi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\mu_{\Phi}(t)\phi_{1},\qquad\frac{\partial\phi_{2}(\mathbf{x},t)}{\partial t}=\mu_{\Phi}(t)\phi_{2},\qquad\quad t_{n}\leq t\leq t_{n+1}, (9.44)

which immediately suggests that the projection constants in (9.42) are chosen as

σ1n+1=σ2n+1,n≥0.\displaystyle\sigma_{1}^{n+1}=\sigma_{2}^{n+1},\qquad n\geq 0. (9.45)

Plugging (9.45) and (9.42) into (9.43), we obtain

σ1n+1=σ2n+1=1‖Φ⁡(⋅,tn+1−)‖2=1‖ϕ1​(⋅,tn+1−)‖22+‖ϕ2​(⋅,tn+1−)‖22,n≥0.\displaystyle\sigma_{1}^{n+1}=\sigma_{2}^{n+1}=\frac{1}{\|\Phi(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\|\phi_{1}(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}^{2}+\|\phi_{2}(\cdot,t_{n+1}^{-})\|_{2}^{2}}},\;n\geq 0. (9.46)

Then, BEFD in section 3.2 can be used to discretize the GFDN (9.41)-(9.42) and we omit the detailed scheme here, as the generalization is straightforward.

9.6. Numerical methods for computing dynamics

To compute dynamics of a two component BEC, finite difference time domain methods in section 4.2 can be directly extended to solve the CGPEs (9.3). Here we focus on the time splitting methods. For n=0,1,…n=0,1,\dots, from time t=tn=n​τt=t_{n}=n\tau to t=tn+1=tn+τt=t_{n+1}=t_{n}+\tau, the CGPEs (9.3) are solved in three splitting steps [195, 181, 183]. One first solves

i∂ψj∂t=−12∇2ψj,j=1,2,\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi_{j}}{\partial t}=-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{2}\psi_{j},\qquad j=1,2, (9.47)

for the time step of length τ\tau, followed by solving

i∂ψj∂t=Vj(𝐱)ψj+∑l=12βj​l|ψl|2ψj,j=1,2,\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi_{j}}{\partial t}=V_{j}({\mathbf{x}})\psi_{j}+\sum_{l=1}^{2}\beta_{jl}|\psi_{l}|^{2}\psi_{j},\qquad j=1,2, (9.48)

for the same time step with V1​(𝐱)=V⁡(𝐱)+δV_{1}(\mathbf{x})=V(\mathbf{x})+\delta and V2​(𝐱)=V​(𝐱)V_{2}(\mathbf{x})=V(\mathbf{x}), and then by solving

i​∂ψ1∂t=−λ​ψ2,i​∂ψ2∂t=−λ​ψ1,\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\psi_{1}}{\partial t}=-\lambda\psi_{2},\quad i\frac{\partial\psi_{2}}{\partial t}=-\lambda\psi_{1}, (9.49)

for the same time step. For time t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}], the ODE system (9.48) leaves |ψ1​(𝐱,t)||\psi_{1}({\mathbf{x}},t)| and |ψ2​(𝐱,t)||\psi_{2}({\mathbf{x}},t)| invariant in tt, and thus it can be integrated exactly to obtain [33, 31, 47, 48, 193], for j=1,2j=1,2 and t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}]

ψj​(𝐱,t)=ψj​(𝐱,tn)​exp⁡[−i⁡(Vj​(𝐱)+∑l=12βj​l​|ψl​(𝐱,tn)|2)​(t−tn)].\displaystyle\psi_{j}({\mathbf{x}},t)=\psi_{j}(\mathbf{x},t_{n})\exp\left[-i\left(V_{j}({\mathbf{x}})+\sum_{l=1}^{2}\beta_{jl}\left|\psi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t_{n})\right|^{2}\right)(t-t_{n})\right]. (9.50)

For the ODE system (9.49), we can rewrite it as

i​∂Ψ∂t=−λ​A​Ψ,withA=(0110)a​n​dΨ=(ψ1ψ2).\displaystyle i\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial t}=-\lambda A\Psi,\qquad\mathrm{with}\quad A=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&1\\ 1&0\end{array}\right)\quad{\mathrm{a}nd}\quad\Psi=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\psi_{1}\\ \psi_{2}\end{array}\right).

Since AA is a real and symmetric matrix, it can be diagonalized and integrated exactly, and then we obtain [15, 195], for t∈[tn,tn+1]t\in[t_{n},t_{n+1}]

Ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=ei​λ​A​(t−tn)​Ψ​(𝐱,tn)=(cos⁡(λ⁡(t−tn))i​sin⁡(λ⁡(t−tn))i​sin⁡(λ⁡(t−tn))cos⁡(λ⁡(t−tn)))​Ψ​(𝐱,tn).\Psi(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{i\lambda A\;(t-t_{n})}\Psi(\mathbf{x},t_{n})=\left(\begin{array}[]{ll}\cos\left(\lambda(t-t_{n})\right)&i\sin\left(\lambda(t-t_{n})\right)\\ i\sin\left(\lambda(t-t_{n})\right)&\cos\left(\lambda(t-t_{n})\right)\\ \end{array}\right)\Psi(\mathbf{x},t_{n}).

Then, time splitting spectral method introduced in sections 4 and 6 can be applied to compute the dynamics of the CGPEs (9.3), by a suitable composition of the above three steps (cf. section 4.1). The detailed scheme is omitted here for brevity.

9.7. Numerical results

In this section, we will report the ground states of (9.15), computed by our numerical methods.
