10. Perspectives and challenges

So far, we have introduced mathematical results and numerical methods for ground states and dynamics of a single/two component rotating/nonrotating BEC with/without dipole-dipole interactions described by mean field GPE. Despite these BEC systems, much progress has been made towards realizing other kinds of gaseous BEC, such as spinor condensates, condensates at finite temperature, Bose-Fermi mixtures, etc. These achievements have brought great challenges to atomic physics community and scientific computing community for modeling, simulating and understanding various interesting phenomenons.

10.1. Spin-1 BEC

In earlier BEC experiments, the atoms were confined in magnetic trap [12, 86, 59], in which the spin degrees of freedom is frozen. In recent years, experimental achievement of spin-1 and spin-2 condensates [50, 124] offers new regimes to study various quantum phenomena that are generally absent in a single component condensate. The spinor condensate is achieved experimentally when an optical trap, instead of a magnetic trap, is used to provide equal confinement for all hyperfine states.

The theoretical studies of spinor condensate have been carried out in several papers since the achievement of it in experiments [115, 128]. In contrast to single component condensate, a spin-FF (F∈ℕF\in{\mathbb{N}}) condensate is described by a generalized coupled GPEs which consists of 2​F+12F+1 equations, each governing one of the 2​F+12F+1 hyperfine states (mF=−F,−F+1,…,F−1,F)(m_{F}=-F,-F+1,...,F-1,F) within the mean-field approximation. For a spin-1 condensate, at temperature much lower than the critical temperature TcT_{c}, the three-components wave function Ψ:=Ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=(ψ1​(𝐱,t),ψ0​(𝐱,t),ψ−1​(𝐱,t))T\Psi:=\Psi(\mathbf{x},t)=(\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t),\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x},t),\psi_{-1}(\mathbf{x},t))^{T} are well described by the following coupled GPEs [124, 36],

i​ℏ​∂tψ1​(𝐱,t)=\displaystyle i\hbar\,\partial_{t}\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)= [−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+(c0+c2)​(|ψ1|2+|ψ0|2)+(c0−c2)​|ψ−1|2]​ψ1\displaystyle\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+(c_{0}+c_{2})\left(|\psi_{1}|^{2}+|\psi_{0}|^{2}\right)+(c_{0}-c_{2})|\psi_{-1}|^{2}\right]\psi_{1}
+c2​ψ¯−1​ψ02,\displaystyle+c_{2}\,{\overline{\psi}}_{-1}\,\psi_{0}^{2}, (10.1)
i​ℏ​∂tψ0​(𝐱,t)=\displaystyle i\hbar\,\partial_{t}\psi_{0}(\mathbf{x},t)= [−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+(c0+c2)​(|ψ1|2+|ψ−1|2)+c0​|ψ0|2]​ψ0\displaystyle\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+(c_{0}+c_{2})\left(|\psi_{1}|^{2}+|\psi_{-1}|^{2}\right)+c_{0}|\psi_{0}|^{2}\right]\psi_{0}
+2​c2​ψ−1​ψ¯0​ψ1,\displaystyle+2c_{2}\,\psi_{-1}\,{\overline{\psi}}_{0}\,\psi_{1}, (10.2)
i​ℏ​∂tψ−1​(𝐱,t)=\displaystyle i\hbar\,\partial_{t}\psi_{-1}(\mathbf{x},t)= [−ℏ22​m​∇2+V⁡(𝐱)+(c0+c2)​(|ψ−1|2+|ψ0|2)+(c0−c2)​|ψ1|2]​ψ−1\displaystyle\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})+(c_{0}+c_{2})\left(|\psi_{-1}|^{2}+|\psi_{0}|^{2}\right)+(c_{0}-c_{2})|\psi_{1}|^{2}\right]\psi_{-1}
+c2​ψ02​ψ¯1,𝐱=(x,y,z)T∈ℝ3.\displaystyle+c_{2}\,\psi_{0}^{2}\,{\overline{\psi}}_{1},\qquad\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)^{T}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. (10.3)

Here V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is an external trapping potential. There are two atomic collision terms, c0=4​π​ℏ23​m​(a0+2​a2)c_{0}=\frac{4\pi\hbar^{2}}{3m}(a_{0}+2a_{2}) and c2=4​π​ℏ23​m​(a2−a0)c_{2}=\frac{4\pi\hbar^{2}}{3m}(a_{2}-a_{0}), expressed in terms of the ss-wave scattering lengths, a0a_{0} and a2a_{2}, for scattering channel of total hyperfine spin 0 (anti-parallel spin collision) and spin 2 (parallel spin collision), respectively. The usual mean-field interaction, c0c_{0}, is positive for repulsive interaction and negative for attractive interaction. The spin-exchange interaction, c2c_{2}, is positive for antiferromagnetic interaction and negative for ferromagnetic interaction. The wave function is normalized according to

‖Ψ‖22:=∫ℝ3|Ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱=∫ℝ3∑l=−11|ψl​(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱:=∑l=−11‖ψl‖22=N,\displaystyle\|\Psi\|_{2}^{2}:=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|\Psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\sum_{l=-1}^{1}|\psi_{l}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\;d\mathbf{x}:=\sum_{l=-1}^{1}\|\psi_{l}\|_{2}^{2}=N, (10.4)

where NN is the total number of particles in the condensate. This normalization is conserved by coupled GPEs (10.1)-(10.3), and so are the magnetization

M⁡(Ψ⁡(⋅,t)):=∫ℝ3[|ψ1​(𝐱,t)|2−|ψ−1​(𝐱,t)|2]​𝑑𝐱≡M⁡(Ψ⁡(⋅,0))=M\displaystyle M(\Psi(\cdot,t)):=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\left[|\psi_{1}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}-|\psi_{-1}(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\right]d\mathbf{x}\equiv M(\Psi(\cdot,0))=M (10.5)

and the energy per particle

E⁡(Ψ⁡(⋅,t))\displaystyle E(\Psi(\cdot,t)) =\displaystyle= ∫ℝ3{∑l=−11(ℏ22​m|∇ψl|2+V(𝐱)|ψl|2)+(c0−c2)|ψ1|2|ψ−1|2\displaystyle\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}\biggl\{\sum_{l=-1}^{1}\left(\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}|\nabla\psi_{l}|^{2}+V(\mathbf{x})|\psi_{l}|^{2}\right)+(c_{0}-c_{2})|\psi_{1}|^{2}|\psi_{-1}|^{2} (10.6)
+c02​|ψ0|4+c0+c22​[|ψ1|4+|ψ−1|4+2​|ψ0|2​(|ψ1|2+|ψ−1|2)]\displaystyle+\frac{c_{0}}{2}|\psi_{0}|^{4}+\frac{c_{0}+c_{2}}{2}\Bigl[|\psi_{1}|^{4}+|\psi_{-1}|^{4}+2|\psi_{0}|^{2}\left(|\psi_{1}|^{2}+|\psi_{-1}|^{2}\right)\Bigr]
+c2(ψ¯−1ψ02ψ¯1+ψ−1ψ¯02ψ1)}d𝐱≡E(Ψ(⋅,0)),t≥0.\displaystyle+c_{2}\left({\overline{\psi}}_{-1}\psi_{0}^{2}{\overline{\psi}}_{1}+\psi_{-1}{\overline{\psi}}_{0}^{2}\psi_{1}\right)\biggr\}\;d\mathbf{x}\equiv E(\Psi(\cdot,0)),\qquad t\geq 0.

Then ground states of spin-1 BEC can be defined as the minimizer of energy EE under the normalization and magnetization constraints [36, 45, 26]. In particular, when the external traps for all the components are the same, ground states for ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic spin-1 BECs can be simplified [26]. Generally speaking, for spin-FF BEC, the complicated nonlinear terms in (10.1)-(10.3) lead to new difficulties for mathematical analysis and numerical simulation [182]. Much work needs to be done in future, especially when rotational frame and dipole-dipole interactions are taken into account in spin-FF BECs [124].

10.2. Bogoliubov excitation

The theory of interacting Bose gases, developed by Bogoliubov in 1947, is very useful and important to understand BEC in dilute atomic gases. One of the key issue is the Bogoliubov excitation.

To describe the condensate, we have the lowest order approximation, i.e., the Gross-Pitaevskii energy by assuming that all particles are in the ground state. However, due to the interactions between the atoms, there is a small portion occupying the excited states. Thus, if a higher order approximation of the ground state energy is considered, excitations have to be included. Using a perturbation technique, Bogoliubov has investigated this problem and shown that the excited states of a system of interacting Bose particles can be described by a system of noninteracting quasi-particles satisfying the Bogoliubov dispersion relation.

To determine the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum, we consider small perturbations around the ground state of Eq. (1.19). For simplicity we assume a vanishing harmonic potential V⁡(𝐱)=0V(\mathbf{x})=0 and homogeneous density ν\nu. A stationary state of the GPE (1.19) is given by ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=ψ⁡(t)=e−i​μ​t​ν\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\psi(t)=e^{-i\mu t}\sqrt{\nu} with the chemical potential

μ=β​ν.\mu=\beta\nu. (10.7)

Now we add a local perturbation ξ⁡(𝐱,t)\xi(\mathbf{x},t) to the stationary state ψ⁡(t)\psi(t), that is, ψ⁡(𝐱,t)=e−i​μ​t​[ν+ξ⁡(𝐱,t)]\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=e^{-i\mu t}[\sqrt{\nu}+\xi(\mathbf{x},t)]. We expand the perturbation in a plane wave basis as ξ⁡(𝐱,t)=∫ℝ3(u𝐪​ei⁡(𝐪⋅𝐱−ω𝐪​t)+v𝐪¯​e−i⁡(𝐪⋅𝐱−ω𝐪​t))​𝑑𝐪\xi(\mathbf{x},t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\bigl(u_{{\bf q}}e^{i({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{x}-\omega_{{\bf q}}t)}+\overline{v_{{\bf q}}}e^{-i({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{x}-\omega_{{\bf q}}t)}\bigr)d{\bf q} and insert ψ⁡(𝐱,t)\psi(\mathbf{x},t) into Eq. (1.19). Here, ω𝐪\omega_{{\bf q}} are the excitation frequencies of quasimomentum 𝐪{\bf q} and u𝐪u_{{\bf q}}, v𝐪v_{{\bf q}} are the mode functions. Keeping terms linear in the excitations u𝐪u_{{\bf q}} and v𝐪v_{{\bf q}} we find the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations

ω𝐪​u𝐪=𝐪22​u𝐪+ν​β​(v𝐪+u𝐪),−ω𝐪​v𝐪=𝐪22​v𝐪+ν​β​(v𝐪+u𝐪).\begin{split}\omega_{{\bf q}}u_{{\bf q}}&=\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2}u_{{\bf q}}+\nu\beta(v_{{\bf q}}+u_{{\bf q}}),\\ -\omega_{{\bf q}}v_{{\bf q}}&=\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2}v_{{\bf q}}+\nu\beta(v_{{\bf q}}+u_{{\bf q}}).\end{split} (10.8)

Then we can find the eigenenergies of Eq. (10.8) by solving the eigenvalue problem. The resulting Bogoliubov energy EB​(𝐪)=ω𝐪E_{B}({\bf q})=\omega_{{\bf q}} is determined by

EB2​(𝐪)=𝐪22​(𝐪22+2​β​ν).E_{B}^{2}({\bf q})=\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{{\bf q}^{2}}{2}+2\beta\nu\right). (10.9)

When an external potential is considered, the Bogoliubov energy would be more complicated. In 1999, the Bogoliubov excitation spectrum was observed for the first time in atomic BEC [170], using light scattering. Later in 2008, observation of Bogoliubov excitations was announced in exciton-polariton condensates [179]. Such elementary excitations are crucial in understanding various phenomenon in BEC.

10.3. BEC at finite temperature

The process of creating a BEC in a trap by means of evaporative cooling starts in a regime covered by the quantum Boltzmann equation (QBE) and finishes in a regime where the GPE is expected to be valid. The GPE is capable to describe the main properties of the condensate at very low temperatures, it treats the condensate as a classical field and neglects quantum and thermal fluctuations. As a consequence, the theory breaks down at higher temperatures where the non-condensed fraction of the gas cloud is significant. An approach which allows the treatment of both condensate and noncondensate parts simultaneously was developed in [190, 39].

The resulting equations of motion reduce to a generalized GPE for the condensate wave function coupled with a semiclassical QBE for the thermal cloud:

i​ℏ​∂tψ⁡(𝐱,t)=[−ℏ22​m​∇2+(nc​(𝐱,t)+2​n​(𝐱,t))​g−i​R​(𝐱,t)]​ψ,∂F∂t+𝐩m⋅∇𝐱F−∇𝐱U⋅∇𝐩F=Q⁡(F)+Qc​(F),\begin{split}&i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi(\mathbf{x},t)=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+(n_{c}(\mathbf{x},t)+2n(\mathbf{x},t))g-iR(\mathbf{x},t)\right]\psi,\\ &\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}+\frac{{\bf p}}{m}\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}F-\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}U\cdot\nabla_{{\bf p}}F=Q(F)+Q_{c}(F),\end{split} (10.10)

where nc​(𝐱,t)=|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2n_{c}(\mathbf{x},t)=|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2} is the condensate density, F:=F⁡(𝐱,𝐩,t)F:=F(\mathbf{x},{\bf p},t) describes the distribution of thermal atoms in the phase space and it gives the particle number with momentum 𝐩{\bf p} at position 𝐱\mathbf{x} and time tt in the thermal cloud. n⁡(𝐱,t)=∫ℝ3F⁡(𝐱,𝐩,t)/(2​π​ℏ)3​𝑑𝐩n(\mathbf{x},t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}F(\mathbf{x},{\bf p},t)/(2\pi\hbar)^{3}d{\bf p}, V⁡(𝐱)V(\mathbf{x}) is the confining potential and g=4​π​ℏ2​as/mg=4\pi\hbar^{2}a_{s}/m. The collision integral Q⁡(F)Q(F) is given by

Q⁡(F)=\displaystyle Q(F)= 2​g2(2​π)5​ℏ7​∫ℝ3×ℝ3×ℝ3δ⁡(𝐩+𝐩∗−𝐩′−𝐩∗′)×δ⁡(ϵ+ϵ∗−ϵ′−ϵ∗′)\displaystyle\frac{2g^{2}}{(2\pi)^{5}\hbar^{7}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}\delta({\bf p}+{\bf p}_{\ast}-{\bf p}^{\prime}-{\bf p}_{\ast}^{\prime})\times\delta(\epsilon+\epsilon_{\ast}-\epsilon^{\prime}-\epsilon_{\ast}^{\prime})
×[(1+F)​(1+F∗)​F′​F∗′−F​F∗​(1+F′)​(1+F∗′)]​d​𝐩∗​d​𝐩′​d​𝐩∗′,\displaystyle\times[(1+F)(1+F_{\ast})F^{\prime}F^{\prime}_{\ast}-FF_{\ast}(1+F^{\prime})(1+F^{\prime}_{\ast})]\,d\,{\bf p}_{\ast}\,d{\bf p}^{\prime}\,d{\bf p}_{\ast}^{\prime},

where ϵ=U⁡(𝐱,t)+𝐩2/2​m\epsilon=U(\mathbf{x},t)+{\bf p}^{2}/2m, U⁡(𝐱,t)=V⁡(𝐱)+2​g​nc​(𝐱,t)+2​g​n​(𝐱,t)U(\mathbf{x},t)=V(\mathbf{x})+2gn_{c}(\mathbf{x},t)+2gn(\mathbf{x},t) and δ⁡(⋅)\delta(\cdot) is the Dirac distribution. Qc​(F)Q_{c}(F) which describes collisions between condensate and non condensate particles is given by

Qc​(F)=\displaystyle Q_{c}(F)= 2​g2​nc(2​π)2​ℏ4​∫ℝ3×ℝ3×ℝ3δ⁡(m​𝐯c+𝐩∗−𝐩′−𝐩∗′)\displaystyle\frac{2g^{2}n_{c}}{(2\pi)^{2}\hbar^{4}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R}^{3}}\delta(m{\bf v}_{c}+{\bf p}_{\ast}-{\bf p}^{\prime}-{\bf p}_{\ast}^{\prime})
×δ⁡(ϵc+ϵ∗−ϵ′−ϵ∗′)​[δ⁡(𝐩−𝐩∗)−δ⁡(𝐩−𝐩′)−δ⁡(𝐩−𝐩∗′)]\displaystyle\times\delta(\epsilon_{c}+\epsilon_{\ast}-\epsilon^{\prime}-\epsilon_{\ast}^{\prime})[\delta({\bf p}-{\bf p}_{\ast})-\delta({\bf p}-{\bf p}^{\prime})-\delta({\bf p}-{\bf p}_{\ast}^{\prime})]
×[(1+F∗)​F′​F∗′−F∗​(1+F′)​(1+F∗′)]​d​𝐩∗​d​𝐩′​d​𝐩∗′,\displaystyle\times[(1+F_{\ast})F^{\prime}F^{\prime}_{\ast}-F_{\ast}(1+F^{\prime})(1+F^{\prime}_{\ast})]\,d\,{\bf p}_{\ast}\,d{\bf p}^{\prime}\,d{\bf p}_{\ast}^{\prime},

where

ϵc​(𝐱,t)=12​m​𝐯c​(𝐱,t)2+μc​(𝐱,t),\displaystyle\epsilon_{c}(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{1}{2}m{\bf v}_{c}(\mathbf{x},t)^{2}+\mu_{c}(\mathbf{x},t), (10.11)

and 𝐯c{\bf v}_{c} is the quantum hydrodynamic velocity, μc\mu_{c} is the effective potential acting on the condensate [190, 108]. R⁡(𝐱,t)R(\mathbf{x},t) is then written as

R⁡(𝐱,t)=ℏ2​nc​∫ℝ3Qc​(F)(2​π​ℏ)3​𝑑𝐩.\displaystyle R(\mathbf{x},t)=\frac{\hbar}{2n_{c}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\frac{Q_{c}(F)}{(2\pi\hbar)^{3}}\,d{\bf p}. (10.12)

Note that for low temperatures T→0T\to 0 we have n,R→0n,R\to 0 and we recover the conventional GPE. The system (10.10) is normalized as Nc​(0)=Nc0N_{c}(0)=N_{c}^{0} and Nt​(0)=Nt0N_{t}(0)=N_{t}^{0} with

Nc​(t)=∫ℝ3|ψ⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱,Nt​(t)=∫ℝ3|n⁡(𝐱,t)|2​𝑑𝐱,t≥0,\displaystyle N_{c}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|\psi(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}\,d\mathbf{x},\quad N_{t}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}|n(\mathbf{x},t)|^{2}d\,\mathbf{x},\quad t\geq 0, (10.13)

where Nc0N_{c}^{0} and Nt0N_{t}^{0} are the number of particles in the condensate and thermal cloud at time t=0t=0, respectively. It is easy to see from the equations (10.10) that the total number of particles defined as Ntotal​(t)=Nc​(t)+Nt​(t)=Ntotal0=Nc0+Nt0N_{\rm total}(t)=N_{c}(t)+N_{t}(t)=N^{0}_{\rm total}=N^{0}_{c}+N^{0}_{t} is conserved. For this set of equations, the GPE part can be solved efficiently, and the main trouble comes from the Boltzmann equation part. Alternatively, projected GPE model is also used for simulating BEC at finite temperature [85, 87].
